subsystems.assessment: The engine core is in genuinely good shape for a single-maintainer project: the step loop is small and readable, the chunk planner and pacer are fuzz-tested, cache ownership is guarded against error paths (CacheRestoreGuard), the prefix cache is collision-safe by construction, and the speculative path keeps exact greedy semantics. The strongest parts are the explicit invariants (prefill-only pool writes, one logits row per sequence, block refcounting) and the tests that pin them. The fragile parts are at the seams between the scheduler, the prefix cache and the allocator: the scheduler reserves nothing (it re-reads num_free per sequence and admits prefills against a count that ignores the decodes it just promised a block to), the prefix cache pins up to 512 blocks per layer with no pressure-driven eviction while the pool floor is 256 blocks, and a single allocation failure inside a forward becomes abort_running() for every in-flight request plus a permanent halving of the prefill cap. Those three together form a reachable failure chain on the default multi-turn server path and are the most important things to fix. The biggest performance lever left in this subsystem is step structure rather than kernels: prefill chunking bounds the GPU submission but not decode latency (decode rows sit in the last chunk and the step does not return until every chunk is drained), the sampler does two Metal round trips per sequence per step instead of one batched readback, and generated tokens never enter the prefix cache so every chat turn re-prefills the previous assistant reply. The per-step CPU costs I specifically looked for (prefix hashing, Vec clones of block ids, HashMap token counts, tensor construction) are all negligible against a 20-30 ms step and need no work. The tokenizer-roundtrip caveat from the May notes is still unmeasured in code: nothing compares turn N+1's ids with turn N's ids plus outputs, and the only skipped-token signal is a debug! line. Finally, gpu_lock.rs's header no longer describes what engine_loop does: the whole step, CPU sampling and constraint-mask building included, runs under the per-device lock.

findings.title: Scheduler double-books the last free KV blocks; the resulting append failure aborts every running request
findings.evidence: src/scheduler/mod.rs:263-266: `for &seq_id in &seqs_needing_block { if self.num_free_blocks() > 0 { if budget > 0 { scheduled.push(... Decode ...)` -- num_free_blocks() is re-read per sequence but nothing is reserved, so with 1 free block and 2 decodes at a boundary both are scheduled. mod.rs:287 `let mut free_blocks = self.num_free_blocks();` then :297 `if blocks_needed > free_blocks { break; }` and :316 `free_blocks = free_blocks.saturating_sub(blocks_needed);` -- prefill admission starts from the same unreserved count, so a prefill can take the block a decode was promised. The block is really taken inside the forward: src/common/paged.rs:1107-1110 `if current_offset == 0 { let id = alloc.allocate()?; ... }` (runs even when skip_pool_write is true). The error propagates: src/engine.rs:571-581 `Err(e) => { if pacer.shrink() { tracing::warn!(...) } return Err(e); }`, and src/server/routes/engine_loop.rs:969 `let aborted_ids = engine.abort_running();` sends EngineEvent::Error to every tracker.
findings.rationale: The pool is sized for max_num_sequences x context (loader.rs:1702), but it is shrunk at runtime by prefix-cache pinning (finding 2), by --max-context-len pinned above what the pool supports (loader.rs:1608 'is served whatever the pool turns out to be'), and by the 256-block floor. Once free blocks are scarce, two decodes crossing a block boundary in the same step (identical-length concurrent requests do this on the same step) or one decode plus a freshly admitted prefill exceed the supply, allocate() fails inside attention, and the whole batch is killed instead of one sequence being preempted. The scheduler's own test comment (fuzz_preemption_and_retirement_give_every_block_back: 'An exhausted pool fails the append ... the scheduler preempts on the next step') describes behaviour the engine does not have.
findings.proposal: Reserve as you schedule: `let mut free = self.num_free_blocks(); for seq needing a block { if free > 0 { free -= 1; schedule } else { preempt } }` and pass `free` into the prefill admission loop instead of re-reading num_free_blocks(). Second, make a per-sequence allocation failure non-fatal to the batch: in run_forward_pass, map a KV-exhaustion error from one sequence to preempting that sequence (clear caches, requeue) rather than returning Err from step(); or at minimum have engine_loop abort only the sequences that were in the failing batch's prefill set rather than abort_running().
findings.expected_benefit: Removes a whole-batch failure mode (N concurrent requests get an error at once) on a supported configuration; after the fix the worst case is one preemption. No throughput cost.
findings.verify_how: Unit test in scheduler/mod.rs: pool of 2 blocks, two sequences each at num_processed_tokens == DEFAULT_BLOCK_SIZE, exactly 1 free block; today both are scheduled as Decode, after the fix one is preempted. E2E on M5: start a model with --max-context-len above the granted pool, send 8 identical 2000-token prompts concurrently with max_tokens 600 and watch for 'engine step failed ... KV cache memory exhausted' followed by 8 error streams.

verdict.reason: Verified in src/scheduler/mod.rs:263-266: each decode on a boundary is scheduled when `self.num_free_blocks() > 0`, nothing is decremented, and mod.rs:287 `let mut free_blocks = self.num_free_blocks();` re-reads the same unreserved count for prefill admission, which deducts only its own `blocks_needed` (mod.rs:316). num_free_blocks (mod.rs:199-204) is `free_list.len() + (max_blocks - num_blocks)` on allocators[0] (paged.rs:601-603). The block is taken only inside the forward: paged.rs:1107-1110 `if current_offset == 0 { let id = alloc.allocate()?; }` runs regardless of skip_pool_write, and allocate() (paged.rs:565-571) returns `KV cache memory exhausted` when the free list is empty. The error leaves run_forward_pass via engine.rs:571-581 (after `pacer.shrink()`), step() propagates it (engine.rs:1055-1063 `?`), and engine_loop.rs:969 `engine.abort_running()` -> scheduler.abort_all_running() (mod.rs:361-368) clears every running sequence and sends EngineEvent::Error to each tracker. The test comment at mod.rs:802-803 reads exactly as quoted. Worth: unpinned pools are fitted so max_num_sequences x context_len <= pool (loader.rs:1573-1577, 1779-1787), but a pinned context is served 'whatever the pool turns out to be' (loader.rs:1606-1608) and the prefix cache pins up to 512 blocks per layer (finding 2), so a scarce-block regime is reachable on a supported configuration, and admission never reserves growth room for decodes, so exhaustion is the designed normal path, not an edge case. Reserving as you schedule (carry one `free` counter through both loops) is a handful of lines and makes allocation failure impossible under correct accounting; that part alone is S. The second half (per-sequence non-fatal failure inside run_forward_pass) is harder than S because the failure surfaces mid-forward after other sequences' appends were staged, and becomes unnecessary once reservation is right; keep abort_running as the backstop.

findings.title: Prefix cache pins up to 512 blocks per layer with no pressure-driven eviction; admission starves and the engine loop hot-spins
findings.evidence: src/engine.rs:890 `PrefixCache::new(512)` (fixed, independent of pool size). src/common/prefix_cache.rs:159-171: `if !self.entries.contains(&h) { for (layer_idx, &bid) in block_ids.iter().enumerate() { allocators[layer_idx].lock().unwrap().share(bid); } if let Some((_, evicted)) = self.entries.push(...)` -- the only eviction is LRU overflow at 512 entries; there is no method that frees entries on allocator pressure. src/common/paged.rs:601-603 `pub fn num_free(&self) -> usize { self.free_list.len() + (self.max_blocks - self.num_blocks) }` -- a shared block (refcount >= 1) is not free. src/scheduler/mod.rs:297 `if blocks_needed > free_blocks { break; }` and :264-284 preempt running decodes instead of asking the prefix cache for blocks. src/models/loader.rs:1708 `let min_blocks: usize = 256;` -- the pool floor is half the prefix cache capacity. src/server/routes/engine_loop.rs:644-646 and :684-687,985: with pending work the loop does try_recv, step() (which returns immediately at engine.rs:1032-1039 when the batch is empty), yield_now(), and repeats.
findings.rationale: Every finished prompt leaves its full blocks pinned by the cache until 512 entries accumulate. On a pool near the 256-block floor (large model at 4K context on 24 GB) one 4000-token conversation pins 250 blocks and the next distinct 4000-token prompt can never be admitted: blocks_needed 250 > free 50, nothing is running to retire, nothing registers to trigger LRU eviction, so the request waits until the client times out while the engine thread spins at 100% of a core holding and releasing the gpu lock. On a 2048-block pool the cache silently removes 25% of the capacity the scheduler was sized for, turning full-context concurrency into preemption storms (finding 1 and 14). This is likely the mechanism behind the roadmap's 'timeout-aborted requests interacting with prefix cache' suspicion.
findings.proposal: Add `PrefixCache::evict_lru(n_blocks, allocators) -> usize` (pop_lru until n blocks are released or the cache is empty) and call it from Scheduler::schedule in two places: before preempting a decode that needs a block, and before giving up on admitting the head of the waiting queue. Size the capacity from the pool: `PrefixCache::new((num_total_blocks / 2).max(64))` instead of 512, and log at info when the cache is trimmed. Also make the idle-spin visible: when step() admitted nothing while work is waiting, engine_loop should block on request_rx with a timeout rather than yield_now().
findings.expected_benefit: Eliminates a starvation/deadlock on a supported path and returns up to 512 blocks x layers to the scheduler under load (on Phi-3-mini's 2048-block pool that is 25% of KV capacity, i.e. two full-context sequences). Removes a 100%-CPU spin while a request is stuck.
findings.verify_how: Unit test: allocators with 300 blocks, PrefixCache::new(512), register a 250-block prompt and retire it, then schedule a different 250-block prompt: today schedule() returns nothing forever. E2E on M5: run a 12B-class model so the pool caps near the floor, send two different 4000-token prompts sequentially, observe the second never gets a first token and top shows the engine thread at 100%.

verdict.reason: Verified: engine.rs:890 `PrefixCache::new(512)` is fixed; prefix_cache.rs exposes only new/disabled/count_cached_blocks/lookup/register (fn list at :40,:50,:59,:86,:121) and the only release is LRU overflow inside register (prefix_cache.rs:164-175). register calls `share(bid)` per layer (:160-162), share bumps ref_counts (paged.rs:576-583) and free only returns a block to free_list at refcount 0 (paged.rs:585-593), so num_free (paged.rs:601-603) excludes every cached block. schedule() breaks at mod.rs:297 `if blocks_needed > free_blocks { break; }` and preempts decodes at :273-283 without ever consulting the cache. The spin is real: engine_loop.rs:644 `if engine.has_pending_work()` (waiting non-empty, mod.rs:400-402) -> try_recv -> step() which returns at engine.rs:1032-1039 when the batch is empty -> `std::thread::yield_now()` at engine_loop.rs:985, taking and dropping gpu_lock (685-688) each iteration. Deadlock geometry: one waiting prompt needing more than pool minus pinned blocks, nothing running to retire, nothing registering to trigger LRU eviction; with min_blocks 256 (loader.rs:1708) and a pinned --max-context-len this is reachable on the maintainer's own 12B-on-24GB case. On a 2048-block pool the cost is milder than 'starvation': 512 pinned blocks leave 6 of 8 full-context sequences runnable, the rest preempt. Sizing the cache from the pool and adding evict-under-pressure is S and correct; note the hot spin is independent of the prefix cache (any head-of-queue prompt that cannot be admitted spins) and the right fix there is to block on request_rx (blocking_recv) when schedule() admitted nothing and running is empty.

findings.title: Decode sequences wait for every chunk of every admitted prefill: chunking bounds the GPU submission but not inter-token latency
findings.evidence: src/engine.rs:491-505 build_batch_input appends decode tokens after all prefill suffixes (`for &seq_id in decode_ids { all_token_ids.push(...); token_counts.push(1); }`), and ChunkPlanner (engine.rs:316-350) walks counts in order, so decode rows land in the last chunk. engine.rs:550-605: `while let Some(chunk) = planner.next(pacer.cap()) { ... if len > chunk.counts.len() { device.synchronize()?; pacer.observe(...) } } Tensor::cat(&rows, 0)` -- step() returns only after all chunks are drained; tokens are delivered by engine_loop only after step() returns (engine_loop.rs:684-705). The pacer doc admits it: engine.rs:202-204 'Splitting a prompt into chunks does not let anything else run: the whole batch belongs to one step either way.' The scheduler bundles up to max_tokens_per_step=4096 prefill tokens per step (manager.rs:1202) and admits a single oversized prompt of any length (scheduler/mod.rs:301-304).
findings.rationale: On a multi-user server, every client currently streaming stalls for the full prefill of any newly admitted prompt: 4096 tokens at the measured ~1-2K tok/s prefill on a 4B checkpoint is 2-4 s with no token; an oversized 16K prompt is 10+ s. The chunk cap (512-1024) already defines the natural step granularity, and all the plumbing for resumable prefill exists: num_processed_tokens, position offsets via num_cached_tokens, set_num_tokens, and ChunkPlanner's finished[] already models 'this sequence contributes no logits row this forward'.
findings.proposal: True chunked prefill across steps: let a Prefill-phase sequence stay in Prefill with num_processed_tokens advancing by at most pacer.cap() per step; schedule() admits 'one chunk of prefill' plus all decodes per step; run_forward_pass runs exactly one forward per step; sample_prefill_outputs samples only sequences whose prompt completed this step; prefix registration happens when the prompt completes. Keep the pacer as the per-step chunk size. Cheaper interim: order decode rows first in build_batch_input and deliver new_tokens per chunk via a callback, which fixes delivery latency without changing the scheduler.
findings.expected_benefit: Worst-case inter-token latency for streaming clients during a long-prompt arrival drops from the whole prefill (seconds, unbounded for oversized prompts) to one chunk (~0.3-0.7 s at 512-1024 tokens). Aggregate throughput unchanged; the number of forwards per prompt is the same as today's chunking.
findings.verify_how: On M5: stream a 500-token answer from client A, then submit a 4000-token prompt from client B mid-stream; record A's max inter-token gap (today ~= B's TTFT; after the fix ~= one chunk time). The server already logs ttft_ms per request; add the max inter-token gap to the request span.

verdict.reason: Accurate: build_batch_input appends decode rows after all prefill suffixes (engine.rs:500-505), ChunkPlanner walks counts in order (engine.rs:331-342), run_forward_pass drains every chunk before `Tensor::cat(&rows, 0)` (engine.rs:550-605) and engine_loop delivers new_tokens only after step() returns (engine_loop.rs:685-705). The pacer doc (engine.rs:200-204) states the limitation. But the 'cheaper interim' does not deliver: moving decode rows to the first chunk makes step k's decode token available one chunk earlier, yet step k+1 (the next token for the same client) still cannot start until all of step k's prefill chunks drain, so the max inter-token gap stays equal to the whole prefill. Only the full cross-step chunking helps, and it is honestly L: it touches schedule() admission (budget = pacer.cap() of prefill tokens per step), PrefillInfo/plan_prefill_inputs (resume from num_processed_tokens, no prefix lookup on resumed chunks), sample_prefill_outputs (sample only completed prompts), prefix registration timing, CacheRestoreGuard, and the pacer's per-chunk accounting. Single-user (the verified primary use on a laptop) is unaffected and aggregate throughput is unchanged, so this is a multi-tenant latency improvement, not a throughput or correctness item.
verdict.corrected_benefit: Worst-case inter-token gap for already-streaming clients drops from the newly admitted prompt's whole prefill (seconds, unbounded for oversized prompts) to one chunk (~0.3-0.7 s). No change for a single user; aggregate throughput unchanged.
verdict.corrected_proposal: Drop the interim (decode-rows-first plus per-chunk delivery) since it cannot shorten the gap. Implement true cross-step chunked prefill: Prefill-phase sequences stay in Prefill with num_processed_tokens advancing by at most pacer.cap() per step; schedule() admits all decodes plus at most one cap's worth of prefill tokens from the head prompt; run_forward_pass runs exactly one forward per step; sample_prefill_outputs samples and registers only sequences whose prompt completed this step; the pacer keeps observing full-cap chunks.

findings.title: Sampling does 2 GPU round trips per sequence per step (greedy) or a full-vocab copy per sequence (non-greedy) instead of one batched readback
findings.evidence: src/engine.rs:697-711 `for (i, &seq_id) in decode_ids.iter().enumerate() { let seq_logits = batch_logits.get(num_prefills + i)?; ... sampling::sample(&seq_logits, ...)` (and the same per-row loop at :628-641 for prefills). src/sampling.rs:105-109: `let token = logits.argmax(D::Minus1)?.to_scalar::<u32>()?; let sum: f32 = logits.sum_all()?.to_dtype(F32)?.to_scalar()?;` -- two Metal commit+wait per row; sampling.rs:120 `let mut logits_vec: Vec<f32> = logits.to_dtype(F32)?.to_vec1()?;` -- one sync plus vocab x 4 bytes (~600 KB on a 150K vocab) per row for any non-greedy request. Also src/engine.rs:585-587,605: `for &row in &chunk.finished { rows.push(out.narrow(0, row, 1)?); } ... Tensor::cat(&rows, 0)` issues N narrows and a cat even when the only chunk already holds one row per sequence (the decode case).
findings.rationale: Each to_scalar/to_vec on Metal is a command-buffer flush and wait, typically 0.1-0.5 ms of fixed latency; at concurrency 8 that is 16 serial syncs per step (plus 9 extra tiny ops from narrow/cat) against a step of ~25-35 ms on the 4B checkpoints the notes measure (30-46 tok/s), i.e. roughly 5-20% of the step spent waiting on readbacks that could be one. The plan comparison's 'GPU-side sampling / top-k prefilter' item is the bigger rewrite; this is the cheap part of it.
findings.proposal: In step(): once per step compute `argmax = batch_logits.argmax(D::Minus1)` ([N] u32) and `sums = batch_logits.sum(D::Minus1)` ([N]), read both back once (two syncs total, or one by folding the NaN check into a single f32 vector readback of [N] sums plus the u32 argmaxes), and hand each greedy/unconstrained sequence its precomputed token; for rows that need CPU sampling (temperature, penalties, logprobs, constraint) do one `index_select(rows).to_dtype(F32).to_vec2()` and sample from slices. Skip narrow/cat in run_forward_pass when the planner produced a single chunk whose finished covers all sequences.
findings.expected_benefit: Per step: 2N syncs -> 2 (greedy) and N vocab copies -> 1 batched copy (non-greedy). Expected 5-15% aggregate throughput at concurrency 8, ~0 at N=1 beyond removing one of the two greedy syncs.
findings.verify_how: Wrap sample_prefill_outputs/sample_decode_outputs in Instant timing behind OXYDLLM_PROFILE_DECODE and compare per-step sampling ms at N=1 and N=8 before/after; compare aggregate tok/s at 8 concurrent requests on Qwen3-4B-AWQ.

verdict.reason: Verified: sample_prefill_outputs and sample_decode_outputs call sampling::sample per row (engine.rs:628-641, 697-711); the greedy fast path is `logits.argmax(D::Minus1)?.to_scalar::<u32>()?` plus `logits.sum_all()?.to_dtype(F32)?.to_scalar()?` (sampling.rs:105-109), two host readbacks per row, and the non-greedy path does `logits.to_dtype(F32)?.to_vec1()?` per row (sampling.rs:120), a full-vocab copy per sequence. The narrow/cat at engine.rs:585-587,605 are extra launches, not syncs. PLAN_COMPARISON §8c shipped only the scalar-cast part; the roadmap does not reject GPU-side sampling. Batching argmax and sum over [N, vocab] once per step and reading back [N] each uses the same candle reduce kernels per row, so greedy tokens are unchanged; the per-row NaN check folds into the [N] sums. Worth: each extra readback on Metal is a commit plus wait_until_completed on a near-empty queue, roughly 0.1-0.3 ms, so at N=8 the 14 avoidable syncs cost ~1.5-5 ms of a ~40-60 ms batched step: 3-10% at concurrency 8 is the honest bound (the finding's 5-15% is the optimistic end); ~0 at N=1 unless both readbacks are folded into one. Effort S is right: it is local to engine.rs and sampling.rs.

findings.title: A 1-token prefill tail chunk skips the pool write but its block is still registered in the prefix cache
findings.evidence: src/common/paged.rs:1084-1086: `// Decode-only: pool writes are only needed for prefix-cache reuse ... let skip_pool_write = self.contig_len > 0 && new_seq == 1;` -- the heuristic treats any 1-token append after the first as decode. ChunkPlanner (src/engine.rs:331-342) can leave a sequence a 1-token tail: counts [497, 16] with cap 512 gives chunk 1 = [497, 15] and chunk 2 = [1]; that second chunk reaches append with contig_len == 15 and new_seq == 1, so token 15 of sequence 2 is never written to the pool. src/engine.rs:664-678 then registers it anyway: `if info.num_full_blocks_total > info.num_cached_blocks { let new_block_ids = ... (info.num_cached_blocks..info.num_full_blocks_total).map(|block_idx| seq.caches.iter().filter_map(|c| c.block_id_at(block_idx)) ...; prefix.register(&seq.all_tokens, ...)` with num_full_blocks_total = 16/16 = 1 (engine.rs:476). A later prompt sharing those 16 tokens hits the block (lookup caps at (seq_len-1)/block_size, engine.rs:435-439), prepopulates it, and append's (None, None) branch gathers all 16 slots from the pool (paged.rs:1216-1221), slot 15 holding zeros or a previous occupant's K/V.
findings.rationale: The condition needs a multi-prefill step where a sequence's remaining tail is exactly one token and its length is a multiple of block_size; with concurrent arrivals and the planner cutting wherever the cap lands, that is a few-percent-of-steps event under load, and the symptom is a silently wrong K/V for one position of a shared prefix (degraded, not garbage output), which no existing test can see because the fake models in engine.rs never read the pool back. Single-sequence prefill is arithmetically safe only because the cap is always a multiple of 16.
findings.proposal: Decide the pool-write policy by phase, not by new_seq: add `PagedKvCache::set_pool_writes(bool)` (or a flag on append) that the engine sets to true for sequences in SequencePhase::Prefill and to false in sample_prefill_outputs where it sets `seq.phase = Decode` (engine.rs:651); drop the new_seq == 1 heuristic. Alternatively, as a contained guard in ChunkPlanner::next, never leave a sequence a 1-token remainder (take one fewer so the tail is >= 2). Add a KvFakeModel-style test that fills blocks through append across a [497,16]/cap-512 plan and asserts the registered block's last slot was written.
findings.expected_benefit: Closes a silent prefix-cache corruption on the chunked multi-prefill path; no performance cost (one bool per append).
findings.verify_how: Unit: construct the [497, 16] / cap 512 plan with a model that writes recognisable K values, run two engine steps with a second prompt sharing the 16-token prefix, read the pool slot via BlockAllocator::gather and assert it equals the written value. E2E: temperature-0 A/B of a shared-prefix pair whose first prompt is forced into that geometry.

verdict.reason: Verified end to end. paged.rs:1086 `let skip_pool_write = self.contig_len > 0 && new_seq == 1;` is the only criterion. ChunkPlanner::next (engine.rs:331-342) takes `min(remaining, room)` so counts [497,16] at cap 512 yields chunk 1 = [497,15], chunk 2 = [1] for the second sequence; flush_caches runs after chunk 1 (engine.rs:588) and the contiguous buffer then holds 15 tokens (paged.rs:1168-1174 contig_len += new_seq), so chunk 2's append has contig_len 15, new_seq 1, and token 15 gets no PendingRun (paged.rs:1113-1127) while cached_slots and num_tokens still advance (:1133-1138). sample_prefill_outputs registers `seq_len / block_size` = 1 full block (engine.rs:476, 664-678) regardless. A later prompt sharing those 16 tokens with seq_len >= 17 passes max_cacheable (engine.rs:444-447), prepopulates the block, and the (None, None) branch gathers all 16 slots from the pool (paged.rs:1221-1226), reading slot 15 as stale. Single-sequence prefill is safe because the cap (512 and its halvings) and cached prefixes are multiples of 16, so a 1-token tail always lands at block offset 0 and is never in a registered block; only multi-prefill steps hit it. The symptom (one stale K/V position in a shared prefix, silent) and the lack of any test that reads the pool back justify medium. The cheapest fix is the planner guard (never leave a remainder of exactly one token for a sequence that spans chunks), three lines with no API change; the phase flag is equally sound.

findings.title: Speculative decode keeps emitting accepted tokens after max_tokens is reached
findings.evidence: src/engine.rs:822-836: `for tok in accepted { seq.append_token(tok); ... let is_stop = ...; if seq.apply_token(tok, is_stop) { new_tokens.push(NewToken {...}) } else { break; } }` -- the loop only breaks when apply_token returns false. src/scheduler/sequence.rs:61-74: apply_token returns false only for is_stop; on the length cap it sets `self.status = SequenceStatus::Finished; self.finish_reason = Some("length".to_string());` and still returns true, and keeps incrementing num_generated on later calls. The function's own doc (engine.rs:764-768) promises 'a stop or length cap drops the remaining accepted tokens'.
findings.rationale: With max_tokens = 10, num_generated = 9 and three accepted tokens, the sequence emits 12 tokens; the client receives up to SPEC_DRAFT_K-1 tokens beyond its max_tokens and completion_tokens over-reports. Only reachable with a draft model configured (opt-in), which is why no test caught it; the batch path appends one token per step so retire_finished catches Finished in time.
findings.proposal: Break when the sequence is finished for any reason: `let emitted = seq.apply_token(tok, is_stop); if emitted { new_tokens.push(...) } if !emitted || seq.status == SequenceStatus::Finished { break; }`. Add an engine test with a FakeModel draft and max_tokens = 1 asserting exactly one NewToken.
findings.expected_benefit: Correct max_tokens semantics on the speculative path; no perf change.
findings.verify_how: The new unit test; E2E with --draft-model: request max_tokens=3 at temperature 0 and count streamed tokens.

verdict.reason: Verified: run_speculative_decode's acceptance loop (engine.rs:822-836) breaks only when `seq.apply_token(tok, is_stop)` returns false, and apply_token (sequence.rs:61-74) returns false only for `is_stop`; on `num_generated >= max_tokens` it sets Finished and `finish_reason = "length"` but returns true and keeps incrementing num_generated on later calls. With max_tokens 10, num_generated 9 and three accepted tokens, all three are pushed as NewToken (12 emitted). The doc at engine.rs:764-768 promises the opposite. Only reachable with a draft model (opt-in, roadmap 'speculative decoding phase 2: parked'), and the batch path is safe because it appends one token per step before retire_finished (engine.rs:1096). The one-line break on `seq.status == SequenceStatus::Finished` and a FakeModel test are S.

findings.title: PrefillPacer halves and freezes the chunk cap on any forward error, including decode-only steps and block exhaustion
findings.evidence: src/engine.rs:571-581: `Err(e) => { if pacer.shrink() { tracing::warn!(tokens = len, new_cap = pacer.cap(), ... "prefill chunk failed; the cap comes down for the next request"); } return Err(e); }` -- called for every chunk error regardless of whether the chunk was a prefill (len > counts.len()) or at the cap. engine.rs:267-275: `fn shrink(&mut self) -> bool { if self.cap <= 32 { return false; } self.cap /= 2; self.best = None; self.settled = true; true }` and engine.rs:244-246 `fn observe(...) { if tokens < self.cap || self.settled { return; }` -- once settled the cap never climbs again for the process lifetime.
findings.rationale: The shrink exists for 'a chunk too large for the device to back', but the same arm fires for a KV-exhaustion error raised by a 1-token decode step (finding 1), for a model-side error, or for any transient failure; three such errors leave the cap at 64 tokens, and the engine's own doc says a 12B checkpoint lost 40% of TTFT to small chunks. The pacer is per model and lives as long as the engine, so one bad minute degrades every later prefill until the model is unloaded.
findings.proposal: Shrink only when the failed chunk was a full prefill chunk (`len >= pacer.cap() && len > chunk.counts.len()`) and the error is a device/allocation failure rather than a KV-pool exhaustion (match on the error message or carry a typed error from paged.rs); after shrinking set `settled = false` with `best = None` so the cap can re-climb up to the failed size minus one doubling, and log the reason.
findings.expected_benefit: Prevents a permanent 2-16x prefill slowdown after transient errors; otherwise behaviour-neutral.
findings.verify_how: Unit: `shrink()` must be a no-op when invoked with a decode-only chunk descriptor; E2E: provoke one 'engine step failed' (e.g. the finding-1 scenario) and then measure TTFT on a 2K prompt before and after; today it roughly doubles.

verdict.reason: Accurate: engine.rs:571-581 calls `pacer.shrink()` on every forward_batch_last error with no check on `len > chunk.counts.len()` or on the error kind; shrink (engine.rs:267-275) halves, clears best and sets settled, and observe (engine.rs:244-246) returns early once settled, so the cap never climbs again for the engine's lifetime. A KV-exhaustion error (paged.rs:565-571) raised by a decode-only chunk therefore halves the prefill cap; the engine's own doc (engine.rs:205-210) records a 40% TTFT loss from small chunks. But the proposal's re-climb (`settled = false` after shrink) contradicts the pacer's stated policy that a size which failed must not be retried, adds state for no clear gain, and once finding 1 is fixed the exhaustion error should not occur at all; a model-side transient error remains the only trigger, and each such error already aborts every running request, so it is a loud, rare event. The minimal gate is the whole fix.
verdict.corrected_benefit: Prevents a permanent 2-16x prefill slowdown after an error that was not a device-capacity failure; otherwise neutral.
verdict.corrected_proposal: Shrink only when the failed chunk was a prefill chunk (`len > chunk.counts.len()`) and the error is not the pool-exhaustion error (carry a typed KvExhausted variant from paged.rs allocate(), or match the 'KV cache memory exhausted' message); keep shrink's settled semantics unchanged and log the reason.

findings.title: Generated tokens never enter the prefix cache, so every chat turn re-prefills the previous assistant reply
findings.evidence: The only registration site is in sample_prefill_outputs: src/engine.rs:664-678 `if info.num_full_blocks_total > info.num_cached_blocks { ... prefix.register(&seq.all_tokens, info.num_cached_blocks, &new_block_ids); }` with num_full_blocks_total computed from the prompt length (engine.rs:476 `let num_full_blocks_total = seq_len / block_size;`). Decode never writes the pool: src/common/paged.rs:1084-1086 `let skip_pool_write = self.contig_len > 0 && new_seq == 1;`, although the block id is still allocated for decode tokens (paged.rs:1107-1110). retire_finished (scheduler/mod.rs:338-357) just frees. Server and REPL rebuild the whole prompt from text each turn (src/server/routes/chat.rs:1690-1707; src/main.rs:1271-1273), so turn N+1's prompt = turn N's prompt + reply N + user N+1, of which only turn N's prompt blocks can hit.
findings.rationale: The LOAD_AND_HISTORY note expects TTFT at turn N to cover only the new user message (10-50 tokens); the code re-prefills the entire previous reply plus the new message every turn. For normal replies that is a few hundred tokens (~0.2-0.5 s of prefill on a 4B checkpoint per turn); for thinking models whose reasoning stays in history it is thousands. The pool blocks for those tokens are already allocated and refcounted; only the bytes are missing.
findings.proposal: At retirement (or when a decode crosses a block boundary), materialise the generated tokens' full blocks: in retire_finished (or a new Engine hook before it) call a `PagedKvCache::commit_contig_to_pool(from_token, to_token)` per layer that slice-copies the contiguous buffer rows into the already-allocated pool blocks (one write per layer per sequence, not per token), then `prefix.register(&seq.all_tokens, prompt_full_blocks, generated_full_block_ids)`. Exclude the sampled stop token (it has no KV). Must run under the gpu lock before clear_caches frees anything; the prefix cache then holds the refcount.
findings.expected_benefit: Multi-turn TTFT drops by the previous reply's prefill: ~0.2-0.5 s per turn for 300-500-token replies, 1-2 s per turn for 2K-token thinking replies, at the cost of one KV copy per layer at retire.
findings.verify_how: RUST_LOG=oxydllm::engine=debug multi-turn session: skipped_tokens at turn N+1 should equal turn N's full prompt plus reply (today it equals turn N's prompt only); compare ttft_ms across 5 turns of a chat with 400-token replies.

verdict.reason: Verified: the only register call is in sample_prefill_outputs (engine.rs:664-678) over `info.num_cached_blocks..info.num_full_blocks_total` with num_full_blocks_total = prompt seq_len / block_size (engine.rs:476); decode appends skip pool writes (paged.rs:1086) although block ids are allocated (paged.rs:1107-1110); retire_finished only clears caches (mod.rs:338-357); chat.rs:1690-1700 rebuilds the prompt from message text each turn. The LOAD_AND_HISTORY note (lines 252-255) expects turn-N TTFT to cover only the new user message, which the code cannot deliver: turn N's reply blocks were never written to the pool, so turn N+1 re-prefills them. Benefit is real but bounded by the note's own caveat (lines 258-300): a hit needs encode(decode(reply)) to match the generated ids block for block, which modern byte-level BPE mostly gives; the reply's last partial block plus template suffix always re-prefills. Mechanism is sound and cheap at retire: per layer one slice copy of the contiguous buffer rows into the already-allocated pool blocks (slots are in table.cached_slots), then register with the prefix cache holding the refcount, excluding the sampled last token (no KV). Caveats that keep it at M: sliding-window layers keep only the window in the contiguous buffer (paged.rs:1149-1160 keep/span), so blocks outside the window cannot be committed from it and must be handled (skip registration for those spans or keep per-token pool writes on windowed layers); the registration must run under gpu_lock before clear_caches; and a fuller cache interacts with finding 2's fixed 512 capacity.

findings.title: gpu_lock is held for the whole step, including CPU sampling and constraint-mask construction; the module header says the opposite
findings.evidence: src/gpu_lock.rs:16-17: `// Scheduling and sampling happen **outside** the lock, so the only serialised // portion is the actual GPU compute.` versus src/server/routes/engine_loop.rs:685-688 `let step_result = { let _gpu = gpu_lock.acquire(); engine.step() };`. Inside step() under that lock: src/engine.rs:634 and :703 `let allowed = seq.constraint.as_ref().map(|c| c.allowed(vocab));` which in src/constrain.rs:1137-1160 walks every vocabulary entry through the byte automaton (`for (id, entry) in self.table.bytes.iter().enumerate().take(vocab_size) { ... if self.walk(&mut m, &mut g, tok_bytes) ...`) per constrained sequence per token; the CPU sampler (sampling.rs:120-260) softmax/top-k/top-p over the full vocab; prefix-cache hashing; and the per-chunk `device.synchronize()` (engine.rs:600) whose chunk may last up to CHUNK_CEILING = 3 s (engine.rs:188).
findings.rationale: With two models resident on the same Metal device (the manager keeps several loaded and evicts by LRU), model B's engine thread cannot start its forward while model A builds a 150K-entry JSON mask (milliseconds per token) or samples on the CPU, and it waits up to a full 3 s prefill chunk. Readbacks must stay under the lock (the roadmap lists candle 0.11 concurrent-synchronize corruption), but the pure-CPU phases need not.
findings.proposal: Split Engine::step into three phases and have engine_loop lock only the middle one: (1) schedule, plan_prefill_inputs, build masks (`allowed()`), build_batch_input; (2) run_forward_pass plus one batched logits readback (finding 4) returning host-side rows; (3) CPU sampling, constraint advance, prefix registration, retire_finished. Expose this as `Engine::prepare() -> Prepared`, `Engine::forward(&Prepared) -> HostLogits` and `Engine::finish(Prepared, HostLogits)`, or accept a closure for the locked section. Fix the gpu_lock.rs header either way.
findings.expected_benefit: On a two-model server the second model's step no longer waits for the first's CPU work: constrained decoding and non-greedy sampling move off the critical section (ms per token per constrained sequence). Single-model servers are unaffected.
findings.verify_how: Load two small models, run a json_schema request on A and a greedy stream on B concurrently; measure B's inter-token time with and without A's constrained traffic.

verdict.reason: Accurate as to the code: gpu_lock.rs:16-17 claims sampling happens outside the lock, engine_loop.rs:685-688 holds `gpu_lock.acquire()` around the whole `engine.step()`, and inside it `c.allowed(vocab)` (engine.rs:634, 703) walks every vocabulary entry through the automaton per constrained token (constrain.rs:1137-1160, no memo; the MASK_CACHE in mask.rs:16,127-130 is the attention-mask cache, unrelated). Worth is narrow: it only matters when two models on the same device serve concurrently, and even then the candle 0.11 concurrent-synchronize hazard keeps every readback inside the lock, so only pure-CPU phases can move. PLAN_COMPARISON §8 (lines 251-270) already settled that pool=1 serializes candle encoding and advised against widening gpu_lock; nothing there asks for narrowing it either. The maintainer's platform is a 24 GB laptop where two resident models decoding concurrently is unusual, and the three-phase refactor is M and touches the whole step. A cheaper S change captures most of it for the one costly CPU phase.
verdict.corrected_benefit: Removes the per-constrained-token vocab walk (milliseconds) from the cross-model critical section and makes gpu_lock.rs truthful; no effect on single-model servers.
verdict.corrected_proposal: Fix the gpu_lock.rs header to say the whole step is serialized. Compute each constrained sequence's `allowed` mask outside the lock: in engine_loop after step() returns (the constraint has already advanced), store it on the SequenceState and have sample_*_outputs consume the stored mask instead of calling allowed() under the lock. Defer the full prepare/forward/finish split until the batched readback (finding 4) exists, at which point CPU sampling can leave the lock as a follow-up.

findings.title: Tokenizer-roundtrip caveat is still unverified in code: no skipped-token metric and no prefix-divergence check in the REPL
findings.evidence: src/engine.rs:41-47 StepOutput carries only `prefix_cache_hits: usize, prefix_cache_misses: usize` (a prefill counts as a hit if a single block matched); the token-level signal is debug-only: engine.rs:461-467 `tracing::debug!(seq_id, cached_blocks = num_cached_blocks, total_blocks = ..., skipped_tokens = num_cached_tokens, "prefix cache hit")`. src/main.rs:1271-1273 `let mut prompt = server::apply_chat_template(&tokenizer, &messages, ...); let mut prompt_tokens = tokenizer.encode(&prompt)?;` re-encodes text each turn with no comparison against the previous turn's ids plus output_ids; src/server/routes/chat.rs:1690-1707 does the same. The only roundtrip check in the tree (src/tokenizer.rs:447-451) is for stop markers.
findings.rationale: The May note flagged encode(decode(ids)) != ids as a potential silent TTFT regression and listed a two-line detection (LCP of the new prompt against the expected prefix). Nothing shipped, and the hit/miss counter cannot distinguish 'skipped 3000 tokens' from 'skipped 16'. With finding 8 fixed the exposure grows, since the reply tokens would then be cache material.
findings.proposal: Add `prefix_cache_skipped_tokens` and `prefill_tokens` to StepOutput, export a Prometheus counter pair and include skipped tokens in the first-token info log in engine_loop; in run_interactive keep `expected_prefix = prev_prompt_tokens ++ output_ids` and warn when the LCP with the new prompt_tokens is shorter than prev_prompt_tokens.len(). Add a tokenizer test that encodes a chat template rendering of a decoded assistant reply (with trailing newlines, code fences, long digit runs) and asserts the prefix ids are stable for the tokenizers shipped with the verified checkpoints.
findings.expected_benefit: Turns an unmeasured risk into a number visible per request; cost is two usize fields per step.
findings.verify_how: Run a 5-turn REPL session with a code-heavy reply and read the new warning / skipped_tokens figure; compare against turn N's prompt length.

findings.title: Prefill admission charges the full prompt length against the step budget even when the prefix cache will skip most of it
findings.evidence: src/scheduler/mod.rs:301-304: `let tokens_needed = seq.all_tokens.len(); if tokens_needed > budget && prefill_scheduled { break; }` while blocks_needed_for_prefill (mod.rs:208-220) already computed `pc.count_cached_blocks(&seq.all_tokens, self.block_size)` and discounted the cached blocks from the block count but not from the token count. The engine then feeds only the uncached suffix (engine.rs:473-474 `let uncached_len = seq_len - num_cached_tokens; let input_tokens = all_tokens[num_cached_tokens..].to_vec();`).
findings.rationale: Multi-turn chat near the context limit is exactly the case where prompts are long and almost entirely cached: two 3800-token turn-N requests arriving together are serialised one per step (the second trips `tokens_needed > budget && prefill_scheduled` after the decodes consume budget) although each runs ~100 uncached tokens; the deferred one pays one extra step plus its own tiny forward instead of sharing a chunk.
findings.proposal: Have blocks_needed_for_prefill return `(blocks_needed, cached_tokens)` and use `tokens_needed = total_tokens - cached_tokens` for the budget check (keeping at least 1).
findings.expected_benefit: Fewer one-step deferrals and fewer tiny separate prefill forwards under concurrent cached arrivals; modest latency win, zero risk.
findings.verify_how: Scheduler unit test with a prefix cache holding a 60-block prompt and budget 128: two cached 1000-token prompts should be admitted in one step after the change.

findings.title: ChunkPlanner splits sequences that would fit whole in the next chunk
findings.evidence: src/engine.rs:331-341: `while self.seq < self.counts.len() && room > 0 { let take = (self.counts[self.seq] - self.done_in_seq).min(room); counts.push(take); room -= take; ...` -- greedy fill always consumes the remaining room from the next sequence. With cap 512 and counts [400, 400, 400] the plan is [400,112], [288,224], [176]: two sequences cut although none exceeds the cap. Each cut costs a contiguous-buffer regrow and copy in paged.rs (contig_buf_capacity(112) = 224 < 400, so the (Some, Some) branch at paged.rs:1172-1205 reallocates and copies) plus a partial-prefix attention pass.
findings.rationale: Mid-sequence cuts are required only for prompts longer than the cap; for batched arrivals of ordinary prompts they add copies and small, inefficient forwards that the pacer's own doc identifies as the cost of chunking.
findings.proposal: In ChunkPlanner::next, when the current sequence has not started (done_in_seq == 0), does not fit in the remaining room, fits in a fresh chunk (count <= cap), and the chunk already holds at least cap/2 tokens, close the chunk instead of taking a partial. Keep fuzz_chunking_preserves_the_batch as the invariant.
findings.expected_benefit: Fewer contig regrows and partial forwards in multi-prefill steps; expect a few percent of prefill time when several prompts arrive together, nothing in the single-prompt case.
findings.verify_how: Add a planner test for [400,400,400]/512 expecting no partial counts; E2E: submit 3 x 400-token prompts simultaneously and compare the step's prefill time before/after.

findings.title: Speculative path pays K+1 CPU round trips per sequence per step and verifies sequences one at a time, which caps the achievable speedup below 1x for small drafts
findings.evidence: src/engine.rs:742-756 greedy_forward ends with `let argmax = logits.squeeze(0)?.argmax(candle_core::D::Minus1)?; argmax.to_vec1::<u32>()` (a full Metal flush+wait); it is called in the draft loop at engine.rs:803-807 `for pos in ((l - 1) as u32..).take(SPEC_DRAFT_K) { let out = greedy_forward(draft, device, &mut seq.draft_caches, &[cur], &[pos])?; cur = out[0]; drafts.push(cur); }` (K = 4 syncs) and once more for the target at :813. run_speculative_decode iterates `for &seq_id in decode_ids` (engine.rs:789) so N spec sequences mean N unbatched target forwards. The draft's catch-up at :794-798 runs the whole prompt gap in one unchunked forward.
findings.rationale: A 0.6B draft forward on Metal is launch-bound (several ms), so four serial draft steps plus their readbacks cost about one target step on a 4B model before any verification; the roadmap's 'no speedup with current 0.6B drafts' is partly structural, not only draft quality, and a better draft will not reveal it until the chain stays on-device and verification is batched.
findings.proposal: Give greedy_forward a Tensor-input variant and feed the argmax tensor straight back as the next draft input (one readback of all K drafts after the loop), run the K draft steps without intermediate synchronisation, and batch the verify forwards across spec sequences (they are independent and the model already supports multi-sequence batches). Route the draft catch-up through the ChunkPlanner.
findings.expected_benefit: Per spec sequence per step: 5 syncs -> 2; verification cost shared across N sequences. Makes the speculative path measurable so phase 2 can be evaluated honestly.
findings.verify_how: With --draft-model on Qwen3-4B + Qwen3-0.6B at temperature 0, log per-step draft loop time vs target step time; today draft loop ~= target step.

findings.title: Preemption victim is whichever decode happens to sit on a block boundary, pushed to the front of the queue to re-prefill everything
findings.evidence: src/scheduler/mod.rs:272-283: `let idx = *self.running_index.get(&seq_id).unwrap(); let mut seq = self.remove_from_running(idx); tracing::warn!(... "sequence preempted due to memory pressure; KV cache cleared and re-queued"); seq.clear_caches(); seq.num_processed_tokens = 0; seq.phase = SequencePhase::Prefill; seq.status = SequenceStatus::Waiting; self.waiting.push_front(seq);` -- the sequence needing the block is itself preempted regardless of its age or length, and running order is perturbed by swap_remove (mod.rs:109-116) so there is no stable notion of youngest.
findings.rationale: Recompute cost is proportional to the victim's length, so preempting a 3000-token sequence to keep a 20-token one is the worst trade, and the re-prefill then re-registers its blocks in the prefix cache, pinning more (finding 2). vLLM preempts the latest-arrived sequence to preserve FCFS and minimise lost work.
findings.proposal: When a decode needs a block and none is free (after finding 2's eviction), preempt the most recently admitted running sequence (track admission order with a monotonic counter on SequenceState) and credit its freed blocks to the current step's reservation (finding 1) so the older sequence proceeds.
findings.expected_benefit: Under pressure, lost work per preemption drops from 'longest sequence' to 'newest sequence'; fairness becomes FCFS. No effect when the pool is not under pressure.
findings.verify_how: Scheduler unit test: two running sequences, the older long and at a boundary, pool exhausted: the newer one should be preempted; E2E: with a deliberately small --max-context-len pool, measure total re-prefilled tokens across a 2-client run from the 'sequence preempted' log.

findings.title: Stale and duplicated commentary around the pacer contradicts the constants it documents
findings.evidence: src/engine.rs:184-188: `/// ... A quarter of a second keeps the desktop responsive /// with room to spare ... const CHUNK_CEILING: Duration = Duration::from_secs(3);` -- the doc describes 250 ms, the value is 3 s. src/engine.rs:589-598: the comment 'A forward returns once the work is queued, not once it has run, so the chunk has to be drained before it can be timed' appears twice in a row with slightly different wording. src/engine.rs:1301-1303: the test doc begins with a leftover sentence from the previous latency-target design ('Contract: the cap follows the machine. A chunk that overran the target shrinks it, a full chunk well inside the target grows it, and a chunk') before the current contract. src/gpu_lock.rs:16-17 (see finding 9).
findings.rationale: The ROADMAP's constant audit asks that policy constants carry their reason; CHUNK_CEILING is the one whose reason text disagrees with its value by 12x, and a reader cannot tell whether 3 s or 250 ms was measured. The duplicated block and the orphaned test sentence are the kind of drift that makes future pacer changes riskier.
findings.proposal: Decide and document the real ceiling (the macOS watchdog argument supports seconds, the responsiveness argument supports hundreds of ms); delete the duplicate comment; rewrite the test doc; update gpu_lock.rs's header to match engine_loop.
findings.expected_benefit: Prevents a future change from 'fixing' the constant to match the comment or vice versa.
findings.verify_how: Read the diff; no runtime check needed.

subsystems.coverage_notes: Read all five scope files in full. Confirmed callees by reading the relevant parts of src/common/paged.rs (allocator allocate/share/free/num_free, PagedKvCache append/flush_pending/clear/prepopulate_block/set_num_tokens/truncate_to, ContigBufferPool, safe_model_kv_ceiling), src/sampling.rs (sample entry and the greedy/non-greedy readback paths), src/models/traits.rs, src/models/gguf_model.rs (StandardTransformer is the sole BatchModel impl and overrides forward_batch_last with LogitRows::LastPerSequence, so the lm_head-over-all-prompt-tokens concern is already addressed), src/common/block.rs (LogitRows and flush_caches), src/server/routes/engine_loop.rs (step loop, gpu_lock acquisition, disconnect/error handling), src/constrain.rs (allowed/advance), src/models/loader.rs (compute_kv_blocks, min_blocks 256), src/main.rs run_interactive and src/server/routes/chat.rs prompt building. Not read: the attention/FA kernels, kv_quant, the rest of paged.rs (gather/write internals, segment growth), constrain.rs automaton internals, engine_loop text decoding/harmony routing, manager.rs. I could not run anything (no Metal, cargo off limits), so every latency/throughput figure is an estimate argued from code structure and the maintainer's own measured numbers in the notes, not a measurement. Items examined and judged negligible (no finding): prefix-cache hashing (3 walks per admission, FxHash of 16 u32s), block_ids Vec clones on lookup, token_counts HashMap upkeep, per-step Tensor::from_vec for ids/positions, stop-sequence suffix checks, running_index HashMap churn, VecDeque abort position scan.
missed: Admission has no growth reservation (no watermark): schedule() admits waiting prompts down to the last free block (src/scheduler/mod.rs:287-316, `free_blocks = self.num_free_blocks()` and `if blocks_needed > free_blocks { break; }` with blocks_needed = div_ceil(prompt_len) minus cached, mod.rs:208-221), while every running decode needs one fresh block per layer at each 16-token boundary (decode_needs_new_block, mod.rs:225-227) and a preempted sequence loses its whole KV, goes to the front of the queue (mod.rs:273-283) and must re-prefill its prompt tail plus all generated tokens (never pool-written, paged.rs:1086). At full occupancy this is a thrash loop rather than graceful degradation: admit A to the last block, next boundary preempt A (freeing its blocks), re-admit A next step (its blocks are free again), re-prefill, hit the next boundary, repeat; A makes at most 16 tokens of progress per full re-prefill while other decodes also compete for the same blocks. The standard fix is a watermark in the admission loop (admit only if free_blocks - blocks_needed >= running.len() + 1, i.e. one growth block per running sequence, or a small fraction of the pool), which with the reservation fix from finding 1 makes preemption a genuine rarity instead of the steady state at high load. It is S, testable with the existing fuzz harness at mod.rs:763 by asserting a bound on preemptions per generated token. Coverage note: I read the cited regions of engine.rs, scheduler/mod.rs, sequence.rs, prefix_cache.rs, gpu_lock.rs, paged.rs (allocate/share/free and append), engine_loop.rs (enqueue, loop body, error path), sampling.rs greedy path, constrain.rs allowed(), loader.rs KV plan, chat.rs prompt rebuild, the ROADMAP rejected/audit/backlog sections, PLAN_COMPARISON §8 and the LOAD_AND_HISTORY multi-turn section; I did not read CacheRestoreGuard, flush_caches, the sliding-window handling in prepopulate/set_num_tokens, or the per-layer allocator construction (whether all layers share one block count, which num_free_blocks assumes by reading allocators[0]).

subsystems.assessment: The paged KV subsystem is well-built where the maintainer has already been burned: block refcounts are conserved (fuzzed), the windowed buffer is bounded and fuzz-tested, the segment-at-a-time pool keeps resident bytes close to the tokens in use, and the sizing now asks the Metal driver instead of a fitted fraction. What is fragile is everything the budget does not see. A running sequence's KV lives twice, once in the block pool (whole blocks, for the prefix cache) and once in a per-sequence contiguous buffer (what every attention kernel actually reads), and only the pool is charged to the budget; the contiguous side carries 25% growth slack, is copied on every regrowth, and its per-layer recycling pool pins the four largest buffers ever seen for the life of the model. For Phi-3-mini that idle retention alone can exceed the entire KV grant. Decode tokens also take pool blocks that are never written or read, so the scheduler's block accounting is right only by coincidence. The single biggest lever is therefore structural: attention kernels that read the pool through a block table, which halves KV memory per sequence and deletes the contiguous buffer, its growth copies and its pool. Below that there are several cheap wins: the free list is LIFO so after the first sequence retires every prefill writes the pool one block at a time; a prefix-cache hit syncs the GPU once per layer to read back an index it uploaded a moment earlier; the global budget on Metal takes the CPU branch because `is_cpu` is derived from the CUDA device list; and the mask cache can pin hundreds of MB of masks per thread. KV quantization is in a holding pattern: the per-token single-norm scheme is numerically unsuited to post-RoPE keys (the maintainer found this and switched Auto to Off), the CPU packing path is single-threaded and allocation-heavy, and the CHANGELOG and the enum's own doc still describe the old behaviour. Locking is not a lever here: one engine thread per model means the allocator mutex is uncontended.

findings.title: KV of a running sequence is stored twice (block pool + contiguous buffer); the second copy is unbudgeted and decode tokens take pool blocks that are never written or read
findings.evidence: paged.rs:1086 `let skip_pool_write = self.contig_len > 0 && new_seq == 1;` (decode never writes the pool) while the same loop still calls `alloc.allocate()` when `current_offset == 0` (1091-1096). paged.rs:1170 `k_buf.slice_set(new_k, 2, at)?;` writes every token into the per-sequence contiguous buffer; paged.rs:1144 `k_src: k_flat.contiguous()?,` keeps a third copy of each prefill batch until flush. The pool is read back only in the `(None, None)` branch via paged.rs:1229 `let (pk, pv) = self.allocator.lock().unwrap().gather(&idx)?;` (first append after a prefix hit). paged.rs:928-934 `contig_buf_capacity` over-allocates: `total_needed * 2` below 1024, `+ (total_needed / 4).min(4096)` above. Attention reads only the contig view (attention.rs:749 `seg.cache.append(..)` / `seg.cache.current()`), and loader.rs:1635 `kv_bytes_per_block` charges only `DEFAULT_BLOCK_SIZE * n_kv_heads * head_dim * dtype * 2` per layer, i.e. the pool alone.
findings.rationale: Every token of a running sequence costs pool bytes (16-token blocks, materialised in whole segments) plus contig bytes (1.25x to 2x the live length), and only the pool is charged against the KV grant or seen by the scheduler. For Phi-3-mini (12 KB/token/layer) a 4096-token sequence holds ~50 MB/layer in the pool and ~63 MB/layer in the contig buffer; across 32 layers that is 1.6 GB charged and ~2 GB uncharged per sequence. The decode-phase pool blocks hold garbage: they exist only so `cached_slots` and block counts stay consistent. This double residency is exactly the regime (weights + KV crowding the device) that produced the silent-corruption bugs in alpha.15, and it is why the contig pool (kv-paged-2) can exceed the grant.
findings.proposal: Make the pool the only copy: give the Metal SDPA-vector (decode) kernel and the FA prefill kernel a block-table argument (`[n_blocks] u32` + block_size) so they gather K/V rows from the layer's pool segment(s) directly, and drop `contig_k/contig_v`, `acquire_contig`, the growth/compaction path and `ContigBufferPool`. Pool writes then happen for decode tokens too (one `slice_set`/custom write per layer per token, same count as today's contig write). Windowed layers keep the window by freeing blocks that fall out of it (refcounted, so prefix-cache sharers are unaffected). The segment list must stay addressable from the kernel (pass per-segment base pointers, or make segment size a kernel constant). As an intermediate step with no kernel work, charge live + pooled contig bytes to the model's footprint so eviction and the ceiling see them.
findings.expected_benefit: KV memory per running sequence roughly halves (pool only, no 25%-100% slack), so the same grant serves ~2x the concurrent sequences or context; the per-regrowth copies (cumulatively ~4x the final length at the 1.25x growth factor) and the contig pool disappear; decode per-token cost is unchanged (a pool write replaces a contig write); prefix hits no longer need `gather` at all.
findings.verify_how: On the M5, log `pool_bytes()` plus the sum of live and pooled contig buffer bytes per layer (add a trace in `acquire_contig`/`release_contig`) while serving 8 concurrent 2k-token requests on Phi-3-mini; compare with the model's reported kv_cache_bytes. After the change, Metal memory gauge for the same load should drop by close to the contig total, with decode tok/s unchanged (OXYDLLM_PROFILE_DECODE).

verdict.reason: Every cited line checks out. paged.rs:1086 `skip_pool_write = self.contig_len > 0 && new_seq == 1` while the loop at 1091-1096 still calls `alloc.allocate()` whenever `current_offset == 0`, so decode tokens take 16-token pool blocks that are never written (no run is pushed at 1098-1115) and never read: `gather` is reached only from the `(None, None)` arm at 1226-1231, i.e. the first append of a cache whose table was prepopulated by a prefix hit. Attention reads only the contig view (attention.rs:745/749 -> `current()` at 1247-1254). `contig_buf_capacity` (928-934) gives 2x below 1024 tokens and 1.25x (capped +4096) above, and `k_src: k_flat.contiguous()?` (1144) is a third transient copy per chunk. Accounting: `kv_cache_bytes` (traits.rs:76-90) sums `reserved_bytes()` = pool ceiling only; loader.rs:1635-1643 charges `DEFAULT_BLOCK_SIZE*n_kv*hd*dtype*2` per layer; grep finds no caller of any contig figure outside paged.rs. So a running sequence costs pool (rounded to 16) + contig (>=1.25x), >=2.25x what the grant sees; on Phi-3-mini (384 KB/token across 32 layers) 8 sequences of ~1.1k tokens (what the 3.25 GB grant admits) carry ~4.2 GB of uncharged contig beside 3.25 GB charged. The CHANGELOG's 'eight concurrent sequences in 3.25 GB' is therefore not the real footprint. Worth: memory is the binding constraint on the 24 GB target and the alpha.15 bugs came from exactly this regime, so high is right. Effort L is honest and if anything optimistic: the decode SDPA on Metal is candle's kernel (attention.rs:829-834 `use_seg_sdpa`), so a block-table variant means a kernel of their own plus the FA prefill kernel, the sink SDPA, the CPU path, windowed layers and spec-decode rollback. The reviewer's intermediate step (charge live+pooled contig bytes into the footprint/ceiling) is S and should land first regardless; a middle ground that avoids kernel work is to stop allocating pool blocks for decode tokens and charge contig growth to the scheduler instead, but that changes the block-based capacity model and is not obviously simpler.

findings.title: ContigBufferPool pins the four largest contiguous K/V buffers ever seen, per layer, for the life of the model
findings.evidence: paged.rs:352 `const MAX_POOL_BUFFERS: usize = 4;` paged.rs:367-376 `fn put(..) { .. let pos = self.buffers.partition_point(|b| b.cap < buf.cap); self.buffers.insert(pos, buf); if self.buffers.len() > self.max_buffers { self.buffers.remove(0); } }` evicts the SMALLEST. paged.rs:1392-1410 `clear()` hands every finished sequence's buffer back: `alloc.release_contig_buffer(k, v, cap)`. The pool is a field of the per-layer `BlockAllocator` (paged.rs:412 `contig_pool: ContigBufferPool`), so the cap is 4 per layer, and nothing bounds it by bytes or reports it (grep: no caller of pool_bytes/contig outside paged.rs).
findings.rationale: After four or more requests complete, each layer keeps its four largest buffers. Phi-3-mini: a 4096-token sequence allocates cap=5120 slots x 32 heads x 96 x 2 B x (K+V) = 63 MB per layer; four of them per layer x 32 layers = ~8 GB retained at idle, larger than the 3.25 GB KV grant the CHANGELOG reports for this model. Realistic 2k contexts still retain ~4 GB. Because the policy keeps the largest, one long request permanently raises the floor. This memory sits beside weights and pool in unified memory, uncharged, which is the oversubscription regime the alpha.15 bugs came from.
findings.proposal: Bound the pool by bytes rather than count, shared across layers (e.g. a single `AtomicUsize` budget of at most ~10% of the model's KV grant, checked in `put`), evict the largest or least-recently-returned buffer when over budget, and drop pooled buffers after an idle interval (the engine loop already has a keep-alive tick). Charge the pooled bytes into the model's footprint. If kv-paged-1 lands, delete the pool entirely.
findings.expected_benefit: Idle footprint after a busy period drops by up to 4 x (largest sequence KV per layer x layers), i.e. gigabytes on a mid-size model; the server's memory stays close to what the budget charged, which is what keeps it out of the silent-corruption regime.
findings.verify_how: Load Phi-3-mini, note Metal memory in use at idle; run sequential requests of ~4000, 3000, 2000, 1000 prompt tokens; wait for all to finish; compare idle memory. Expect several GB retained today and ~zero after the change.

verdict.reason: Verified: `MAX_POOL_BUFFERS = 4` (paged.rs:352), `put` inserts sorted by cap and evicts index 0 = the smallest (367-376), the pool is a field of the per-layer `BlockAllocator` (412), `release_contig_buffer` (637-639) has no byte bound, and `clear()` (1392-1410) returns every finished sequence's buffer. The arithmetic holds: a 4096-token Phi-3-mini sequence gets cap 5120 (928-934) = 5120*32*96*2B*2 = 63 MB per layer, 4 per layer x 32 layers = 8 GB retained at idle; realistic 2k traffic retains ~4 GB. I also checked that nothing else would hold the memory if the pool let go: candle 0.11's `drop_unused_buffers` (metal_backend/device.rs:131-150) runs on every `wait_until_completed`/`flush_and_wait_current` (175, 185), evicting buffers with strong_count == 1 from the map and the residency set, and the engine syncs after every prefill chunk (engine.rs:598), so dropped ContigBuffers are freed promptly and the 'near zero after the change' expectation is sound. The ROADMAP lists `MAX_POOL_BUFFERS` under 'C. deliberate policy: document why', not under rejected. The uncharged bytes are seen by `available_memory_bytes()` in `safe_model_kv_ceiling` (paged.rs:265-275), so the failure mode is the next model's pool being squeezed rather than corruption, but gigabytes of idle retention beside a 3.25 GB grant is still high. A per-allocator byte cap (e.g. pooled bytes <= `reserved_bytes()/8`) avoids the cross-layer atomic and is the cheapest form; S effort stands.

findings.title: gather() across pool segments uploads the slot index to the GPU and immediately reads it back, forcing a full GPU sync per layer on every prefix-cache hit
findings.evidence: paged.rs:1226-1229 builds the index on device from a CPU slice it already has: `let slots = &self.table.cached_slots[..]; let idx = Tensor::from_slice(slots, (from_old,), &self.device)?; let (pk, pv) = self.allocator.lock().unwrap().gather(&idx)?;`. paged.rs:812 (multi-segment Full pool) then does `let slots: Vec<u32> = slot_indices.to_device(&Device::Cpu)?.to_vec1()?;` and paged.rs:854 (quantized) `let indices: Vec<u32> = slot_indices.to_device(&Device::Cpu)?.to_vec1()?;`. candle-core 0.11 metal_backend/mod.rs:2004-2018 `to_cpu` issues a blit then `self.device.flush_and_wait_current()?` (drains the queue). Segments are one sequence's context each (loader.rs:1349 `ctx.div_ceil(DEFAULT_BLOCK_SIZE)`), so the multi-segment branch is the norm once more than one sequence has ever been admitted.
findings.rationale: A prefix-cache hit calls `append` -> `gather` once per layer, and in the multi-segment case each call drains the Metal queue before the forward can continue, so the GPU idles while the CPU builds the next layer. For 32-48 layers that is 32-48 pipeline drains added to TTFT on exactly the requests that are supposed to be fast (multi-turn chat). Each drain is on the order of 0.2-1 ms plus the lost overlap, i.e. tens of milliseconds per prefix-hit request.
findings.proposal: Change `gather` to take `&[u32]` (the caller holds `cached_slots` on the CPU) and build only the device-side index tensors it needs: for one segment a single `Tensor::from_slice`; for several, partition on the CPU slice as now, build per-segment index tensors and the inverse permutation from CPU data, never calling `to_device(Cpu)`. The quantized arm consumes the slice directly.
findings.expected_benefit: Removes num_layers GPU syncs per prefix-hit request; TTFT on cached-prefix requests drops by the sync cost (estimated 10-50 ms on 32-48 layer models) and GPU/CPU overlap is restored across layers.
findings.verify_how: Admit two concurrent requests once (so a second segment exists), then time the first token of a repeated identical prompt (prefix hit) before and after; alternatively count `flush_and_wait_current` calls per request in Instruments.

verdict.reason: Verified: the caller builds the index on the device from a CPU slice it already holds (paged.rs:1228 `Tensor::from_slice(slots, (from_old,), &self.device)`), then `gather` reads it straight back: 812 `slot_indices.to_device(&Device::Cpu)?.to_vec1()?` in the multi-segment Full arm and 854 in the Quantized arm. candle 0.11 `to_cpu` (metal_backend/mod.rs:2004-2018) issues a blit and `flush_and_wait_current()`, which also runs the whole-map `drop_unused_buffers` sweep (device.rs:185). The branch is keyed on `segments_k.len() == 1` (795), not on where the requested slots live, and a segment is one sequence's context (loader.rs:1349), so once a second segment has ever been materialised every prefix-hit gather pays the drain. Frequency is right: once per layer per prefix-hit request, mid-forward, with the allocator mutex held across the sync (1229). The proposal (take `&[u32]`, partition on the CPU, `Tensor::from_vec` per segment and for the inverse) changes nothing numerically and is S. Benefit is the lost CPU/GPU overlap plus drain latency per layer, tens of ms of TTFT on the multi-turn path that is supposed to be fastest; medium is fair.

findings.title: LIFO free list hands blocks out in descending order after the first sequence retires, defeating run coalescing so each prefill flush issues one copy kernel per 16-token block per layer
findings.evidence: paged.rs:587-596 `pub fn free(..) { .. if self.ref_counts[block_id] == 0 { self.free_list.push(block_id); } }` and paged.rs:564-575 `allocate` does `self.free_list.pop()`. paged.rs:1403 `clear()` frees `for &bid in &self.table.block_ids` in ascending order, so the next `allocate` sequence returns the highest id first. Runs coalesce only when paged.rs:1109-1113 `prev.dst_slot + prev.n_tokens == dst_slot && prev.src_offset + prev.n_tokens == written` holds, which fails for descending slots. Each run becomes one `alloc.write` (paged.rs:1277) -> `slice_set` -> candle `copy2d` kernel dispatch (candle metal_backend/mod.rs:1795-1808: the blit fast path needs `dst_s == d2`, which never holds here).
findings.rationale: Fresh segments are handed out ascending (`free_list.extend((first..num_blocks).rev())`), so the first request writes each layer's prefill in one kernel; every request after a `clear()` writes n/16 kernels per layer per chunk. A 1024-token chunk on a 32-layer model goes from 32 to 2048 copy dispatches; at ~5-15 us of encode per Metal dispatch that is 10-30 ms of CPU encode per chunk, a few percent of the chunk, and it also multiplies the `items` in the quantized flush.
findings.proposal: Return a sequence's blocks so that the next sequence receives an ascending run: iterate `self.table.block_ids.iter().rev()` in `clear()` (paged.rs:1403) and in `truncate_to` (paged.rs:1460), and have `prefix_cache` eviction free in the same order. Add a test that a second sequence's `PendingBatch.runs.len() == 1` after a first one has been cleared. Longer term, replace per-run `slice_set` with one custom scatter kernel per layer (candle's `scatter_set` needs a full-size index tensor, so it is not a fit).
findings.expected_benefit: Per-flush copy dispatches drop from n/16 per layer to ~1 per layer in the common case; prefill CPU encode time drops by tens of ms per chunk on mid-size prompts (a few percent), more on many-layer models.
findings.verify_how: Add a trace counter of `runs.len()` per `flush_pending`; run two identical 1024-token prompts back to back and confirm the second shows 64 runs per layer today and 1 after; compare prefill time of the second request with OXYDLLM_PROFILE_DECODE/Instruments.

verdict.reason: Verified the mechanism end to end: `grow` extends the free list with `(first..num_blocks).rev()` (paged.rs:519) so pops are ascending for a fresh segment; `free` pushes (595) and `allocate` pops (568); `clear()` frees `block_ids` in ascending order (1403-1405) so the next sequence receives the highest id first; runs coalesce only under the `prev.dst_slot + prev.n_tokens == dst_slot` test (1109-1113), which fails for descending slots; each run becomes one `alloc.write` (1330) -> `slice_set` on dim 0 (777-778) -> candle `copy2d` where the blit fast path needs `dst_s == d2` (metal_backend/mod.rs:1795), impossible here since dst stride is the whole segment. So after one churn a 1024-token chunk goes from 1 to 64 copy dispatches per layer (2048 vs 32 on 32 layers). Worth: the reviewer's 'few percent' is a reasonable bound but not measured; CPU encode of the flush overlaps the still-running forward, and the GPU-side cost is the fixed per-dispatch overhead on ~2000 tiny kernels, likely single-digit to low-double-digit ms per chunk, made visible by the `device.synchronize()` at engine.rs:598. Reversing the iteration in `clear()`/`truncate_to` fixes the common case but not interleaved retirements or prefix-cache evictions (prefix_cache.rs:171-175 frees one block per layer per entry); a min-ordered free list (BTreeSet, or keep the Vec sorted descending so `pop` yields the smallest id) gives ascending runs regardless of free order at the same S effort and is the form I would recommend. Also note that prefix-cache sharing and `max_cacheable` interleaving still fragment a sequence's first blocks; that is inherent.

findings.title: Mask LRU caches up to 32 full [q, kv] tensors per thread and rebuilds a fresh mask (2 uploads + 6 kernels + cast) for every new shape
findings.evidence: mask.rs:16 `const MASK_CACHE_CAP: usize = 32;` mask.rs:126-133 three `thread_local!` `LruCache<.., Tensor>` keyed by exact `(query_len, kv_len, ..)`. mask.rs:55-64 `causal_mask_prefixed` builds `Tensor::from_vec(row ..)`, `Tensor::from_vec(col ..)`, `broadcast_sub`, `affine`, `tanh`, `affine`, `affine`, `reshape`; mask.rs:225 `map.push(key, mask.clone())` keeps the dtype-cast result. Consumed on the generic attention path (attention.rs:936-958) when `seg.num_tokens > 1`, which on Metal is the sinks model (gpt-oss, attention.rs:835 `use_metal_fa = .. && self.sinks.is_none()`) and any shape FA does not serve, and always on CPU.
findings.rationale: With chunked prefill every chunk of every prompt has a distinct `(q, kv)`, so each is a miss: four f32 temporaries of q*kv*4 B plus the kept BF16 mask of q*kv*2 B. At q=1024, kv=8192 an entry is 16 MB; 32 entries pin 512 MB of GPU memory per engine thread, never released while the model is loaded, uncharged to any budget, and the build itself costs ~7 dispatches over q*kv elements per new shape.
findings.proposal: Keep one large mask per (device, dtype, window): build `[Qmax, KVmax]` once on the CPU (a Vec of 0 / -1e30 in the target dtype, uploaded once) with prefix `KVmax - Qmax`, and serve any `(q, kv)` as the bottom-right view `mask.narrow(2, Qmax - q, q)?.narrow(3, KVmax - kv, kv)?`, which is exactly the prefixed causal mask for prefix `kv - q` (and for the window mask the same identity holds when the big mask is built with that window). `broadcast_add` accepts the strided view. Grow Qmax/KVmax on demand (rare) and drop the three LRUs.
findings.expected_benefit: Mask memory becomes one buffer per dtype (e.g. 1024 x 32768 x 2 B = 64 MB) instead of up to 32 shape-specific tensors; no per-shape GPU construction, removing ~7 dispatches and 4 transient q*kv*4 B allocations per prefill chunk on the generic path.
findings.verify_how: Serve gpt-oss-20b with prompts of 20 different lengths and watch the Metal memory gauge climb by the mask sizes today; after the change it should stay flat. Count calls to `causal_mask_prefixed` per request.

verdict.reason: Verified: three thread-local LRUs of 32 (mask.rs:16, 126-133) keyed by exact shape; `causal_mask_prefixed` (55-64) does two `from_vec` uploads, `broadcast_sub`, `affine`, `tanh`, `affine`, `affine`, `reshape`, and the cached entry is the dtype-cast result (225). Consumption: attention.rs:936-958 consults the LRU only when the caller passes no mask (block.rs:63/400 thread `mask: Option<&Tensor>` through; the engine/model forwards pass none) and `seg.num_tokens > 1`; on Metal that is the sinks model since `use_metal_fa` requires `self.sinks.is_none()` (attention.rs:811) plus any head_dim/dtype the FA hardware path refuses, and always on CPU. With the pacer's chunk cap at 512/1024 (engine.rs:197, 227) every prompt length yields distinct `(q, kv)` keys, so the prefix LRU fills under varied traffic; at q=1024, kv=8192 a BF16 entry is 16 MB and 32 of them pin 512 MB that nothing charges (candle frees dropped buffers at the next sync, device.rs:131-150, so the LRU is the only holder). The windowed LRU stays small because `truncate_kv_window` bounds kv <= w + q. I checked the proposed identity: the bottom-right `narrow(2, Qmax-q, q).narrow(3, KVmax-kv, kv)` view of a `[Qmax, KVmax]` mask with prefix `KVmax-Qmax` opens exactly `j' <= i' + (kv-q)`, and for the window form the `pos < j + w` condition transforms identically, so results are bit-identical; candle Metal binary ops accept strided views, and the broadcast over heads is already strided today. ROADMAP lists `MASK_CACHE_CAP` as a policy to document, not rejected. Medium is right for gpt-oss-class models (the memory-tight Metal case), low elsewhere; S effort stands.

findings.title: Quantized-pool flush runs single-threaded, allocation-heavy scalar quantization on the CPU after every prefill chunk, with a GPU sync per layer
findings.evidence: paged.rs:1317-1325 `let k_vec: Vec<f32> = k_cat.to_device(&Device::Cpu)?.to_dtype(DType::F32)?.flatten_all()?.to_vec1()?;` (and v) per layer per flush; paged.rs:1345-1363 `for t in 0..total_tokens { for h in 0..nkv { .. quantizer.quantize_key(..); .. quantizer.quantize(..) } }` with no parallelism. kv_quant.rs:235-300 `quantize_key` allocates `packed` (248), `residual` (264), `qjl_bits` (286), calls `quantize_mse` (339: allocs `y` 361, `indices` 377, packed Vec) and `dequantize_mse` (385: allocs indices + `y` 403) and the 1-bit pack: ~9 heap allocations and two WHT passes per key vector, ~4 per value vector. `flush_caches` runs after each chunk (engine.rs:588) before `device.synchronize()`. The CHANGELOG's '1 percent' cost was measured on decode, where paged.rs:1086 skips pool writes entirely, so the prefill cost was never measured.
findings.rationale: For Phi-3-mini (32 KV heads x 32 layers) each prompt token needs 2048 head-vector quantizations; at an estimated 1-3 us each (allocations, WHT, 96 binary searches, residual pass) that is 2-6 ms of serial CPU per prompt token, i.e. 2-6 s added to the TTFT of a 1024-token prompt, during which the GPU is idle. The path is opt-in today (`--kv-quant lossless|balanced|aggressive`) but it is the only way to get the 4x capacity the feature promises.
findings.proposal: In `flush_pending`, quantize with `rayon::par_chunks_mut` over tokens (rayon is already a dependency), writing packed bytes straight into the `*_staged` slices; give `KvQuantizer` allocation-free entry points that take `&mut [u8]` / stack `[f32; 512]` scratch instead of returning Vecs, and skip the redundant dequantize-for-residual by computing the residual from the centroid indices directly.
