Collapse `write_staged`'s per-token loop (paged.rs:666-684) into one `copy_from_slice` per run since slots in a run are contiguous. Optionally run the quantization on a worker and join before the next read.
findings.expected_benefit: 8-10x from parallelism on an M5 plus ~2x from removing allocations: TTFT penalty of quantized pools drops from seconds to a few hundred ms on a 1k-token prompt; the GPU->CPU sync per layer remains but no longer gates seconds of CPU work.
findings.verify_how: Time first-token latency for a 2048-token prompt on Phi-3-mini with `--kv-quant lossless` vs `off`; the difference today should be seconds and after the change a few hundred ms. Profile `flush_pending` with OXYDLLM_PROFILE_DECODE or Instruments to confirm it dominates.

verdict.reason: The code reading is accurate: per layer per flush `k_cat.to_device(Cpu)?.to_dtype(F32)?.flatten_all()?.to_vec1()?` (paged.rs:1317-1325) is a GPU drain, the `for t { for h { quantize_key; quantize } }` loop (1345-1363) is single-threaded, and `quantize_key` (235-300) + `quantize_mse` (339-383) + `dequantize_mse` (385-420) allocate roughly nine Vecs per key vector; `flush_caches` runs after every prefill chunk (engine.rs:588) before the sync, and `write_staged` (650-684) copies token by token although a run's slots are contiguous. Two things cut the worth. First, the path is opt-in: `resolve_kv_quant` returns `Off` for `Auto` (loader.rs:1678-1683) because, per the maintainer's own diagnosis and commit 70df9c2, keys quantized by this scheme answer the second request with garbage; making a path faster that produces wrong output is premature and should ride along with the quantizer redesign (kv-paged-7), which touches the same staging code. Second, the cost estimate is somewhat high for the named model: Phi-3-mini's head_dim 96 is not a power of two so `use_hadamard` is false (kv_quant.rs:150) and no WHT passes run; ~1 us per head vector still gives ~1-2 s per 1k prompt tokens, so the order of magnitude holds. Cheaper first cut not in the proposal: batch all layers' staged tensors of a flush into one readback instead of one `to_vec1` sync per layer. Corrected: severity low until the quantizer is correct again, then medium; effort M for parallelism + allocation-free entry points done together with the redesign.

findings.title: Per-token single-norm key quantization cannot represent post-RoPE outlier channels, which is why Auto no longer quantizes; the scheme needs per-channel (KIVI-style) key scales
findings.evidence: kv_quant.rs:348-383 `quantize_mse`: `let norm = { .. s += v * v; .. s.sqrt() }; .. y.push(v * inv_norm); .. wht_inplace(&mut y); .. *idx = Self::find_nearest(boundaries, yv);` one scalar norm per head vector, then uniform Lloyd-Max bins. Maintainer's own diagnosis in loader.rs:1663-1683 `resolve_kv_quant`: 'after rotary embedding a handful of channels sit twenty to sixty times above the rest, the single norm a token's four-bit code is scaled by is set by those channels, and every other channel lands in the central bins .. the score against a query is off by four to nine units' and `KvQuantMode::Auto => Off` (commit 70df9c2). The Hadamard rotation does not fix this: after normalisation the outlier contributes ~1/sqrt(d) to every rotated coordinate while the informative channels contribute ~0.016, below one 4-bit bin width (~0.028 in the rotated domain), so they are quantized to noise.
findings.rationale: The quantized pool is the only mechanism for the 4x capacity the CHANGELOG advertises, and it is currently correct only for values. Keys fail on exactly the distribution real models produce, so any operator who opts in gets the second-request garbage the commit describes. The fix is a known design: KIVI quantizes keys per channel (scale/zero per (head, channel) over a group of tokens) and values per token, which is a natural fit for 16-token blocks.
findings.proposal: Add a per-channel key mode: for each (head, channel) within a 16-token block store a scale (and zero) as f16, quantize the 16 values of that channel to 4 bits; keep values per token as now. Storage per key head per token: 64 B of codes + hd*2*2/16 = 32 B of scales at hd=128, still 2.7x below BF16. Dequantize in `gather` per block. Keep the Hadamard/QJL path for values or delete it if measurement shows no benefit. Add a kv_quant test with an outlier-channel key (one channel at 40x) asserting the dequantized dot product against a random query stays within a bound of ~0.1 units; the present sinusoid tests (kv_quant.rs:649-720) pass on the broken scheme.
findings.expected_benefit: Restores a usable lossless mode so Auto can quantize again when the grant is short: ~2.7-4x KV capacity at bounded score error on real keys instead of the current all-or-nothing choice between exact blocks and corrupt output.
findings.verify_how: Re-run the failing probe from commit 70df9c2 (Phi-3.5-mini and Qwen2.5 with `--kv-quant lossless`, two requests sharing a prefix) and the 30-checkpoint coherence sweep; measure softmax score error on real post-RoPE keys dumped from one layer.

verdict.reason: Verified: `quantize_mse` (kv_quant.rs:348-383) computes one L2 norm per head vector, normalises, optionally applies a randomized Hadamard (only when head_dim is a power of two, 150), and bins every coordinate against the same Lloyd-Max N(0,1) boundaries (57-70, 422-434); `quantize_key` (235-300) adds a 1-bit QJL residual on top of a 3-bit MSE code. The maintainer's rustdoc at loader.rs:1663-1677 and commit 70df9c2 state the failure on real post-RoPE keys (channels 20-60x above the rest, scores off by 4-9 units, second request garbage) and that `Auto` now never quantizes, so the 4x-capacity feature the CHANGELOG advertises is effectively unavailable and the opt-in modes are a correctness trap. The reviewer's Hadamard argument is loose in its constants but right in direction, and for d=96 the rotation is not even applied, so the outlier saturates the bins directly. Per-channel key scales per 16-token block (KIVI) is the established fix and fits the block layout; the storage figure (64 B codes + 32 B f16 scale/zero per head per token at hd=128, ~2.7x under BF16) is correct; `gather` dequantises on the CPU already (854-895) so a per-block scale lookup slots in. Effort M is honest (staging layout, write_staged, gather, loader byte accounting at loader.rs:1644-1657, tests, two-request probes). The outlier-key test must land with the fix, not before, to keep the suite green.

findings.title: On Metal the global KV budget never consults the device working set: is_cpu is derived from the CUDA device list, which is empty on every Mac
findings.evidence: paged.rs:70-89 `pub fn detect_system_kv_budget(memory_budget_bytes, is_cpu) { if !is_cpu && let Some(budget) = device_working_set_bytes() { .. } let physical = ..; let kv_fraction: f64 = if is_cpu { 0.65 } else { 0.55 }; ..}`. manager.rs:313 `let is_cpu = cuda_devices.is_empty(); let kv_total = detect_system_kv_budget(memory_budget_bytes, is_cpu);` main.rs:119-132 `resolve_devices` returns `vec![]` unless `--devices`/`OXYDLLM_DEVICES` is given, while loader.rs:747 `select_device_at` picks `Device::new_metal(0)` regardless. By contrast paged.rs:265-275 `safe_model_kv_ceiling` and 232-237 `safe_total_commitment_bytes` do use `device_working_set_bytes()`.
findings.rationale: On the only verified platform the global budget is `physical * 0.65 - 512 MB` (15.1 GB on a 24 GB M5), the CPU share, not `min(recommendedMaxWorkingSetSize, free)` as the function's doc and the per-model ceiling assume. The three sizing figures therefore come from two different models of the machine; the ROADMAP classes these constants as D1 (wrong value corrupts output silently), and a 16 GB or 128 GB machine will get a different mismatch. Today the effect is bounded (15.1 GB vs 17.76 GB) but it also means the `free` reading is never applied to the global budget.
findings.proposal: In `detect_system_kv_budget`, try `device_working_set_bytes()` first regardless of `is_cpu` (it already returns `None` off Metal), or have the manager derive `is_cpu` from the device `select_device_at` actually returns. Fix the manager's warning text at manager.rs:316-321, which still says the budget derives from free memory at startup.
findings.expected_benefit: All three sizing paths agree on the device's own figure; the global budget tracks `recommendedMaxWorkingSetSize` and free memory on Metal as documented, removing one fitted fraction from the supported path.
findings.verify_how: On the M5 read the startup log line `global KV cache budget configured`: today it reports ~15.1 GB; after the fix it should report min(17.76 GB, free at startup).

verdict.reason: The code does what is claimed: manager.rs:313 `let is_cpu = cuda_devices.is_empty();` is true on every Mac without `--devices`, and `detect_system_kv_budget` (paged.rs:70-89) takes the device branch only when `!is_cpu`, so the server's global budget on Metal is `physical*0.65 - 512 MB` (15.1 GB on 24 GB) while `safe_model_kv_ceiling` (265-275) and `safe_total_commitment_bytes` (232-237) use `device_working_set_bytes()`; main.rs:1138 derives `is_cpu` from the real device, so the CLI and the server disagree too. But the proposal is unsound against the file's own contract: the function's doc (paged.rs:40-66) and the test `kv_budget_is_deterministic_across_calls` (1490-1495, 'budget must not vary with free memory') exist precisely because alpha.15 removed free-memory-dependent sizing, and the device branch does `budget.min(free)`, so routing Metal through it would reintroduce the startup-dependent budget the maintainer measured as a swap-and-corrupt failure. There is no corruption risk today: the physical-fraction figure is the smaller of the two on every machine size (0.65x-512 MB vs recommendedMaxWorkingSetSize ~0.74x). What is real is maintainability: a device branch that is unreachable in the server, a stale warning at manager.rs:316-321 that still blames free memory, and `is_cpu` meaning 'no CUDA' rather than 'CPU'. Corrected: severity low, category maintainability, effort S: derive `is_cpu` from the device `select_device_at` returns, either delete the device branch or drop its free-memory min to honour the deterministic contract, fix the warning text, and pin the Metal server path's figure in a test.

findings.title: Device-path ceiling drops the MIN_USEFUL_KV floor: weights at or above the working set get a zero KV ceiling and a misleading error
findings.evidence: paged.rs:265-280 `pub fn safe_model_kv_ceiling(weights_bytes) { if let Some(budget) = device_working_set_bytes() { let by_device = budget.saturating_sub(weights_bytes); return match available_memory_bytes() { Some(free) => by_device.min(free), None => by_device }; } .. }` while the floor paged.rs:140 `const MIN_USEFUL_KV: usize = 1 << 30;` is applied only in the non-device fallback (paged.rs:286-288 `.max(MIN_USEFUL_KV)`). loader.rs:1710-1748: a zero ceiling gives `capped_bytes = 0`, `granted_blocks = 0 < min_blocks` and bails with 'start the server with --memory-budget <MB>', but `retry_cap` (loader.rs:1711) can only lower the ceiling.
findings.rationale: A checkpoint whose resident bytes approach `recommendedMaxWorkingSetSize` (streamed models report resident + expert cache as `weights_bytes`) is refused with advice that cannot help. The old path kept such models servable with a 1 GB pool; the doc of MIN_USEFUL_KV still says it does.
findings.proposal: Apply `.max(MIN_USEFUL_KV)` on the device path too (or refuse explicitly with a message naming the working-set figure and the weights), and make the exhaustion message point at the actual remedy.
findings.expected_benefit: Predictable behaviour for large resident models and an error that names the cause; removes a silent divergence between the two sizing paths.
findings.verify_how: Unit test: with `device_working_set_bytes()` stubbed to 16 GB, `safe_model_kv_ceiling(17 << 30)` should not be 0; on the M5 load a checkpoint whose weights exceed ~17.7 GB resident and read the error.

findings.title: Dead quantized arm in BlockAllocator::write duplicates the flush quantization loop; contig_start is write-only state
findings.evidence: paged.rs:725-790 `pub fn write(..)` has a `KvPool::Quantized { .. }` arm (751 `let k_cpu = data_k.to_device(&Device::Cpu)?;` through the per-head quantize loop). Its only production caller is paged.rs:1277 inside `if self.quantizer.is_none() { .. alloc.write(..) }`; the quantized flush goes through `write_staged` (paged.rs:1374). The other caller is the Full-pool test at paged.rs:1614. `contig_start` is assigned 0 at paged.rs:1024, 1216, 1235, 1414 and read at 1168, 1169, 1178, 1255 but never advanced.
findings.rationale: Two copies of the quantization bookkeeping (byte offsets, norm indices, residual handling) must be kept in sync by hand, and the dead one is the one tests cannot reach. `contig_start` suggests a ring-buffer design that does not exist, which misleads the next edit of the windowed path.
findings.proposal: Restrict `write` to the Full pool (bail on Quantized) and delete the arm; remove `contig_start` and use 0 directly in `append`/`current`.
findings.expected_benefit: ~60 fewer lines of unreachable quantization code and one fewer invariant to reason about in the windowed buffer.
findings.verify_how: `cargo test` after deletion; grep confirms no other caller.

findings.title: Documentation contradicts shipped behaviour: garbled constant docs, Auto mode doc, CHANGELOG and ROADMAP all describe superseded KV sizing/quantization
findings.evidence: kv_quant.rs:3-12 doc of `KvQuantMode::Auto`: 'keeps blocks unquantized while the pool .. fits the safe ceiling, and drops to [Lossless] when it does not' but loader.rs:1679-1683 `resolve_kv_quant` returns `KvQuantMode::Off` for Auto. CHANGELOG.md 'Unreleased' repeats the stale claim ('quantize losslessly when it does not'). paged.rs:96-116: the doc on `KV_POOL_FRACTION` is two doc blocks concatenated ('Where a model's first attempt at a KV pool starts..' immediately followed by 'Largest share of physical memory one model's KV pool may occupy'); same at paged.rs:118-131 for `KV_TOTAL_FRACTION` and in the test doc at paged.rs:1516-1518. ROADMAP 'Version B: grow the KV pool lazily (not done..)' while paged.rs:426 `BlockAllocator::growing` shipped in commit 81e2169. manager.rs:316-321 warns the budget 'derives from the memory free at startup', which paged.rs:55-67 says it no longer does.
findings.rationale: The maintainer relies on doc comments as the record of measurements; several now assert things the code does not do, including the user-facing claim that Auto quantizes. The next person sizing a pool or choosing a KV mode will reason from the wrong description.
findings.proposal: Rewrite the `Auto` doc and CHANGELOG line to match `resolve_kv_quant` (Auto == Off until a per-channel scheme lands); split the two constant docs back into their intended paragraphs and note they apply only off-Metal; mark Version B as shipped (growth) with shrinking still open; fix the manager warning text.
findings.expected_benefit: Removes four contradictions between code and record on the memory-sizing path the ROADMAP calls the most dangerous.
findings.verify_how: Review diff; `cargo doc` renders the constants with single coherent paragraphs.

findings.title: GDN recurrent state (~2 MB per linear layer per sequence) is allocated fresh per sequence and charged to no budget
findings.evidence: paged.rs:969-976 `pub struct RecurrentState { pub conv: Tensor, pub s: Tensor }` with `s: [num_v_heads, head_k_dim, head_v_dim], F32`. gdn.rs:350 `None => Tensor::zeros((h, dk, dv), DType::F32, &device)?` and gdn.rs:596 `Tensor::zeros((1, k - 1, conv_dim) ..)` on first use; paged.rs:1395 `clear()` sets `self.recurrent = None` (dropped, not pooled). Linear layers alias the first full layer's allocator (loader.rs:1343-1345) so scheduler admission (scheduler/mod.rs:199-203 `allocators[0].lock().unwrap().num_free()`) counts only attention blocks, and loader.rs:1635 `kv_bytes_per_block` sums only `layer_kv_specs`.
findings.rationale: For Qwen3.5-4B (27 linear layers, 32 x 128 x 128 F32 = 2 MB each) a sequence holds ~54 MB of state outside the KV accounting; eight concurrent sequences hold ~430 MB that the plan never subtracted, plus per-sequence zero-fill and buffer churn through candle's pool at every admission.
findings.proposal: In `compute_kv_blocks`, subtract `max_num_sequences * per_sequence_state_bytes` (from the GDN config) from the capped bytes before converting to blocks, and keep a small free list of state tensors on the allocator (as the contig pool does) so retire/admit reuse buffers instead of allocating.
findings.expected_benefit: KV plan stays honest for hybrids (hundreds of MB at 8 sequences), and admission no longer triggers 27 zero-fills per sequence.
findings.verify_how: Run Qwen3.5-4B with 8 concurrent requests; compare the Metal memory gauge delta against the plan's kv_cache_bytes; the gap should match sequences x state bytes today and close after the change.

findings.title: Per-token decode append is two separate copy kernels per layer (K then V)
findings.evidence: paged.rs:1170-1171 `k_buf.slice_set(new_k, 2, at)?; v_buf.slice_set(new_v, 2, at)?;` each is a candle `slice_set` -> `copy2d` with `dst_s = cap * hd != d2`, so the strided-kernel path (candle metal_backend/mod.rs:1802-1808), one dispatch each. The K and V buffers are separate tensors from paged.rs:1037-1047 `acquire_contig` (`Tensor::zeros(dims ..)` twice).
findings.rationale: On a 32-layer model every decode token encodes 64 small copy dispatches purely for cache writes; at ~5-10 us of encode each that is ~0.3-0.6 ms of a ~22 ms token on Phi-3-mini (1-3%). If kv-paged-1 is done this becomes a pool write and the same optimisation applies there.
findings.proposal: Allocate K and V as one `[2, nkv, cap, hd]` buffer (narrow on dim 0 gives contiguous K and V views for the kernels) and add a tiny custom Metal kernel `kv_append` that writes both heads' rows in one dispatch; alternatively build the K/V projection output already in that layout so the write is a single `slice_set`.
findings.expected_benefit: Halves cache-write dispatches per token (64 -> 32 on 32 layers); ~1% decode throughput on small models, more on many-layer models where dispatch overhead dominates.
findings.verify_how: OXYDLLM_PROFILE_DECODE per-phase timing of `attn` before/after on Phi-3-mini and a 48-layer model; count dispatches per token in a Metal capture.

findings.title: Test gaps around the behaviours above: contig-pool memory bound, run coalescing after churn, outlier-channel keys, and the Metal budget path
findings.evidence: paged.rs tests cover block conservation (fuzz), windowed correctness, segment gather order and quantized round trips, but no test bounds total contig bytes across sequences (`contig_pool_evicts_smallest_on_overflow` at paged.rs:2159 only checks count/order), none asserts `PendingBatch.runs.len()` after a cleared sequence, and `kv_budget_is_deterministic_across_calls` (paged.rs:1499) calls `detect_system_kv_budget(None, false)` whereas production passes `is_cpu = true` on Metal (manager.rs:313). kv_quant.rs tests (649-720) quantize smooth sinusoids only; the maintainer's commit 70df9c2 notes synthetic keys passed while real keys failed.
findings.rationale: Each of the memory and sizing findings in this report is invisible to the current suite: the suite would stay green while idle memory grows by gigabytes, prefill writes fragment 64x, or the budget takes the wrong branch. The quantizer test gap is the one that let a user-facing corruption ship under Auto.
findings.proposal: Add (a) a test that after N cleared sequences the per-layer pooled contig bytes stay under a configured byte cap; (b) a test that a second sequence's flush produces a single run per layer after the first was cleared; (c) a kv_quant test with one channel at 40x asserting the dequantized key's dot product with a unit query is within ~0.1 of the exact one (expected to fail today, documenting the known defect); (d) a test that `detect_system_kv_budget` with the production `is_cpu` value equals the device-path figure when `device_working_set_bytes()` is Some.
findings.expected_benefit: Turns the three silent-regression classes on this path (memory growth, write fragmentation, quantizer error on real keys) into failing tests.
findings.verify_how: Tests fail on current HEAD for (b), (c), (d) as described and pass after the corresponding fixes.

verdict.reason: The gaps are real as described: `contig_pool_evicts_smallest_on_overflow` (paged.rs:2159-2173) checks only count and order, no test inspects `PendingBatch.runs` after churn (the struct is private, 943-947, so a `#[cfg(test)]` accessor is needed), `kv_budget_is_deterministic_across_calls` (1490-1495) passes `is_cpu = false` while the server passes true, and the kv_quant tests (649-720) use smooth sinusoids. But the proposed tests are not all sound as stated. (b) is good and S. (a) presupposes the byte cap from kv-paged-2 and should be written with it. (c) 'expected to fail today' cannot be committed under a green-suite rule and documents nothing if `#[ignore]`d; it belongs with the kv-paged-7 fix. (d) asserts that the production `is_cpu` path equals the device-path figure, which contradicts the deterministic-budget contract the existing test already pins (see kv-paged-8); the right test is one that fixes whatever policy is decided for the Metal server path. Corrected: severity low, effort S, proposal: add (b) now, (a) with the pool byte cap, (c) with the per-channel quantizer, and replace (d) with a test of the decided Metal budget policy plus a test that the contig bytes charged to a model's footprint track live + pooled buffers once kv-paged-1's accounting step lands.

subsystems.coverage_notes: Read-only review on Linux without Metal; nothing was executed and no cargo commands were run. Scope files (paged.rs, kv_quant.rs, mask.rs) were read in full. Callers were read selectively: attention.rs forward_batch (append/current, mask routing, FA/SDPA gating), engine.rs (prefix prepopulate, registration, spec-decode rollback, chunked forward + flush ordering, allocator construction), loader.rs (compute_kv_blocks, resolve_kv_quant, kv_bytes_per_block, allocator construction, device selection), manager.rs (budget construction, is_cpu), scheduler admission accounting, prefix_cache register, block.rs flush_caches and mask origin, gdn.rs state allocation, main.rs resolve_devices, and candle-core 0.11 Metal internals for slice_set/copy2d, index_select, zeros, host upload and to_cpu sync. Not covered: the Metal SDPA/FA kernel sources (so the feasibility of a block-table argument in kv-paged-1 is argued from the kernel signatures, not from kernel code), prefix_cache lookup/eviction beyond register, the scheduler preemption path in full, CUDA paths, and the embeddings/encoder runtime. All timing figures (dispatch cost, quantization microseconds, sync cost) are estimates argued from the code and candle's implementation, not measurements; the memory figures are computed from model geometry and the code's capacity formulas.
missed: The most valuable thing the reviewer did not raise is a latent silent-corruption path at the seam between `skip_pool_write` and prefix-cache registration. paged.rs:1086 decides 'decode' by `self.contig_len > 0 && new_seq == 1`, but the prefill chunk planner packs several sequences into one forward with `take = (remaining).min(room)` (engine.rs:318-343), so a sequence's trailing piece in a chunk can be exactly one token (e.g. at cap 512 a 497-token prompt A leaves room 15, so a 528-token prompt B is split 15 / 512 / 1). That final 1-token append is written to the contig buffer (1167-1172) but never to the pool (no run pushed at 1098-1115), while the engine registers `num_full_blocks_total = seq_len / block_size` = 33 blocks (engine.rs:473, 665-677 -> prefix_cache.rs:132-170) because 528 is a multiple of 16. A later prompt that extends B's prefix (a multi-turn follow-up; `max_cacheable` at engine.rs:447 only limits same-length lookups) prepopulates all 33 blocks and `gather` (paged.rs:1226-1231) reads slot 527 from the segment, which holds the zeros of `Tensor::zeros` (483) or a previous sequence's stale row: one wrong key/value at one position, no error, exactly on the prefix-hit path the maintainer uses two-request probes for. The pacer cap only ever takes power-of-two values (engine.rs:227, 259, 267-275) so a single-sequence prompt cannot trigger it; concurrent arrivals can. Fix (S): keep a `pool_tokens` counter in `PagedKvCache` that advances only on appends that queued runs (and on `prepopulate_block`), and have the engine register `min over layers of pool_tokens / block_size` blocks; or pass an explicit phase from the engine so `append` skips only true decode. Test: two sequences packed so one ends in a 1-token piece, then a third sequence hitting the full prefix must gather K/V equal to what the contig buffer held.

subsystems.assessment: The HTTP layer is not where decode throughput is lost: per token the engine thread re-decodes a 5-token window, does one channel send and one small JSON serialization (a handful of allocations, single-digit microseconds), which is well under 1% of a Metal step, and the manager mutex is held only for a HashMap lookup on the hot path. Request validation is thorough (sampling ranges, tool and schema shapes, strict mode, allowed_tools) and the compat tests pin the wire shapes well. What is fragile is lifecycle and edge behaviour rather than CPU. The incremental decoder's stable-window freeze decodes one token at a time into permanently frozen text, so any character the tokenizer splits into byte tokens becomes U+FFFD and then misaligns the emitted suffix (duplicated or truncated text) in both streaming and non-streaming responses. A prompt longer than the context is not rejected but enqueued with max_tokens clamped to 0; if it needs more KV blocks than the pool it sits at the head of the FIFO scheduler, blocks every later request on that model, and makes the engine thread spin at full CPU until the 300 s request timeout. A non-streaming client that disconnects is never noticed because the collectors are detached tasks, so the engine finishes the whole generation for nobody while holding KV blocks. Those three are the biggest levers because each costs whole requests or minutes of GPU time rather than microseconds. The second tier is prompt-side cost: the Jinja environment is rebuilt and the template recompiled per request, rendering plus tokenization run inline on a tokio worker, and tool definitions are rendered twice (template plus injected instruction) with contradictory format guidance, which inflates prefill on every agent turn. Observability is good (per-request spans, TTFT and prefix-cache metrics) with one wrong series: queue depth is a single global gauge overwritten by every resident model's loop. Embeddings and model discovery hold locks longer than needed (a whole batch under the GPU lock with one forward per input; GGUF header parsing under the manager mutex when /v1/models is polled). Finally the four SSE emitters are copy-pasted and have already drifted, so the streaming tool-call pass-through the roadmap wants will be cheaper after a small ChunkWriter refactor.

findings.title: Stable-window freeze corrupts multi-token UTF-8 characters and misaligns the streamed suffix
findings.evidence: engine_loop.rs:443 `let new_stable_end = all_ids.len().saturating_sub(DECODE_STABLE_LOOKBACK);` then :452-454 `let delta_ids = &all_ids[*stable_end..new_stable_end]; let delta = decode_with_neutral_prefix(tokenizer, delta_ids, ...); stable_text.push_str(&delta);` — with one new token per step the delta is a single token, so the frozen text is literally a concatenation of per-token decodes. decode_with_neutral_prefix (:414-431) decodes `[neutral, tok]` and strips the neutral text; tokenizer.rs:335-338 `self.inner.decode(ids, true)` is HF's lossy decode, which turns a lone leading byte (F0 9F) or a lone continuation byte into U+FFFD. :491 `let full = format!("{}{}", stable_text, window_text);` then emit_suffix(&full, decoded_len) uses a byte offset computed against the previous step's correctly decoded `full` (where the window still held both halves and decoded the real character). The maintainer's own test at :548 (`["caf\u{FFFD}", "café", ...]`) shows their tokenizers do split characters across tokens.
findings.rationale: When a character spans tokens t_k, t_k+1 (SentencePiece byte-fallback for '’', '€', emoji, CJK outside the vocab; byte-level BPE for rarer emoji/ZWJ sequences), the step at which the boundary crosses between them freezes t_k alone as U+FFFD (3 bytes) and decodes t_k+1 alone as another U+FFFD; the previously emitted correct character (2-4 bytes) is now represented by 6-9 bytes in `full`, so `decoded_len` lands inside already-sent text and emit_suffix re-emits a fragment of it (duplicated text) plus the FFFDs; the completion flush (:812-827) re-decodes correctly but with the wrong `decoded_len` and truncates. Non-streaming content is the concatenation of these deltas (chat.rs:1443) so it is corrupted too. Nothing tests prefix_decode_incremental with a tokenizer; only emit_suffix is unit-tested with hand-written strings.
findings.proposal: In advance_stable_window, refuse to advance a boundary that is not UTF-8 complete: if `delta` (or, on the first freeze, the whole decoded prefix) ends with or contains U+FFFD, or if the window decode of `all_ids[new_stable_end..]` begins with U+FFFD, leave `stable_end` unchanged this step so the window keeps both halves together; retry on later steps (the window grows by a few tokens at most). Alternatively freeze bytes, not text: decode `all_ids[stable_end-LOOKBACK..new_stable_end]`, strip the known tail, and only commit when the result is valid UTF-8. Add a unit test that builds a ByteLevel BPE tokenizer whose vocab splits 'é' and an emoji into byte tokens and asserts the cumulative emitted text equals tokenizer.decode(all_ids) for sequences longer than DECODE_STABLE_LOOKBACK.
findings.expected_benefit: Removes visible garbage (U+FFFD, duplicated or missing tail text) from streamed and non-streamed output on any byte-split character; zero cost in the common case since the boundary only pauses for the 1-3 steps a split character is in flight.
findings.verify_how: On the M5 with a Phi-3/Llama-2 family GGUF (SentencePiece byte fallback) ask for 30 emoji or a line of '’' and '€' in a 200-token answer, with stream=true; compare the concatenated SSE deltas against the same prompt at stream=false and against a client-side decode of the ids. Today both responses contain U+FFFD and a repeated fragment right after each split character; after the fix they match.

verdict.reason: Verified in code. advance_stable_window (engine_loop.rs:443-456) advances the boundary by exactly the tokens added since the last step, so after the first freeze (`*stable_end == 0` branch, :447-450) every later delta is `&all_ids[*stable_end..new_stable_end]` = one token per normal decode step, decoded in isolation by decode_with_neutral_prefix (:414-431) and appended to stable_text (:454). The window is decoded separately (:485-490) and the two strings are concatenated (:491) before emit_suffix computes the suffix from the previous step's byte offset (:394-404). Tokenizer::decode is HF lossy decode (tokenizer.rs:335-338) and the GGUF-built tokenizers use ByteFallback (tokenizer.rs:605) or ByteLevel (:624) decoders, both of which turn an isolated lead/continuation byte token into U+FFFD. So for any character spanning two tokens, the step where the lead token crosses the boundary turns a correctly decoded 2-4 byte char (previous `full`) into 6+ bytes of FFFD in the new `full`; decoded_len is clamped back into the FFFD (clamp_to_char_boundary :381-387) and emit_suffix re-emits the window text that was already sent (:396-400; only a trailing FFFD is trimmed). Non-streaming content is the concatenation of these Token events (collect_one_completion_inner chat.rs:1443-1450), so it is corrupted too. The completion flush (:832-840) uses the misaligned decoded_len against a correct full decode. Frequency: once per split character, for every byte-fallback tokenizer (Phi-3/Llama-2/Mistral/Gemma GGUFs) on any emoji or out-of-vocab CJK/accented char, and for byte-level BPE on rarer glyphs. The existing tests (:496-575) only exercise emit_suffix with hand-written strings and never reach this path. Proposal is sound: hold the boundary when the delta or the start of the window decodes to U+FFFD; add a cap (e.g. window > 4x lookback forces advance) so a model emitting genuinely invalid bytes cannot grow the re-decoded window without bound. Effort S, severity high are honest: it is a visible correctness bug on the primary supported path.

findings.title: Over-long prompts are enqueued with max_tokens 0, head-of-line block the scheduler and make the engine thread spin until the timeout
findings.evidence: chat.rs:1777-1782 `let remaining = handle.max_seq_len.saturating_sub(prompt_len); let max_tokens = body.max_completion_tokens.or(body.max_tokens).unwrap_or(remaining).min(remaining);` — no check that prompt_len < max_seq_len or that the prompt fits the pool; the request is sent at :1826. scheduler/mod.rs:291-298 `let seq = match self.waiting.front() {...}; let blocks_needed = self.blocks_needed_for_prefill(seq, prefix_cache); if blocks_needed > free_blocks { break; }` — FIFO head, nothing behind it is considered. scheduler/mod.rs:400-402 `has_pending_work = !self.waiting.is_empty() || !self.running.is_empty()`. engine_loop.rs:684-688 `if engine.has_pending_work() { let step_result = { let _gpu = gpu_lock.acquire(); engine.step() };` and :984-985 `metrics::QUEUE_DEPTH.set(...); std::thread::yield_now();` — engine.rs:1038-1046 returns an empty StepOutput immediately when nothing was scheduled, so the loop re-steps without blocking. main.rs:724 default request timeout 300 s; 0 disables it.
findings.rationale: A prompt that needs more KV blocks than the pool holds can never be scheduled, yet it is a valid waiting sequence: every request that arrives after it on that model waits behind it, and the engine loop spins (lock acquire, schedule, return, yield) at 100% of a core for up to 300 s (forever with --request-timeout 0) until the client's collector times out, drops its receiver, and the closed-channel check at :656-661 aborts it. A prompt that merely exceeds max_seq_len but fits the pool is prefilled past the model's context (positions beyond the trained range) and answers with one 'length' token instead of a 400. Both are user-triggerable with a single curl.
findings.proposal: In chat_completions, after `prompt_len` is known: if `prompt_len >= handle.max_seq_len` return 400 with type `invalid_request_error`, code `context_length_exceeded` (OpenAI wording: 'This model's maximum context length is N tokens, however you requested M'), and clamp `max_tokens` to at least 1. Also carry the pool's total block capacity (or max prefill tokens) on ReadyHandle so a prompt that cannot fit the pool is refused at the handler. In engine_loop, when a step produced no tokens, no completions and `engine` has nothing running, fall back to `blocking_recv` (or `recv_timeout`) instead of re-stepping, so an unschedulable head never spins the thread.
findings.expected_benefit: Eliminates a trivially triggered multi-minute stall of a whole model and a 100% CPU spin on the engine thread; gives clients the standard 400 they already handle.
findings.verify_how: Start with --max-context-len 2048, send a 3000-token prompt (stream=false), then a normal request on the same model from a second terminal: today the second request waits ~300 s and `top` shows the engine thread at 100%; after the fix the first returns 400 immediately and the second is served.

verdict.reason: Verified. chat.rs:1777-1781 computes `remaining = max_seq_len.saturating_sub(prompt_len)` and `max_tokens = ...unwrap_or(remaining).min(remaining)` with no check that prompt_len < max_seq_len; grep for max_seq_len/context length finds no other guard in chat.rs, engine_loop.rs, scheduler/mod.rs or engine.rs (the only hits are :1777 and scheduler doc comments). enqueue_request passes prompt_tokens straight to engine.add_request_* (engine.rs:940-983 -> scheduler.add_request_*, which only stores the values, scheduler/mod.rs:123-187). The scheduler admits only the FIFO head and `break`s when `blocks_needed > free_blocks` (scheduler/mod.rs:290-298), so a prompt needing more blocks than the pool holds blocks everything behind it forever. has_pending_work is `!waiting.is_empty() || !running.is_empty()` (:400-402), so the engine loop takes the non-blocking try_recv branch (engine_loop.rs:644-654), calls step under gpu_lock (:684-688), step returns an empty StepOutput when nothing was scheduled (engine.rs:1038-1046), and the loop yields and repeats (:984-985): a 100% spin with a lock acquire per iteration. The only exit is the closed-channel check (:669-682) after the client's collector drops its receiver on the 300 s timeout (collect_one_completion chat.rs:1403-1418, main.rs:724 default 300, 0 disables); combined with server-http-3 (non-streaming receivers are never dropped on disconnect) and `--request-timeout 0` the model is wedged permanently. A prompt that exceeds max_seq_len but fits the pool is prefilled with positions beyond the model's context (I did not verify RoPE table sizing, so whether that errors or silently degrades is open; if it errors it also trips server-http-14 and aborts neighbours). Proposal is sound and standard (400 context_length_exceeded; clamp max_tokens >= 1). I would refine the engine-side part: do not switch to blocking_recv when nothing is running (that would hide a stuck head until the next request arrives); instead have the scheduler fail a head whose blocks_needed exceeds the pool's total capacity (not just free blocks) so it is aborted with an Error event, which removes the spin and the head-of-line block in one place. Severity high, effort S confirmed.

findings.title: Non-streaming requests detach their collectors, so a client disconnect never aborts generation
findings.evidence: chat.rs:2540-2543 `let mut handles = Vec::with_capacity(n); for rx in completion_rxs { handles.push(tokio::spawn(collect_one_completion(rx, req_timeout))); }` then :2549-2556 `let data = handle.await.map_err(|_| error_response(... "Task panic" ...))??;`. The engine's only disconnect signal is engine_loop.rs:656-661 `trackers.iter().filter_map(|(&seq_id, tracker)| tracker.tx.is_closed().then_some(seq_id))`. Contrast the streaming path, where `response_rx` lives inside the task that fails on `sse_tx.send` once the SSE body is dropped (:2104-2108).
findings.rationale: When the HTTP connection closes (user cancels, client timeout shorter than the server's 300 s, proxy reset), hyper drops the handler future, which drops the Vec<JoinHandle>; dropping a JoinHandle detaches rather than aborts, so each spawned collector keeps owning its `rx`, `tx.is_closed()` stays false, and the engine generates all n completions to max_tokens (default `remaining`, i.e. thousands of tokens) or to the 300 s timeout, occupying a scheduler slot and KV blocks the whole time. The same detachment means an early `?` return on choice i leaves choices i+1..n running. Spawning buys nothing here: collect_one_completion only awaits channel receives.
findings.proposal: Await the collectors inline so that dropping the handler drops the receivers: `let results = futures::future::join_all(completion_rxs.into_iter().map(|rx| collect_one_completion(rx, req_timeout))).await;` (or a tokio::task::JoinSet wrapped in a guard whose Drop calls abort_all). The has_tools streaming path already aborts siblings explicitly (:1898-1900); do the same on the first error in the non-streaming loop.
findings.expected_benefit: Cancelled non-streaming requests stop costing GPU time within one step instead of up to max_tokens steps; frees KV blocks and a max_num_seqs slot immediately, which directly raises throughput for the remaining clients under cancel-heavy workloads.
findings.verify_how: `curl -m 2` a stream=false request with max_tokens 1500 on the M5; with RUST_LOG=oxydllm=debug today you see no 'request aborted' line and a 'request completed' line ~1500 tokens later, with oxydllm_queue_depth staying at 1; after the fix 'request aborted ... response channel closed' appears within one step of the disconnect.

verdict.reason: Verified. chat.rs:2539-2543 spawns one tokio task per receiver (`tokio::spawn(collect_one_completion(rx, req_timeout))`) and awaits the JoinHandles in order (:2549-2556). Dropping a tokio JoinHandle detaches the task, so when hyper drops the handler future on connection close, each spawned collector keeps owning its receiver and `tracker.tx.is_closed()` (engine_loop.rs:670-673) stays false until Finish/StreamEnd or the 300 s timeout fires inside collect_one_completion (:1413-1418). collect_one_completion_inner (:1426-1470) does nothing but `rx.recv().await`, so spawning buys nothing and awaiting the futures inline (futures::future::try_join_all, or a JoinSet whose Drop aborts) makes the drop propagate: the receiver is dropped, the engine loop's closed-channel check aborts the sequence on its next iteration. Also verified that the early `?` on choice i (:2549-2556) leaves choices i+1..n detached. Contrast the n==1 streaming path, which keeps response_rx inside the task that fails on sse_tx.send once the SSE body drops (:2136-2171, :2098-2104), and the n>1 streaming forwarders which break on merged_tx send failure (:2325-2335). Cost of the bug: one scheduler slot plus the prompt's KV blocks for up to max_tokens steps (default `remaining`, i.e. the whole remaining context) per cancelled request, directly reducing batch capacity for other clients. Note `futures` is not currently a dependency (Cargo.toml:27-31 lists tokio/tokio-stream/minijinja only), so either add it or use tokio::task::JoinSet with an abort-on-drop guard. Severity high, effort S, confirmed.

findings.title: Chat template is recompiled per request and rendering plus tokenization run inline on the tokio worker
findings.evidence: chat.rs:1690-1696 `let prompt = apply_chat_template(&handle.tokenizer, &messages_for_prompt, ...)` and :1707 `let prompt_tokens = handle.tokenizer.encode(&prompt)` both execute directly inside the async handler. chat_template.rs:26-38 (called from chat.rs:1537) `let template = preprocess_template(template); let mut env = Environment::new(); env.set_unknown_method_callback(...); env.add_filter(...); ... env.add_template("chat", &template).context("Failed to compile chat template")?;` — a new minijinja Environment and a full compile of the (5-20 KB) Jinja template on every request, twice on the system-role retry (chat.rs:1551-1562). tokenizer.rs:300-306 encode is the HF Rust tokenizer, synchronous.
findings.rationale: Per request this costs one template parse+compile (hundreds of microseconds to a couple of ms for Llama-3/Qwen/gpt-oss sized templates) plus the render of the whole conversation plus the encode of the whole prompt (tens of ms at 10-30k tokens, since every turn re-renders and re-tokenizes the full history). All of it runs on a tokio worker thread, so concurrent SSE streams scheduled on that worker see their chunks delayed by the same amount (visible jitter), and the handler already logs template_ms/encode_ms because the maintainer suspected it. The compile part is pure waste: the template is immutable per tokenizer.
findings.proposal: Cache the compiled template per tokenizer: store a `OnceLock<Arc<minijinja::Environment<'static>>>` (or an owned `Environment` built once in Tokenizer::from_dir / from_gguf_file) and have chat_template::apply_chat_template take `&Environment` and only build the context and render. Then run `apply_chat_template` + `encode` (+ stop-string encodes and SchemaArena::compile) in `tokio::task::spawn_blocking` for every request, returning the prompt ids; this keeps tokio workers free for SSE fan-out.
findings.expected_benefit: Saves roughly 0.3-2 ms of TTFT per request from the compile alone and removes up to tens of ms of inter-chunk jitter on other streams when a long-context request arrives; modest in absolute terms, but it is the one per-request cost in this layer that is simply avoidable.
findings.verify_how: RUST_LOG=oxydllm=debug and read `template_ms` for a 2-message request on Qwen3 or gpt-oss before/after caching; for the blocking effect, stream a long answer while firing a 20k-token prompt at the server and plot SSE inter-chunk gaps (a one-off gap equal to encode_ms appears today).

verdict.reason: Accurate mechanism: chat_template::apply_chat_template (chat_template.rs:21-38) runs preprocess_template, builds a fresh minijinja Environment, registers callbacks/filters and compiles the template on every call; the chat.rs wrapper (:1283-1322) calls it once and again without the system message on failure, so up to two compiles per request. Rendering and HF encode (:1690-1713) run on the tokio worker. But the benefit is overstated: a 5-20 KB template compiles in well under a millisecond on an M-series core, while TTFT is dominated by prefill at hundreds of ms, so the compile is <1% of TTFT; the maintainer already logs template_ms/encode_ms (:1716-1724) and would have seen it if it mattered. The jitter argument is weak too: tokio's work stealing lets idle workers pick up queued SSE tasks while one worker encodes, so the inter-chunk gap only appears when all workers are busy. Cache the compiled Environment once per Tokenizer (OnceLock<Environment<'static>> built with add_template_owned) as cheap hygiene; spawn_blocking for encode is optional and only worth it for very long prompts.
verdict.corrected_benefit: Removes ~0.1-1 ms per request of pure waste (template parse+compile, x2 on the system-role retry); no measurable TTFT change in practice.
verdict.corrected_proposal: Store a compiled minijinja Environment on Tokenizer (OnceLock, built via add_template_owned on first use) and have chat_template::apply_chat_template take &Environment and only build the context and render; skip the spawn_blocking part unless encode_ms for the maintainer's long-context workloads shows >10 ms.

findings.title: Tool definitions are rendered twice: native template `tools` plus an injected JSON instruction that contradicts the template's call format
findings.evidence: chat.rs:1641-1643 `let tools_value = (!tool_config.tools.is_empty()).then(|| serde_json::to_value(&tool_config.tools).ok()).flatten();` is passed to the template (:1695), and unconditionally :1653-1655 `if needs_tool_instr { extra_parts.push(tools_system_instruction(&tool_config.tools, &tool_config)); }` prepends a system block built at :646-647 `let tools_json = serde_json::to_string_pretty(tools)` that says 'respond ONLY with a valid JSON object ... {"tool_calls": [...]}'. chat_template.rs:60 `tools: opts.tools` renders them natively for Qwen/Llama-3.1/Mistral-class templates. The parser comment at :735-737 records the consequence: 'a `{"tool_calls": [...]}` object when the model echoes the injected system-prompt instruction inside the tags' (observed E2E on Qwen2.5-1.5B).
findings.rationale: For any model whose template consumes `tools` (every modern tool-calling checkpoint), the prompt carries the tool schemas twice, the injected copy pretty-printed (more tokens than compact), so a 10-tool agent turn pays roughly 2-5k extra prefill tokens per request and doubles the prefix-cache footprint of the system prompt; on an M5 at ~1-2k prefill tok/s that is 1-4 s of TTFT on a cold prefix. The injected format also contradicts the native `<tool_call>{"name","arguments"}</tool_call>` convention the model was fine-tuned on, which is exactly the mixed-shape output the parser has grown special cases for.
findings.proposal: Inject the instruction only when the template does not reference tools: `let template_handles_tools = tokenizer.chat_template().is_some_and(|t| t.contains("tools"));` and skip `tools_system_instruction` (keeping only the one-line choice/parallel constraint, which templates do not express) when it does; keep the injected block for templates without tool support and for the fallback formats. Use compact JSON (`to_string`) in the injected block when it is used.
findings.expected_benefit: Halves tool-definition tokens per agent request (1-5k tokens for realistic tool sets), proportionally lowering TTFT on cold prefix and prefix-cache usage; removes a documented source of malformed tool-call shapes.
findings.verify_how: Send the compat tests' base_tools plus 8 more realistic tools to Qwen3 and read `prompt_tokens` in `usage` before/after; run the E2E tool-call battery and count outputs that needed the instruction-echo parser branch.

verdict.reason: Duplication verified: tools_value is passed to the template (chat.rs:1641-1643, :1695) and, unconditionally when has_tools (:1648-1655), tools_system_instruction prepends a system block containing `serde_json::to_string_pretty(tools)` inside <tools> tags plus a `{"tool_calls": [...]}` format instruction (:646-676). For templates that consume `tools` (chat_template.rs:60 passes them into the context) the schemas appear twice, pretty-printed once. The parser comment (:716-742) confirms the mixed-shape consequence (`{"tool_calls": ...}` echoed inside <tool_call> tags). However the proposal is risky as stated: the injected JSON format is the parser's primary contract (parse order at :794 tries <tool_call> tag blocks first, then the JSON object), and dropping the whole instruction for any template containing the substring "tools" removes the format instruction for models whose native call format the parser does not handle (e.g. Llama-3.1 python_tag, Mistral [TOOL_CALLS]; grep finds no parser support for either). The token estimate is also high: a realistic tool definition is ~80-150 tokens compact, so 10 tools cost ~1-2k extra tokens once per cold prefix, and the system prefix is prefix-cached across turns of a conversation, so the per-turn cost is mostly paid once. Cheaper, safer change: when the template references tools, keep the format/choice/parallel instruction but omit the duplicated <tools> schema listing; always emit compact JSON.
verdict.corrected_benefit: Roughly 1-2k fewer prompt tokens per cold prefix for a 10-tool agent (about 0.5-1 s of TTFT on M5-class prefill) and a smaller prefix-cache footprint, without changing the parser contract.
verdict.corrected_proposal: In tools_system_instruction take a `template_renders_tools: bool` (tokenizer.chat_template().is_some_and(|t| t.contains("tools"))): when true, emit only the format + parallel + choice lines and no <tools> block; when false, keep the block but use serde_json::to_string (compact). Keep the format instruction in both cases so parse_tool_calls' primary shape still applies; re-run the E2E tool-call battery on Qwen2.5/Qwen3 before shipping.

findings.title: Embeddings hold the device GPU lock across the whole batch with one forward per input and no input cap
findings.evidence: embeddings.rs:58-69 `tokio::task::spawn_blocking(move || { let gpu = gpu_lock_for(...); let _gpu = gpu.acquire(); ... for text in &batch { let ids = handle_for_embed.tokenizer.encode_with_special_tokens(text)?; prompt_tokens += ids.len(); vectors.push(handle_for_embed.model.embed(&ids)?); } ...` — encoder.rs:117 and :249 `pub fn embed(&self, ids: &[u32]) -> Result<Vec<f32>>` take a single sequence. gpu_lock.rs:25-30 is a plain `Arc<Mutex<()>>`; engine_loop.rs:685-687 holds the same lock around each `engine.step()`. No limit on `inputs.len()` or total tokens (:36-45 only reject empty).
findings.rationale: Every chat engine loop on the device waits for the embeddings task to release the lock, and it only does so after N separate forward passes (each with its own command-buffer submission and sync), with tokenization done inside the critical section. A RAG ingestion batch of 128-512 chunks therefore freezes all chat streams for the whole batch (hundreds of ms to seconds), and an unbounded `input` array can hold the device indefinitely. OpenAI caps inputs at 2048 per request.
findings.proposal: Tokenize all inputs before taking the lock; acquire the lock per input (or per chunk of ~8) so decode steps interleave; add `embed_batch(&[Vec<u32>])` to EncoderModel with right-padding and an attention mask (bidirectional encoders batch trivially; the causal last-token pooler needs per-row gather) so a batch is one forward; reject more than 2048 inputs or more than a configured token total with 400.
findings.expected_benefit: Chat inter-token gaps during embedding traffic drop from batch-length to one-item length (S fix), and embedding throughput rises several-fold from batching (M fix); bounded worst case per request.
findings.verify_how: Stream a chat answer while POSTing /v1/embeddings with 256 inputs on the M5; record the longest SSE inter-chunk gap (today roughly the whole embeddings wall time) and the embeddings request latency before/after.

verdict.reason: Code verified: embeddings.rs:56-71 acquires `gpu_lock_for(device)` once inside spawn_blocking, then loops over every input doing tokenizer.encode_with_special_tokens and model.embed(&ids) (single-sequence API, encoder.rs:117 and :249) under the lock; only an empty input is rejected (:40-47). The engine loop takes the same per-device lock around each step (engine_loop.rs:598, :686; gpu_lock.rs:43-45 keys locks by device), so every chat stream on that device stalls for the whole embeddings batch, with tokenization inside the critical section. The S part of the proposal (tokenize before locking, acquire per input or per small chunk, cap inputs at 2048 and total tokens) is sound and captures most of the latency benefit. The M part (embed_batch with padding and masks) needs caution the finding does not mention: the maintainer verifies embedding models as bitwise-deterministic against sentence-transformers (CHANGELOG alpha.15 and Unreleased 'Tests'); padded batched GEMMs change reduction shapes and may perturb vectors at the ULP level, so batching must be re-verified against that sweep and is a separate decision. The ROADMAP rejection ('embeddings via the decoder engine') does not cover this.
verdict.corrected_benefit: Chat inter-token gaps during embedding traffic drop from the full batch duration (seconds for 256 chunks) to one item's forward (ms); a bounded worst case per request. Batching throughput gains are a separate M-sized follow-up gated on the determinism sweep.
verdict.corrected_proposal: Tokenize all inputs before taking the lock; acquire the device lock per input (or per chunk of ~8) around model.embed; return 400 for more than 2048 inputs or more than a configured total-token budget. Consider embed_batch later only with re-verification of the bitwise-deterministic embedding sweep.

findings.title: /v1/models re-scans the models directory and parses every GGUF header under the manager mutex on a tokio worker
findings.evidence: handlers.rs:15 `let (discovered, registry) = state.manager.lock().await.discovered_with_registry();` (same at :51 for get_model). manager.rs:416-425 `let fresh = self.discovery_cache.as_ref().is_some_and(|c| c.refreshed_at.elapsed() < DISCOVERY_CACHE_TTL); if !fresh { self.discovery_cache = Some(DiscoveryCache { discovered: loader::discover_models(&self.models_dir), ... }); }` with `DISCOVERY_CACHE_TTL` = 5 s (:156). loader.rs:66-105 walks two directory levels; :186-193 per GGUF stem group calls `discover_gguf_model`, which at :604-606 does `GgufHeader::read(gguf_path)` → gguf_header.rs:273-280 mmaps the file and parses the entire header (metadata including `tokenizer.ggml.tokens` arrays). chat.rs:1577-1581 takes the same `state.manager.lock().await` to obtain a handle.
findings.rationale: Chat UIs (Open WebUI, LibreChat) poll /v1/models every few seconds, i.e. slower than the 5 s TTL, so each poll re-parses N GGUF headers of several MB each (vocab and merges live in the header) synchronously while holding the async mutex that chat_completions needs before it can even render a prompt; with a models directory of a dozen quant variants that is tens to hundreds of ms per poll on a tokio worker, and every chat request arriving in that window waits for it.
findings.proposal: Refresh discovery off the lock: when stale, drop the guard, run `loader::discover_models` in `spawn_blocking`, then re-lock to install the cache (serve the stale snapshot to concurrent callers meanwhile). Alternatively let the eviction task refresh it periodically and make `discovered_with_registry` read-only. Also have `discover_gguf_model` stop parsing at the tensor table or skip array-valued metadata it does not use.
findings.expected_benefit: Removes a periodic multi-ms to hundreds-of-ms stall of the manager lock and of one tokio worker; chat TTFT no longer depends on the UI's polling schedule.
findings.verify_how: With 10+ GGUF variants in the models dir, time `curl /v1/models` twice 6 s apart (second call is a cold refresh) and measure chat TTFT for a request fired 10 ms after the refresh starts; compare to a request fired in a fresh window.

verdict.reason: Verified. handlers.rs:15 and :51 call `state.manager.lock().await.discovered_with_registry()`; models/manager.rs:410-428 refreshes synchronously under that `&mut self` when the cache is older than DISCOVERY_CACHE_TTL = 5 s (:156), via loader::discover_models -> discover_gguf_model -> GgufHeader::read (loader.rs:603-604) -> mmap + parse (gguf_header.rs:273-279). parse (:184-210) materialises every metadata value with `c.value(tag, 0)` into a HashMap, including the full tokenizer.ggml.tokens/scores/merges arrays, i.e. on the order of 100k String allocations per GGUF file per refresh, tens of ms per file. chat_completions takes the same async mutex for get_or_load (chat.rs:1588-1591) and get_model (handlers.rs:51) also triggers the refresh. With UIs polling /v1/models at intervals longer than 5 s, every poll is a cold refresh and any chat request arriving in that window waits. Effect is bounded (tens to a few hundred ms for a dozen GGUFs, only for requests coinciding with a poll) so medium is right; S effort is honest. The cheapest fix is in the parse path: discovery needs architecture, layer count and vocab size, so a discovery-mode parse that skips array values (counting elements without allocating) would cut the refresh cost by an order of magnitude before any lock restructuring.

findings.title: n>1 enqueues n identical prompts in one burst, so all n prefill in the same step and miss the prefix cache; per-completion work is repeated n times
findings.evidence: chat.rs:1786-1850 `for i in 0..n { ... .map(SchemaArena::compile) ... handle.request_tx.try_send(IncomingRequest { prompt_tokens: prompt_tokens.clone(), ... extra_stop_token_ids: extra_stop_token_ids.clone(), ... })` — n sends back to back. engine_loop.rs:645-653 drains them all with try_recv before one step. engine.rs:1036 `plan_prefill_inputs(scheduler, prefix_cache, &prefill_ids, block_size)` looks up the cache for every scheduled prefill before the forward, and registration happens only afterwards in `sample_prefill_outputs` via `PrefixRegistry` (:1059-1071). scheduler/mod.rs:301-303 only limits *additional* prefills when the prompt exceeds the step budget, so short prompts are batched together.
findings.rationale: For prompts shorter than max_tokens_per_step the scheduler admits all n in one step; each does a full lookup-miss prefill, so the prompt is computed n times instead of once plus n-1 block reuses, and n copies of the prompt's KV blocks are allocated. SchemaArena::compile (constrain.rs:564) is also run n times for the same schema. n>1 is rare but it is exactly the sampling-comparison use case, where the prompt is often the expensive part.
findings.proposal: Engine side (cleanest): in plan_prefill_inputs, detect sequences in the same step whose `all_tokens` share a prefix with an earlier scheduled prefill and defer them one step so they hit the cache the first one registers; or share the prefill forward and copy block ids. Handler side (cheap): enqueue completion 0, wait for its first Token event (its blocks are registered), then enqueue 1..n; compile the SchemaArena once per request and clone the Arc.
findings.expected_benefit: Prefill cost for n>1 drops from n× to ~1× plus block reuse: for a 600-token prompt with n=4 that is ~1800 fewer prefill tokens per request; KV usage for the prompt part drops n×.
findings.verify_how: Send n=4 with a 600-token prompt and watch `oxydllm_prefix_cache_requests_total{result="miss"}`: it rises by 4 today; after the change by 1 with 3 hits; compare TTFT of the response.

verdict.reason: Partially accurate. chat.rs:1786-1853 does try_send n requests back to back and SchemaArena::compile runs inside the loop (:1818-1820), and plan_prefill_inputs (engine.rs:431-447) looks up the cache for all prefills before any registration (register happens in sample_prefill_outputs :678). But the claimed outcome depends on the engine being busy: when the engine is idle it is blocked in request_rx.blocking_recv() (engine_loop.rs:655-667), takes only request 0, steps (prefilling it alone and registering its blocks), and only on the next iteration drains 1..n via try_recv (:644-654), so on an idle engine completions 1..n already hit the prefix cache. The n-fold miss only happens when has_pending_work() is already true at drain time. n>1 is rare (OpenAI clients mostly use n=1), so this is a low-severity, rarely-taken-path item. The engine-side proposal (M) is disproportionate; the handler-side stagger is S.
verdict.corrected_benefit: On a busy engine, prefill for n>1 drops from n x prompt to 1 x prompt plus block reuse; SchemaArena compiled once per request instead of n times. No change on an idle engine, which already reuses.
verdict.corrected_proposal: In chat_completions compile the JsonSpec/SchemaArena once and clone it per completion; enqueue completion 0 first and the remaining n-1 after its first Token or Finish event (their lookups then hit the registered blocks). Alternatively, in plan_prefill_inputs defer a prefill whose all_tokens share >= one block with an earlier prefill in the same step.

findings.title: Multi-token `stop` strings are silently ignored although the engine already matches token sequences
findings.evidence: chat.rs:1727-1741 `// Single-token stops only. let extra_stop_token_ids: Vec<u32> = match &body.stop { Some(StopParam::Single(s)) => { let ids = handle.tokenizer.encode(s).unwrap_or_default(); if ids.len() == 1 { ids } else { Vec::new() } } ...` — no error, no warning. The engine already has sequence matching: engine.rs:163 `stop_token_sequences: Vec<Vec<u32>>`, :172 `fn has_matching_stop_sequence(tokens, stop_sequences)`, :652 `stop.matches(next_token, &seq.extra_stop_token_ids, &seq.all_tokens)`, but per-request state only carries ids (sequence.rs:34 `pub extra_stop_token_ids: Vec<u32>`).
findings.rationale: `stop: ["\n\nUser:", "###"]` is one of the most common OpenAI parameters (completion-style prompting, ReAct agents); today such a request generates past the marker up to max_tokens and returns text the client did not want, with no indication the parameter was dropped. Because BPE boundaries differ in context, token-sequence matching alone is also unreliable; the tokenizer already exposes `stop_text_markers` (tokenizer.rs:410) for the engine-level case.
findings.proposal: Add `extra_stop_sequences: Vec<Vec<u32>>` and `stop_strings: Vec<String>` to IncomingRequest and SequenceState; extend StopRules::matches to check per-sequence token sequences, and in the engine loop check the decoded tail (`out_stable_text`+window) for the stop strings, finishing the sequence with reason 'stop' and trimming the marker from the emitted text (OpenAI semantics). Return 400 for more than 4 stop strings.
findings.expected_benefit: Correct OpenAI `stop` semantics; shorter generations for completion-style clients (fewer wasted decode steps).
findings.verify_how: Request with `stop: ["\n\nQ:"]` on a prompt that elicits a Q/A list; today the answer runs past the marker, after the fix it ends before it with finish_reason 'stop'.

verdict.reason: Verified. chat.rs:1727-1741 keeps only stop strings that encode to exactly one token and silently drops the rest (no warning, no 400); types.rs:145-148 StopParam accepts Single/Multiple strings. The engine already supports token-sequence stops globally: engine.rs:163 stop_token_sequences, :172 has_matching_stop_sequence, built from extra_stop_sequences at construction (:877-881) and checked per sampled token via stop.matches(next_token, &seq.extra_stop_token_ids, &seq.all_tokens) (:652, :719, :825), but per-request state only carries single ids (IncomingRequest -> add_request_with_stop :946-960). Because BPE boundaries differ in context, the finding is right that token-sequence matching alone is insufficient and a text-level check on the emitted text is needed; that check must run on `full` before emit_suffix emits (hold back any suffix that is a prefix of a stop string), which is why M is the honest effort. OpenAI clients commonly send multi-token stops, so medium api-ux is right. Not on the ROADMAP backlog or rejected list.

findings.title: `messages[].content` rejects the OpenAI content-parts array with a 422

findings.title: Streaming with tools buffers the whole completion, so clients see nothing until generation ends
findings.evidence: chat.rs:1870-1883 `if has_tools { let buffered_rxs = completion_rxs; ... let mut handles = buffered_rxs.into_iter().map(|rx| Some(tokio::spawn(collect_one_completion(rx, req_timeout)))).collect();` then :1914 the role chunk is only sent after every completion has finished; content is replayed as one chunk at :2034-2060. The ROADMAP near-term backlog lists this ('Streaming tool calls (today tool-call responses buffer fully...)'), so this records the mechanism rather than re-proposing the goal.
findings.rationale: Every agent turn carries tools, so for agent clients streaming is effectively disabled: TTFT equals total generation time, reasoning_content never streams, and the client cannot show progress or cancel early (which, combined with server-http-3's detached collectors, also means the 'cancel' it does send is ignored). Most responses in an agent loop are plain text, so the buffering is paid even when no tool call occurs.
findings.proposal: Pass-through until a tool-call opener is observed: keep a small pending buffer (the stable text) and stream Token deltas as content while the trimmed prefix does not start with `<tool_call>`, `{`, or `` ``` ``; once an opener is seen, switch to buffering and parse at Finish as today. Reasoning tokens stream immediately in either mode. For ForcedFunction/Required stay in buffered mode (the output is a call by construction).
findings.expected_benefit: Restores real streaming for the majority of agent turns (plain text), with no change in the tool-call wire shape; also lets the disconnect path see the client leave.
findings.verify_how: Stream a tools-bearing request whose answer is prose on the M5 and time the first content delta: today it equals the full completion time; after the change it is one TTFT.

verdict.reason: Verified. chat.rs:1870-1883 moves all receivers into spawned collectors when has_tools, awaits every one to completion (:1884-1905), and only then emits the role chunk (:1908-1920) and replays content as a single chunk (:2043-2062), so TTFT equals full generation time for every tools-bearing request, including the majority that answer in prose. The ROADMAP backlog (line 555) already lists streaming tool calls as a known gap, so the finding's contribution is the mechanism and the pass-through design, which is sound: stream content while the trimmed prefix does not start with an opener (<tool_call>, { or ```), switch to buffering once one is seen, keep ForcedFunction/Required buffered. Caveat: with the injected JSON instruction (tools_system_instruction :646-676) a pure tool-call answer begins with `{`, which the opener rule covers; prose that legitimately starts with `{` would be buffered, which is harmless. Effort M and medium severity are honest.

findings.title: oxydllm_queue_depth is one global gauge overwritten by every resident model's loop
findings.evidence: metrics.rs:44-50 `pub static QUEUE_DEPTH: LazyLock<Gauge> = LazyLock::new(|| register_gauge!("oxydllm_queue_depth", "Current number of sequences in the inference engine (waiting + running)...")` — unlabelled, unlike every other series (`&["model"]`). engine_loop.rs:984 `metrics::QUEUE_DEPTH.set(engine.queue_depth() as f64);` runs after each step of each model's loop; mod.rs/manager allow several models resident with LRU eviction.
findings.rationale: With two models serving, the series alternates between their depths at step rate and the scrape sees whichever loop stepped last; a model that goes idle never resets it either, so a stale depth persists after the busy loop stops stepping. Dashboards built on it mislead exactly in the multi-model case the server advertises.
findings.proposal: Make it a GaugeVec labelled by model (consistent with TTFT/TPS), set it per loop, and remove the series when the loop exits (the drain at :1001-1009 is the place), mirroring `refresh_memory_gauges`' reset discipline.
findings.expected_benefit: Correct per-model utilisation metric; no stale series after unload.
findings.verify_how: Load two models, run a 4-sequence burst on one, scrape /metrics repeatedly: the value flips between 0 and 4 today; after the change `oxydllm_queue_depth{model=...}` reads 4 and 0 respectively.

findings.title: usage.completion_tokens_details.reasoning_tokens counts text deltas, not tokens, and is absent in streaming
findings.evidence: chat.rs:1446-1449 `EngineEvent::ReasoningToken(text) => { data.reasoning_content.push_str(&text); data.reasoning_tokens += 1; }` — one increment per event, and engine_loop.rs:761-769 emits a ReasoningToken only when prefix_decode_incremental returns new text (held-back U+FFFD, speculative multi-token steps and the final flush at :830-843 all change the event count). The streaming usage chunks at :2242-2250 and :2466-2476 hard-code `completion_tokens_details: None`.
findings.rationale: The value drifts from the real token count by the number of coalesced or split deltas, and streaming clients never get it at all, while the engine already knows the exact number (`tracker.thinking_ids.len()`).
findings.proposal: Add `reasoning_tokens: usize` to EngineEvent::Finish (set from `tracker.thinking_ids.len()`), carry it into CompletionData and into the streaming usage chunk when include_usage is set.
findings.expected_benefit: Accurate reasoning accounting in both modes.
findings.verify_how: Non-streaming request with enable_thinking on Qwen3; compare reasoning_tokens with `tokenizer.encode(reasoning_content).len()` (they differ today) and check the streaming usage chunk gains the field.

findings.title: A single step error aborts every running sequence, so one request's failure kills its neighbours
findings.evidence: engine_loop.rs:946-981 `Err(e) => { consecutive_errors += 1; ... if consecutive_errors >= MAX_CONSECUTIVE_ERRORS { let aborted_ids = engine.abort_all(); ... } else { let aborted_ids = engine.abort_running(); for id in aborted_ids { if let Some(tracker) = trackers.remove(&id) { ... tracker.tx.send(EngineEvent::Error(e.to_string())); ...` — the error is opaque (`anyhow`), so the loop cannot tell a per-sequence failure from a device failure. engine.rs:1050-1070 `sample_prefill_outputs(...)?; sample_decode_outputs(...)?;` propagate sampler/constraint errors for one sequence as a whole-step error; the alpha.15 changelog describes router-index validation that 'fails the request instead of panicking' through this same path.
findings.rationale: Under continuous batching the common per-sequence failure modes (constraint/sampler error, invalid router index for one sequence's tokens, a logit-bias id out of vocab) are returned as a step error and every concurrent request on the model receives a 500 'engine step failed' and loses its partial output, even though their state is intact. A device-level fault does warrant the batch abort; a sampler error does not.
findings.proposal: Give Engine::step a typed error: `StepError::Sequence { seq_id, source }` for failures raised while sampling or advancing one sequence (abort just that id, send Error to its tracker, keep the batch), and `StepError::Device(source)` for forward-pass failures (current behaviour). The engine already has the seq_id at the failure site in sample_prefill_outputs/sample_decode_outputs.
findings.expected_benefit: Isolates failures to the offending request; removes the collateral 500s under load.
findings.verify_how: Run 4 concurrent streams and inject a per-sequence failure (e.g. a logit_bias with a token id above vocab_size if that errors in the sampler, or the router-index test fault); today all 4 receive the error, after the change only one.

verdict.reason: Mechanism verified: engine_loop.rs:942-981 treats any Err from engine.step() as batch-wide: below MAX_CONSECUTIVE_ERRORS it calls engine.abort_running() (:969, engine.rs:1121-1123 = scheduler.abort_all_running) and sends Error+StreamEnd to every running tracker; step() propagates sampling errors with `?` (engine.rs:1050-1070). Per-sequence error sources do exist: sampling.rs:111/123 bail on NaN logits (a single row can be NaN) and :635 bails on an empty distribution after filtering, which one request can trigger with logit_bias/min_p/a grammar mask. So the risk is real but on a rarely-taken path (medium by the rubric). The typed-error proposal is heavier than needed: the seq_id is in hand at the sampling call sites in sample_prefill_outputs/sample_decode_outputs, so catching the error there and reporting failed ids in StepOutput avoids changing Engine's error type across the crate.
verdict.corrected_benefit: A sampler/constraint failure in one sequence aborts only that sequence; concurrent requests keep their partial output and continue, and forward-pass (device) failures keep today's batch abort.
verdict.corrected_proposal: In sample_prefill_outputs/sample_decode_outputs wrap the per-sequence sample call in a match; on Err push (seq_id, message) into a new `StepOutput.failed: Vec<(SequenceId, String)>`, abort that sequence via scheduler.abort_sequence, and continue the loop. In engine_loop, after a successful step, send EngineEvent::Error + StreamEnd to the trackers listed in `failed` and record the error metric; leave the Err(e) branch for forward-pass failures.

findings.title: Four copy-pasted SSE/response emitters have already drifted; a ChunkWriter would collapse ~500 lines and the per-token clones
findings.evidence: Each emitter builds `ChatCompletionChunk { id: chat_id.clone(), object: "chat.completion.chunk".to_string(), created, model: model_id_clone.clone(), ..., system_fingerprint: Some(fp.clone()) }` and `sse_tx.send(Ok(Event::default().data(serde_json::to_string(&chunk).unwrap())))`: tools-buffered path :1905-2104, n==1 path :2112-2300, n>1 path :2302-2520, plus the non-streaming assembly :2540-2700. The n==1 path emits the usage chunk on Finish (:2242) while the n>1 path emits it only after all StreamEnds (:2466); the n>1 path handles `Error` by ending the whole stream after one choice's error without the sibling cleanup the tools path does (:1898).
findings.rationale: Every streaming feature (tool pass-through, reasoning usage, logprobs in n>1) must be written three times and tested three times, and the drift above shows that is already not happening. Per token the pattern also clones four Strings and serializes a struct whose id/model/fingerprint never change; this is microseconds and not a throughput issue, but the writer makes it free to fix.
findings.proposal: Introduce `struct ChunkWriter { tx, id: Arc<str>, model: Arc<str>, fp: Arc<str>, created }` with `fn role(&self, idx) -> bool`, `fn delta(&self, idx, Delta, logprobs) -> bool`, `fn finish(&self, idx, reason) -> bool`, `fn usage(&self, Usage) -> bool`, `fn error(&self, msg)`, `fn done(&self)`; route all three streaming paths through one `stream_events(rx_merged, n, writer)` loop and keep the tools path as a pre-pass that buffers then replays through the same writer.
findings.expected_benefit: Roughly 500 fewer lines, one place to add streaming features, consistent usage/error semantics across n==1, n>1 and tools; incidental removal of 3-4 allocations per token.
findings.verify_how: http_compat_tests streaming cases stay green; add a test asserting the usage chunk position is identical for n=1 and n=2.

findings.evidence: engine_loop.rs:503-575 `mod streaming_decode_tests` calls only `emit_suffix` with hand-written cumulative strings; no test calls `prefix_decode_incremental`/`advance_stable_window` (grep finds them only in the production path at :761/:782). subsystems.assessment: The sampler is in genuinely good shape for the single-sequence case: the greedy path leaves only an argmax and a scalar NaN-guard on the GPU, the non-greedy filters are in-place with thread-local scratch, top-p has a proven-exact threshold fast path with a bitwise property test, and seeded determinism and tie-breaking are deliberate and tested. The constrained decoder is small, Copy-state, and sound in the sense that was fuzzed, and the schema arena falls back to syntax-only for anything it cannot compile. The fragility sits in two places. First, the per-step cost model: sample() is called once per sequence row and every call is its own Metal command-buffer commit plus CPU wait (two for greedy), so batched decode pays 2B synchronous readbacks per step; likewise JsonConstraint::allowed() re-walks every vocabulary token's bytes from scratch each step with no cache, trie, or first-byte pruning, which on a 150k vocabulary is a millisecond-class cost serialized on the engine thread, not the 'microsecond class' the module doc claims; the ROADMAP's mask-cache and byte-trie items are confirmed not shipped (MASK_CACHE_CAP is the attention-mask LRU in common/mask.rs, unrelated to GCD). Second, one real soundness hole in the automaton's events: a number immediately followed by ',' never raises EV_OBJ_COMMA, so a closed object whose last remaining property is numeric can be driven into a whitespace-only dead end that burns max_tokens and returns unparseable output, and the fuzz test's 'if !finished { continue }' is shaped precisely to hide it. Around those there are smaller items worth doing: the schema compiler and the HTTP validator expand $ref graphs as trees with only a depth cap (a 200-byte self-referential schema spins the handler for hours), NodeId truncation is silent, the repetition penalty compounds penalty^count over the whole history by default (far stronger than every reference implementation), n>1 seeded completions share a one-step-shifted random stream, and SentencePiece vocabularies (Gemma, Phi-3, Ministral, Llama-2 family) get no constraint at all with only a log line to say so. The biggest throughput lever is batching the logits readback and overlapping mask construction with the forward; the biggest correctness lever is the comma event fix plus a fuzz that refuses whitespace-only masks.

findings.title: Number followed by ',' skips the key-availability check: closed objects dead-end into whitespace-only masks
