findings.evidence: constrain.rs:274-277 (step_ev): `b',' => { if matches!(before_state, S::ObjNext) { ev |= EV_OBJ_COMMA; } }` -- the comma event is raised only when the state BEFORE the byte was ObjNext. constrain.rs:441-445 (step_inner, S::Num arm): `if n.complete() { self.state = self.after_value(); return self.step(b, mode); }` -- a number terminated by ',' goes Num -> ObjNext -> ObjComma inside one step_inner call, so before_state is S::Num(_) and EV_OBJ_COMMA is never set (only EV_SCALAR_END via lines 302-306). constrain.rs:850: `if ev & EV_OBJ_COMMA != 0 && !self.has_available_key(arena) { return false; }` is therefore skipped. constrain.rs:985-997 has_available_key returns false when additionalProperties is false and every property is emitted. Contrast: a string/literal value lands in ObjNext before the ',' byte, so the check fires correctly for them.
findings.rationale: With a strict-mode schema (additionalProperties:false, the OpenAI strict norm) whose last un-emitted property is numeric, compact output like {"name":"Ada","age":36 lets the model emit ',' (allowed) and then nothing but whitespace is legal: ObjComma accepts only ws or '"', and every '"' token is rejected by has_available_key at EV_KEY_START, while '}' is illegal in ObjComma. The sequence then emits whitespace tokens until max_tokens (each step paying the full-vocab mask walk), finishes with finish_reason=length and unparseable JSON (strict -> content_filter). The fuzz test cannot see it: constrain.rs:1416 asserts only !choices.is_empty() (whitespace satisfies it) and constrain.rs:1431 `if !finished { continue; }` silently drops walks that never reach a stop.
findings.proposal: Derive the comma event from the resulting state rather than the prior one: in step_ev replace the `b','` arm with `if b == b',' && self.state == S::ObjComma { ev |= EV_OBJ_COMMA; }` (ObjComma is reachable only via ObjNext, whether directly or through number completion). Add a unit test: schema {a: integer, additionalProperties:false}, walk `{"a":1`, assert ',' is masked and '}' allowed. Harden the fuzz: assert that from every reached state at least one non-whitespace non-stop token is allowed, and fail (not continue) when a walk does not finish within the step budget.
findings.expected_benefit: Removes a reachable dead end on the supported json_schema path that today costs a full max_tokens of decode and returns invalid output; makes the 'valid by construction' guarantee hold for numeric-last objects.
findings.verify_how: On the M5: Qwen3-4B with response_format json_schema {"type":"object","properties":{"name":{"type":"string"},"age":{"type":"integer"}},"required":["name","age"],"additionalProperties":false}, strict:true, a prompt that asks for name, age and email, temperature 0; today the completion that tries to continue past age ends as content_filter/length with trailing whitespace. Also the new unit test fails before the fix and passes after.

verdict.reason: Verified in code. step_ev (constrain.rs:242-247) snapshots `before_state` and calls step_inner; the S::Num arm (441-444) on a terminating ',' sets `self.state = self.after_value()` (ObjNext) and re-dispatches through `self.step(b, mode)`, and `step` is `self.step_ev(b, mode).is_some()` (236-238), so the inner call's EV_OBJ_COMMA is computed and discarded. Back in the outer step_ev the `b','` arm (274-277) tests `matches!(before_state, S::ObjNext)` with before_state == S::Num(_), so only EV_SCALAR_END (302-306) is raised and on_byte's `ev & EV_OBJ_COMMA` guard (850) never runs. Once in ObjComma the arm at 350-360 accepts only ws or '"'; '"' raises EV_KEY_START (258-259) and is rejected at 856-858 by has_available_key (985-997, false when additionalProperties is false and all props emitted); '}' is illegal (`_ => false`). So the dead end is real and reachable by a single allowed ',' token after a numeric last property. Literals and strings are unaffected because their transition to ObjNext happens on the last value byte and the ',' is a separate step. The fix is sound: S::ObjComma is assigned only at 464 from the ObjNext arm, so testing the post-state is equivalent to the intended pre-state check; use `matches!(self.state, S::ObjComma)`. The fuzz (1398-1431) indeed cannot see it: `!choices.is_empty()` is satisfied by whitespace and `if !finished { continue; }` drops the walk. Severity high stands: json_schema with additionalProperties:false is the strict-mode norm and a numeric last field is common.

findings.title: allowed() rebuilds the full-vocabulary mask by walking every token's bytes each step: no cache, no trie, no first-byte pruning, 150 KB allocation per step
findings.evidence: constrain.rs:1137-1160: `let mut allowed = vec![false; vocab_size]; for (id, entry) in self.table.bytes.iter().enumerate().take(vocab_size) { ... let mut m = self.machine; let mut g = self.guide; if self.walk(&mut m, &mut g, tok_bytes) { allowed[id] = true; } }`. walk (1121-1132) calls step_ev + guide.on_byte per byte. GuideState (791-796) is [Level; 8] (16 B each) + ValCtx, ~160 B; JsonMachine (107-111) is u128 + u8 + S, 32 B: both are copied per token. No cache structure exists anywhere in the file; the module doc at line 8 claims 'microsecond class'. Called from engine.rs:634 and :703 once per constrained sequence per step, before the GPU readback, on the engine thread. ROADMAP lines 549-552 list the automaton-state mask cache and byte trie as not yet done.
findings.rationale: In the dominant in-string state nearly every token is legal, so every token is walked to its last byte: for a 152k Qwen vocabulary that is on the order of 600k-900k step_ev/on_byte pairs (each a 15-25-branch state machine) plus 152k x ~190 B struct copies plus a 152 KB zeroed Vec<bool> that sample() then re-scans to write -inf. That is roughly 2-8 ms per step per constrained sequence, serialized on the engine thread and (in today's call order) not overlapped with the GPU. On a 30 ms decode step that is 5-25 percent; on a 10 ms small-model step it dominates. The in-string state repeats for every byte of every string value, so it is exactly the case a state-keyed cache or a precomputed set serves.
findings.proposal: Three layered changes, cheapest first. (a) Static string-safe set: at TokenByteTable::build precompute for each token the index of its first '"' or '\\' and whether every byte before it is >= 0x20; the mask for S::Str{esc:false,uni:0} with ValCtx::Free is then a build-time bitset (tokens with no special byte and a clean prefix) OR-ed with walks of only the few thousand tokens that contain a quote or backslash, started at that byte. (b) First-byte pruning for structural states: probe the 256 single bytes from the current state, then walk only tokens in the per-first-byte buckets that passed (after '{' only ws and '"' buckets, i.e. a few thousand tokens). (c) An LRU keyed by (JsonMachine, GuideState) -- both are Copy and can derive Hash/Eq -- holding the finished bitset, for key-scan/enum states that recur. Return a reusable Vec<u64> bitset (or a per-sequence buffer) instead of a fresh Vec<bool>, and have sample() iterate set bits of the complement.
findings.expected_benefit: In-string and structural states drop from millisecond-class full walks to a bitset copy plus a few thousand walks: expected 10-50x reduction of mask cost, i.e. constrained decode throughput within a few percent of unconstrained instead of 5-25 percent below.
findings.verify_how: Add a #[cfg(feature = "metal")]-free micro-bench test: build TokenByteTable from the Qwen3 tokenizer.json, advance a JsonConstraint into `{"name":"Ad`, time 100 calls of allowed(151936) before/after; also compare tok/s of a json_schema request vs the same prompt unconstrained on Qwen3-4B (the gap today is the mask cost).

verdict.reason: Accurate: allowed() (1137-1160) allocates `vec![false; vocab_size]`, iterates every table entry, copies JsonMachine (105-111, u128+u8+S) and GuideState (790-796, [Level;8]+ValCtx, ~170 B) per token and walks every byte through step_ev + on_byte (1121-1132); no cache, trie or first-byte pruning exists in the file. Called once per constrained sequence per step from engine.rs:634 and :703. Two corrections that do not change the verdict: (1) for the first row the mask runs before the first readback (engine.rs:703 then sampling.rs:120), so on Metal it partially overlaps the forward's tail; only rows after the first are strictly serial. (2) ROADMAP 549-552 already lists the state-keyed mask cache and byte trie as near-term backlog ('biggest practical win'), so this is planned, not rejected. Worth: with ~152k tokens, ~5 bytes/token, two function calls per byte plus a ~200 B struct copy per token, 2-6 ms per step on one core is a sound first-principles estimate, i.e. 5-20% of a 30 ms step and more on small models; the alpha.15 changelog contains no measurement of this cost. Proposal (c), the (JsonMachine, GuideState)-keyed cache, is the maintainer's own plan and the cheapest to land (both types are plain Copy data; derive Hash/Eq). Proposal (a) is sound only for value strings (key:false) with ValCtx::Free (on_byte's Free arm at ~905 is a no-op), excluding tokens containing '"', '\\' or bytes < 0x20 and excluding KeyScan key strings; the `uni` escape counter must also be 0. Effort M is honest.

findings.title: One Metal commit-and-wait per sequence row in the sampler: batched decode pays 2B synchronous readbacks per step instead of 1-3
findings.evidence: sampling.rs:104-110: `if params.is_plain_greedy() && allowed.is_none() { let token = logits.argmax(D::Minus1)?.to_scalar::<u32>()?; let sum: f32 = logits.sum_all()?.to_dtype(F32)?.to_scalar()?;` -- two device readbacks per row. sampling.rs:120: `let mut logits_vec: Vec<f32> = logits.to_dtype(F32)?.to_vec1()?;` -- one 600 KB readback per non-greedy/masked row. engine.rs:697-708 (sample_decode_outputs) and :627-641 (sample_prefill_outputs) loop `for (i, &seq_id) in decode_ids.iter().enumerate() { let seq_logits = batch_logits.get(num_prefills + i)?; ... sampling::sample(&seq_logits, ...)`. candle-core 0.11.0 metal_backend/mod.rs:2004-2019 to_cpu: allocates a staging buffer, blits, `self.device.flush_and_wait_current()?` (commit + CPU wait), and device.rs:131-155 drop_unused_buffers then walks every pooled buffer list under two write locks on each call.
findings.rationale: Each readback is a full command-buffer commit, GPU completion wait, staging-buffer allocation and a pool sweep; the GPU idles while the CPU runs the previous row's sampler and, for constrained rows, the full-vocab mask walk (engine.rs:703 runs allowed() before the readback). With B sequences the step pays 2B (greedy) or B (sampled) such round trips, each in the ~100-300 us class on Apple Silicon plus the pool sweep, i.e. roughly 1.5-5 ms per step at B=8 against ~0.3 ms if batched. The maintainer's note that the sampler is negligible (PERFORMANCE_INVESTIGATION_GGUF line 354) was for single-stream decode, where B=1 and this cost is one round trip.
findings.proposal: Split sample() into a batched device prelude and a CPU core. Prelude, once per step over the [B, vocab] tensor: `argmax(D::Minus1)` -> to_vec1 (one readback), `sum(D::Minus1).to_dtype(F32)` -> to_vec1 (per-row NaN attribution kept, one readback), and for rows that are not plain-greedy-unmasked an index_select of those rows cast to F32 -> to_vec2 (one readback). Then call a `sample_row(&[f32] | argmax, params, ...)` per sequence on the CPU. Compute all constrained masks (rayon over sequences) before the prelude so they overlap the forward instead of sitting between readbacks. greedy_forward (engine.rs ~744) already follows this one-readback shape for speculative decode.
findings.expected_benefit: Per-step sync count independent of batch size: at B=8 roughly 1.5-4 ms saved per step (5-10 percent of a 4B-model step, 15-25 percent of a sub-1B step); B=1 unchanged.
findings.verify_how: Wrap sample_prefill_outputs + sample_decode_outputs in a timer under OXYDLLM_PROFILE_DECODE and run 8 concurrent greedy requests on Phi-3-mini (the soak configuration in the Unreleased changelog); compare the per-step sampler time and aggregate tok/s before and after; expect the sampler time to stop scaling with B.

verdict.reason: Accurate. sampling.rs:104-110: plain-greedy unmasked rows do `logits.argmax(D::Minus1)?.to_scalar()` and `logits.sum_all()?.to_dtype(F32)?.to_scalar()` (two device readbacks); line 120 does one `to_vec1` for every other row. engine.rs:697-708 and :627-641 call sample() per row in a loop, so a step pays 2B or B synchronous readbacks. candle-core 0.11.0 metal_backend/mod.rs:2004-2019 to_cpu allocates a staging buffer, blits and calls `flush_and_wait_current`, which (device.rs:180-186) also runs drop_unused_buffers (131-155): two write locks and a retain() over every pooled buffer list, on every readback. greedy_forward (engine.rs:749-762) already shows the one-readback shape with a batched argmax. Worth: once the first readback has drained the GPU, each further commit+wait is pure latency (order 100 us on Apple Silicon) plus the pool sweep; at B=8 greedy that is 16 round trips, ~1.5-3 ms against a ~30-40 ms batched step, so >5% is plausible on the server's main (concurrent) path; B=1 is unchanged, which is why the PERFORMANCE_INVESTIGATION note ('sampler negligible', single stream) does not contradict it. The proposal is implementable with candle (`batch_logits.argmax(D::Minus1)?.to_vec1::<u32>()`, `sum(D::Minus1)` keeps per-row NaN attribution, `index_select` for non-greedy rows then `to_vec2`), and the per-row argmax is the same reduce kernel per row so greedy output is unchanged. A cheaper first step covering most of the greedy win: hoist the NaN-guard sum and the argmax to one batched readback each before the loop (S), leaving the non-greedy index_select for later. Caveat per the maintainer's measure-first rule: the per-roundtrip cost is estimated, not measured; the proposed OXYDLLM_PROFILE_DECODE timer should come first.

findings.title: Schema compile expands $ref as a tree with only a depth cap and truncates NodeId with 'as u16'; the validator shares the shape, so a tiny self-referential schema spins the handler
findings.evidence: constrain.rs:588 `if depth > 32 { return ANY; }`; 596-603 `if let Some(name) = r.strip_prefix(prefix) { ... return self.compile_node(target, root, depth + 1); }` with no memo of resolved refs and no visit/node budget; 505 `pub type NodeId = u16;` and 555/624/661/669-689 `(self.nodes.len() - 1) as NodeId` silently wrap past 65535. chat.rs:355-360 validate_schema_shape_inner has the same recursion (`if depth > 64 { Err }` then `resolve_schema_ref` -> recurse depth+1, properties -> recurse depth+1) with no cycle detection, and chat.rs:268-280 resolve_schema_ref follows any '#/...' pointer.
findings.rationale: A ~200-byte schema `{"$ref":"#/$defs/n","$defs":{"n":{"type":"object","properties":{"a":{"$ref":"#/$defs/n"},"b":{"$ref":"#/$defs/n"}}}}}` passes every keyword check and is visited 2^32 times by the validator (each visit allocates a format!() path) before compile is reached: a single unauthenticated request pins a tokio worker for hours. Schemas with fan-out that the validator survives still reach compile with the same exponential shape, where nodes.len() can exceed u16 and the 'as NodeId' wrap makes later ids alias earlier nodes, i.e. guidance against the wrong node (possible stuck masks or over-permissive guidance).
findings.proposal: In compile_node: memoize resolved $ref targets by pointer string to NodeId (insert a placeholder, compile once, patch), and add a node budget (e.g. 4096; beyond it return ANY) with NodeId::try_from instead of 'as'. In the validator: carry a HashSet of (ref string) on the current path to reject cycles with a 400, and a total visit budget. Both are local changes; the compile side keeps GUIDED_DEPTH semantics because recursion beyond 8 levels is syntax-only anyway.
findings.expected_benefit: Closes a request-level denial of service and a silent id-aliasing bug; recursive schemas (lists of nodes, trees) become compilable and guided to GUIDED_DEPTH instead of being unrolled.
findings.verify_how: Post the schema above to /v1/chat/completions with a 5 s client timeout: today the server thread does not return; after the fix it answers 400 (cycle) or compiles in microseconds. Unit test: compile a two-way self-referential $defs schema and assert nodes.len() stays under the budget.

verdict.reason: Accurate on both sides. compile_node (constrain.rs:582-603): `if depth > 32 { return ANY; }`, `$ref` resolution recurses with depth+1 and no memo; object properties recurse with depth+1 (637-640); every push uses `(self.nodes.len() - 1) as NodeId` with `pub type NodeId = u16` (505). For the two-way self-referential schema each nesting costs 2 depth units, so 17 object levels are expanded: 2^17-1 = 131071 Object nodes, which exceeds u16 and the `as` cast silently wraps, aliasing later ids onto earlier nodes (root() at 554-556 is also a wrapped id). Validator (src/server/routes/chat.rs:348-361 and the properties/items recursion at ~409-426): `depth > 64` cap, `resolve_schema_ref` follows any '#/...' pointer (268-281) and recurses with depth+1, properties recurse with depth+1, no visited set: 32 levels of fan-out 2 = 2^32 visits, each allocating a `format!()` path, before compile is reached. That is an unauthenticated request-level DoS on a tokio worker and a silent id-aliasing bug; medium is fair because the trigger is a pathological schema. The proposal is sound: a pointer-string -> NodeId memo with placeholder produces a cyclic arena, which the walker tolerates (nesting bounded by MAX_DEPTH 64 and guidance by GUIDED_DEPTH 8 via `overflow`), plus a node budget and NodeId::try_from; cycle detection in the validator via a path set. Effort S.

findings.title: repetition_penalty compounds as penalty^count over the full history by default, unlike every reference implementation
findings.evidence: sampling.rs:341-354 apply_repetition_penalty_with_counts: `let factor = penalty.powf(count as f32); logits[idx] = if l > 0.0 { l / factor } else { l * factor };` and 328-336 apply_repetition_penalty_cpu applies the division once per occurrence in prev_tokens. engine.rs:636-640 always passes `&seq.all_tokens` (prompt + output) and `Some(&seq.token_counts)` (scheduler/mod.rs:163-165 pre-counts the prompt). chat.rs:1768-1769 defaults repetition_window to 0 = full history; README 480-481 documents only 'Repetition penalty (default: 1.0)'.
findings.rationale: HF transformers and vLLM apply the divisor once per token present in the context; llama.cpp applies it once per unique token in the last repeat_last_n (64) tokens. Here a token seen 30 times in a 500-token context at penalty 1.1 is divided by 17, at 1.3 by 2600: after a few hundred tokens ',', '.', ' the' and the prompt's own frequent tokens are effectively banned, so clients porting repetition_penalty=1.1 from vLLM get degraded, drifting text and no documentation says why. Validation only enforces > 0, so the compounding is unbounded.
findings.proposal: Make the per-unique-token semantics the default: factor = penalty (count >= 1), keeping repetition_window as is; if the compounding form is wanted, expose it explicitly (e.g. repetition_penalty_mode: 'unique' | 'per_occurrence') and document both in README and the SamplingParams doc. frequency_penalty already covers the count-scaled case.
findings.expected_benefit: Parity with the ecosystems clients come from, no silent quality collapse on long generations with a modest penalty, and the two code paths (counts vs window slice) become trivially equivalent.
findings.verify_how: Generate 1k tokens from Qwen3-4B with repetition_penalty 1.1, temperature 0.7, same seed, before/after; compare the fraction of punctuation tokens and a judge-model coherence score, and diff against vLLM's output on the same request.

verdict.reason: Code verified: apply_repetition_penalty_cpu (sampling.rs:328-336) divides once per occurrence in the window slice and apply_repetition_penalty_with_counts (341-354) uses `penalty.powf(count)`; engine.rs:636-640/703-708 always pass `&seq.all_tokens` plus `Some(&seq.token_counts)` and the window default is 0 = full history (chat.rs:1769, README 480-481). The doc comment at 327 calls this 'classic', but the CTRL formulation, HF's RepetitionPenaltyLogitsProcessor (gather/scatter, one division regardless of duplicates), vLLM (mask of present tokens) and llama.cpp's penalties sampler (one division per token in the ring buffer, counts only feed frequency penalty) all apply it once per unique token. 1.1^30 = 17.4x on frequent punctuation after a few hundred tokens is a real, undocumented quality divergence for clients porting vLLM settings, and validation only enforces > 0. Not mentioned in ROADMAP/CHANGELOG as a decision. Proposal is S and makes the two paths trivially equivalent (count > 0 -> one division; window slice -> dedup). It is a behaviour change for existing users, so it belongs in the changelog; medium api-ux is the right severity.

findings.title: SentencePiece vocabularies get no byte table, so Gemma, Phi-3, Ministral and Llama-2-family requests silently lose the constraint
findings.evidence: constrain.rs:708-748 TokenByteTable::build maps each token's chars through gpt2_char_to_byte (line 727 `match char_to_byte.get(&ch)`) and returns None when `(mapped as f64) < vocab_size as f64 * 0.9` (742); SentencePiece tokens are spelled with U+2581 and '<0xNN>' which the GPT-2 alphabet does not contain. engine_loop.rs:624-630 logs tracing::info! once and enqueue_request (299-313) builds no constraint when byte_table is None; the HTTP response carries no signal. README verified list includes gemma-2b/2-2b/3-1b/4-E2B, Phi-3.5-mini, Phi-3-mini GGUF and Ministral-3-3B (all SPM-style vocabularies); tokenizer.rs:726 already identifies SPM for GGUF (`model_kind == "llama" || "gemma4"`).
findings.rationale: The changelog headline is 'structured output is guaranteed rather than validated after the fact', but for roughly a third of the verified checkpoints the guarantee degrades to post-hoc validation with only a log line to say so; a json_schema strict request on Phi-3 can end as content_filter where the same request on Qwen cannot.
findings.proposal: Add a second mapping in TokenByteTable::build: if the GPT-2 mapping covers < 90 percent, try SPM: '▁' -> 0x20, '<0xNN>' -> that byte, everything else the token's UTF-8 bytes; accept whichever mapping covers >= 90 percent, and expose which (if any) was used so the chat handler can report it (e.g. a 'constrained: false' warning field or a metrics counter). Verify on Phi-3-mini GGUF and gemma-3-1b with the e2e adversarial battery.
findings.expected_benefit: Constrained decoding on every verified text model instead of byte-level BPE only; the guarantee the changelog states becomes true across the supported set.
findings.verify_how: After the change, POST a strict json_schema request to Phi-3-mini-4k-instruct-Q4 and gemma-3-1b-it and confirm the log no longer reports 'JSON-constrained decoding unavailable' and that an adversarial prompt (ask for extra keys) still yields schema-valid output with finish_reason stop.

verdict.reason: Accurate: TokenByteTable::build (constrain.rs:708-748) maps token chars only through gpt2_char_to_byte and returns None below 90% coverage; U+2581 and '<0xNN>' pieces are outside the GPT-2 alphabet, so SentencePiece vocabularies fail. src/server/routes/engine_loop.rs:624-630 logs one tracing::info! and enqueue_request (296-334) silently builds no constraint when byte_table is None; nothing in the request path marks the response as unconstrained. README lists gemma-2b/2-2b/3-1b/4-E2B and Phi-3.5-mini/Phi-3-mini GGUF among verified models (lines 95-99), all SPM; tokenizer.rs:720-728 already recognises SPM GGUFs. One overstatement: Ministral 3 (Tekken, byte-level) and Llama-2 (README 88: unverified) should not be counted, so it is ~6 of 32 verified checkpoints, not a third. The proposed SPM mapping is sound: a leading '▁' that the decoder strips at sequence start only turns an allowed ' {' into '{', still valid JSON, so the mask stays sound. Effort M is honest because verification must run on the Metal battery; medium api-ux stands.

findings.title: The full-vocabulary exp() pass is now the dominant CPU term of non-greedy sampling; a GPU softmax (no extra sync) or a SIMD exp removes it
findings.evidence: sampling.rs:280-293 softmax_probs: `let mut probs: Vec<f32> = logits.iter().map(|&l| ((l - max_logit) / temp).exp()).collect();` over the whole row, called at 219 for every sampled token; 120 copies the F32 row from the GPU just before. candle already has a Metal softmax kernel (used by the attention paths) that could run in the same command buffer as the lm_head before the single readback of 120.
findings.rationale: After the alpha.15 work removed the ln pass and the full sort, what remains per sampled token is: F32 cast+copy (~0.1-0.2 ms), NaN scan (~0.02 ms), 152k scalar expf calls (libm, not vectorized by rustc: ~3-5 ns each, ~0.5 ms), top-p fast path (~0.05 ms) and the categorical scan. The exp pass is therefore roughly half or more of the ~0.4 ms the changelog measures per sampled token, and it is pure CPU work on the engine thread.
findings.proposal: When no penalties, logit_bias or mask apply (the common temperature>0 request), compute `softmax_last_dim(logits / temperature)` on the device and read probabilities instead of logits (NaN still propagates for the guard; max/sum are not needed on the CPU). For the penalized/masked path, replace the scalar loop with a 4-lane NEON exp polynomial (1e-6 relative error is far below sampling noise) or a chunked exp from a vetted crate. Keep the existing full-sort reference property test and add one comparing fast-exp softmax to std within 1e-5.
findings.expected_benefit: Roughly 0.3-0.4 ms per sampled token removed from the engine thread (most of the remaining sampled-vs-greedy gap); at 30 tok/s that is 1 percent, at 100 tok/s on small models 3-4 percent.
findings.verify_how: Run the existing sampling_cost_decomposition test (Metal-gated) and read 'softmax+ln' minus 'ln pass alone' to get the exp cost on the M5; then compare sampled tok/s (temperature 0.7, top_p 0.95) vs greedy before and after.

verdict.reason: The code is as described (softmax_probs, sampling.rs:280-293, scalar `.exp()` over the full row, called at 219 for every sampled token after the F32 readback at 120) and a device softmax helper already exists (src/common/linear.rs:248 softmax_last_dim). But the quantitative claim is inconsistent with the maintainer's own measurement: CHANGELOG line 184 says the whole sampled-over-greedy overhead is ~0.4 ms/token, so the exp pass cannot be ~0.5 ms; from the same numbers it is at most ~0.2-0.3 ms, i.e. <1% at 30 tok/s and ~2-3% only on sub-1B models at 100 tok/s. The existing `sampling_cost_decomposition` test (sampling.rs:693, prints 'softmax+ln' and 'ln pass alone') already isolates it on the M5, so the honest first step is to read that number. The device-softmax variant also changes numerics between the penalised (CPU) and unpenalised (GPU) paths for the same seed, which the maintainer will want called out.
verdict.corrected_benefit: At most ~0.2-0.3 ms per sampled token on the engine thread (<1% at 30 tok/s, ~2-3% on 100 tok/s small models); only worth doing if the decomposition test shows exp dominating.
verdict.corrected_proposal: Run sampling_cost_decomposition on the M5 and subtract 'ln pass alone' from 'softmax+ln' to get the exp cost. Only if it exceeds ~0.2 ms: in the no-penalty/no-bias/no-mask branch, cast the row to F32 and apply the existing softmax_last_dim on the device (one extra kernel in the same command buffer, same single readback), reading probabilities instead of logits; keep the CPU softmax for the penalised/masked path and add a test comparing both within 1e-5.

findings.title: Post-softmax filters still touch the full vocabulary three times per token (top-k scratch copy, top-p zeroing, categorical scan) and top_logprobs allocates 1.2 MB per token
findings.evidence: sampling.rs:446 `scratch.extend_from_slice(probs);` copies the whole row for select_nth; 535-537 keep_top_p_prefix `for p in probs.iter_mut() { *p = 0.0; }` then rewrites the kept prefix; 618-629 categorical_sample `for (i, &p) in probs.iter().enumerate() { cumulative += p; if r < cumulative ...` scans from index 0 across the full row even though after top-p typically 6-7 entries are non-zero (changelog line 184); 308-321 top_k_by_logprob builds `Vec<(u32, f32)>` for the full vocabulary on every call when top_logprobs is requested.
findings.rationale: The dense pipeline costs three full-row passes (~150-250 us at 152k) after the softmax even though the candidate set is already sparse after the threshold scan in apply_top_p; the ordering min_p -> top_k -> top_p -> draw could operate on the (index, prob) candidate list that apply_top_p already builds in IDX_SCRATCH.
findings.proposal: Build the candidate list once (indices with p >= max*1e-4, falling back to full when their mass is short), apply min_p/top_k/top_p on that list, draw from its prefix sums, and only index into the full row for the returned token; for top_logprobs, select the k best directly from the candidate list (a full-row select only in the fallback). Keep the full-sort reference property test as the oracle.
findings.expected_benefit: About 0.1-0.2 ms per sampled token and zero large allocations when logprobs are requested; modest alone, additive with finding 7.
findings.verify_how: Extend sampling_cost_decomposition with a 'filters+draw' line and compare before/after; property-test the sparse pipeline against the current dense functions on peaked and flat distributions.

findings.title: Seeded n>1 completions draw from one-step-shifted copies of the same random stream
findings.evidence: sampling.rs:618-621 categorical_sample: `Some(s) => splitmix64_f32(s.wrapping_add(step))` with step = prev_tokens.len() (sampling.rs:231); 516-519 tie_break_seed `base.wrapping_add(step) ^ TIE_BREAK_NAMESPACE`; chat.rs:1789 `let seed = base_sampling_params.seed.map(|s| s.wrapping_add(i as u64));` gives completion i the seed s+i.
findings.rationale: Completion i at generated position t uses key s+i+L+t and completion i+1 at position t-1 uses s+i+1+L+t-1: the same key, so the uniform draws of the n completions are the same sequence offset by one token. The outputs differ because contexts diverge, but the streams are not independent, which is what a 'distinct seed per completion' is meant to provide and what a reproducibility consumer would assume.
findings.proposal: Mix the seed before combining with the step: key = splitmix64_u64(splitmix64_u64(seed) ^ (step << 1)) or simply splitmix64_u64(seed).wrapping_add(step) so neighbouring seeds map to unrelated keys; apply the same to tie_break_seed. Note in the changelog that seeded outputs change once.
findings.expected_benefit: Statistically independent completions under seed with n>1; one-line change, no runtime cost.
findings.verify_how: Unit test: for seed s and steps 0..1000 assert the key sequence for seed s+1 shares no element with seed s shifted by one (today it shares all of them).

findings.title: Constrained decoding is tested only against a synthetic 97-token single-byte table, the fuzz hides dead ends, and the non-greedy mask path has no test
findings.evidence: constrain.rs:1347-1356 guided() builds TokenByteTable::from_raw with one byte per token; no test calls TokenByteTable::build on a real tokenizer.json, so multi-byte tokens such as '":', '"},', '\n  "', bytes >= 0x80 through the GPT-2 alphabet, the 90 percent threshold, and the padded-vocab path (allowed() takes `.take(vocab_size)` at 1140 with model vocab 151936 vs tokenizer 151665) are unexercised. constrain.rs:1416 asserts only `!choices.is_empty()` and 1431 `if !finished { continue; }` skips walks that never reach a stop. sampling.rs tests never call sample() with Some(allowed) and temperature > 0, and no test asserts apply_repetition_penalty_cpu == apply_repetition_penalty_with_counts.
findings.rationale: Finding 1 is exactly the class of bug these gaps admit: a whitespace-only mask passes the fuzz, and a real vocabulary's multi-byte structural tokens are the ones that cross state boundaries within one token. The sampler's masked non-greedy path is the production path for json_schema with temperature > 0 and is untested.
findings.proposal: (a) Add a test gated on a tokenizer.json being present (like the existing SentencePiece GGUF round-trip test) that builds the real table, checks coverage >= 0.9, walks a compact nested document with multi-byte tokens, and checks allowed() never marks an id >= tokenizer vocab. (b) In the fuzz, assert that every state allows at least one non-whitespace token or a stop, and fail on unfinished walks. (c) Add sample() tests: with a mask and temperature 0.8 over 1000 seeds, a masked token is never returned; with an all-false mask the call errors. (d) Property-test the two repetition-penalty paths for equality over random histories.
findings.expected_benefit: Would have caught finding 1 and guards the mask-cache/trie refactor in finding 2.
findings.verify_how: The new fuzz assertion fails on current main for the person_schema when 'age' is emitted last followed by ','; passes after finding 1's fix.

verdict.reason: Verified: guided() (constrain.rs:1306-1315) builds the table with from_raw from one byte per token (0x20..0x7F plus '\n', stop id 96); no test in src/ or tests/ calls TokenByteTable::build (grep found only the definition and the engine_loop call), so the GPT-2 alphabet mapping, multi-byte structural tokens, the 90% threshold and `.take(vocab_size)` padding (1140) are unexercised. The fuzz (1398-1431) asserts only `!choices.is_empty()` and `continue`s on unfinished walks, which is exactly how finding 1 slipped through. In sampling.rs no test passes `Some(allowed)` into sample() (the only `if let Some(allowed)` is production code at 126) and apply_repetition_penalty_with_counts is referenced only at its definition (341) and call site (152), so the counts/window equivalence is untested. All four proposed tests are S and the fuzz hardening would fail on current main for the person_schema when age is emitted last followed by ','.

findings.title: Greedy-with-mask path silently emits a token when the mask allows nothing, while the sampled path errors
findings.evidence: sampling.rs:128-141: after masking, `if params.is_plain_greedy() { let token = logits_vec.iter().enumerate().max_by(|a, b| a.1.total_cmp(b.1)).map(|(i, _)| i as u32).unwrap_or(0); return Ok(...)` -- with every logit at -inf, max_by returns the last index (vocab-1, often a padded id above the tokenizer vocabulary). The sampled path instead reaches categorical_sample's bail at 630 ('distribution is empty').
findings.rationale: An all-false mask is reachable today through finding 1 only indirectly (whitespace stays legal), but any vocabulary lacking some single-byte tokens (special-marked bytes, non-byte-level tables once SPM support lands) can produce it, and then greedy JSON mode emits an arbitrary id and advance() silently keeps state (constrain.rs:1173 only commits when the walk succeeds), producing garbage with no error.
findings.proposal: After masking, if no entry of allowed is true, bail with a clear error ('constraint admits no token at this state') for both paths; cheap (one any() over the mask) and makes the two paths consistent.
findings.expected_benefit: Fails loudly instead of emitting a padded token id and desynchronising the constraint.
findings.verify_how: Unit test: sample() with allowed = all false and temperature 0 must return Err, not Ok(vocab-1).

findings.title: Small dead code and avoidable per-token allocation in the constraint and penalty paths
findings.evidence: constrain.rs:307-309 `if before_depth < self.depth { // already flagged via byte match above }` is an empty branch. constrain.rs:1170 advance(): `let bytes = tok_bytes.clone();` heap-copies the token bytes per accepted token although walk() takes &self and &[u8] (no borrow conflict). constrain.rs:127-130 `match mode { JsonMode::Object => S::Value, JsonMode::Value => S::Value }` both arms identical. sampling.rs:358-374 apply_frequency_presence_penalty (builds a HashMap per token) is unreachable from the engine, which always passes Some(token_counts) (engine.rs:639, 708); apply_repetition_penalty_cpu is reached only when repetition_window is set, so two penalty implementations must be kept in sync by hand (see finding 5).
findings.rationale: None of these cost throughput today; they are the kind of duplication and leftover that will cost review time during the mask-cache refactor and the penalty semantics change.
findings.proposal: Delete the empty branch and the redundant match; walk the table slice directly in advance(); make the no-counts penalty variants #[cfg(test)] or derive them from the counts variant by building counts once from the window slice.
findings.expected_benefit: Smaller surface for the two upcoming changes in this file; one fewer allocation per constrained token.
findings.verify_how: cargo clippy and the existing tests; no behaviour change expected.

subsystems.coverage_notes: Read both scope files in full (sampling.rs 1024 lines, constrain.rs 1497 lines) plus the call sites that matter: engine.rs sample_prefill_outputs/sample_decode_outputs/step/run_forward_pass/greedy_forward, scheduler/sequence.rs and add_request_full, engine_loop.rs byte-table build and enqueue_request, chat.rs sampling-param construction, validate_sampling_params, validate_schema_shape_inner, resolve_schema_ref and json_mode construction, tokenizer.rs helpers used by TokenByteTable, and candle-core 0.11.0's Metal to_cpu / flush_and_wait_current / drop_unused_buffers to confirm per-readback sync cost. Read the ROADMAP 'Rejected', 'Constant and flag audit' and 'Near-term backlog' sections, the CHANGELOG Unreleased/alpha.15 sections, and grepped the four other maintainer notes for sampling/sync mentions (PLAN_COMPARISON lists GPU-side sampling as a candidate, not rejected; PERFORMANCE_INVESTIGATION's 'sampler negligible' is a single-stream measurement). Not done: no code was executed (no cargo, no rustc), so every timing figure is an analytic estimate with a verification recipe rather than a measurement; did not read the HTTP json_schema compat tests beyond their request bodies (they use a scripted engine and do not exercise the constraint); did not audit the harmony/thinking opt-out logic in engine_loop beyond the enqueue_request match; did not examine candle's Metal argmax/sum kernels for BF16 accumulation precision (only relevant to the NaN guard, where NaN propagation is dtype-independent); did not review the speculative-decode path's interaction with sampling beyond confirming it is excluded for constrained and non-plain-greedy sequences.
missed: The constraint's stop set and the engine's stop set are built from different sources, and the mask only ever whitelists the former. TokenByteTable::build stores `stop_ids: tokenizer.stop_token_ids()` (constrain.rs:745-747; that list is the tokenizer's eos plus a hard-coded name list at tokenizer.rs:377-407), and allowed() enables only `self.table.stop_ids` at an accepting state (constrain.rs:1151-1156), while every special token has `bytes = None` (constrain.rs:723-725) and so can never be walked. The engine, however, stops on `model.stop_token_ids()` merged with engine-level extras (engine.rs:873-875, 1049-1051) and on each request's `extra_stop_token_ids` (engine.rs:719). Any id in the engine's set that the tokenizer list lacks (a model whose end-of-turn token is not one of the hard-coded names, e.g. Phi-3's `<|end|>`, which becomes relevant as soon as finding 6 lands SPM support; or a request `stop` that resolves to a special id) is therefore masked at exactly the moment the model wants to emit it; the only legal tokens are whitespace (S::Done accepts ws, constrain.rs:~491) and the tokenizer's own eos, so a model that prefers its end-of-turn token pads whitespace until max_tokens and returns finish_reason=length. The fix is small: build the table (or JsonConstraint) with the engine's merged stop set rather than the tokenizer's, and union the sequence's extra_stop_token_ids in allowed(); add a test that a stop id present in the engine set but absent from tokenizer.stop_token_ids() is allowed at an accepting state.

subsystems.assessment: The loading subsystem is in genuinely good shape structurally: the two-phase safetensors load (parallel CPU decode, sequential device transfer), the pread-based parallel GGUF materialisation with the crate's own header reader, the owned IQ weight path, the drain-then-fingerprint retry loop, and the GGUF rope-table sharing all show measured reasoning, and the constants carry their provenance. What is fragile is everything that happens on the device after upload and everything the memory accounting cannot see: the safetensors block build concatenates q/k/v and gate/up into new device tensors while ModelWeights still holds the originals, so a dense checkpoint peaks at roughly 1.65x its weight bytes right before the KV pool is grown, which is exactly the pressure regime the maintainer traced silent corruption to; the tied-lm_head RTN reads the uploaded embedding back and builds two F32 copies of it; the safetensors path still builds one RoPE table per layer (the fix shipped only for GGUF); and Llama-family GGUF q/k rows are read back, shuffled and re-uploaded layer by layer. On time, the two biggest costs are the FP8 scale fold, which runs single-threaded over three full-size F32 temporaries after a lossless detour through BF16, and the fact that on both paths the model-sized memcpy into MTLBuffers is serialised (by the global metal_alloc_lock on GGUF, by design on safetensors) and preceded by a redundant heap copy. The dead Metal branches and the every-16-tensors drains in weights.rs describe a candle that no longer exists (0.11's to_device is a synchronous newBufferWithBytes with nothing to drain), which is harmless today but will mislead the next person who touches the lock cadence. The fingerprint check that the whole retry loop rests on samples one 8-16 KB norm buffer out of thousands. The biggest single lever is to separate allocation from filling on Metal: allocate buffers serially under the lock, drain once, then pread or memcpy in parallel straight into the shared buffers' contents (all the needed candle 0.11 constructors are public); that removes one full copy, the serialisation and the per-thread heap transient on both loaders at once. The second lever is to move every post-upload transform (qkv/gate_up fusion, FP8 fold, RTN, depermute) into the parallel CPU phase before upload, where it is cheaper, parallel and transient-free.

findings.title: Safetensors block build holds the per-projection originals and the fused q/k/v and gate/up copies on the device at the same time (~1.65x weights transient, right before the KV pool is grown)
findings.evidence: loader.rs:1111 `let weights = ModelWeights::load(&weight_path_refs, device, dtype, expert_stream)?` is a local that lives until `load_standard_safetensors` returns (after the closure ending at :1446); weights.rs:452 `fn resolve_name<'a>(&'a self, name: &str) -> Option<&'a Tensor>` and the `get`/`try_get` API only borrow from the immutable `tensors: FxHashMap<String, Tensor>` (:38), nothing can remove an entry. Per layer, loader.rs:1311 `TransformerBlock::load(&block_cfg, i, &weights)` reaches attention.rs:191 `let qkv_w = Tensor::cat(&[q_w, k_w, v_w], 0)?;` and ffn.rs:100 `let gate_up_w = Tensor::cat(&[&gate_w, &up_w], 0)?;`, each a new device allocation. The KV pool's first segment is allocated in the same closure (loader.rs ~1346 `BlockAllocator::growing` -> paged.rs:474-476 `if max_blocks > 0 { this.grow()?; }`) while `weights` is still alive. candle only releases dropped buffers at `wait_until_completed` (candle device.rs:131/175/185 `drop_unused_buffers`), i.e. at loader.rs:858.
findings.rationale: For a dense decoder q+k+v+gate+up is ~65% of a layer's parameters (Qwen3-4B: 65.5M of 101M per layer), so at the end of the block loop the device holds the originals plus the fused copies, ~1.65x the weight bytes, and this peak overlaps the KV pool growth. compute_kv_blocks sizes the pool from `weights.runtime_size_bytes()` (originals only), so the ceiling logic cannot see this transient; it is precisely the allocation pressure the alpha.15 notes trace the silent weight corruption to, and it shrinks the set of checkpoints that load without a halving retry on 24 GB.
findings.proposal: Fuse before upload instead of after: in ModelWeights::load, after apply_weight_scale_inv and before phase 2, concatenate the CPU tensors of each layer's q/k/v (and biases/scale_inv) into `...self_attn.qkv_proj.weight` and gate/up into `...mlp.gate_up_proj.weight`, removing the parts, so phase 2 uploads only fused tensors; attention.rs:171-186 already accepts the fused `qkv_proj` name, ffn needs the symmetric branch. Minimal alternative: give ModelWeights a `take(&self, name) -> Option<Tensor>` over a `Mutex<FxHashMap>` and have Attention::load/Ffn::load take the parts they fuse, so each original is dropped as soon as its copy exists.
findings.expected_benefit: Transient device peak drops from ~1.65x to ~1.0x weights plus one layer; 2L queued cat kernels disappear from the load; no numerical change. On a 24 GB M5 this is several GB of headroom for 8-9B BF16 or FP8-dequantized checkpoints and fewer pool-halving retries.
findings.verify_how: Instrument the end of the block loop vs. after `load_standard_safetensors` returns with the Metal device's pooled bytes (or `footprint`/vm_stat) on a dense BF16 checkpoint such as Qwen3-4B BF16: expect ~13 GB vs ~8 GB today, ~8 GB vs ~8 GB after. Then re-run a checkpoint that currently triggers 'weights did not survive this KV pool; retrying' and confirm it loads first try with the same fingerprint.

verdict.reason: Mechanism verified: `weights` is a local at loader.rs:1111, borrowed by the closure at :1203 and used as late as :1371-1410 (per-layer Gemma projections), so it lives until the function returns; attention.rs:191 `Tensor::cat(&[q_w, k_w, v_w], 0)` and ffn.rs:100 `Tensor::cat(&[&gate_w, &up_w], 0)` allocate fused device copies per layer (Linear::new at linear.rs:160 only takes a `.t()` view, no third copy); the KV pool grows inside the same closure (loader.rs:1346 -> paged.rs:474-476 -> :499-500 `Tensor::zeros` on the device) with no drain between (no drain_metal/synchronize in attention.rs or ffn.rs); candle releases pooled buffers only in `drop_unused_buffers` from `wait_until_completed` (device.rs:131-150, :175). The AWQ branch returns early at attention.rs:160, so this is the BF16/FP8-dequantized dense path. Arithmetic holds (~65% of layer params fused; ~1.58x with the embedding). Severity high stands for 8-9B BF16 on 24 GB, but the stated proposal (fuse on the CPU before upload, M) is more than needed: a `take(&self, name)` over a `Mutex<FxHashMap>` used by Attention::load/Ffn::load, plus moving the allocator construction after the last `weights` use and a `drop(weights); drain_metal(..)` before `BlockAllocator::growing`, removes the overlap and the duplicates in under a day. Note the pool cannot reuse the dropped originals (sizes differ from the fused buffers), so the drain before growing is what actually frees them.
verdict.corrected_benefit: Same peak reduction (~1.6x -> ~1.0x weights plus one layer at pool-growth time) without touching the tensor-naming contract; the per-layer fused copies still exist transiently during the block loop but never coexist with the KV pool.
verdict.corrected_proposal: Add `ModelWeights::take(&self, name) -> Option<Tensor>` (interior mutability) and have Attention::load/Ffn::load take q/k/v and gate/up after the `Tensor::cat`; move the `allocators` construction (loader.rs:1343-1360) to after the last `weights` use (:1410), then `drop(weights)` and `drain_metal(device, "pre-pool")` before `BlockAllocator::growing`. Fuse-before-upload can follow later if the transient during the block loop itself proves to matter.

findings.title: FP8 scale folding runs single-threaded over three full-size F32 temporaries, after a lossless detour through BF16
findings.evidence: weights.rs:253 `for weight_name in weight_names {` is a plain sequential loop; :267 `let weight_f32 = weight.to_dtype(DType::F32)`, :230 `.broadcast_as((s_out, block_out, s_in, block_in))?.contiguous()?` materialises a scale grid the size of the weight, then `.mul(weight)` and :283 `let scaled = scaled_f32.to_dtype(weight_dtype)`. Phase 1 at :365-373 (`par_iter`, `&Device::Cpu`) has already cast every F8 tensor F8->F32->BF16 (:150-157). candle 0.11 cpu_backend/utils.rs:221-231 `unary_map` is `vs.iter().map(|&v| f(v)).collect()`; rayon in candle-core's CPU backend is used only by conv/matmul, so to_dtype/mul here are single-threaded.
findings.rationale: Per FP8 weight the fold costs BF16->F32 (write 4 B/elem), the grid (write 4 B/elem), the product (read 8, write 4 B/elem) and ->BF16 (read 4, write 2 B/elem): roughly five passes and ~14 B/elem of transient, on one core, after the parallel phase already produced the BF16. For a 4B-parameter FP8 checkpoint that is on the order of 100 GB of single-threaded memory traffic, likely the dominant term of its load time. F8E4M3 values are exactly representable in BF16, so f8->f32->bf16->f32 is the identity and `bf16(f32(f8) * scale)` is bitwise identical to the current chain.
findings.proposal: Fold inside the phase-1 rayon closure: when `f8_names.contains(name)` and a `_scale_inv` companion exists (known from `scale_inv_names`), produce the BF16 tensor in one pass over the F8 bytes, `bf16::from_f32(f32::from(f8) * scale[o / block_out][i / block_in])`, computing the block index from the element index instead of building the broadcast grid; keep apply_weight_scale_inv only for non-F8 weights that ship a scale. Put the per-element math in one helper that expert_stream.rs:445-461 (which replicates the chain for byte identity) also calls. Drop the folded `*_scale_inv` entries before phase 2: linear.rs:544-548 ignores scale_inv for non-F8 weights, so on Metal they are dead yet uploaded as hundreds of buffers.
findings.expected_benefit: FP8 safetensors load time bounded by one parallel pass instead of five sequential ones (several seconds on Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507-FP8); per-weight transient from ~14 B/elem to ~3 B/elem; bitwise-identical weights.
findings.verify_how: Time `ModelWeights::load` on Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507-FP8 before/after; add a test that folds a random F8 block-scaled tensor through both the old chain and the new helper and asserts byte equality (the Fp8Resident-vs-Standard harness in expert_stream.rs already does this shape of check); re-run the FP8 model in the regression sweep.

verdict.reason: Verified end to end. weights.rs:253 is a plain `for weight_name in weight_names`; :267 `weight.to_dtype(DType::F32)`, :228-231 `.broadcast_as(...).contiguous()` builds a weight-sized F32 grid, `.mul(weight)`, :283 `to_dtype(weight_dtype)`; :291 `drain_metal(scaled.device(), ..)` is a no-op on CPU. Phase 1 (:365-378) runs with `&Device::Cpu` and `preserve_fp8_weight && !device.is_metal()` == false on Metal, so :150-157 has already cast every F8 tensor F8->F32->BF16 in parallel. candle 0.11's CPU `to_dtype`/`mul`/`contiguous` go through `unary_map`/`binary_map`/strided copy (cpu_backend/utils.rs:221-231, plain `.iter().map().collect()`); rayon appears in cpu_backend/mod.rs only in conv (:975, :1206, :1280). So the fold is ~5 sequential passes, ~28 B/elem of traffic, single core: for ~3.6B FP8 elements that is ~100 GB at single-thread memcpy speed, i.e. several seconds, plausibly the dominant term of an FP8 safetensors load. Numerics: every F8E4M3 value (incl. subnormals) is exactly representable in BF16, so `bf16(f32(f8))` is the identity and `bf16(f32(f8) * scale)` is bitwise identical to the current chain. linear.rs:544-548 confirms `from_weight_with_scale_inv` drops scale_inv for non-F8 weights, so the folded `*_scale_inv` entries uploaded in phase 2 are dead on Metal (small bytes, hundreds of residency inserts). Effort M is honest (rayon closure, shared helper with expert_stream.rs:449-461, byte-equality test).

findings.title: GGUF: metal_alloc_lock is held across the MTLBuffer memcpy, so the whole file is copied on one thread while the rayon readers block holding tensor-sized heap buffers
findings.evidence: gguf_weights.rs:655-658 `let _guard = device.is_metal().then(|| crate::common::weights::metal_alloc_lock().lock().unwrap()); let (qt, staged) = qtensor_with_staged(dtype, &bytes, entry.dims.clone(), device)`; :532 `QStorage::from_data(Cow::Borrowed(bytes), device, dtype)` -> candle quantized/metal.rs:458-466 `load_quantized` -> `new_buffer_builder().with_data(data)` -> candle device.rs:253-257 `new_buffer_with_data` which calls `newBufferWithBytes` (the full memcpy) and only then `buffers.write()` + `residency_set.insert`; candle-metal-kernels residency_set.rs:32-37 `insert` is `addAllocation` + `commit()` with no lock, so the lock is needed for the insert, not for the copy. :623-625 `let mut bytes = vec![0u8; size_in_bytes]; file.read_exact_at(&mut bytes, start as u64)` allocates and zero-fills a heap copy per tensor first. The owned path does the same at :700-701.
findings.rationale: The parallel part of the GGUF load is only the pread; every byte is then memcpy'd into Metal under one global mutex, so the device copy of a 15 GB file is a ~1.5 s single-threaded phase, preceded by calloc page zeroing, with up to one tensor-sized Vec<u8> per rayon worker alive while they queue on the lock (hundreds of MB transient on top of the file).
findings.proposal: Separate allocation from filling. Serially under the lock: `QMetalStorage::zeros(md, elem_count, dtype)` per entry (pooled allocation plus a queued fill blit, no memcpy), then one `drain_metal`. In parallel without the lock: `pread` each tensor straight into `storage.buffer().contents()` (shared storage, CPU-writable on unified memory), then `QTensor::new(QStorage::Metal(storage), dims)` and `StagedWeight::new(buffer.clone(), ..)`. For owned IQ weights use `md.allocate_buffer(size)` (pooled, inserted in the residency set, not filled) and `StagedWeight::of_kind`. `QStorage::Metal`, `QTensor::new`, `QMetalStorage::zeros`/`buffer`, `Buffer::contents` and `MetalDevice::allocate_buffer` are all public in candle 0.11, so no fork is needed.
findings.expected_benefit: One full-file memcpy and the calloc disappear, the remaining copy becomes N-way parallel, and the per-worker heap transient goes away; roughly 1-2 s on a 15 GB UD file and a corresponding share of the 2.7 s measured on the 4B Q4_K_M.
findings.verify_how: Time `GgufWeights::load` on Qwen3-4B-Q4_K_M (2.7 s in the May note) and on a 15 GB UD-Q4_K_M; peak RSS during load; temp-0 output and `weight_fingerprint` must be unchanged. Keep the IQ parity tests.

verdict.reason: The lock-across-memcpy claim is accurate: gguf_weights.rs:655-658 takes `metal_alloc_lock` and only then calls `qtensor_with_staged` -> :532 `QStorage::from_data` -> candle quantized/metal.rs:458-466 `load_quantized` -> `new_buffer_builder().with_data()` -> device.rs:398-401 -> :253-262 `new_buffer_with_data` (memcpy via newBufferWithBytes, then `buffers.write()` + `residency_set.insert`); build_owned does the same at :700-701. I could not open candle-metal-kernels on this Linux checkout (not vendored without the metal feature), so 'insert is unsynchronised' rests on the maintainer's comment at weights.rs:52-54, which is consistent with the ordering in device.rs. The proposal is implementable: `QMetalStorage::zeros` (quantized/metal.rs:14) and `buffer()` (:36) are pub, `MetalDevice::allocate_buffer` (device.rs:294) is pub and uses `StorageModeShared` (device.rs:74-76), so CPU writes through `contents()` are legal; QMetalStorage's fields are private so `zeros()` is the only constructor route and its fill blit must be drained before the parallel writes or it overwrites them (the reviewer orders this correctly). Worth is smaller than 'high': the serial part is one memcpy of the file at ~10-15 GB/s, ~0.2 s of the 2.7 s measured on the 4B Q4_K_M (PERFORMANCE_INVESTIGATION_GGUF.md:388) and ~1-1.5 s on a 15 GB file, load-time only, bought with raw-pointer writes into Metal buffers. Medium.
verdict.corrected_benefit: ~8-10% of GGUF load time (0.2 s on the 4B Q4_K_M, ~1-1.5 s on a 15 GB UD file) and removal of the per-worker tensor-sized Vec transient; no change to weights or output.
verdict.corrected_proposal: As stated, but prefer `md.allocate_buffer(size)` (no fill blit, no drain needed) wherever a constructor accepts a raw buffer (owned IQ weights via `StagedWeight::of_kind`), and use `QMetalStorage::zeros` + one drain only for candle-typed tensors; measure the serial memcpy share first with a timestamp around the locked region before committing the unsafe path.

findings.title: load_tensor_with_dtype's Metal branches are unreachable and the phase-2 every-16-tensors drains drain nothing on candle 0.11
findings.evidence: The only caller passes the CPU device: weights.rs:373 `&Device::Cpu,` inside the par_iter at :365. Hence :94 `if file_is_f8 && device.is_metal() && !keeps_file_dtype(name)` never fires, the guards at :119, :160 and :190 `let _guard = device.is_metal().then(|| metal_alloc_lock()...)` never lock, every `drain_metal(device, name)` inside is a no-op, and the :173 `Err(device_cast_err) => { ... reload on CPU ... }` fallback is dead. Phase 2 at :392-403: `let dev_t = cpu_t.to_device(device)` then `if i % 16 == 15 { drain_metal(device, name)?; }` and `drain_metal(device, "post-load")`; candle 0.11 `storage_from_cpu_storage` (metal_backend/mod.rs:2179) uses `new_buffer_builder().with_data()` -> `new_buffer_with_data` = synchronous `newBufferWithBytes`, no command buffer, so nothing is queued to drain. The comment at :344-356 ('staging buffers are only reclaimed at sync points') describes a path this candle does not take.
findings.rationale: About sixty lines of guarded device code, locks and drains that cannot execute encode a mental model of the loader that is wrong for the candle in Cargo.toml; the ROADMAP even plans to 'delete the loader drains' once upstream fixes staging reclamation, while on this path they already do nothing. Each vestigial drain commits and waits an empty command buffer (126 of them on a 2011-tensor checkpoint).
findings.proposal: Make `load_tensor_with_dtype` CPU-only (remove the device parameter, the FP8-on-Metal early path, the three guarded blocks and the device-cast fallback), delete the `% 16` drain, keep exactly one drain after the model build/KV pool (load_batch_model:858 already does it), and rewrite the two-phase comment to state the real constraints: residency-set insert is unsynchronised (hence the lock in parallel paths) and `to_device` queues nothing.
findings.expected_benefit: Smaller, truthful loader; tens of ms saved on high-tensor-count checkpoints; removes a trap for whoever tunes the drain cadence next.
findings.verify_how: cargo test; load gemma-4-E2B-it and Qwen3-4B-FP8 and compare `weight_fingerprint` and load time (equal or slightly lower).

verdict.reason: The only caller is weights.rs:370-378 and it passes `&Device::Cpu` (:373); grep finds no other call site. Hence :94 `file_is_f8 && device.is_metal()` never fires, the `device.is_metal().then(|| metal_alloc_lock()...)` guards at :119, :160, :190 never lock, every inner `drain_metal(device, name)` is a no-op (drain_metal at :60-66 only synchronizes a Metal device), and the :173 CPU-fallback arm is dead because the cast at :162 already runs on the CPU. Phase 2 (:391-403) calls `to_device` -> `storage_from_cpu_storage` (metal_backend/mod.rs:2179) -> `new_buffer_builder().with_data()` -> device.rs:398-401 -> `new_buffer_with_data` (:253), a synchronous newBufferWithBytes with no command buffer, so the `% 16` drains commit and wait on empty command buffers (and `drop_unused_buffers` finds nothing: `cpu_t` has no device buffer). The two-phase comment at :344-356 describes a staging path this candle does not take. Low risk, small win, better model of the loader. Keep the final drain at loader.rs:858 (it does matter for the queued cats/zeros).

findings.title: Safetensors path builds one RoPE cos/sin table per layer; the GGUF rope_sharing_plan fix was not applied here
findings.evidence: loader.rs:1326-1338 `let ropes = (0..cfg.num_hidden_layers).map(|i| RotaryEmbedding::new_with_scaling(per_layer_rotary_dims[i], ctx, per_layer_rope_thetas[i], cfg.rope_scaling.clone(), dtype, device))`; rope.rs:217-224 builds `positions.matmul(&inv_freq)` then `freqs.cos()?.to_dtype(dtype)` and `freqs.sin()?.to_dtype(dtype)`, two `[ctx, dim/2]` tables per call plus F32 intermediates. gguf_model.rs:328 `fn rope_sharing_plan` dedups by (dim, theta) and :609-640 clones one table per layer, with the doc noting 268 MB per table at Gemma 4's declared context and 12.9 GB when built per layer. `RotaryEmbedding` is `Clone` (rope.rs:69).
findings.rationale: Each layer's table costs ctx x rotary_dim x 2 bytes. With `--max-context-len 40960` on Qwen3-4B (36 layers, dim 128) that is 36 x 21 MB = 755 MB where 21 MB would do; a Gemma-4-class safetensors checkpoint (48 layers, dim 256/512) with a long pinned or granted context reproduces the multi-GB failure the GGUF path already fixed. The tables also cost 5 queued GPU ops per layer at load.
findings.proposal: Reuse `rope_sharing_plan` keyed on (rotary_dim, theta) (rope_scaling is uniform across layers in the HF config) and clone the shared `RotaryEmbedding` per layer, mirroring gguf_model.rs:609-640; move the helper to rope.rs so both loaders share it.
findings.expected_benefit: Device memory for rope tables drops from L tables to the number of distinct geometries (1-2): ~0.7 GB on Qwen3-4B at 40960 ctx, GBs on Gemma-4 at long contexts; fewer load-time kernels.
findings.verify_how: Load Qwen3-4B (safetensors) with `--max-context-len 40960` and compare the device's committed bytes after load before/after (expect ~0.7 GB less); outputs unchanged since the tables are identical.

verdict.reason: Mechanism verified: loader.rs:1326-1338 builds one `RotaryEmbedding` per layer; rope.rs:217-224 materialises `freqs.cos()?.to_dtype(dtype)` and `.sin()` as two `[ctx, dim/2]` tables in the runtime dtype plus F32 intermediates (which the candle pool recycles across layers since they are same-sized and dropped); gguf_model.rs:328 `rope_sharing_plan` and :605-631 share tables in the GGUF path only; `RotaryEmbedding` is `Clone` (rope.rs:69). The size claim is 2x too high: per layer cos+sin = ctx * (dim/2) * 2 tables * 2 B = ctx * dim * 2 B = 10.5 MB at 40960 x 128, so Qwen3-4B costs 377 MB (not 755 MB) where 10.5 MB would do. Gemma-4-class safetensors (dim 256/512, long context) still reaches GBs, which is the case the GGUF note documents. Proposal sound: `cfg.rope_scaling` is uniform, thetas differ per layer (local/global), so 1-2 distinct geometries.
verdict.corrected_benefit: ~0.37 GB on Qwen3-4B safetensors at 40960 ctx (36 tables -> 1); multi-GB on Gemma-4-class safetensors at long contexts; 5 queued load-time ops per layer become 5 per distinct geometry; tables identical so output unchanged.
verdict.corrected_proposal: Move `rope_sharing_plan` to rope.rs and reuse it in load_standard_safetensors keyed on (per_layer_rotary_dims[i], per_layer_rope_thetas[i]), cloning the shared table per layer exactly as gguf_model.rs:632-633 does.

findings.title: 4-bit tied lm_head RTN quantizes the already-uploaded embedding: device readback plus two F32 copies of the full vocabulary table on the CPU
findings.evidence: loader.rs:1245 `let raw = crate::common::awq::rtn_quantize_awq(&embed_weight, 128)?;` runs after phase 2 moved `embed_weight` to the device. awq.rs:656-662 `let w: Vec<f32> = weight.to_device(&Device::Cpu)?.to_dtype(DType::F32)?.flatten_all()?.to_vec1()?` is a readback, an F32 tensor and a second F32 Vec; :668-670 `vec![0u8; out_features * in_features]` nibbles; :711-712 packed i32; :726-735 `.t()?.contiguous()?` copies each output once more before `AnyLinear::from_awq` uploads it.
findings.rationale: For a 248k x 4096 embedding (Qwen3.5-class, the case the comment at :1234-1239 cites) that is ~2 GB read back from the device, ~4 GB + ~4 GB of F32, 1 GB of nibbles and ~0.5 GB packed, i.e. ~11 GB of CPU transient during an INT4 load on a 24 GB machine, plus the 0.3-5 s the May note measured. The F32 tensor exists only to be copied into a Vec.
findings.proposal: Run the RTN in phase 1 on the CPU BF16 tensor before upload (hook in ModelWeights::load behind the same quant-scheme gate, or give the loader the CPU copy): read `to_vec1::<bf16>()` once and convert per element inside the existing rayon row loop, skipping the F32 tensor; produce qweight/qzeros/scales directly in AWQ layout so the `.t().contiguous()` passes go away. Longer term, a small Metal kernel doing RTN+pack on the device removes the CPU pass entirely.
findings.expected_benefit: No device readback, ~6 GB less CPU transient on large-vocab INT4 models, and a shorter AWQ/CT4 load; numerically identical (same per-element F32 math).
findings.verify_how: Peak RSS and load time for Qwen3-4B-AWQ and a Qwen3.5 INT4 checkpoint before/after; assert the produced qweight/qzeros/scales are byte-identical to the current function on a fixed input.

verdict.reason: Verified: loader.rs:1245 runs `rtn_quantize_awq(&embed_weight, 128)` on the device tensor after phase 2; awq.rs:656-662 does `to_device(Cpu).to_dtype(F32).flatten_all().to_vec1()` (readback + an F32 tensor + an F32 Vec, 8 B/elem), :668-670 nibbles (1 B/elem), :711-712 packed words, :726-735 `.t().contiguous()` CPU transposes of the packed outputs. The transient estimate (~11 GB for a 248k x 4096 table) is right; the F32 tensor exists only to be copied into the Vec. The per-element RTN math is in F32 already so converting bf16->f32 per row inside the existing `par_chunks_mut` loop is bitwise identical. The cheaper fix is to keep the call site and change `rtn_quantize_awq` to read the weight in its own dtype (`to_vec1::<bf16>()`, or match on dtype) and convert per row; that removes the F32 tensor and F32 Vec (8 B/elem of the ~11 B/elem) with no plumbing of quant scheme/tie config into ModelWeights::load. The readback itself is a blit of 2 B/elem on unified memory and is cheap; the `.t().contiguous()` copies are 0.5 B/elem and minor.
verdict.corrected_benefit: CPU transient during INT4 load drops by ~8 B/elem (≈6 GB on a 248k x 4096 table, ≈3 GB on Qwen3-4B's 151936 x 2560), plus the single-threaded F32 cast and copy disappear; output bitwise identical.
verdict.corrected_proposal: In `rtn_quantize_awq`, replace the `to_dtype(F32).flatten_all().to_vec1::<f32>()` with a dtype-native `to_vec1::<bf16>()` (and F16/F32 arms) and convert each row to f32 inside the rayon row loop; optionally emit qweight/qzeros/scales directly in AWQ layout to drop the three `.t().contiguous()` passes. Moving the call into phase 1 can follow if the device readback shows up in a trace.

findings.title: Llama-family GGUF q/k de-interleave happens after upload: per-layer device readback, single-threaded shuffle, re-upload, and the originals stay resident until GgufWeights drops
findings.evidence: gguf_weights.rs:434 `tensor.data()?.into_owned()` (candle quantized/metal.rs:441-454: a `blit_to_cpu` encoder, wait, `read_to_vec`), :440 `let mut out = vec![0u8; data.len()];` followed by the sequential row loop, then :452 `qtensor_with_staged(tensor.dtype(), &out, vec![rows, k], device)` allocates a second device buffer; the original stays in `gguf.tensors` until `gguf` is dropped at the end of `load_batch_model_gguf` (loader.rs:1552). Called per layer from attention.rs:490-491 `if cfg.gguf_qk_permuted { crate::common::gguf_weights::depermute_qk_rows(&weight, heads, hd, device)? }` inside the sequential block loop.
findings.rationale: Two blit-and-wait round trips and two re-uploads per layer, on one thread: Llama-3-8B Q4_K_M is 64 tensors / ~380 MB read back, shuffled and re-uploaded, and held twice on the device until the loader returns. The shuffle is a pure byte permutation the loader could apply to the bytes it already has in hand before uploading.
findings.proposal: Apply the row permutation in `build_tensor` on the pread bytes (inside rayon, before the Metal allocation) when the file's architecture has `gguf_qk_permuted` set: read `general.architecture`, `attention.head_count`, `attention.head_count_kv` and `attention.key_length` from the header and pass a per-name `(n_heads, head_dim)` predicate into `parallelise_tensor_load`. Keep `depermute_qk_rows` as the reference implementation for the existing inverse-permute test.
findings.expected_benefit: Removes 2L device round trips and the duplicate q/k buffers for llama/mistral/granite GGUFs; the shuffle becomes parallel and free of GPU waits.
findings.verify_how: Time the block build for a Llama-3 or Mistral GGUF before/after; assert the uploaded q/k bytes equal `depermute_qk_rows`'s output; temp-0 output unchanged.

verdict.reason: Verified: gguf_weights.rs:434 `tensor.data()?.into_owned()` -> candle quantized/metal.rs:441-454 (`blit_to_cpu` encoder, `flush_and_wait_current`, `read_to_vec`); :440 `vec![0u8; data.len()]` then a sequential row copy; :452 `qtensor_with_staged` uploads a second device buffer; attention.rs:488-497 calls `depermute_qk_rows` for q and for k per layer from the sequential block loop whenever `cfg.gguf_qk_permuted`; the originals remain in `gguf.tensors` (Arc<QTensor>) until `gguf` drops at the end of load_batch_model_gguf (:1552), after the KV pool has been grown inside `load_gguf`. So 2L GPU waits, 2L readbacks, 2L re-uploads and ~380 MB of duplicated q/k on Llama-3-8B Q4_K_M, on one thread. Doing the row shuffle on the pread bytes in `build_tensor` (and in `build_owned` for IQ q/k) before the Metal allocation is a pure byte permutation and parallel for free; the loader needs the arch/head-count predicate that currently lives in the model config, which should be passed in rather than duplicated. Effort S-M; keep `depermute_qk_rows` as the reference for the existing test.

findings.title: GGUF materialises every tensor in the file, including blocks the model never uses (NextN prediction heads), before the topology says which ones matter
findings.evidence: gguf_weights.rs:547-565 `parallelise_tensor_load` builds `entries.iter().collect()` with no name filter; loader.rs:1490 `let gguf = GgufWeights::load_shards(&gguf_path_strs, device)?` runs before :1503 `parse_gguf_topology(&gguf)`, which at gguf_model.rs:247-253 reads `{arch}.nextn_predict_layers` and drops the trailing blocks only from `num_hidden_layers` ('Qwen3.8-27B ships 65 blocks for a 64-layer model'). The safetensors path has the equivalent filter at weights.rs:349-354 (`model.visual.`, `mtp.`).
findings.rationale: The unused block is read, zero-filled, memcpy'd into Metal, inserted into the residency set and then dropped with `gguf`: on a 16 GB 65-block file that is ~250 MB of device memory held through the KV sizing and ~1/65 of the load time, for nothing. The same applies to any future vision or MTP tensors llama.cpp emits.
findings.proposal: After `GgufHeader::parse`, read `general.architecture`, `{arch}.block_count` and `{arch}.nextn_predict_layers` from `header.content.metadata` and skip `blk.N.*` entries with N >= block_count - nextn (plus known non-text prefixes) before `parallelise_tensor_load`; make `total_size_bytes` reflect what was loaded.
findings.expected_benefit: ~1.5% load time and ~250 MB transient on Qwen3.8-27B-class files; a clean hook for skipping other unused tensor families.
findings.verify_how: Load a nextn-carrying GGUF and log the materialised tensor count and `total_size_bytes` before/after; confirm `estimate` and generation are unchanged.

verdict.reason: Accurate: `parallelise_tensor_load` (gguf_weights.rs:547-565) builds `entries.iter().collect()` with no name filter, `GgufWeights::load_shards` runs at loader.rs:1490 before `parse_gguf_topology` at :1503, which drops `nextn_predict_layers` only from `num_hidden_layers` (gguf_model.rs:247-253); `gguf` stays alive through `load_gguf` so the unused block coexists with the KV pool. But the benefit is one block of 65 (~1.5% of bytes and load time, ~250 MB transient) on the single model family that ships NextN heads; llama.cpp emits vision towers in separate mmproj files, so there is no wider class of dead tensors in a text GGUF today. Real, cheap, low impact.
verdict.corrected_benefit: ~1.5% load time and ~250 MB load-time transient on NextN-carrying GGUFs only; nothing on other files.
verdict.corrected_proposal: As stated: filter `blk.N.*` with N >= block_count - nextn_predict_layers after `GgufHeader::parse` and before `parallelise_tensor_load`; keep `total_size_bytes` consistent with what was materialised.

findings.title: KV pool is sized (and can fail) only after the weights are fully materialised, although both headers give the sizes up front
findings.evidence: GGUF: loader.rs:1490 `GgufWeights::load_shards` then :1501 `let weights_size = gguf.total_size_bytes();` then :1516 `compute_kv_blocks(...)` which bails at :1740 'KV cache budget exhausted'. Safetensors: :1111 `ModelWeights::load` then :1167 `compute_kv_blocks`. The sizes are header-derivable: :940-968 `expert_split_runtime_bytes` already sums `view.data().len()` scaled by dtype from the safetensors header without touching data, and `GgufHeader.tensors` carries dims and type id per tensor.
findings.rationale: When the global budget cannot grant the 256-block minimum (several models resident, or a draft reserving half the budget at manager.rs:1068-1070), the failure is reported only after a 5-30 s load that read and uploaded every weight, and the failed-load path then has to drop and drain all of it.
findings.proposal: Compute `weights_bytes` from the header(s) (reuse `expert_split_runtime_bytes` for safetensors, a dims x type-size sum over `header.tensors` for GGUF), run `compute_kv_blocks` and acquire the budget before materialising, release it on any load error; keep the post-load drain/fingerprint retry as is.
findings.expected_benefit: Budget refusals surface in milliseconds instead of after a full load; no behaviour change on the success path.
findings.verify_how: Start the server with a tiny `--memory-budget`, request a model, and time the refusal before/after.

verdict.reason: The ordering is as claimed (GGUF: loader.rs:1490 load_shards then :1501/:1516 compute_kv_blocks; safetensors: :1111 then :1167) and the sizes are header-derivable (`expert_split_runtime_bytes` :939-968 already does it for safetensors, `TensorEntry` dims/type for GGUF; `runtime_size_bytes` at weights.rs:576-581 is the same sum modulo the F32-pinned scalars). But the path is rare: the manager now evicts idle models before loading (CHANGELOG 'Unreleased'), so 'KV cache budget exhausted' (:1738-1748) surfaces only when the budget is tiny or a draft reserves it, and the dominant cost in the failure story is the retry loop (:822-890), which re-reads and re-uploads all weights per halving by design and which this proposal does not touch. api-ux polish, S.
verdict.corrected_benefit: A budget refusal returns in milliseconds instead of after a full load on the rare configurations that still hit it; no change on the success path.
verdict.corrected_proposal: Compute `weights_bytes` from the headers (reuse `expert_split_runtime_bytes`; add a dims x type-size sum over `GgufHeader.tensors`), run `compute_kv_blocks` and acquire the budget before materialising, release on any error; keep the post-load drain/fingerprint retry unchanged.

findings.title: gguf_probe's skip_value recurses without a depth bound on untrusted remote bytes and ignores the GGUF version (v1 lengths are 4 bytes)
findings.evidence: gguf_probe.rs:153-168 `fn skip_value(&mut self, tag: u32) -> Option<()> { match tag { ... 9 => { let elem = self.u32()?; let n = self.u64()?; for _ in 0..n { self.skip_value(elem)?; } ...` has no depth counter, whereas the local reader has gguf_header.rs:96 `const MAX_DEPTH: usize = 64;` and :159-160 `if depth >= MAX_DEPTH { anyhow::bail!(...) }`. :183 `let (Some(_version), Some(n_tensors), Some(n_kv)) = (c.u32(), c.u64(), c.u64())` discards the version and :147-148 `fn string(&mut self) -> Option<String> { let n = self.u64()? as usize;` always reads 8-byte lengths, while gguf_header.rs:134-139 reads 4 bytes for `GgufV1`. The bytes come from a 96 MB range request (:242, :256) to a third-party repository.
findings.rationale: A header whose metadata nests arrays of arrays costs 12 bytes per level, so a few MB of hostile or merely odd bytes recurse hundreds of thousands of frames and abort `oxydllm pull` with a stack overflow instead of returning `Unknown`; the `hostile_bytes` fuzz never nests, so the gap is untested. A v1 file misparses and most likely yields `Unknown`, silently skipping the check that exists to save a download.
findings.proposal: Thread a `depth` argument through `skip_value` and return `None` past 64 (mirror gguf_header.rs); read the version and use 4-byte counts/lengths for v1; add a deeply nested case to `hostile_bytes` and a v1 header case to the tests.
findings.expected_benefit: The probe honours its 'never fails' contract on any input; v1 files get a real verdict.
findings.verify_how: Unit test: a header with 300k nested empty arrays returns `HeaderVerdict::Unknown` without overflowing; a v1-encoded header of plain K-quants returns `Loadable`.

verdict.reason: gguf_probe.rs:153-168 `skip_value` recurses on tag 9 with no depth argument, while the local reader bounds depth (gguf_header.rs:96 `MAX_DEPTH = 64`, :159-160 bail). A nested array costs 12 bytes per level (4-byte elem tag + 8-byte count with n=1), so an 8 MB prefix of the 96 MB range (:242, :256) yields ~700k frames and aborts `oxydllm pull` with a stack overflow instead of `Unknown`, violating the 'never fails' contract at :244-247; the fuzz helper (:310-330) emits random bytes and never constructs nesting, so the gap is untested. The v1 half is accurate (:147-148 always 8-byte lengths, :183 discards `_version`, gguf_header.rs:134-139 reads 4 bytes for V1) but nearly worthless: in v1 `n_tensors`/`n_kv` are also u32 so the probe misparses immediately and returns `Unknown`, the download proceeds and the local reader handles v1; keep it only for consistency. Medium (process abort on hostile input from a third-party repo), S.

findings.title: The full GGUF header (tokenizer vocab and merges arrays) is parsed on every model-list refresh per file and twice per load; load_shards deep-copies it
findings.evidence: loader.rs:603-606 `fn discover_gguf_model` -> `GgufHeader::read(gguf_path)`, whose parser (gguf_header.rs:192-205) decodes every metadata value, including `tokenizer.ggml.tokens`/`merges`/`scores` arrays, `Vec::with_capacity` per array, to read three fields. It runs per variant from scan_model_entry (:204), which manager.rs:420-424 refreshes whenever `DISCOVERY_CACHE_TTL` (5 s, manager.rs:156) expires, and at startup (routes/mod.rs:204, manager.rs:300). Per GGUF load the header is parsed by tokenizer.rs:226 `GgufHeader::read(gguf_path)` and again by gguf_weights.rs:130 `GgufHeader::parse(&mmap[..])`. gguf_weights.rs:313 `metadata = header.content.metadata.clone();` deep-copies the map for sharded files.
