findings.rationale: A 150k-token vocabulary is ~450k heap allocations per parse (tens of ms per file); a models directory with ten GGUF variants pays that on every listing window and every `oxydllm list`, and each GGUF load pays it twice (plus a copy for shards). Small, but it is pure overhead on the request path of `/v1/models`.
findings.proposal: Add a discovery-mode parse that skips metadata values other than a few `general.*`/`{arch}.block_count` scalars (reuse gguf_probe's skipping cursor or a `skip_arrays` flag in `Cursor::value`), cache discovery by (path, mtime), hand the tokenizer's parsed `Content` to `GgufWeights::load` (or vice versa), and move rather than clone the metadata in load_shards.
findings.expected_benefit: Listing cost per file drops from tens of ms to under a ms; one fewer full parse per load; no behaviour change.
findings.verify_how: Time `oxydllm list` and `GET /v1/models` after the cache expires on a directory with ~10 GGUF variants; time the tokenizer+loader header steps on one load.

findings.title: The post-load consistency check fingerprints a single hidden_size-element norm buffer, so a lost write anywhere else passes
findings.evidence: loader.rs:917-928 `fn weights_read_consistently` calls `model.weight_fingerprint()` twice around a drain and compares; gguf_model.rs:689-691 `fn weight_fingerprint(&self) -> Option<f64> { self.norm.fingerprint() }`; norm.rs:39-51 reads `self.weight` (one tensor of hidden_size elements, 8-16 KB) to the CPU and sums `(i+1)*x`. The retry loop at :858-890 halves the pool only on this signal or a failed drain. The ROADMAP's own design ('the loader knows each weight's checksum from the CPU side for free ... read one small tensor back and confirm the upload survived') is only partly implemented: nothing is compared against a CPU-side value.
findings.rationale: The check samples one buffer out of thousands and only tests that two reads agree across a drain; the buffers most likely to be crowded by a pool allocation are the large ones. The maintainer's three positive cases happened to touch the norm; a corruption confined to attention or FFN weights would load 'successfully' and produce garbage, which is the exact failure the loop exists to prevent.
findings.proposal: Compute a cheap CPU-side checksum for a handful of large tensors during phase 1 (safetensors) or in `build_tensor` (GGUF: the bytes are in hand), e.g. the embedding and the first and last layer's down/qkv projections, and after the final drain compare against a device-side reduction of the same tensors (a strided `sum_all` or a tiny kernel reading the raw bytes); have `weight_fingerprint` return the vector of expected/actual pairs so the retry loop can name the tensor that lost writes.
findings.expected_benefit: Detection probability scales with the sampled bytes instead of one 8 KB buffer; the retry loop and the D1 memory constants gain a trustworthy oracle.
findings.verify_how: Reproduce the oversized-pool case from the alpha.15 notes (Qwen3-4B-FP8 with a forced 12 GB pool) and confirm detection with the norm excluded from the sample; run the 32-model sweep to confirm no false positives.

verdict.reason: Verified: loader.rs:917-928 compares two `weight_fingerprint()` reads a drain apart; gguf_model.rs:703-705 returns `self.norm.fingerprint()`; norm.rs:39-51 reads one hidden_size-element tensor (8-16 KB). Both reads happen after the full drain at :858, so the check does not compare against a known-good value: a buffer whose writes were lost before the first read returns the same wrong bytes twice and passes; what the maintainer observed (first read 5_592_404_480, later reads 9_073_553) is a first readback that failed, not a stable corruption, so the oracle is empirical and narrow. The ROADMAP D1 text asks for a CPU-side checksum. The reviewer's device-side reduction is unnecessary: on unified memory reading back a few tens of MB is milliseconds, so hash the raw bytes of K large tensors where they are already in hand (GGUF: `build_tensor` bytes; safetensors: the CPU tensor before `to_device`), read them back after the final drain and compare. Keep the norm check. Confidence that this changes outcomes is moderate since the failure mode is undocumented; sweep must show no false positives.
verdict.corrected_benefit: Detection covers hundreds of MB of the buffers most exposed to pool pressure instead of one 8 KB tensor, with a CPU-side ground truth; the retry loop can name the tensor that lost writes.
verdict.corrected_proposal: Compute a cheap byte hash (e.g. xxh3/FNV over raw bytes) for the embedding and the first/last layer's largest projections at load (GGUF in `build_tensor`, safetensors just before `to_device`), store them beside the model, and after the :858 drain read those tensors back (`to_vec`/`QStorage::data`) and compare; return the mismatching names through `weight_fingerprint`-style trait method so the halving loop logs them.

findings.title: Safetensors same-dtype tensors are copied twice (page cache to Vec in parallel, then Vec to MTLBuffer on one thread in hash order)
findings.evidence: Phase 1 at weights.rs:365-373 calls `mmap.load(name, &Device::Cpu)` -> candle safetensors.rs:115-123 `convert_slice` -> `Tensor::from_slice(data, shape, device)` (copy into a Vec; for a BF16 file at BF16 runtime nothing else happens, :144-146 short-circuit). Phase 2 at :391-397 `let names: Vec<String> = tensors.keys().cloned().collect(); for (i, name) in names.iter().enumerate() { let cpu_t = tensors.remove(name)...; let dev_t = cpu_t.to_device(device)` is a single-threaded `newBufferWithBytes` per tensor (candle device.rs:253-257) walked in FxHashMap order.
findings.rationale: For the common BF16-in/BF16-out checkpoint phase 1 exists only to feed phase 2; the second copy is ~1 s per 10 GB on one core plus 2000 `residency_set.commit()` calls, i.e. a sizeable share of the 9.2 s measured on gemma-4-E2B-it (the May note already attributed ~3 ms/tensor to the Metal side).
findings.proposal: Same shape as loading-3: for tensors whose file dtype equals the runtime dtype and that carry no scale, skip phase 1; in phase 2 call `md.allocate_buffer(bytes)` serially (residency insert under the lock) for all of them, then copy from the mmap slice (or pread) into `buffer.contents()` in parallel with rayon, wrapping with `MetalStorage::new(buffer, device, count, dtype)` (candle metal_backend/mod.rs:1908, pub) and `Tensor::from_storage` (tensor.rs:601, pub). Keep the CPU phase for casts, FP8 and scale folds.
findings.expected_benefit: One full-model copy removed and the other parallelised; on a 9.5 GB checkpoint roughly 0.5-1 s, more on high-tensor-count models where per-tensor overhead dominates.
findings.verify_how: Time `ModelWeights::load` on gemma-4-E2B-it (9.2 s baseline) and Llama-3.2-1B; `weight_fingerprint` and temp-0 output unchanged.

verdict.reason: Accurate: phase 1 (weights.rs:365-378) calls `mmap.load(name, &Device::Cpu)` -> candle safetensors.rs:115-123 `convert_slice` -> `Tensor::from_slice` (heap copy), and for BF16-in/BF16-out the dtype short-circuit at :144-146 means that copy is the only work; phase 2 (:391-403) then walks `tensors.keys()` in hash order on one thread with `to_device` -> `new_buffer_with_data` (device.rs:253). Also, `entries` holds the whole checkpoint in the heap before phase 2 starts. The parallel proposal is implementable (`MetalStorage::new` pub at metal_backend/mod.rs:1908, `Tensor::from_storage` pub at tensor.rs:601 with `BackpropOp::none()` pub at op.rs:1096, `allocate_buffer` pub and StorageModeShared) but is unsafe-pointer work for ~0.5-1 s of a 9.2 s load. A much cheaper first step gets the memory win and one of the two copies: for tensors whose file dtype equals the runtime dtype, carry no scale and are not `keeps_file_dtype`, skip phase 1 and call `mmap.load(name, device)` in phase 2 (one memcpy from the page cache into the MTLBuffer, no heap Vec). Measure, then parallelise only if the serial memcpy still dominates.
verdict.corrected_benefit: One full-model copy and the full-model heap transient between the phases disappear for same-dtype checkpoints (most BF16 models); ~0.3-0.6 s on gemma-4-E2B-it's 9.2 s, more where per-tensor overhead dominates; fingerprint and output unchanged.
verdict.corrected_proposal: In `ModelWeights::load`, partition `names` into 'direct' (file dtype == runtime dtype, no `_scale_inv` companion, not keeps_file_dtype, not F8) and 'cast'; run phase 1 only on 'cast'; in phase 2 upload 'direct' tensors with `mmap.load(name, device)` under the existing sequential loop and the others with `to_device`. Revisit the rayon `allocate_buffer` + `contents()` fill if a timestamp around phase 2 still shows >0.5 s.

findings.title: The pre-download header probe fetches up to 96 MB before parsing a byte, through a client with no timeout
findings.evidence: gguf_probe.rs:242 `const HEADER_PROBE_BYTES: u64 = 96 * 1024 * 1024;`, :256 `format!("bytes=0-{}", HEADER_PROBE_BYTES - 1)`, :261 `match req.send().and_then(|r| r.bytes()) { Ok(b) => inspect_header(&b), ...}` buffers the whole range before `inspect_header` runs. The client comes from hub.rs:336-337 `reqwest::blocking::Client::builder().timeout(None)` and is passed at hub.rs:435 `probe_remote(&client, &url, ...)`.
findings.rationale: A real header (vocab plus merges) is 5-30 MB, so most probes download 3-20x more than the verdict needs: 96 MB is 8-80 s on a 10-100 Mbit/s link, in front of a check sold as 'answers in seconds', and a connection that stalls hangs `pull` indefinitely, contradicting the 'never fails' contract of the function.
findings.proposal: Fetch progressively (2 MB, then x4 up to 96 MB), running `inspect_header` after each step and stopping at the first non-Unknown verdict, through a probe-specific client with a ~15 s timeout; or stream the body and parse incrementally with the existing cursor.
findings.expected_benefit: Typical probe cost drops to a few MB and a couple of seconds; a dead network can no longer wedge `pull`.
findings.verify_how: Time `oxydllm pull` of a UD variant on a throttled link before/after; simulate a stalled server and confirm the probe returns `Unknown` within the timeout.

verdict.reason: Verified: gguf_probe.rs:242 `HEADER_PROBE_BYTES = 96 MB`, :256 `bytes=0-{}` range, :261 `req.send().and_then(|r| r.bytes())` buffers the whole range before `inspect_header`; the client is built at hub.rs:336-337 with `.timeout(None)` and passed at :435. Real headers are 7-10 MB for a 151k vocab and ~15-20 MB for 262k, so 96 MB is 5-10x what the verdict needs (8 s at 100 Mbit/s before the first byte is parsed), and a stalled connection hangs `pull` with no timeout, against the function's own 'never fails' doc (:244-247). `inspect_header` already returns `Unknown` on truncation (:171-174, :205-217), so a progressive fetch (8 MB -> 32 MB -> 96 MB, stop at the first non-Unknown) through a probe-specific client with a 15-30 s timeout is correct and small.

subsystems.assessment: The manager is small, well-commented and its locking discipline is right where it matters: the tokio mutex is taken only around slot bookkeeping, loads run on their own OS threads, the chat route awaits the oneshot outside the lock, and the per-device gpu lock serializes warm-up against other engines. The hub's resume logic is careful and well tested, and the new header probe before download is exactly the right instinct. What is fragile is the lifecycle glue around eviction, which has drifted out of step with the engine loop and the device-sizing work: the alpha.15 slot guard holds a strong channel sender on the engine thread, so an idle engine told to shut down blocks forever in blocking_recv and never frees its weights while the manager has already released its KV budget and will load the next model on top of it; and the manager decides "CPU or GPU" from --devices being empty, which is always true on Metal, so every first load of an unregistered model is projected at the CPU F32 expansion (2x safetensors, up to 7.5x+ GGUF) and evicts everything resident, and the global KV ceiling never consults the device working set the maintainer built for exactly this purpose. Those two together are the biggest lever in this subsystem: fixing them makes eviction and the implicit memory ceiling actually mean what the CHANGELOG says they mean, which also matters for the silent-corruption class the maintainer has been chasing, since oversubscription is its known trigger. Second tier: Loading slots are invisible to the budget so concurrent loads oversubscribe, keep-alive counts in-flight generation as idle, aliases double-load the same weights, and the warm-up comment still defends an ordering against a candle SDPA path the decoder no longer takes while leaving the MPP GEMM, batched GEMV and long-KV FA kernels to be built on the first real request. The CLI (run) duplicates the engine assembly and a quadratic version of the streaming decoder the server already solved; env-var scope diverges per subcommand. The estimate command is honest about being a label lookup for quality but its KV figure ignores hybrid layers and the loader's actual ceiling. None of these touch the per-token GPU path; the headroom here is memory correctness, cold-start latency and operator trust rather than tok/s.

findings.title: Evicted idle engines never exit: slot guard keeps the request channel open while the loop blocks in blocking_recv
findings.evidence: manager.rs:1184 `let engine_tx = request_tx.clone();` ... :1256-1261 `let _slot_guard = EngineSlotGuard { manager: manager_thread, model_id: ..., request_tx: engine_tx, }; engine_loop(engine, tokenizer, request_rx, shutdown, model_id_thread);` (guard lives on the engine thread for the whole loop). src/server/routes/engine_loop.rs:640 `if shutdown.load(Ordering::Acquire) { break; }` is only reached after :656 `match request_rx.blocking_recv() { Some(req) => ..., None => break }`, which blocks until a request arrives or every Sender is dropped. The three eviction sites only remove the slot and set the flag, sending nothing: manager.rs:570-573 (`self.kv_budget.release(kv_bytes); self.slots.remove(&id); ... s.store(true, Ordering::Release)`), :702-705 (evict_expired), :1336-1345 (post-load over-budget). The guard's own `engine_tx` is a strong Sender, so after the slot's sender is dropped the channel still has one sender and blocking_recv never returns None.
findings.rationale: Keep-alive eviction by definition targets idle engines, i.e. ones parked in blocking_recv. After eviction the manager has released the model's KV-budget bytes (:570, :702, :1273) and dropped it from total_loaded_bytes, so the next get_or_load will load another model (or a fresh copy of the same one) while the old thread still owns its weights and KV pool on the GPU. Every evict/reload cycle leaks one model-sized footprint; this is the oversubscription pattern the maintainer identified as the trigger of silent output corruption. The unit tests only check the slot map (engine_panic_removes_stale_slot, evict_expired_removes_idle_slot), never that the engine thread terminates, so nothing catches it.
findings.proposal: Hold a `tokio::sync::mpsc::WeakSender` in the guard instead of a Sender: `request_tx: request_tx.downgrade()` and compare with `WeakSender::same_channel_as_sender(&slot_tx)` (available in the locked tokio 1.52.2, bounded.rs:1913). With no strong sender on the engine thread, removing the slot drops the last Sender (once in-flight ReadyHandle clones finish) and blocking_recv returns None, so the loop exits exactly when evicted. Belt and braces: make the idle wait observe the flag, e.g. loop on `blocking_recv` from a channel whose Receiver the evictor can `close()` (store a `tokio::sync::Notify`/`AbortHandle` in the slot), or have the evictor send a sentinel `IncomingRequest::Shutdown`. Add a test that installs a Ready slot backed by a real engine_loop on a thread, calls evict_expired, and asserts the thread joins within a bounded time.
findings.expected_benefit: Eviction and the implicit memory ceiling start actually freeing memory. On the M5 this is the difference between a 24 GB machine holding one model after keep-alive and holding N stale copies; it removes an entire class of oversubscription that the KV/weight sizing constants were fitted around.
findings.verify_how: On the M5: start with --keep-alive 10, send one chat request, wait 60 s. /v1/models/running is empty and the log says 'evicting idle model', but `ps -o rss` / Activity Monitor for the oxydllm process and `sudo powermetrics`/`vm_stat` show the weights still resident and no 'engine loop exited' log line. Repeat load/evict three times and watch RSS grow by one model each time. After the WeakSender change the thread exits and memory returns within a second of eviction.

verdict.reason: Verified line by line. manager.rs:1184 `let engine_tx = request_tx.clone();` and :1256-1261 build `EngineSlotGuard { request_tx: engine_tx, .. }` on the engine thread and keep it alive across `engine_loop(...)`. engine_loop.rs:640 checks the shutdown flag only at the top of the loop, and when `!engine.has_pending_work()` the loop parks in `request_rx.blocking_recv()` (:656-664), which returns `None` only when every `Sender` is gone. All three evictors do exactly slot-remove + flag-store and nothing else: :570-573 (LRU), :702-705 (evict_expired), :1341-1345 (post-load over-budget). Removing the slot drops the slot's Sender, but the guard's own strong Sender keeps the channel open, so an idle engine never wakes, never sees the flag, and never drops its weights/KV pool, while `kv_budget.release` and `total_loaded_bytes` (:365-376, Ready-only) already count the memory as free. Keep-alive eviction targets idle engines by definition, so this is the common path, not a race. The tests at :1585-1630 only exercise the guard's Drop in isolation, never an engine parked in blocking_recv. The proposal is implementable as stated: tokio 1.52.2 bounded.rs:1547 `Sender::downgrade` and :1913 `WeakSender::same_channel_as_sender` both exist, and ReadyHandle clones (:625-629) are dropped at request end, so the last strong Sender disappears exactly at eviction. The only path where the flag alone can work is the post-load unload (:1322-1360) when it wins the race against the loop's first iteration. Severity high is right: every evict/reload cycle leaks one model footprint on the GPU, and the released KV budget then lets the next load allocate a second pool beside a live one, the silent-corruption pattern the ROADMAP D1 section describes.

findings.title: Manager decides CPU-vs-GPU from `--devices` being empty, which is always true on Metal: first-load projections use CPU F32 expansion and the KV ceiling skips the device query
findings.evidence: manager.rs:313-314 `let is_cpu = cuda_devices.is_empty(); let kv_total = detect_system_kv_budget(memory_budget_bytes, is_cpu);` and :485 `let is_cpu = self.cuda_devices.is_empty();` followed by :500-507 `if is_cpu { if let Some(gguf_path) = find_gguf_file(model_path) { let factor = gguf_cpu_expansion(&gguf_path); ((gpu_bytes as f64 * factor) as usize, factor) } else { (gpu_bytes * 2, 2.0) } } else { (gpu_bytes, 1.0) }`. main.rs resolve_devices returns `vec![]` unless --devices/OXYDLLM_DEVICES is given; loader.rs:735-760 select_device_at ignores the index on Metal. paged.rs:70-72 `if !is_cpu && let Some(budget) = device_working_set_bytes()` is therefore skipped on every Mac and the budget falls to `physical * 0.65 - 512 MB`. estimate.rs:698-716 gguf_cpu_expansion returns 7.5 for Q4_K/Q5_K/Q6_K, 10-13 for Q2/Q3. The projection is then passed to :639 `self.evict_lru_for_bytes(needed_bytes)` whose loop (:548-575) evicts until `used + needed <= budget`.
findings.rationale: On the only verified platform the manager believes it is on CPU. A first load of a 15 GB Q4_K_M GGUF is projected at ~113 GB, which can never fit the 17.76 GB implicit ceiling, so the loop evicts every resident model before each first load of any unregistered model (the registry hides this for models the maintainer has loaded before, which is why it goes unnoticed on the sweep set). A BF16 safetensors model is projected at 2x. The global KV ceiling also stops being 'what the device says' as documented in paged.rs and becomes a fitted fraction, the very thing the ROADMAP's D1 item is trying to retire. `run_interactive` gets it right (main.rs:1135 `matches!(device, Device::Cpu)`), so the two entry points disagree.
findings.proposal: Give ModelManager an explicit `is_cpu: bool` computed once in `new` by selecting the device the loader will select (`loader::select_device_at(first_idx, require_gpu).map(|d| d.is_cpu())`, or cache the Device itself since engines run on one device) and use it in both sites; drop the `cuda_devices.is_empty()` heuristic. Log the projected size with its source so an operator can see it. Combine with finding 3 so GGUF projections sum only the chosen variant.
findings.expected_benefit: Stops wholesale eviction on first loads (each unnecessary reload of a 4-15 GB model costs 5-60 s of load plus warm-up), and routes the server's KV ceiling through recommendedMaxWorkingSetSize as designed. Removes a silent divergence between `run` and `start` memory sizing.
findings.verify_how: On the M5: delete `.oxydllm_registry.json`, start the server with two models resident, then request a third never-loaded GGUF. Current log shows `model not in registry, using projected memory size ... cpu_expansion_factor=7.5` and one 'evicting LRU model due to memory pressure' line per resident model; after the fix the factor is 1.0 and only what is needed is evicted. Also compare the 'global KV cache budget configured' line before/after: it should move from physical*0.65-0.5 GB to min(17.76 GB, free).

verdict.reason: Mechanism verified: manager.rs:313 and :485 both use `cuda_devices.is_empty()` as `is_cpu`; main.rs:119-132 `resolve_devices` returns `vec![]` without --devices/OXYDLLM_DEVICES and :839 passes it through; loader.rs:735-753 ignores the index on Metal; paged.rs:70-89 skips `device_working_set_bytes()` when `is_cpu` and returns physical*0.65-512MB; estimate.rs:698-713 returns 7.5 for Q4_K/Q5_K/Q6_K. So on every Mac a registry miss projects a Q4_K_M GGUF at ~7.5x and a safetensors model at 2x. But the consequences are smaller than claimed. (a) The implicit eviction ceiling is `safe_total_commitment_bytes()` (paged.rs:242-250), which does consult `device_working_set_bytes()` regardless of is_cpu, so the LRU ceiling is already device-derived; only the global KV sum uses the fitted fraction, and on a 24 GB M5 that gives 15.1 GB instead of min(17.76 GB, free), i.e. more conservative, not dangerous. (b) The inflated projection only makes `evict_lru_for_bytes` (:528-546) evict every Ready slot once, then the load proceeds anyway (`None => break`); this is a one-time cost per never-loaded model id, hidden after the first success by the registry (:476-479). On the maintainer's one-model-at-a-time sweep it is invisible; in multi-model serving it costs one spurious reload of each resident model per first load (5-60 s). That is a real defect on the only verified platform but not a >5% steady-state or corruption risk on its own; it becomes dangerous only through finding 1 (each spurious eviction leaks a model). Proposal is sound and cheap; `device_working_set_bytes()` already creates a Metal device at startup, so `is_cpu` can come from the same probe.
verdict.corrected_benefit: No wholesale eviction of resident models on the first load of an unregistered model (one spurious reload of each resident model, 5-60 s each, per new model id); KV global ceiling becomes device-derived (15.1 GB -> min(17.76 GB, free) on a 24 GB M5), a sizing consistency fix rather than a throughput gain. Combined with finding 1 it removes a leak trigger.
verdict.corrected_proposal: In ModelManager::new, derive `is_cpu` from the device the loader will actually pick: `loader::select_device_at(cuda_devices.first().copied().unwrap_or(0), require_gpu).map(|d| d.is_cpu()).unwrap_or(true)` (or reuse the Metal probe that `device_working_set_bytes` already performs), store it on the manager, and use it at :313 and :485; delete the `cuda_devices.is_empty()` heuristic. Log `projected_gb` with `source=registry|disk` and the factor so an operator sees it.

findings.title: First-load projection for a GGUF folder sums every variant on disk and carries no KV term, so it disagrees with both the loader and the registry
findings.evidence: manager.rs:484 `let disk_bytes = estimate_model_size(model_path);` where estimate_model_size (:233-247) sums every `.safetensors` or `.gguf` in the directory; resolve_model_path returns the directory for a variant id (loader.rs:368-400), and the loader then picks one variant via select_gguf_paths. Registry hits return `entry.size_bytes + entry.kv_cache_bytes` (:476-479) while the disk path returns weights only. estimate.rs:77-85 already shows the right call: `let chosen = crate::models::loader::select_gguf_paths(dir, model_id, all)?;`. hub.rs select_variant actively encourages multi-variant folders ('Already downloaded: ✓ Q4_K_M' then pick another).
findings.rationale: A folder holding Q4_K_M (15 GB) + Q8_0 (27 GB) projects 42 GB for a 15 GB load, which under the 17.76 GB implicit ceiling evicts everything (independently of finding 2). In the other direction, safetensors first loads project without the pool the loader will ask for (compute_kv_blocks asks for max_num_sequences x context up to safe_model_kv_ceiling), so the LRU pass makes too little room and relies on the GlobalKvBudget to refuse, which then fails the load with 'KV cache budget exhausted' instead of evicting.
findings.proposal: In projected_size_bytes: for GGUF dirs use `find_gguf_files` + `select_gguf_paths(model_path, model_id, files)` and sum only those shards; add a KV term using the same arithmetic the loader uses (expose a pure `kv_request_bytes(weights_bytes, context, seqs)` from loader/paged that applies safe_model_kv_ceiling) so registry-less and registry-backed projections have the same shape. Keep the registry as the exact override.
findings.expected_benefit: Eviction pressure proportional to the model actually loading; no spurious full evictions in multi-variant folders; fewer 'budget exhausted' failures that eviction could have prevented.
findings.verify_how: Pull two variants of one GGUF repo into one folder, remove the registry file, load the smaller variant next to a resident model: log 'projected_gb' currently equals the folder total; after the fix it equals the chosen file (+KV).

verdict.reason: Verified. manager.rs:233-247 `estimate_model_size` sums every `.safetensors`/`.gguf` in the directory; :484 feeds that into the projection; the registry path (:476-479) returns `size_bytes + kv_cache_bytes` while the disk path has no KV term at all. loader.rs:299-303 `select_gguf_paths` is `pub(crate)` and estimate.rs:77-85 already uses it to pick the variant the server would load, so the manager can do the same. The `find_gguf_file` at :490 only picks the factor source (gguf.index first entry or first .gguf, loader.rs:578-596), the sum still counts all variants. hub.rs's variant picker makes multi-variant folders normal. Effort S and medium severity are honest: the effect is spurious eviction (via :528-546) on first loads of multi-variant folders, and under-reservation for safetensors first loads that the GlobalKvBudget then refuses instead of evicting. For the KV term, approximate with the same ceiling the loader applies (`safe_model_kv_ceiling`-style arithmetic); exactness is not needed for an eviction heuristic.

findings.title: Loading slots carry no projected bytes, so two concurrent loads both pass the eviction check against the same total
findings.evidence: manager.rs:365-376 total_loaded_bytes sums only `SlotState::Ready { weights_size_bytes, kv_cache_bytes, .. }`; :639 `self.evict_lru_for_bytes(needed_bytes);` then :644-647 `self.slots.insert(model_id.to_string(), SlotState::Loading { waiters: vec![tx] });` stores nothing about size. evict_lru_for_bytes (:548-575) considers only Ready slots for both `used` and LRU candidates. The post-load check (:1322-1360) runs only `if let Some(budget) = mgr.memory_budget_bytes`, i.e. not under the implicit ceiling.
findings.rationale: Client A requests model X (15 GB) and client B requests model Y (12 GB) within the same load window (typical for a UI that lists models and immediately chats, or two users): both see `used = 0`, both evict nothing, both load, and 27 GB is committed on a 17.76 GB ceiling with no unload. With an explicit --memory-budget the second is unloaded only after its full load and warm-up, wasting 10-60 s and the device drain. The loader's own 'weights survived the pool' check is per load and does not see the sibling load.
findings.proposal: Store `projected_bytes` in `SlotState::Loading` and count it in a `committed_bytes()` that evict_lru_for_bytes and the post-load check use instead of total_loaded_bytes; when the loop cannot make room (no Ready slot left and still over), fail the waiters immediately with the same 'exceeds memory budget' message rather than proceeding. On install, replace the projection with the measured size.
findings.expected_benefit: Serialises memory commitment correctly under concurrent first requests; prevents the implicit-ceiling oversubscription path and the wasted second load under an explicit budget.
findings.verify_how: Start the server with two unregistered models that together exceed the implicit ceiling, fire two chat requests for them in parallel; currently both reach Ready and /v1/models/running reports total_loaded_bytes above safe_total_commitment_bytes. After the fix the second waits or is refused with a clear error.

verdict.reason: Verified. manager.rs:365-376 `total_loaded_bytes` counts only `SlotState::Ready`; :644-647 inserts `SlotState::Loading { waiters: vec![tx] }` with no size; the LRU loop :533-546 reads `used = self.total_loaded_bytes()` and considers only Ready slots; the post-load check :1322 runs only `if let Some(budget) = mgr.memory_budget_bytes`, so under the implicit ceiling nothing corrects a double commitment. No load-serialising lock exists (grep for a load mutex in manager.rs/loader.rs returns nothing; each load is its own OS thread, :1029+). Two first requests for different unregistered models inside one load window therefore both pass the check against the same `used` and both load. The shared `GlobalKvBudget` (Arc, :1081) bounds the KV pools collectively, so the oversubscription is weights-only, which is still the dangerous kind on unified memory. Storing `projected_bytes` in `Loading` and counting it is a small, local change; medium/S is right.

findings.title: Keep-alive treats an in-flight generation as idle: a per-request keep_alive override can evict the model mid-stream
findings.evidence: manager.rs:620 `*last_used = Instant::now();` is the only bump and happens when get_or_load returns the handle (request arrival), plus :1306 at install. :683-688 `SlotState::Ready { last_used, effective_keep_alive, .. } if now.duration_since(*last_used) > *effective_keep_alive => Some(id.clone())`. The override comes straight from the body: chat.rs:1589 `let keep_alive_override = body.keep_alive.map(Duration::from_secs);` (types.rs:126 `pub keep_alive: Option<u64>`), and :622-624 overwrites `effective_keep_alive` for the slot. spawn_eviction_task ticks every 30 s (:1385-1393). engine_loop.rs:640 breaks on the flag at the next step and then drains every tracker with `EngineEvent::Error("Model unloaded")` (:990-1000).
findings.rationale: A client sending `keep_alive: 0` (ollama semantics: unload after this request) or a small value gets its own stream killed at the next 30 s tick because `now - last_used > 0` is already true while tokens are still being generated; a long generation under the default 900 s with `--request-timeout 0` has the same exposure. README:401 documents keep-alive as 'Idle seconds before model eviction', and a model producing tokens is not idle.
findings.proposal: Put an `Arc<AtomicU64>` last-activity timestamp (or an in-flight counter) in the Ready slot and pass it to engine_loop, which stores `Instant`-derived millis after each step and on each completion; evict_expired compares against `max(last_used, last_active)` and never evicts a slot whose in-flight counter is non-zero. Optionally interpret `keep_alive: 0` as 'evict once the engine goes idle' by letting the engine loop set the shutdown flag itself when `has_pending_work()` becomes false.
findings.expected_benefit: No mid-stream 'Model unloaded' errors from the eviction task; keep-alive semantics match the documentation and the ollama-compatible field clients already send.
findings.verify_how: Send a chat request with `keep_alive: 0`, `max_tokens: 2000`, stream on, against a small model; within 30 s the stream ends with an error event and the log shows 'evicting idle model (keep-alive expired)'. After the fix the stream completes and eviction follows.

verdict.reason: Verified. The only `last_used` writes are manager.rs:620 (on get_or_load returning Ready) and the Ready install (:1306 area); :683-688 evicts when `now - last_used > effective_keep_alive` with no in-flight check; :1404-1412 ticks every 30 s; chat.rs:1589 takes `keep_alive` straight from the body (types.rs:126) and :622-624 overwrites the slot's `effective_keep_alive`, which is also sticky for every later client of that model. engine_loop.rs:640 breaks on the flag at the next iteration and :989-997 drains every tracker with `EngineEvent::Error("Model unloaded")`. So `keep_alive: 0` (ollama semantics) or any value shorter than the generation kills the client's own stream at the next tick. Rare path (needs a per-request override or a >900 s generation), so medium is right. The proposal is sound: engine_loop already has `trackers` (non-empty == in flight), so an `Arc<AtomicUsize>` in-flight counter or an `Arc<AtomicU64>` last-activity stamp passed through the slot is enough; also consider resetting `effective_keep_alive` to the server default after an override expires so one client's 0 does not stick.

findings.title: Warm-up comment defends an SDPA ordering the decoder no longer exercises, and the three phases skip the kernels the first real request builds (MPP GEMM at M>=64, batched GEMV, long-KV FA)
findings.evidence: manager.rs:840-842 `/// ... Phase 3 (full prefill) MUST be last: a Metal candle bug emits NaN logits on the first call_sdpa_full after a call_sdpa_vector call without an intervening full.` and :907 `const FULL_WARMUP_TOKENS: usize = 16;`. But candle's SDPA op is reached only from attention.rs:884 `super::metal_ops::sdpa(` inside the `use_seg_sdpa` branch, which requires attention.rs:833 `&& seg.num_tokens == 1`; metal_ops.rs:135-137 selects `call_sdpa_full` only for `q_seq > 8`, so the full kernel is unreachable from the decoder; multi-token segments go to `use_metal_fa` (attention.rs:810-826) or the naive matmul. Meanwhile metal_ops.rs:2546 `pub const MPP_GEMM_MIN_M: usize = 64;` with :2831 `dims[0] < MPP_GEMM_MIN_M` fallback, and MPP pipelines are built per kernel on first use (metal_ops.rs:2655 get_or_compile_mpp_pipeline -> newComputePipelineStateWithFunction); attention.rs:33 `const METAL_FA_MIN_KV: usize = 1024;` gates the FA decode path; the warm-up uses batch 1, 8/16 tokens, KV 16.
findings.rationale: The maintainer asked whether the NaN workaround is still needed: on the current code the decoder cannot trigger the vector->full transition because full is never called, so the ordering constraint is vestigial and the comment misleads the next reader (the 2026-05-16 investigation predates the FA gating). The real cost is what warm-up does not touch: the first prompt of >=64 tokens pays a TensorOps pipeline build per weight kind, the first concurrent request pays the batched GEMV kernels, and the first >1024-token context pays the FA decode kernel, all on the user's TTFT after 'model ready' was logged. The warm-up doc promised 'otherwise the first real request pays multi-second compilation latency' and that promise is only kept for the paths it happens to run.
findings.proposal: Rewrite the doc comment to the current rationale (JIT coverage: FA prefill, vector decode, quant GEMV; note the retired candle-full dependency and the date). Set phase 3 to `MPP_GEMM_MIN_M` tokens (64, well below any context) so the staged GEMM pipelines for every weight kind in the model are built; add a two-sequence decode step (two PagedKvCache slices, token_counts [1,1]) to build the batched GEMV kernels; optionally, when context_len >= 1024+16, run a 1024-token prefill followed by one decode so the FA decode path compiles too. Keep everything non-fatal as now.
findings.expected_benefit: Moves kernel-build latency from the first user prompt into load time where it is already reported as warmup_s. Magnitude on the M5 is unmeasured here; the maintainer's own comment calls the SDPA case multi-second, and TensorOps pipelines are heavier than plain compute pipelines.
findings.verify_how: After a fresh load, send a 200-token prompt and read the `ttft_ms` field of the 'first token emitted' log line; send the same prompt again. The difference is the un-warmed build cost. Repeat for two concurrent requests (batched GEMV) and for a 1500-token prompt + decode (FA decode). After widening the warm-up, first and second TTFT should match within noise and warmup_s should grow by roughly the same amount.

verdict.reason: The vestigial-comment claim is verified and datable: attention.rs:830-836 `use_seg_sdpa = ... && seg.num_tokens == 1 ...` is the only path to `metal_ops::sdpa` (the single caller is attention.rs:884), and metal_ops.rs:135-137 routes to `call_sdpa_full` only for `q_seq > 8`, so the full kernel (metal_ops.rs:277) is unreachable from the decoder. `git log -S` dates the `seg.num_tokens == 1` gate to commit 42943bf (2026-08-26), after the 2026-05-16 NaN investigation and after the ROADMAP's 2026-08-13 note that `FULL_WARMUP_TOKENS` 16 'exists because a bisect showed n=8 produced NaN and n=9 did not'; the comment at manager.rs:839-842 now describes a transition that cannot happen. The MPP gap is also real and larger than the reviewer thought: `mpp_library` compiles the kernel library from source (`newLibraryWithSource_options_error`, metal_ops.rs:2592) and pipelines via `newComputePipelineStateWithFunction` (:2655-2690) on first use, and warm-up at 8/16 tokens (:852, :907) never reaches `MPP_GEMM_MIN_M` 64 (:2546, :2831), so the first long prompt pays a Metal source compile plus per-kind pipeline builds after 'model ready'. Downgrades: (1) the proposed 64-token phase is insufficient, `min_m` (:3083-3091) is 64 only for Q4_0/Q4_1/Q5_0/Q5_1/Q4K, `MPP_MATVEC_MAX_M+1` for IQ kinds and 128 for everything else, so the warm prefill must be >= 128 tokens (or the model's max `min_m`); (2) the batched-GEMV and FA-decode (KV >= 1024) warm-ups are unverified here, a 1024-token warm prefill costs load time and pool on every load, and the maintainer's measure-first rule applies; keep those out until TTFT deltas are measured. Magnitude is unmeasured on either side; a source compile is typically hundreds of ms to a few seconds, once per process, which is why it belongs in warmup_s.
verdict.corrected_benefit: First-prompt TTFT after a fresh load no longer includes the TensorOps library compile and per-kind pipeline builds (once per process, hundreds of ms to seconds, unmeasured); the warm-up doc stops describing a path that no longer exists.
verdict.corrected_proposal: Rewrite the manager.rs:839-842 comment to the current rationale (FA prefill, vector decode, quant GEMV JIT; note that candle's `call_sdpa_full` has been unreachable since 42943bf). Raise the phase-3 prefill to 128 tokens (max of `min_m` across weight kinds, or compute it from the model's kinds) so the MPP library and staged-GEMM pipelines build during load; keep it non-fatal. Measure first-vs-second TTFT on a 200-token prompt before adding any batched-GEMV or 1024-KV phases.

findings.title: /v1/models rescans the models directory, parsing every GGUF header including tokenizer arrays, under the global manager lock on a tokio worker
findings.evidence: manager.rs:410-430 `pub fn discovered_with_registry(&mut self)` ... `if !fresh { self.discovery_cache = Some(DiscoveryCache { discovered: loader::discover_models(&self.models_dir), ... }) }` with DISCOVERY_CACHE_TTL = 5 s (:171); called as `state.manager.lock().await.discovered_with_registry()` (handlers.rs:15, :51), the same mutex every chat request takes at chat.rs:1588. discover_models -> scan_model_entry -> loader.rs:206 `discover_gguf_model(&effective_id, &paths[0])` per variant -> loader.rs:604 `GgufHeader::read(gguf_path)`, and gguf_header.rs:158-168 parses every array element (`for _ in 0..n { items.push(self.value(elem, depth + 1)?); }`), which includes tokenizer.ggml.tokens/merges (hundreds of thousands of strings). Startup scans twice: routes/mod.rs:204 and manager.rs:300 (ModelManager::new).
findings.rationale: Any client that polls /v1/models (Open WebUI and most desktop clients do, every few seconds) turns each TTL lapse into a synchronous multi-megabyte parse per GGUF variant executed on a runtime worker while holding the lock that get_or_load needs, so chat requests queue behind filesystem work that has nothing to do with them. The cost scales with the number of GGUF files in ~/.oxydllm/models, which for this maintainer is dozens.
findings.proposal: (1) Scan outside the lock: snapshot models_dir, `tokio::task::spawn_blocking(discover_models)`, then lock only to store the result (coalesce concurrent refreshes with a 'refresh in flight' flag). (2) Replace the 5 s TTL with mtime-based invalidation (models_dir mtime plus each model dir's mtime) so unchanged trees are never rescanned. (3) Give discover_gguf_model a metadata-only reader that skips array payloads (a `skip_value` in gguf_header that advances past arrays without materialising them) since discovery needs only general.architecture, block_count and the token_embd shape. (4) Pass the startup scan into ModelManager::new instead of scanning twice.
findings.expected_benefit: Removes O(#GGUF variants x header size) of parsing from the request path; with 20-30 GGUF files that is tens to hundreds of milliseconds of lock hold per refresh, repeated every 5 s under polling. Startup time drops by one full scan.
findings.verify_how: With 20+ GGUF files present, time `curl /v1/models` cold vs within 5 s; then run a 1 Hz /v1/models poller while sending chat requests and watch the `manager_ready_ms` debug field (chat.rs:1597) spike on refresh ticks. After the change it stays flat.

verdict.reason: Verified. manager.rs:156 `DISCOVERY_CACHE_TTL = 5 s`; :410-430 rescans inside `&mut self` (so under the manager mutex) whenever the cache is stale; handlers.rs:15 and :51 call it via `state.manager.lock().await`, the same mutex chat.rs:1588 takes for get_or_load. loader.rs:206 calls `discover_gguf_model` per variant, which at :604 does `GgufHeader::read` (mmap + full parse); gguf_header.rs:158-168 materialises every array element, so tokenizer token/merge arrays (hundreds of thousands of Strings) are allocated per GGUF per refresh. Startup scans twice (routes/mod.rs:204 and manager.rs:300). A 1 Hz /v1/models poller therefore puts O(#GGUF x header size) of synchronous parsing on a tokio worker under the global manager lock every 5 s, and chat requests queue behind it. ROADMAP lists the TTL under 'deliberate policy, document it', not as rejected. Effort M is honest for the full set, but steps (1) spawn_blocking outside the lock with a refresh-in-flight flag, (2) mtime invalidation and (4) passing the startup scan into new() are each S and deliver most of the win; the skip-arrays reader (3) is the M part and can follow.

findings.title: pull never verifies downloaded bytes although the HF listing already supplies each file's sha256, and resume appends to whatever is on disk
findings.evidence: hub.rs:599-630 list_repo_files reads only `let size = s["lfs"]["size"].as_u64().or_else(|| s["size"].as_u64())` from the `?blobs=true` response, whose `lfs` object also carries `oid` (the sha256). hub.rs:701 `if have > 0 && expected == Some(have) { ... return Ok(()); }` accepts any file of the right length without reading it; :764 `.append(true)` continues from the existing tail on 206; is_incomplete_download (:266-324) compares sizes only. There is no hashing anywhere in hub.rs or gguf_probe.rs (grep for sha/oid returns nothing). sha2 0.10.9 is already in Cargo.lock.
findings.rationale: Resume made partial files first-class, which is good, but it also made 'length matches' the only acceptance criterion for 16 GB weights that are then mmapped and trusted. A crash that extended the file with zeros before the data landed, a proxy that served a 200 with a different body, or a bit flip on disk all produce a file the server loads and that emits garbage, a symptom the maintainer has already spent days triaging in other guises. The hash is free to obtain and cheap to compute relative to the download.
findings.proposal: Capture `lfs.oid` per file in list_repo_files; hash while writing (feed each chunk to a Sha256 state; on resume, hash the existing prefix first, which is a sequential read at disk speed) and compare at completion; on mismatch delete the file and refetch once before failing. Persist the verified digest in a `.sha256` sidecar or an extra column in gguf.index so is_incomplete_download can also require it. While there, use the single async client + runtime for the listing and the probe too (hub.rs:336-347 builds a blocking client, an async client and a runtime; probe_remote takes the blocking one).
findings.expected_benefit: Download integrity becomes verified rather than assumed; a corrupt weight file is caught at pull time with a clear message instead of surfacing as nonsense tokens at inference. Cost: one extra sequential read of the resumed prefix and SHA-256 throughput (GB/s class on Apple Silicon) during pull only.
findings.verify_how: Pull a small GGUF, truncate it by 1 MB and append 1 MB of zeros (same length), re-run pull: today it is reported complete and the model loads; after the change pull reports a digest mismatch and refetches. Time a 15 GB pull before/after to confirm hashing hides behind network time.

verdict.reason: Verified. hub.rs:599-630 `list_repo_files` reads only `lfs.size`/`size` from the `?blobs=true` listing and discards the rest of the `lfs` object; :701-705 accepts any file whose length equals the listing (`have > 0 && expected == Some(have)`) without reading it; :762-766 opens with `.append(true)` on a 206 and splices the remote tail onto whatever is on disk; `is_incomplete_download` (:266+) is size-based; grep for sha256/oid/digest over hub.rs and gguf_probe.rs returns nothing. sha2 0.10.9 is in Cargo.lock (transitively, not a direct dependency, so one Cargo.toml line is needed). The CHANGELOG 'Unreleased' entry confirms resume shipped with exactly these acceptance rules. The risk is real on a supported path (a resumed or pre-existing file of the right length is mmapped and trusted) and the fix hides behind network time; medium/M is right. Hash-while-writing plus hashing the resumed prefix is the correct shape; a persisted digest sidecar lets `is_incomplete_download` and `load` reuse it.

findings.title: run_interactive re-decodes the whole response (and the whole thought) on every token, duplicating a quadratic version of the streaming decoder the server already fixed
findings.evidence: main.rs:1343-1345 `output_ids.push(tok.token); let full = tokenizer.decode(&output_ids)?; let start = clamp_to_char_boundary(&full, decoded_len);` and :1328-1330 `thought_ids.push(tok.token); let full = tokenizer.decode(&thought_ids)?;` run once per generated token; tokenizer.rs:335-338 decode is the full HF `inner.decode(ids, true)`. The server's engine_loop.rs:460-470 doc states the same problem ('re-decoding the full sequence every step is quadratic') and solves it with prefix_decode_incremental (:466-493) keeping a stable prefix and re-decoding only a lookback window; main.rs:1107 clamp_to_char_boundary duplicates the engine_loop helper.
findings.rationale: For an n-token answer the CLI performs n(n+1)/2 token decodes: a 2k-token answer is ~2M token-decodes, a 6k-token reasoning trace is ~18M. At single-digit microseconds per token this is seconds of CPU per turn and, at the tail, several milliseconds per step against a ~25-35 ms decode step for a 4B model, i.e. a visible slowdown late in long answers, growing with length. The server path pays nothing comparable.
findings.proposal: Move prefix_decode_incremental, advance_stable_window, decode_with_neutral_prefix, emit_suffix and clamp_to_char_boundary out of engine_loop.rs into a shared `stream_decode` module (or tokenizer.rs) and use it in run_interactive for both the answer and the thought channel; delete the CLI copies. The stop-marker hold-back logic can stay as is on top of the emitted suffix.
findings.expected_benefit: CLI streaming cost becomes O(n) with a constant lookback window; removes ~60 lines of divergent duplicate logic (the CLI and server will stop drifting on Strip-decoder edge cases).
findings.verify_how: `oxydllm run <4B model>` with a prompt that yields a 2000-token answer; sample the process with `sample` or Instruments and look at time in tokenizers::decode, or print per-step wall time: today it grows roughly linearly with output length, after the change it is flat.

verdict.reason: Verified. main.rs:1328-1330 and :1343-1345 call `tokenizer.decode(&thought_ids)` / `tokenizer.decode(&output_ids)` on the whole accumulated id list for every token; tokenizer.rs:335-339 is the full HF `inner.decode(ids, true)`. engine_loop.rs:460-470 documents this exact problem and :382-493 holds the incremental decoder (`clamp_to_char_boundary`, `emit_suffix`, `decode_with_neutral_prefix`, `advance_stable_window`, `prefix_decode_incremental`); main.rs:1107 is a verbatim duplicate of engine_loop.rs:382. For an n-token answer the CLI does n(n+1)/2 token-decodes; at ~1 us/token the 2000th step decodes 2000 tokens, ~2 ms against a 25-35 ms step, and a 6k-token thought is ~18M token-decodes. CLI-only, so medium; moving the helpers to a shared module and deleting the CLI copies is S and also removes drift between the two decoders.

findings.title: Environment-variable and option handling diverge per subcommand: OXYDLLM_MODELS_DIR is honored only by `start`, and the load options are parsed twice
findings.evidence: main.rs:696-698 parse_start_args: `let mut models_dir: Option<PathBuf> = std::env::var("OXYDLLM_MODELS_DIR").ok().map(PathBuf::from);` and :704 `env_usize("OXYDLLM_MAX_CONTEXT_LEN")`; parse_run_args :853-860 starts from `max_context_len = None`, `kv_quant = Auto` and reads no models-dir/context/kv-quant/draft env; parse_pull_args, parse_estimate_args, parse_rm_args use `models_dir.unwrap_or_else(default_models_dir)`; `list` (:1448-1453) does `args[2..].windows(2).find(|w| w[0] == "--models-dir")` and ignores everything else. README:400 lists `--models-dir <DIR> | OXYDLLM_MODELS_DIR | ~/.oxydllm/models` without a start-only caveat. The eight load options (--models-dir, --devices, --max-context-len, --kv-quant, --allow-cpu, --draft-model, --stream-experts, --expert-cache-mb) are implemented twice with copy-pasted validation (main.rs:720-800 and :870-960).
findings.rationale: An operator who runs the service with OXYDLLM_MODELS_DIR=/Volumes/ssd/models (the natural setup for a launchd/systemd install) and then types `oxydllm pull ...` or `oxydllm list` from a shell writes to and reads from ~/.oxydllm/models; the server never sees the new model and `list` says 'No models found'. The duplicated parsers are where this divergence came from and will keep producing it.
findings.proposal: One `fn models_dir_default() -> PathBuf` that consults OXYDLLM_MODELS_DIR for every subcommand; a `CommonLoadOpts` struct with a single `parse_common_opt(args, &mut i, &mut opts) -> Result<bool, String>` used by both start and run (returning false for flags it does not own), with env defaults applied in one place; make `list` use the same arg loop so unknown flags error like everywhere else. Keep the usage text, but state env scope once.
findings.expected_benefit: Removes a trap operators hit on day one and ~80 lines of duplicate parsing; `run` gains the env defaults the usage text already implies for --devices.
findings.verify_how: `OXYDLLM_MODELS_DIR=/tmp/empty oxydllm list` currently lists ~/.oxydllm/models; after the change it lists /tmp/empty. Unit-test parse_common_opt once for both subcommands.

verdict.reason: Verified. main.rs:697-698 is the only place `OXYDLLM_MODELS_DIR` is read (grep confirms); :88-90 `default_models_dir()` ignores it; parse_run_args :853-856 starts every load option at `None`/`Auto` with no env defaults except OXYDLLM_ALLOW_CPU and OXYDLLM_EXPERT_CACHE_MB (:861, :870); `list` (:1448-1453) does an ad-hoc `windows(2)` scan for `--models-dir` and ignores everything else. One nuance: README:400 sits under the '## Server Options' heading, so the docs are arguably start-scoped, but the operator trap stands: a launchd/systemd server with the env set and a shell `oxydllm pull`/`list`/`rm` disagree on the directory. The duplicate option parsing (start :720-800, run :870-960) is where the divergence originates. Medium api-ux, S effort, proposal sound; the ROADMAP's flag section does not reject it (it wants fewer, not divergent, knobs).

findings.title: Engine assembly is duplicated between run_interactive and spawn_load (and `run` skips warm-up), with dead qjl plumbing threaded through every config struct
findings.evidence: main.rs:1200-1215 builds SchedulerConfig `{ max_num_sequences: 1, max_tokens_per_step: 4096 }`, stop controls and `engine::Engine::new_with_stop_controls(...)` plus optional draft; manager.rs:1123-1130 and :1212-1250 do the same with `max_tokens_per_step: 4096` and `max_num_seqs.unwrap_or(8)`; the draft vocab check diverges (main.rs:1189-1193 bails, manager.rs:1232-1240 warns and disables); `run` never calls warm_up_model (private to manager.rs:843). main.rs:710 and :860 `let qjl_quantization = false;` are then carried through StartArgs, RunArgs, StartServerArgs (routes/mod.rs:162), ModelManagerConfig, ModelManager, SpawnLoadParams and LoadBatchOptions although the CHANGELOG removed the only way to set it.
findings.rationale: Two copies of the engine-construction logic have already drifted in behaviour and the CLI lacks the warm-up that the server considers necessary for first-request latency and kernel coverage. The qjl field is a constant false carried through six structs; it costs reading time on every change to those signatures and suggests a configurable behaviour that does not exist.
findings.proposal: Add `pub(crate) fn build_engine(loaded: LoadedModel, tokenizer: &Tokenizer, draft: Option<LoadedModel>, max_seqs: usize) -> (Engine, DraftOutcome)` in models/ (or engine.rs) and `pub(crate) fn warm_up_model` reused by `run`; define `MAX_TOKENS_PER_STEP` once. Remove `qjl_quantization` from the public config structs and keep KvQuantizer::new_with_qjl internal with a single call site deciding it from KvQuantMode.
findings.expected_benefit: One code path for engine setup; the CLI inherits warm-up and the forgiving draft handling; ~70 lines deleted; fewer fields to thread on the next option.
findings.verify_how: cargo test; `oxydllm run` first-turn TTFT drops by the warm-up amount; grep shows a single construction site.

findings.title: Slots and registry are keyed by the raw request string while path resolution accepts aliases, so two spellings of one model load it twice
findings.evidence: chat.rs:1504 `let model_id = body.model.as_deref().unwrap_or("").to_string();` with no canonicalisation; manager.rs:644-647 `self.slots.insert(model_id.to_string(), SlotState::Loading { ... })` and :1296 `mgr.update_registry(&model_id, ...)` use that string, while loader.rs:453-470 resolve_model_path accepts `dir_name.starts_with(&needle) || needle.starts_with(&dir_name)` (case-insensitive prefix in either direction, shortest wins) and case-insensitive GGUF stems. manager.rs:305 `registry.retain(|id, _| valid_ids.contains(id));` keeps only discovered ids at startup.
findings.rationale: Requests for `Ministral-3B` and `Ministral-3B-Instruct-2512`, or `qwen3-4b-q4_k_m` and `Qwen3-4B-Q4_K_M`, resolve to the same directory but occupy two slots, two engine threads and two copies of the weights and KV pool; the gpu lock then time-slices them. Registry entries keyed by an alias are also pruned at the next start, so alias users always fall to the disk projection (findings 2 and 3). The ergonomics of prefix matching are good; the bookkeeping just needs to key on the resolved identity.
findings.proposal: In get_or_load, resolve first to a canonical id (the DiscoveredModel.id for the resolved directory/variant, or the canonical path string) and use it for slot lookup, insertion, registry and the engine's model_id; return the canonical id in the response `model` field (or keep echoing the request string but key internally by canonical id).
findings.expected_benefit: One engine per model regardless of spelling; registry projections hit for alias requests; no silent double memory use.
findings.verify_how: Send two chat requests with the two spellings; /v1/models/running currently lists two entries with identical architecture and total_size_bytes and memory doubles; after the fix one entry.

verdict.reason: Verified. chat.rs:1504 takes `body.model` verbatim; manager.rs:610 `self.slots.get_mut(model_id)` and :644-647 insert key on that raw string; `update_registry` (:783-799) keys the registry on it too; loader.rs:447-458 matches GGUF stems case-insensitively and :462-470 accepts a directory-name prefix in either direction, so `qwen3-4b-q4_k_m`/`Qwen3-4B-Q4_K_M` or `Ministral-3B`/`Ministral-3B-Instruct-2512` resolve to one path but get two slots, two engine threads, two weight copies and two KV pools, time-sliced under gpu_lock. manager.rs:300-305 prunes registry entries not in `discover_models` ids, so alias-keyed entries never survive a restart and alias users always fall into the disk projection (findings 2/3). Keying slots/registry on the resolved canonical id (DiscoveredModel.id or canonical path) while echoing the request string is S and sound.

findings.title: Ready slot can be installed before the engine (and its guard) exist: a panic between the result send and engine_loop leaves a dead channel the guard cannot clean
findings.evidence: manager.rs:1198 `let _ = result_tx.send(Ok(result));` precedes the draft load (:1212-1250), `Engine::new_with_stop_controls` (:1251-1255) and the guard construction (:1256-1260). The install task's only protection is :1266 `Ok(Ok(result)) if result.request_tx.is_closed() => {` evaluated once at receive time. If the thread panics after that check (draft loader, Engine::new), request_rx is dropped with the slot already Ready, and chat.rs:1828-1851 maps `TrySendError::Closed` to 503 'Engine unavailable' until keep-alive expiry.
findings.rationale: This is the same stuck-503 failure the alpha.15 guard was written to eliminate, surviving in a narrower window. It is rare (a panic in draft loading or engine construction) but the fix is a reordering.
findings.proposal: Move the result send to just before engine_loop: build the engine and the EngineSlotGuard first, then `result_tx.send(Ok(result))`. Waiters then also get Ready only when the engine is actually consuming. Alternatively, have the install task re-check `is_closed()` after inserting and remove the slot if it flipped.
findings.expected_benefit: Closes the last window where a slot can be registered without an owner that will clean it up.
findings.verify_how: Unit test: a stub whose Engine construction panics after the result is sent; assert no Ready slot remains. On the M5, configure --draft-model with a deliberately broken draft directory that panics in load and request the model twice.

findings.title: `estimate` KV figure counts every layer at BF16 and ignores the loader's actual sizing (hybrid linear layers, the device ceiling, auto KV quant)
findings.evidence: estimate.rs:527-540 `fn kv_cache_bytes(g: &ModelGeometry, ctx_len, num_seqs)` = 2 x num_layers x num_kv_heads x head_dim x 2 x ctx x seqs; :496-521 parse_geometry_from_json reads only num_hidden_layers, num_key_value_heads, head_dim/hidden_size, never layer_types or full_attention_interval; :343 prints 'KV cache: {} ctx x {} seq (BF16)'. The loader excludes linear layers (loader.rs:1139-1162 `layer_is_linear` filter into `layer_kv_specs`), caps the request at `safe_model_kv_ceiling(weights_bytes)` and the global budget (loader.rs:1710-1734), and may select lossless 4-bit under --kv-quant auto (CHANGELOG, Unreleased).
findings.rationale: For Qwen3.5/3.6 hybrids three of four layers hold recurrent state, so the estimate overstates KV 4x; for every model it describes a pool the server will not allocate on this machine. The tool exists to tell a user whether a model fits; the weights half is accurate, the KV half is not.
findings.proposal: Expose a pure sizing function from the loader (`kv_plan_preview(layer_kv_specs, declared_ctx, pinned_ctx, seqs, weights_bytes, mode)`) built from the same inputs compute_kv_blocks uses, parse the config through hf_parser::parse (already handles layer_types and text_config), and print two lines: 'KV requested (ctx x seq, exact)' and 'KV this machine would grant (ceiling, mode)'. For GGUF read the same keys from the header (qwen35 full_attention_interval).
findings.expected_benefit: The estimate matches what `start` logs at load; hybrid models stop looking 3x heavier than they are.
findings.verify_how: `oxydllm estimate Qwen3.5-4B --context-len 4096` vs the 'KV request capped' / 'model loaded kv_cache_gb' log lines from loading it: today they differ by roughly the linear-layer share and the ceiling; after the change the granted figure matches.

findings.title: pull drops every repository file that lives in a subfolder, hiding the foldered split-GGUF variants bartowski/unsloth publish for large models
findings.evidence: hub.rs:631-633 `fn is_relevant_file(f: &str) -> bool { if f.contains('/') || f.starts_with('.') { return false; }` applied to the whole listing at :352-354 before variant grouping; shard naming is otherwise handled (strip_split_suffix/has_split_suffix :35-53, group_gguf_variants :114-137) and the test at :945 pins the exclusion for `sub/config.json` only.
findings.rationale: Repositories whose quants exceed one file place them in `<model>-Q4_K_M/<model>-Q4_K_M-00001-of-00002.gguf` (bartowski) or `UD-Q4_K_XL/...` (unsloth); for those the menu omits the large variants or says 'No compatible model files found', with no hint that files exist one level down. As the project targets 27B-class models on 24 GB this will be met.
findings.proposal: Accept `.gguf` paths with exactly one directory component, group them by stem as today, and download each to the flat destination basename (shards of one variant share a stem so collisions are not possible); keep the exclusion for non-GGUF nested files. Mention the folder in the menu line.
findings.expected_benefit: Foldered split variants become pullable without the user downloading by hand and writing gguf.index themselves.
findings.verify_how: `oxydllm pull bartowski/<any 70B -GGUF repo>` currently lists only the flat small quants; after the change the foldered Q4_K_M shards appear as one variant with 'N shards'.

findings.title: RegistryEntry.last_used_secs is written only at load time yet exposed by /v1/models as last-used
findings.evidence: manager.rs:787-800 update_registry sets `entry.last_used_secs = now_unix_secs();` and is called only from the install task (:1296) and tests; get_or_load's Ready branch bumps only the in-memory `last_used` Instant (:620). handlers.rs:21 `let last_used_secs = registry.get(&m.id).map(|e| e.last_used_secs).unwrap_or(0);` and :36 `"last_used_secs": last_used_secs` publish it.
findings.rationale: The field is semantically last-loaded; clients using it to sort by recency get load order instead. Fixing it by writing the registry per request would put a file write on the request path, which is the wrong trade, so the fix is a rename or a lazy persist.
findings.proposal: Either rename the JSON field to last_loaded_secs (and the struct field, with a serde alias for old files) or keep an in-memory last-used unix timestamp in the Ready slot, report that for running models, and persist it into the registry at eviction/shutdown time only.
findings.expected_benefit: API field means what it says; no new hot-path I/O.
findings.verify_how: Load a model, wait, send a request, GET /v1/models: last_used_secs does not change today.

subsystems.assessment: The compute graph is in genuinely good shape for a single-stream, single-token decode on BF16/AWQ checkpoints: one architecture-agnostic forward, fused RMSNorm/RoPE/gated-activation/softcap kernels, FlashAttention (TensorOps where available) for prefill, logits projected only for the last row per sequence, adaptive prefill chunking, and a contiguous-buffer KV path that hands the attention kernels views rather than copies. The remaining headroom is almost entirely in the three small places where candle, not the crate, still serves a hot op. First, GGUF decode: every QLinear call casts activations BF16->F32 and the output F32->BF16 around candle's F32-only QMatMul (linear.rs:348,375; candle asserts F32), ~500 casts per token on a 36-layer model, while the 26 bf16-native gguf_*_gemv/gemv_batch/mul_mm kernels that the alpha.12 changelog measured at +7-13% sit unreferenced in quant_kernels.metal, and any batch of 2+ sequences flips every GGUF linear onto candle's 32-row tile GEMM. Second, dense BF16 decode has no GEMV at all: M<64 falls to candle's call_mlx_gemm (linear.rs:133), the shape where the crate's own W4A16 GEMV already reaches 71% of bandwidth. Third, attention performs 7+2N avoidable copy dispatches per layer (fused-qkv narrow+reshape, qk-norm after transpose, the q|k cat for RoPE, per-segment q copies and slice_sets, the final transpose-reshape) and serialises one SDPA launch per sequence, so batched decode scales worse than the batched GEMMs it sits between. Two model-specific gaps are large on their models: gpt-oss prefill always takes the materialised fallback with repeat_kv because no FA kernel accepts sinks, and the safetensors loader allocates a full-context cos/sin table per layer with no sharing (hundreds of MB to GB, uncounted by the KV plan) where the GGUF loader already dedups. Fragile spots are documentation-level: METAL_FA_MIN_KV cannot decide anything, two SDPA predicates are tautologies, the mask parameter is dead in production, and the routing table has no unit test, so the ROADMAP is planning to measure a threshold that has no effect. Numerically the graph follows HF conventions (BF16 residual stream, BF16 cos/sin), which is defensible, but the GGUF lm_head computes F32 logits and rounds them to BF16 before the sampler argmaxes them, which manufactures ties on borderline tokens. The biggest single lever is owning the small-M GEMV/gemv-batch for BF16 and GGUF (re-attaching the existing kernels where they exist), followed by a decode-layout pass in attention; together they plausibly buy 10-20% on single-stream decode and more on batched decode.

findings.title: GGUF decode casts activations to F32 and back around candle's QMatMul on every linear; the crate's bf16-native GGUF gemv kernels are compiled but never dispatched
findings.evidence: linear.rs:263 doc: `Small batches go to candle's QMatMul, which is memory bound down to a single token and serves decode.` linear.rs:348 `let x_f32: &Tensor = if x.dtype() != DType::F32 { x_f32_owned = x.to_dtype(DType::F32)?; ...` ; linear.rs:375 `out.to_dtype(self.out_dtype)?` in `finish`. candle-core-0.11.0/src/quantized/metal.rs:390 `assert_eq!(storage.dtype(), DType::F32);` (F32 input mandatory, F32 output). src/common/quant_kernels.metal still defines `gguf_q4k_gemv_bf16` (l.1235), `gguf_q4k_gemv_batch_bf16` (l.1333), `gguf_q4k_mul_mm_bf16` (l.2736) and 23 siblings for Q4_0/Q4_1/Q5_0/Q5_1/Q8_0/Q2K/Q3K/Q5K/Q6K; `grep -rl` over src/**/*.rs finds no reference to any of the 26 names, and metal_ops.rs:1612 compiles the whole `QUANT_METAL_SOURCE` with `new_library_with_source` at first use. CHANGELOG alpha.12 (l.278-284): the fast path measured Qwen3-4B-Q4_K_M 28.8->31.5 tok/s, Qwen2.5-1.5B 81.5->92.5. The shallow history (51 commits) and CHANGELOG alpha.13-unreleased record no retirement.
findings.rationale: Per token on a 36-layer GGUF model with Separate q/k/v: 7 linears x 2 casts = 14 tiny dispatches per layer, ~500 per token, each a full read+write of an [N, hidden] or [N, out] tensor. The maintainer's own note (PERFORMANCE_INVESTIGATION_GGUF, F2 pilot) measured these casts at 1-2 ms/token, 3-6% at 30 tok/s, and the alpha.12 changelog measured +7-13% from removing them. At HEAD the kernels that removed them exist in the .metal source but QLinear routes decode (M < StagedWeight::min_m, i.e. < 64 or < 128) exclusively through candle. Either the suite was retired for an unrecorded reason, in which case ~2,400 of 3,934 lines of Metal are dead weight compiled on every process start, or decode is paying an overhead already measured and fixed once.
findings.proposal: Re-attach decode to the existing kernels: for `GgufMatmul::Candle` with a `staged` handle (the loader already retains the raw Metal buffer for every Q4_0..Q6K weight, see `StagedWeight { buffer, kind }`), add a CustomOp that dispatches `gguf_<kind>_gemv_bf16` at M=1 and `gguf_<kind>_gemv_batch_bf16` for 2<=M<=GGUF_BATCH_MAX with BF16 in/out, falling back to candle only for kinds without a kernel and for M between GGUF_BATCH_MAX and min_m. Keep `out_dtype`/bias handling in `finish`. If the suite was retired deliberately, delete the 26 kernels and the F2 narrative in the notes instead, so the compile cost and the misleading documentation go away.
findings.expected_benefit: Removes ~500 cast dispatches per token on a 36-layer GGUF model: +6-13% decode throughput by the maintainer's earlier measurement (CHANGELOG alpha.12 l.278-284, note F2), larger on small models. Deleting instead saves first-use compile time of ~60% of quant_kernels.metal.
findings.verify_how: On M5: `OXYDLLM_PROFILE=1` decode on Qwen3-4B-Q4_K_M and count dispatches per layer with Metal System Trace (expect 14 fewer per layer); A/B tok/s single-stream before/after; the existing `batched GGUF GEMV parity for all ten quant types` test (CHANGELOG alpha.12.1) is the correctness gate if it still exists, otherwise re-add a parity test against candle's QMatMul.

verdict.reason: Verified in code: linear.rs:347-358 casts x to F32 (`x.to_dtype(DType::F32)`) and calls `candle_core::Module::forward(inner, &x_2d)`; `finish` (371-377) casts the F32 result back to `out_dtype` (BF16 on Metal, loader.rs:1495-1499). `maybe_staged_quant_matmul` (metal_ops.rs:3182-3192) only takes `dims[0] >= weight.min_m()`, and `min_m` (3082-3091) is 64 for Q4_0/Q4_1/Q5_0/Q5_1/Q4K and 128 for the rest, so every decode M falls to candle; the owned matvec (mpp_gemm.metal:958-960, metal_ops.rs:2631) decodes only IQ4_NL/IQ4_XS/IQ3_S. `grep -rn` over src/**/*.rs finds zero references to any `gguf_*_gemv_bf16`, `gguf_*_gemv_batch_bf16` or `gguf_*_mul_mm_bf16` symbol (26 kernels at quant_kernels.metal:734-3058), while `get_or_compile_quant_pipeline` (metal_ops.rs:1611-1612) compiles the whole QUANT_METAL_SOURCE. The GGUF kernels reduce with simd_sum and contain no atomics (the 6 `atomic_fetch_add` in the file are the retired AWQ/GPTQ `*_atomic` bench kernels), so re-attaching them does not violate the determinism rule. No retirement is recorded in CHANGELOG (alpha.13-Unreleased) and the shallow history has no commit touching `GgufFastPath`. On WORTH: the maintainer's own F2 note (PERFORMANCE_INVESTIGATION_GGUF l.415-417) puts the two casts at 1-2 ms/token = 3-6% and says the +6% of the pilot was exactly the cast removal; alpha.12 measured +9% on Qwen3-4B and +13% on a 1.5B. So the realistic bound is 5-9% on a 4B model, 13% on small ones; still >5%, severity high stands. Deleting instead is the honest alternative if candle's matvec is preferred, since the rules forbid dead code.

findings.title: gpt-oss prefill always takes the materialised fallback with 8x repeat_kv and five score-sized temporaries because no FA/SDPA kernel accepts attention sinks
findings.evidence: attention.rs:810-811 `let use_metal_fa = metal_fa_base_ok && self.sinks.is_none()`; 830-831 `let use_seg_sdpa = sdpa_base_ok && self.sinks.is_none()`; the sink kernel is gated to decode only: `use_sink_sdpa = ... && seg.num_tokens == 1` (l.843-849). The fallback then does attention.rs:909 `let k_seg = self.repeat_kv(k_seg)?;` (expand+reshape = copy to n_heads), 912-914 `q_seg.matmul(&k_seg.transpose(..))?.affine(self.scale, 0.)?`, 972 `let with_sink = Tensor::cat(&[&scores, &sink_col], D::Minus1)?;` then `softmax_last_dim(&with_sink)?.narrow(D::Minus1, 0, sk)?.contiguous()?`. engine.rs:197 `const CHUNK_MAX: usize = 1024;` bounds the chunk.
findings.rationale: gpt-oss-20b (published config: 24 layers, 64 q heads, 8 kv heads, head_dim 64, every other layer windowed at 128) has 12 full-attention layers. For a 1024-token chunk at 8k context each of those layers materialises scores [1,64,1024,8192] in BF16 = 1 GiB, then affine, mask add, sink cat, softmax and narrow+contiguous each allocate another score-sized tensor (~5 GiB of traffic per layer per chunk), plus repeat_kv copies K and V to 64 heads. That is ~60 GB of memory traffic per 1024-token chunk across the 12 layers, ~0.4 s at 150 GB/s, where FlashAttention would read K/V once per query tile. TTFT on long prompts for the flagship MoE model is dominated by this.
findings.proposal: Add a per-head `sinks` input to the crate-owned FlashAttnPrefill and MppFlashAttn kernels: initialise the online-softmax running max to m_i = sink_h and the denominator to l_i = 1 (the extra logit has no value row), which is exactly how the gpt-oss reference formulates it. Route `use_metal_fa` to it when `self.sinks.is_some()`, keep the fallback for CPU. Parity-test against the existing fallback on random data with GQA 64/8 and head_dim 64.
findings.expected_benefit: gpt-oss prefill attention drops from ~5 score-sized passes per full layer to one fused pass; expect multi-x reduction of the attn phase on prompts >2k tokens and bounded transient memory (no 1 GiB score tensors).
findings.verify_how: `OXYDLLM_PROFILE=1` prefill of a 4k and 8k prompt on gpt-oss-20b: compare the `attn` phase per chunk before/after, and peak Metal allocation; the regression sweep's gpt-oss byte-identity will change at rounding level, so compare top-1 agreement over the prompt's logits.

verdict.reason: attention.rs:810-811 `use_metal_fa = metal_fa_base_ok && self.sinks.is_none() ...`, 830-832 `use_seg_sdpa = sdpa_base_ok && self.sinks.is_none() ...`, 843-849 `use_sink_sdpa = ... && seg.num_tokens == 1`, so any prefill segment of a sink model takes the else branch at 908-983: `repeat_kv` on k and v (copies to n_heads), `q_seg.matmul(k^T).affine`, mask `broadcast_add`, `Tensor::cat(&[&scores, &sink_col])`, `softmax_last_dim`, `.narrow(..).contiguous()`, then `attn.matmul(v_seg)`. That is five score-sized full passes plus the K/V expansion per layer per chunk, exactly as claimed. One correction that makes it worse, not better: `truncate_kv_window` (attention.rs:117-121) narrows only when `num_tokens == 1`, so during prefill the windowed gpt-oss layers also see the full KV and materialise full `[64, chunk, kv_len]` scores with a sliding-window mask; the proposal fixes the 12 full layers (the windowed ones also need the FA window path, which commit 42943bf left switched off after a parity failure). The sink formulation (init m_i = sink_h, l_i = 1, no value row) is the standard one and the kernel is crate-owned (flash_attn.metal), so effort M is honest. engine.rs:197 confirms CHUNK_MAX = 1024, so a 1 GiB BF16 score tensor per full layer at 8k context is real. Not rejected in ROADMAP.

findings.title: Safetensors loader builds a full-context RoPE cos/sin table per layer with no sharing; GGUF loader already dedups
findings.evidence: rope.rs:69-73 `#[derive(Clone)] pub struct RotaryEmbedding { cos: Tensor, sin: Tensor }`; rope.rs:216-225 builds `[max_seq_len, head_dim/2]` cos and sin in `dtype`. Caller loader.rs:1326-1336 `let ropes = (0..cfg.num_hidden_layers).map(|i| { RotaryEmbedding::new_with_scaling(per_layer_rotary_dims[i], ctx, per_layer_rope_thetas[i], cfg.rope_scaling.clone(), dtype, device) })` with `ctx` = the KV plan's `context_len` (loader.rs:1185), computed from `weights_bytes: weights_size` (l.1176) before the ropes exist. The GGUF path dedups: gguf_model.rs:328-344 `fn rope_sharing_plan` and 631-632 `per_layer_table.iter().map(|&t| tables[t].clone())`.
findings.rationale: Per layer: ctx x rotary_dim/2 x 2 B x 2 tables. Qwen3-4B (36 layers, d=128) at ctx 40960: 10.5 MB/layer = 377 MB. A 128k-context Gemma-3-12B (48 layers, d=256) if the plan grants the full context: 67 MB/layer = 3.2 GB. All layers of a dense model share (dim, theta, scaling), so this is n_layers identical copies, allocated after the KV budget was sized and therefore eating the safety envelope the ROADMAP's D1 section worries about. Per-layer table construction also runs 5 device kernels and F32 temporaries per layer at load.
findings.proposal: Move `rope_sharing_plan` into rope.rs as `RotaryEmbedding::per_layer(specs: &[(dim, theta, &RopeScaling)], ctx, dtype, device) -> Vec<RotaryEmbedding>` that builds each distinct (dim, theta, scaling) once and clones the Tensor handles (Arc-shared storage) per layer; use it from both loaders. Count the tables in the model's reported footprint.
findings.expected_benefit: Resident memory down by (n_layers-1) x table size: ~370 MB on Qwen3-4B at 40k context, up to GBs on 128k-context Gemma; load time drops by n_layers-1 table builds.
findings.verify_how: Log Metal allocated bytes (or `oxydllm` footprint report) after loading a BF16 safetensors model with a large context before/after; assert in a unit test that two layers with equal (dim, theta) share `cos` storage (same `Tensor::id` or pointer).

verdict.reason: loader.rs:1326-1336 maps `(0..cfg.num_hidden_layers)` to `RotaryEmbedding::new_with_scaling(per_layer_rotary_dims[i], ctx, per_layer_rope_thetas[i], cfg.rope_scaling.clone(), dtype, device)` with `ctx` = `KvPlan.context_len` (loader.rs:1181-1186), and rope.rs:216-225 materialises `[max_seq_len, head_dim/2]` cos and sin in `dtype` per call (two tables, five device ops and two F32 temporaries each). `#[derive(Clone)]` on `RotaryEmbedding` (rope.rs:69-73) clones Arc-backed Tensors, so sharing is free. The GGUF path already dedups via `rope_sharing_plan` (gguf_model.rs:328-344) and its doc records the real-world cost: 'one pair of cos/sin tables is 268 MB, so building one per layer cost 12.9 GB'. Arithmetic checks: Qwen3-4B at ctx 40960, d=128: 40960*64*2B*2 = 10.5 MB/layer, 377 MB over 36 layers. The sharing key must include `rope_scaling` (per-layer differences exist for Gemma local/global), which the proposal does. Effort S, benefit scales with context; high is justified for long-context safetensors models and it also removes a load-time cost.

findings.title: Dense BF16 decode has no GEMV: M<64 falls to candle's call_mlx_gemm tile kernel
