findings.evidence: linear.rs:128-134 `fn matmul_with_bias ... match super::metal_ops::maybe_mpp_matmul(x2, weight_t)? { Some(y) => Ok(y), None => x2.matmul(weight_t) }`; metal_ops.rs:2831 `if dims.len() != 2 || dims[0] < MPP_GEMM_MIN_M || !x.is_contiguous() { return Ok(None); }` with `MPP_GEMM_MIN_M = 64` (l.2546). candle-core-0.11.0/src/metal_backend/mod.rs:1730-1770 `fn matmul` calls `candle_metal_kernels::call_mlx_gemm` unconditionally; no `gemv` symbol exists in that file. Contrast: the crate's own `PackedQuantLinear::forward` routes `m <= self.gemv_max_m()` to `chunked_batch_gemv` (linear.rs:484, 447-470) and the maintainer measured that path at 71% of bandwidth vs 46-50% for paths served by candle (PERFORMANCE_INVESTIGATION_GGUF, Ipotesi 3 table).
findings.rationale: At M=1 a 32-row tiled GEMM stages a 1-row A tile and a BK x BN B tile through threadgroup memory per step and launches only N/BN threadgroups, so a memory-bound matvec runs at a fraction of the bandwidth a simdgroup-per-row GEMV reaches; MLX itself routes M==1 to its gemv kernels for this reason and candle ported only the gemm. Every BF16 safetensors model (Qwen3, Llama, Gemma, Phi, Granite, the embeddings in Qwen3.5 hybrids) decodes through this path for all 7 projections per layer plus lm_head, and the tied BF16 lm_head alone reads vocab x hidden per token (the loader comment at loader.rs:1229-1234 notes 1.27 GB/token on the 248k-vocab Qwen3.5).
findings.proposal: Add `bf16_gemv` / `bf16_gemv_batch` kernels to quant_kernels.metal (one simdgroup per output row, bfloat4 vector loads, F32 accumulate, fixed-order simd_sum reduction like the deterministic AWQ family) and route them from `matmul_with_bias` when `x.dtype()==BF16 && m <= 8 && weight_t.stride()==[1,k]`; optionally let the lm_head variant emit F32 (see compute-graph-8).
findings.expected_benefit: If the kernel reaches the 70% of bandwidth the crate's W4A16 GEMV already reaches, single-stream BF16 decode improves roughly in proportion to the current gap (the maintainer's own data point: a 1.4 GB BF16 model at 54 tok/s is ~50% of 150 GB/s), i.e. +20-40% on dense BF16 checkpoints.
findings.verify_how: Micro-bench `[1,K]x[K,N]` BF16 for Qwen3-4B shapes (K=2560, N in {2560, 9728, 151936}) via candle `matmul` vs the new kernel with the existing paired bench harness; then end-to-end tok/s on Qwen3-4B BF16 and Llama-3.2-1B BF16.

verdict.reason: Code verified: linear.rs:128-134 routes `matmul_with_bias` to `maybe_mpp_matmul` only when it returns Some, and metal_ops.rs:2831 rejects `dims[0] < MPP_GEMM_MIN_M` (64, l.2546), so every decode M goes to `x2.matmul(weight_t)`; candle-core-0.11.0/src/metal_backend/mod.rs:1730-1754 `fn matmul` dispatches `candle_metal_kernels::call_mlx_gemm` unconditionally with no gemv branch. No BF16 dense matvec exists in the crate (mpp_gemm.metal has only the IQ owned matvec at 958-960; quant_kernels.metal has packed-int, F8 and MXFP4 gemvs). The ROADMAP does not reject it. The WORTH caveat is that nobody has measured candle's BF16 M=1 GEMM against the bandwidth roofline on M5: the maintainer's table (PERFORMANCE_INVESTIGATION_GGUF l.117-119) only has candle Q4_K at 46% vs the crate's W4A16 at 71%, and the '1.4 GB BF16 at 54 tok/s' point is implicit. MLX itself routes M==1 to gemv for this reason, so +20-40% is plausible but unproven; per the maintainer's verify-by-execution rule the shape micro-bench in verify_how should gate the kernel work (half a day) before the M-effort kernel. With that ordering the finding stands as high/M.

findings.title: Attention performs 7+2N avoidable copy dispatches per layer: qkv narrow+reshape, qk-norm after transpose, q|k cat for RoPE, per-segment q copies and slice_sets, final transpose-reshape
findings.evidence: attention.rs:686-694 `let q = q_raw.reshape((b, total_seq, self.n_heads, hd))?.transpose(1, 2)?;` (and k, v) where q_raw/k_raw/v_raw are `out.narrow(D::Minus1, ..)` views (l.613-616); candle tensor.rs:2534-2549 `reshape` copies when `!self.is_contiguous()`. attention.rs:700,704 `Some(norm) => norm.forward(&q)?` on the transposed view -> norm.rs:100 `let x_c = x.contiguous()?;` (copy). rope.rs:302-303 `let qk = Tensor::cat(&[q, k], 1)?; let qk_c = qk.contiguous()?;` (copy of q+k). attention.rs:857/885/900 `&q_seg.contiguous()?` and 865/893/906 `out_buf.slice_set(&seg_out.contiguous()?, 2, q_offset)?` once per segment; 986-988 `let out = out_buf.transpose(1, 2)?.reshape((b, total_seq, self.n_heads * hd))?` (reshape of a transposed tensor = copy). metal_ops.rs:340-345 and 482-484 show RmsNormOp and RopeOp bail on non-contiguous input, which is why the copies exist.
findings.rationale: Per layer per step with N decode sequences: 3 (reshape) + 2 (qk-norm contiguous) + 1 (rope cat) + N (q_seg) + N (slice_set) + 1 (final transpose) = 7+2N dispatches that move no information. The only necessary kernels on this path are 2 norms, 1 rope, the cache append, N SDPA launches. Using the maintainer's own cost figure for tiny kernels (1-2 ms for ~360 casts, i.e. 3-5 us each), 9 avoidable dispatches x 36 layers at N=1 is ~1-1.5 ms per token: 4-6% at 40 tok/s, 10%+ at 90 tok/s on a 1.5B model, and it grows with N.
findings.proposal: (a) Apply per-head qk_norm before `transpose(1,2)` on the contiguous [b,T,h,d] tensor the reshape produced (RMS is over d in either layout): -2 dispatches, S. (b) Replace the `Tensor::cat(&[q,k],1)` with two `rope_fused` dispatches on the already-contiguous q and k (same dispatch count, no copy) or a two-input RopeOp: -1 copy, S. (c) Decode fast path when every segment has num_tokens==1: keep q in [b,T,h,d] where `q.narrow(1,i,1)` is contiguous and bit-identical to the [1,h,1,d] SDPA input, lay `out_buf` out as [b,T,h*d] so each segment's [1,h,1,d] output lands with one slice_set and the final transpose-reshape disappears: -(N+1), M. (d) Longer term, own the rms_norm and rope kernels with a row-stride parameter so the three qkv reshape copies go too.
findings.expected_benefit: -5 dispatches/layer at N=1 (-7-2N at larger N): roughly 0.7-1.5 ms per token on a 36-layer model, 3-6% single-stream, more under batching; no numerical change.
findings.verify_how: `OXYDLLM_PROFILE=1` attn phase per layer on Qwen3-4B (qk_norm) decode before/after each step; Metal System Trace dispatch count per layer; byte-identical output on the regression sweep (the reorderings do not change arithmetic).

verdict.corrected_benefit: At N=1 the avoidable copies per layer are 2 (Llama GGUF: rope cat + slice_set) to 7 (Qwen3 safetensors with Fused qkv and per-head qk-norm), not 9: roughly 70-250 dispatches per token on a 36-layer model, ~0.3-1 ms, 1-3% single-stream; the per-segment q copies and the final transpose only cost at N>1, where they add 2N per layer.
verdict.corrected_proposal: (a) Apply PerHead qk-norm on the contiguous [b,T,h,d] tensor before `transpose(1,2)` (attention.rs:686-705): -2 copies on qk-norm models, S, bit-identical. (b) When `segments.len() == 1` skip `out_buf`/`slice_set` and use the kernel output directly as `out` (the sdpa/FA result is already contiguous [1,h,T,d]): -1 copy on every model, S. Drop the 'two rope_fused dispatches' idea: RopeOp (metal_ops.rs:483-485) requires contiguous inputs and after transpose q and k are views, so two calls would need two contiguous copies, i.e. more than the single cat. Keep (c) the [b,T,h,d]-native decode layout and (d) strided norm/rope kernels as M-effort follow-ups for the batched case.
verdict.reason: Mechanism partly verified, counts overstated. Verified: Fused qkv narrows (attention.rs:572-577) are non-contiguous so `reshape` at 686-694 copies; PerHead qk-norm runs on the transposed view (700-705) and norm.rs:100 `x.contiguous()` copies; rope.rs:302-303 cats q and k (one copy); `slice_set` at 865/893/906 is one copy per segment. Refuted parts: with b=1 and T=1 (single-stream decode) `q.narrow(2, q_offset, 1)` keeps contiguity because candle's `Shape::is_contiguous` skips dims of size 1, so `q_seg.contiguous()` is a no-op; likewise `out_buf.transpose(1,2).reshape(..)` at 986-988 on a [1,h,1,d] tensor is a view, not a copy; `seg_out.contiguous()` after sdpa is a no-op. The 3 reshape copies only happen with `QkvProjection::Fused` (safetensors Float path, attention.rs:281, and GGUF only when `attn_qkv` exists, l.480); GGUF Llama/Qwen are `Separate` (l.506) and `q.forward(x)` returns contiguous output. So the 'N=1: 9 dispatches' figure is 2-7 depending on model, and proposal (b) as written would add a copy rather than remove one. The cheap parts (a) and the single-segment bypass get most of the N=1 benefit for S effort.

findings.title: GGUF decode with 2..min_m-1 batched tokens hits candle's 32-row tile mul_mm instead of a batched GEMV; the crate's gguf_*_gemv_batch_bf16 kernels (GGUF_BATCH_MAX=8) are unreferenced
findings.evidence: linear.rs:320-359: QLinear::forward routes `GgufMatmul::Candle` to `maybe_staged_quant_matmul` only when `dims[0] >= weight.min_m()` (metal_ops.rs:3188), where metal_ops.rs:3082-3091 `fn min_m` returns MPP_GEMM_MIN_M (64) for Q4_0/Q4_1/Q5_0/Q5_1/Q4K and 128 for the rest; otherwise `candle_core::Module::forward(inner, &x_2d)` (l.358). candle quantized/metal.rs:372-374 `if src_shape.dim(D::Minus2)? == 1 { return self.fwd_mv(...) }` then `call_quantized_matmul_mm_t` for any M>=2. metal_ops.rs:6384-6387 `/// Max batch the batched-decode gemv kernels handle ... pub const GGUF_BATCH_MAX: usize = 8;` and quant_kernels.metal:1333 `kernel void gguf_q4k_gemv_batch_bf16(` with no Rust reference (grep over src/**/*.rs). The IQ kinds and AWQ/GPTQ do get batched GEMVs (metal_ops.rs:3004 MPP_MATVEC_MAX_M=8; linear.rs:447-470 chunked_batch_gemv).
findings.rationale: With two concurrent sequences, every GGUF linear switches from a memory-bound matvec to a tile GEMM that stages activations through threadgroup memory and computes 32 rows for 2 real ones; at M=2..8 the batched GEMV reads the weight once and amortises the activations in registers, which is the whole point of continuous batching. Q5_K/Q6_K/Q8_0/Q2K/Q3K stay on candle's mm up to M=127. The ROADMAP's claim that the server 'serves eight concurrent sequences' is measured on Phi-3-mini in BF16, not on this path.
findings.proposal: Route 2<=M<=GGUF_BATCH_MAX through the existing `gguf_<kind>_gemv_batch_bf16` kernels (same CustomOp as compute-graph-1), and measure the staged GEMM crossover for M in (8, min_m) per kind with `staged_quant_crossover_probe` so min_m can drop where it wins. Keep candle's mm only as the last fallback.
findings.expected_benefit: Per-step time for N=2..8 GGUF decode should stay close to N=1 (memory-bound) instead of jumping to the tile-GEMM regime; aggregate throughput under concurrency scales near-linearly up to 8.
findings.verify_how: Run 1, 2, 4, 8 concurrent streams on Qwen3-4B-Q4_K_M and Qwen3-4B-Q6_K; plot per-step ms vs N before/after. A step at N=2 that costs ~2x N=1 today is the signature of the mm path.

verdict.reason: Verified: linear.rs:338-344 only tries the staged GEMM, which `maybe_staged_quant_matmul` (metal_ops.rs:3188) refuses below `min_m` = 64 (Q4_0/Q4_1/Q5_0/Q5_1/Q4K) or 128 (Q5K/Q6K/Q8_0/Q2K/Q3K); everything below goes to candle `QMatMul`, whose Metal `fwd` (candle-core-0.11.0/src/quantized/metal.rs:372-374) takes `fwd_mv` only when `dim(D::Minus2) == 1` and otherwise calls `call_quantized_matmul_mm_t` (l.414), the llama.cpp mul_mm tile kernel. `GGUF_BATCH_MAX` (metal_ops.rs:6387) is used only by the MXFP4 op (6762, 6943) and the ten `gguf_*_gemv_batch_bf16` kernels have no Rust caller. The maintainer measured this exact regime in alpha.12.1 ('two batched tokens 3.7x more expensive than two serial ones', aggregate 14.9 to 52.1 tok/s at concurrency 2 once the batch GEMVs were wired), so the present state is a silent regression of a shipped fix on every GGUF model under concurrency; that is arguably high rather than medium. Shares the CustomOp with compute-graph-1, so the combined effort is one M item. The `staged_quant_crossover_probe` measurement for M in (8, min_m) is a sensible add-on.

findings.title: Batched decode attention is serialised: one SDPA launch plus two copies per sequence per layer
findings.evidence: attention.rs:841 `for (i, seg) in segments.iter().enumerate() {` wraps the whole kernel selection; 884-892 `super::metal_ops::sdpa(&q_seg.contiguous()?, &k_in, &v_in, None, seg.num_tokens > 1, ...)` is called once per segment, followed by 893 `out_buf.slice_set(&seg_out.contiguous()?, 2, q_offset)?`. metal_ops.rs:165-200 shows the vector kernel additionally allocating `sdpa_2pass_intermediate/sums/maxs` buffers per call when `k_seq >= TWO_PASS_K_THRESHOLD`. KV contiguous buffers are separate per-sequence tensors from `ContigBufferPool` (paged.rs:1037-1040, 634-639), so there is no single base pointer a multi-sequence kernel could index today.
findings.rationale: At N=8 sequences and 36 layers a decode step issues 288 vector-SDPA launches (each only n_heads threadgroups wide, poor GPU occupancy) plus 576 copy dispatches, while the surrounding GEMMs already batch all 8 rows into one launch each. Attention is the part of the step whose cost grows linearly with N in dispatches rather than in bytes. candle's vector kernel also allocates three scratch buffers per call for long contexts (108+ allocations per step per sequence over 1024 tokens).
findings.proposal: A crate-owned batched decode SDPA kernel: one launch per layer over all single-token segments, taking an argument buffer of per-sequence (k_base, v_base, kv_len, head_stride) entries (Metal argument buffers / `device const T* const*`), writing directly into a [N, h, d] output; or, simpler, carve all contig KV buffers from one slab so the kernel can take (offset, len) pairs. The sink variant for gpt-oss follows the same shape. Pair with compute-graph-5(c) so no per-segment copies remain.
findings.expected_benefit: Per-step attention cost at N=8 goes from ~864 dispatches to ~36 across 36 layers (~3-4 ms per step at the maintainer's per-dispatch cost) and GPU occupancy rises from n_heads to N*n_heads threadgroups per launch; single-stream unaffected.
findings.verify_how: Measure per-step ms at N=1,4,8 on Phi-3-mini (the model the changelog uses for 8-way concurrency) with `OXYDLLM_PROFILE=1`; the attn phase should flatten with N after the change. Parity test against per-segment sdpa on random GQA inputs with unequal kv_len.

verdict.reason: Verified: the whole kernel selection and launch sit inside `for (i, seg) in segments.iter().enumerate()` (attention.rs:794); the vector path issues `super::metal_ops::sdpa(&q_seg.contiguous()?, ...)` once per segment (884-892) followed by `out_buf.slice_set(&seg_out.contiguous()?, 2, q_offset)` (893); with T = N > 1 the `q.narrow(2, q_offset, 1)` view is non-contiguous (stride T*d on dim 1), so the `contiguous()` is a real copy, giving 3 dispatches per segment per layer, 864 at N=8 over 36 layers as claimed. metal_ops.rs:165-200 shows three `device.new_buffer` scratch allocations per call when `k_seq >= 1024` (pool hits mostly, but still per-call). K/V contig buffers are per-sequence tensors, so a single-launch kernel needs either an argument buffer of per-sequence pointers or a shared slab, which makes L the honest effort. Because the engine serialises GPU work, the benefit is dispatch overhead plus occupancy (n_heads threadgroups per launch today), not parallelism; 3-4 ms per N=8 step is a reasonable upper estimate. Not rejected by ROADMAP; pairs naturally with compute-graph-5(c).

findings.title: GGUF lm_head rounds its native F32 logits to BF16 before the sampler argmaxes them, manufacturing ties on borderline tokens and spending two casts over N x vocab
findings.evidence: linear.rs:371-377 `finish`: `let out = if out.dtype() != self.out_dtype { out.to_dtype(self.out_dtype)? }` where candle's QMatMul produced F32 (quantized/metal.rs:385 `.with_size_for(dst_shape.elem_count(), DType::F32)`); gguf_model.rs:515-523 builds the lm_head with `QLinear::from_gguf(w, None, dtype)` where `dtype` is BF16 on Metal (loader.rs:1496-1499). sampling.rs:105 `let token = logits.argmax(D::Minus1)?.to_scalar::<u32>()?;` runs on that BF16 tensor; sampling.rs:120 `let mut logits_vec: Vec<f32> = logits.to_dtype(candle_core::DType::F32)?.to_vec1()?;` casts it straight back for every non-greedy request.
findings.rationale: BF16 keeps 8 significant bits: logits of magnitude 16-32 are quantised to steps of 0.125, 32-64 to 0.25. Two candidates whose F32 gap is below the step become an exact tie and argmax resolves it by index, so a token the F32 head would choose deterministically can flip, which is the 'borderline token flip' the changelog records repeatedly on GGUF checkpoints. The F32 values already exist; the cast is only there because `out_dtype` is the model dtype. The dense BF16 path cannot avoid BF16 logits without a mixed-precision GEMV (compute-graph-4), but the GGUF path can today, and it also saves a BF16 write + F32 read of N x 152k values per step.
findings.proposal: Give the lm_head QLinear `out_dtype = DType::F32` in gguf_model.rs (both the `output.weight` and the tied `token_embd` branches); nothing downstream needs BF16 logits. On the dense path, let the BF16 GEMV of compute-graph-4 emit F32 for the lm_head call site.
findings.expected_benefit: Removes 2 casts over N x vocab per step and restores F32 argmax resolution on GGUF models; expect fewer run-to-run and quant-vs-reference top-1 disagreements on near-tied steps.
findings.verify_how: On Llama-3.2-1B-Q4_K_M (the changelog's known flipper) dump top-2 logits in F32 and BF16 over a few hundred greedy steps: count steps where the BF16 gap is 0 and the F32 gap is not; rerun the 10x byte-identity probe before/after.

verdict.reason: Verified end to end: candle's quantized Metal fwd writes F32 (quantized/metal.rs:385-390 `with_size_for(.., DType::F32)`, `assert_eq!(storage.dtype(), DType::F32)`); `QLinear::finish` (linear.rs:371-377) casts to `self.out_dtype`, which gguf_model.rs:515-523 sets to `dtype` = BF16 on Metal (loader.rs:1495-1499) for both the `output.weight` and tied `token_embd` branches; block.rs:660-680 then applies only `logits / s` (Granite) and `softcap_fused`, which has an F32 variant (metal_ops.rs:880 `softcap_f32`), so F32 logits would flow through unchanged; engine.rs:629/699 hands `batch_logits.get(row)` to `sampling::sample`, whose greedy branch (sampling.rs:105) argmaxes the BF16 tensor and whose non-greedy branch (l.120) casts straight back to F32. `LogitRows::LastPerSequence` (block.rs:646-658) narrows to at most num-sequences rows before the lm_head, so the staged GEMM (M >= 64) never serves it and the F32 values always exist. The tie mechanism is real (BF16 spacing 0.125 at |logit| in [16,32)), the cost of the two vocab-sized casts is real, and the change is a one-line dtype in gguf_model.rs. The regression sweep's byte-identity on GGUF checkpoints will shift on near-tied steps, which the maintainer has accepted before for the F8 GEMV. Medium/S as stated.

findings.title: Fp8Linear::forward dequantises the entire weight on every call; reachable on CPU (and CUDA) where the loader preserves F8
findings.evidence: linear.rs:184-232: `pub fn forward(&self, x: &Tensor)` does `cast_f8e4m3_to_f32(&self.weight)` / `self.weight.to_dtype(DType::F32)` (l.189-193), `weight_f32 = apply_scale_inv(&weight_f32, &scale_for_mul)?` (l.228), `let weight_t = weight_f32.to_dtype(x.dtype())?.t()?;` (l.231), then `matmul_with_bias`. weights.rs:367-375 `let preserve_fp8_weight = name.ends_with(".weight") && scale_inv_names.contains(...)` passed as `preserve_fp8_weight && !device.is_metal()`, and weights.rs:144-146 `if t.dtype() == DType::F8E4M3 { if preserve_fp8_weight { return Ok(t); }`; `apply_weight_scale_inv` skips FP8 weights (test `apply_weight_scale_inv_skips_fp8_weights`, weights.rs:700). linear.rs:531-536 `from_weight_with_scale_inv` builds `Self::Fp8` for any F8E4M3 weight.
findings.rationale: On Metal the loader never produces an Fp8Linear, so the hot Metal path is unaffected, but on the CPU runtime (stated as working) and on CUDA every FP8 projection re-materialises an F32 copy of its weight, multiplies it by the scale grid and casts it again for every token: for a 4B FP8 model that is ~16 GB of F32 writes per token plus a transient F32 weight per layer, so FP8 checkpoints are effectively unusable off Metal, silently. The per-call work is identical every time.
findings.proposal: Dequantise once: in `Fp8Linear::new` (or a `OnceCell` on first forward) compute and keep `weight_t` in the runtime dtype and drop the F8 bytes; or remove the `preserve_fp8_weight` branch and let CPU/CUDA take the same dequant-at-load path Metal does. Keep `Fp8Linear` only if a native F8 kernel is planned for CUDA.
findings.expected_benefit: Off-Metal FP8 decode goes from one full-weight dequant per linear per token to zero; memory stops oscillating by a full F32 weight per layer.
findings.verify_how: Run an FP8 checkpoint with `--device cpu` on the M5 (or any box) and time 10 decode tokens before/after; assert in a unit test that two consecutive forwards do not call the cast (e.g. count via a test hook) or simply that the second forward is not slower than a Float linear.

verdict.reason: Verified: linear.rs:184-232 `Fp8Linear::forward` recomputes `cast_f8e4m3_to_f32`/`to_dtype(F32)`, `apply_scale_inv`, `to_dtype(x.dtype())` and `.t()` on the full weight every call with no cache; linear.rs:540-546 `from_weight_with_scale_inv` builds `Self::Fp8` for any `F8E4M3` weight; weights.rs:367-375 passes `preserve_fp8_weight && !device.is_metal()` so only CPU/CUDA keep F8 (weights.rs:144-146 returns the F8 tensor untouched when preserved). The per-token work is one full F32 materialisation of every projection, so FP8 checkpoints off Metal are unusable in practice, silently. Medium is right per the rubric (rarely-taken path). One refinement to the proposal: on CPU the runtime dtype is F32 (loader.rs:1495), so 'dequantise once' quadruples the F8 bytes; the cheapest consistent fix is to drop `preserve_fp8_weight` and take Metal's dequant-at-load path, after which `Fp8Linear` has no production constructor and must be deleted under the no-dead-code rule (keep it only if a CUDA F8 kernel is actually planned). Effort S either way.

findings.title: Gemma 4 value normalisation runs as 8 unfused candle ops with F32 temporaries instead of the fused RMSNorm kernel
findings.evidence: attention.rs:138-145 `fn rms_norm_no_weight(x: &Tensor, eps: f64)`: `x.contiguous()?.to_dtype(F32)?` then `.sqr()?.mean_keepdim(D::Minus1)?`, `broadcast_div(&(variance + eps)?.sqrt()?)?`, `.to_dtype(dtype)`; used at 711-713 `let v = if self.v_norm { rms_norm_no_weight(&v, self.rms_norm_eps)? }` on the transposed `v` view (l.692-694). arch_defaults.rs:312-321 sets `v_norm: true` for gemma4. By contrast q/k use `norm.forward` which on Metal is one `rms_norm_fused` (norm.rs:98-102).
findings.rationale: Per attention layer per step: contiguous copy of v, cast to F32, square, reduction, add, sqrt, broadcast divide, cast back = 8 dispatches and two F32 temporaries of [b,kv_h,T,d] (in prefill, T x kv_dim x 4 B each), where the q and k norms beside it cost one fused dispatch each. On a 30-40 layer Gemma 4 that is ~250 extra dispatches per token.
findings.proposal: Hold a ones weight `[head_dim]` per Attention (or add `RMSNorm::identity(d, eps)`) and call `rms_norm_fused(&v_c, &ones, eps)` on Metal, keeping the candle chain for CPU; apply it before the transpose so the contiguous copy also disappears (see compute-graph-5a).
findings.expected_benefit: -7 dispatches and two F32 temporaries per attention layer on Gemma 4; ~1 ms/token on a 34-layer model, more in prefill.
findings.verify_how: `OXYDLLM_PROFILE=1` attn phase on gemma-4 decode before/after; outputs should match to BF16 rounding (fused kernel reduces in F32 like the candle chain).

verdict.reason: Verified: attention.rs:138-145 `rms_norm_no_weight` = `contiguous` + `to_dtype(F32)` + `sqr` + `mean_keepdim` (sum + scale) + `+ eps` + `sqrt` + `broadcast_div` + `to_dtype` = 8-9 dispatches with F32 temporaries, called at 711-713 on the transposed `v` view (692-694), while q/k beside it use `RMSNorm::forward`, which on Metal is `rms_norm_fused` on one contiguous copy (norm.rs:98-102). `v_norm` is wired from config in all three constructors (attention.rs:295/434/562, gguf_model.rs:407/555) and arch_defaults.rs:312-321 sets it for gemma4, so this is the live Gemma 4 path on both safetensors and GGUF. The fused kernel multiplies by the weight after an F32 reduction, so a ones weight reproduces the chain to F32 rounding before the BF16 cast; moving it before the transpose also removes the contiguous copy. S effort, ~8 dispatches per layer per token saved, as claimed.

findings.title: GGUF q/k/v and gate/up projections stay Separate even when their ggml types match, costing extra matvec launches and activation re-reads per layer
findings.evidence: ffn.rs:336-352 `load_gguf`: whenever `ffn_gate` exists it builds `GateUpProjection::Separate { gate: AnyLinear::Quantized(gate), up: AnyLinear::Quantized(up) }` unconditionally; ffn.rs:415-423 forward runs `gp.forward(x)?` and `up_p.forward(x)?` then `silu_mul_fused`. attention.rs:525-556 `load_gguf` builds `QkvProjection::Separate` whenever `attn_qkv` is absent (every Llama/Qwen/Gemma GGUF), and `qkv_split` (l.618-625) runs three forwards over the same x. gguf_weights.rs:514-530 `qtensor_with_staged(dtype, bytes, dims, device)` already constructs a QTensor (plus staged handle) from raw block bytes, and the AWQ path already fuses at load (ffn.rs:250 `concat_awq_along_out`, attention.rs:420-430).
findings.rationale: GGUF block quantisation runs along the input dimension, so concatenating two weights of the same ggml type along the output dimension is a byte concatenation of their raw buffers; the result is one matvec reading x once instead of three (qkv) or two (gate/up), and the FFN can use `gated_silu_fused` on the packed output as the safetensors path does. Per layer per token that is 3 fewer matvec dispatches and, while compute-graph-1 stands, 6 fewer casts. Mixed-type files (UD quants, Q4_K_M with Q6_K attn_v) keep the Separate shape.
findings.proposal: In `FeedForward::load_gguf` and `Attention::load_gguf`, when the candidate weights share a `GgmlDType` and whole-block rows, read their raw bytes, concatenate along out, and build one `QLinear` via `qtensor_with_staged` (for Llama, after `depermute_qk_rows`); keep Separate otherwise. For QkvProjection, fuse q+k even when v differs.
findings.expected_benefit: -3 matvec dispatches per layer (~100 per token on a 32-layer model, ~0.4 ms) plus fewer activation reads; enables the packed gated-activation kernel on GGUF.
findings.verify_how: tok/s on Qwen3-4B-Q4_K_M (uniform gate/up types) before/after; parity test: fused QLinear output equals `cat(gate.forward, up.forward)` to F32 rounding; `oxydllm estimate` composition tells which files qualify.

verdict.reason: Verified: ffn.rs:331-352 builds `GateUpProjection::Separate` whenever `ffn_gate` exists, and the forward (415-423) runs two QLinear forwards over the same x before `silu_mul_fused`; the `Fused` branch (390-405) already has `gated_silu_fused`/`gated_gelu_tanh_fused` on the packed output, so the fused activation exists for the proposal to reuse. attention.rs:506 builds `QkvProjection::Separate` when `attn_qkv` is absent (480 is the fused Phi-3 case) and `qkv_split` (579-585) runs three forwards. `qtensor_with_staged` (gguf_weights.rs:514-532) constructs a QTensor plus staged handle from raw block bytes, and the depermute changelog entry confirms blocks run along the input dimension, so out-dimension concatenation is a byte concat for every GGML type. Benefit is modest as the finding itself states (3 launches per layer, fewer small low-occupancy K/V launches, plus the cast savings only while compute-graph-1 stands; after it lands the standalone gain is ~1-2%). Mixed-type files (Q6_K attn_v in Q4_K_M) must stay Separate, which the proposal handles. Medium/M is honest.

findings.title: METAL_FA_MIN_KV can never decide the attention route, two SDPA predicates are tautologies, and the mask/optional-rope plumbing has no production caller
findings.evidence: attention.rs:810-826 `let use_metal_fa = metal_fa_base_ok && self.sinks.is_none() && if seg.num_tokens > 1 { flash_attention_uses_hardware_path(..) } else { !sdpa_base_ok } && mask.is_none() && kv_len >= seg.num_tokens && (kv_len >= METAL_FA_MIN_KV || seg.num_tokens > 1 || (seg.num_tokens == 1 && !sdpa_base_ok));` : when num_tokens==1 the middle clause requires `!sdpa_base_ok`, which makes the third disjunct true; when num_tokens>1 the second disjunct is true, so `kv_len >= METAL_FA_MIN_KV` (l.33, documented as a measured crossover) is dead. attention.rs:830-835 `use_seg_sdpa = ... && seg.num_tokens == 1 && !(seg.num_tokens > 1 && kv_lengths[i] > seg.num_tokens) && (self.attn_softcap.is_none() || seg.num_tokens <= 8)` : both trailing clauses are always true under `seg.num_tokens == 1`. block.rs:640 passes `None,` for the mask on every layer; grep finds no production caller of `forward_batch` with a mask or of `forward_batch_optional_rope` outside attention.rs. ROADMAP D2 lists METAL_FA_MIN_KV among thresholds to measure.
findings.rationale: The routing predicate is the most consequential branch in the forward and it currently reads as if a 1024-token crossover and an 8-token softcap limit exist; the ROADMAP schedules measuring one of them. Anyone tuning decode attention (e.g. trying FA for long-context decode, which the comment claims is the intent) will change the constant and see nothing. Dead parameters threaded through TokenMixer, TransformerBlock and Attention cost review time on every change.
findings.proposal: Extract the route decision into a pure `fn attention_route(num_tokens, kv_len, sdpa_ok, fa_ok, hw_path, has_sinks, softcap, mask) -> Route` and table-test it (compute-graph-13); delete METAL_FA_MIN_KV and the two tautologies, or make the constant real by letting a single-token segment with kv_len >= threshold take FA when the hardware path exists (then measure it). Drop the `mask` parameter from the production signature or move it to a test-only entry; make `forward_batch_optional_rope` private unless the encoder is meant to use it.
findings.expected_benefit: Routing becomes readable and testable; the ROADMAP's D2 item for METAL_FA_MIN_KV resolves without a benchmark; fewer parameters on the hot signature.
findings.verify_how: Unit test over the predicate table; `cargo build` with the constant removed compiles and the regression sweep is byte-identical (no route changes).

verdict.reason: Predicate algebra verified against attention.rs:810-826: for `num_tokens > 1` the middle clause reduces to `hw_path` and the last disjunction is satisfied by `seg.num_tokens > 1`; for `num_tokens == 1` the middle clause requires `!sdpa_base_ok`, which satisfies the third disjunct, so `kv_len >= METAL_FA_MIN_KV` (l.33, documented as a measured crossover) can never decide the route. In `use_seg_sdpa` (830-835) `!(seg.num_tokens > 1 && ..)` and `seg.num_tokens <= 8` are both implied by `seg.num_tokens == 1`. `mask` is threaded through TokenMixer and TransformerBlock (block.rs:67, 408) and the only production caller, block.rs:635-641, passes `None`; `grep` finds no caller of `forward_batch_optional_rope` outside attention.rs (the encoder has its own attention). ROADMAP D2 lists METAL_FA_MIN_KV as a threshold to measure, so resolving it by code reading is in scope. Pure-function extraction plus table test is S and route-neutral (byte-identical sweep).

findings.title: No unit test pins which attention kernel a segment reaches, nor the batched-decode (M=2..8) linear routing
findings.evidence: attention.rs tests (l.1030-1257) all run on `Device::Cpu` (`forward_batch_prefill_output_is_correct_shape_and_finite` l.1156, `forward_batch_with_softcap_produces_finite_output` l.1200) and so never evaluate `use_metal_fa`/`use_seg_sdpa`/`use_sink_sdpa` (l.810-849), which are `#[cfg(feature = "metal")]`; the only Metal checks are end-to-end sweeps. linear.rs tests cover M in {1, 9, 200} for owned weights (l.700) and {1, 8, MPP_GEMM_MIN_M, 200} for staged (l.786) but assert equality only, not which kernel ran, and nothing covers `AnyLinear::forward` at M=2..8 on a `GgufMatmul::Candle` weight.
findings.rationale: The dead conditions in compute-graph-12 and the silent batched-decode regime in compute-graph-6 both survived because the routing is only observed through tok/s. A table-driven test over a pure routing function costs nothing on CI (no GPU) and would have caught both; a Metal-gated test that asserts the kernel name dispatched for M=1,2,8,9,64 per weight kind would make the batched regime visible.
findings.proposal: Factor the attention route and the QLinear/PackedQuantLinear M-routing into pure functions returning an enum, and table-test them on CPU; add a Metal-only test that records the kernel chosen (a test hook or the profiler's phase name) for representative (num_tokens, kv_len, sinks, softcap) and (kind, M) grids.
findings.expected_benefit: Routing regressions become CI failures instead of throughput anomalies; the D2 threshold documentation pass gets an executable spec.
findings.verify_how: Add the tests; they should fail on the current tautologies if written against the intended table (e.g. 'decode with kv_len >= 1024 and FA hardware path takes FA') and pass after compute-graph-12.

verdict.reason: Verified: every attention test that exercises `forward_batch` builds on `Device::Cpu` (attention.rs:1156-1157, 1200-1201), and the three routing predicates are `#[cfg(feature = "metal")]` (810-849), so no unit test observes which kernel a segment reaches; the only staged-vs-candle linear test (`a_staged_handle_changes_the_kernel_and_not_the_answer`, linear.rs:700) asserts equality only. The two confirmed silent regimes (compute-graph-6's M=2..8 fallthrough to candle's mm and compute-graph-12's dead threshold) are exactly the class a pure routing function with a table test would catch on CPU CI. Medium/S as stated; depends on the extraction in compute-graph-12.

findings.title: cos/sin rows are gathered by position twice per layer per step although every layer sharing a table gathers the same rows
findings.evidence: rope.rs:299-300 `let cos = self.cos.index_select(position_ids, 0)?; let sin = self.sin.index_select(position_ids, 0)?;` inside `apply_qk_with_positions`, called from attention.rs:731 once per layer; block.rs:636-642 passes the same `position_ids` to every layer. gguf_model.rs:631-632 clones one table per distinct geometry across layers; loader.rs:1326-1336 builds identical tables per layer.
findings.rationale: Two gather dispatches per layer per step (72 on a 36-layer model) that produce identical [T, d/2] rows for every layer sharing (dim, theta). Each is tiny but is pure launch overhead (~3-5 us each by the maintainer's cast measurement), ~0.3 ms per token.
findings.proposal: Gather once per forward per distinct table: either cache `(position_ids tensor id) -> (cos_rows, sin_rows)` in a `RefCell` on `RotaryEmbedding` (tables are shared across layers after compute-graph-3), or own the rope kernel and pass `position_ids` so it indexes the full table directly with no gather.
findings.expected_benefit: -2(L-1) dispatches per step, ~0.3 ms/token on a 36-layer model; no numerical change.
findings.verify_how: Dispatch count per step in Metal System Trace; `OXYDLLM_PROFILE=1` attn phase delta.

findings.title: Qwen3.5 gated attention copies both halves of q and computes the sigmoid gate as four candle kernels
findings.evidence: attention.rs:673-681 `let q = q_full.narrow(D::Minus1, 0, hd)?.contiguous()?; let gate = q_full.narrow(D::Minus1, hd, hd)?.contiguous()?.reshape(..)`; attention.rs:989-991 `Some(gate) => (out * super::linear::sigmoid(gate)?)?`; linear.rs:244-246 `pub fn sigmoid(x) { ((x.neg()?.exp()? + 1.0)?).recip() }`. metal_ops.rs:648 `struct SiluMulOp` shows a fused two-input elementwise op of the same shape already exists.
findings.rationale: Per gated attention layer per step: 2 strided copies of q-sized tensors plus neg, exp, add, recip, mul = 7 dispatches where one fused `sigmoid_mul` over the gate view would do; only ~1/4 of Qwen3.5/3.6 layers are attention, so the total is ~60 dispatches per token on a 40-layer hybrid (~0.2 ms).
findings.proposal: Add `sigmoid_mul_fused(out, gate)` as a sibling of `SiluMulOp` (sigmoid(gate)*out, not silu) that accepts the gate as a strided view with row stride 2*hd, and keep the `q` half copy only if the downstream reshape needs it (it does not for the decode layout of compute-graph-5c).
findings.expected_benefit: -5 to -6 dispatches per gated attention layer; ~0.2 ms/token on Qwen3.5-4B-class hybrids.
findings.verify_how: Profile attn phase on a Qwen3.5 checkpoint; parity test of the fused op against `out * sigmoid(gate)` in F32.

findings.title: Gemma 3n KV-shared layers still load and compute K/V projection columns whose results are discarded
findings.evidence: attention.rs:743-749 `let (full_k, full_v) = if seg.reuse_cache { seg.cache.current()? } else { ... seg.cache.append(&seg_k, &seg_v)? };` after `qkv_split` (l.656) has already projected q, k and v from the fused `qkv_proj` built in `load` (l.186-236: `Tensor::cat(&[q_w, k_w, v_w], 0)`); block.rs:613-626 sets `reuse_cache: use_shared_cache` from `kv_shared_layer_map`. Nothing in `Attention::load` consults the map.
findings.rationale: For every layer whose map entry is `Some`, 2*kv_dim*hidden weights stay resident and are read per token to produce k and v that are dropped. On Gemma-3n (roughly the last 40% of layers share) that is a few percent of weight bytes per token and resident memory; small, but free to remove.
findings.proposal: Pass the layer's `kv_shared` flag into `Attention::load`/`load_gguf`; when set, build the projection from `q_proj` only (QkvProjection::Fused of q alone, kv_dim 0) and skip the K/V weight tensors; `forward_batch` already tolerates `reuse_cache`.
findings.expected_benefit: ~2*kv_dim*hidden*n_shared_layers bytes less resident and read per token on Gemma 3n (on the order of 1-3%).
findings.verify_how: Resident bytes after loading gemma-3n before/after; byte-identical output on the regression sweep.

findings.title: Granite's residual_multiplier and logits_scaling run as separate elementwise kernels per sub-layer and per step
findings.evidence: block.rs:414-416 `if let Some(m) = self.residual_multiplier { attn_out = (attn_out * m)?; }` and 432-434 the same for `ffn_out`; block.rs:663-665 `if let Some(s) = c.logits_scaling { logits = (logits / s)?; }` over the [N, vocab] logits each step; block.rs:569-571 `if let Some(scale) = c.embed_scale { x = (x * scale)?; }`.
findings.rationale: Two extra full-hidden-state passes per layer (80 dispatches per token on a 40-layer Granite) plus one over N x vocab per step; each is pure launch overhead. `logits_scaling` can be folded into the lm_head weight (W/s) exactly up to one BF16 rounding of the weight, and `residual_multiplier` into o_proj/down_proj (W*m) with the same caveat; `embed_scale` cannot be folded when embeddings are tied.
findings.proposal: At load, scale the lm_head weight by 1/logits_scaling and the o_proj/down_proj weights by residual_multiplier (skipping the fold when the sandwich norms sit between the projection and the multiply), and drop the runtime multiplies; document that this changes Granite output at BF16 rounding level.
findings.expected_benefit: -2 dispatches per layer and -1 per step on Granite (~0.3 ms/token); no change for other architectures.
findings.verify_how: Granite-3.3-2b tok/s and top-1 agreement over a prompt before/after; the `arch_regression` Granite test must be loosened from byte-identity to a logit tolerance if the fold lands.

subsystems.coverage_notes: Read the entire scope (block.rs, attention.rs, ffn.rs, norm.rs, rope.rs, linear.rs, config.rs) and the callees needed to confirm each mechanism: candle 0.11 tensor.rs reshape (copies non-contiguous), quantized/metal.rs fwd (F32-only input, mv only at M==1), metal_backend/mod.rs matmul (mlx gemm only); metal_ops.rs only in the regions named (Sdpa/RmsNorm/Rope ops, FA entry points and their contiguity bails, maybe_mpp_matmul, maybe_staged_quant_matmul, min_m, GGUF_BATCH_MAX, sink SDPA, quant pipeline compile) plus a kernel-name inventory of quant_kernels.metal; paged.rs append/current/contig pool; weights.rs FP8 preserve logic; gguf_weights.rs LinearWeight/qtensor_with_staged; loader.rs rope/ctx/lm_head construction; gguf_model.rs rope sharing and lm_head; traits.rs; sampling.rs sample(); engine.rs PrefillPacer; profile.rs phase/barrier. Not covered: gdn.rs, moe.rs, mask.rs, encoder.rs, the scheduler and engine_loop batch composition (whether prefill and decode segments mix in one forward), paged.rs block-pool writes and flush_pending, the Metal kernel bodies themselves (FA, sdpa_vector_sink, mpp_gemm.metal), and the LOAD_AND_HISTORY and PLAN_COMPARISON notes (only ROADMAP, the GGUF performance note and the NaN note were read in the relevant sections). Nothing was executed. Quantitative estimates lean on the maintainer's own figure of 1-2 ms per ~360 tiny dispatches; the claim that candle's mlx gemm is markedly slower than a GEMV at M=1 (compute-graph-4) could not be verified from source because candle-metal-kernels is not in the Linux registry, hence its 0.6 confidence. gpt-oss-20b geometry (24 layers, 64/8 heads, head_dim 64, alternating 128-token windows) is taken from the published config, not from a local file. The shallow git history (51 commits) does not show when or why the GgufFastPath was removed, so compute-graph-1 is phrased as either a regression or dead code.
missed: The reviewer did not propose hoisting or fusing the per-layer RoPE table gather. rope.rs:299-300 runs `self.cos.index_select(position_ids, 0)?` and `self.sin.index_select(position_ids, 0)?` inside `apply_qk_with_positions`, i.e. two gather dispatches per layer per step (plus the cat and the rope kernel, four launches per layer), while the layer loop in block.rs:635-641 passes the same `position_ids` to every layer and, on dense models, `c.ropes[layer_idx]` are byte-identical tables (the GGUF loader already clones one table per distinct geometry, gguf_model.rs:631-632; compute-graph-3 would make the safetensors path the same). Gathering once per forward in `run_transformer_layers_batch` and handing the `[T, d/2]` cos/sin rows to each layer, or extending `RopeOp` (metal_ops.rs:470-490) to take `position_ids` and the full table and read `cos[pos[t]]` in-kernel, removes ~2*(n_layers-1) dispatches per token (about 70 on a 36-layer model, ~0.2-0.4 ms, roughly 1% at 40 tok/s, more on small models) with bit-identical output and S effort; it composes with compute-graph-5 to bring the attention prologue down to norm + rope + cache append.

subsystems.assessment: The moe/gdn/expert-stream/encoder slice is correct, well-tested against reference fixtures, and unusually honest about its own hazards (the corrupted-readback check in moe.rs, the graveyard in expert_stream.rs, the blocked inversion in gdn.rs all document a measured failure). What it is not yet is launch-efficient: every one of the three hot paths is dominated by small candle ops rather than by bandwidth. MoE decode (`dispatch_naive`) still routes on the CPU: two device-to-host syncs per MoE layer per step plus a per-expert loop of ~8 launches and one host-to-device upload, so a 1.3B-active OLMoE spends ~80% of its ~100 ms token outside the weight reads; the ROADMAP's "decode still naive dense-gate" is stale in wording (the dense scatter_add gate is gone; the module doc still describes it) but right in substance. MoE prefill (`dispatch_sparse`) has a hidden O(E) cost: candle's Metal `index_add` is out-of-place, so each active expert copies the whole `[n_tokens, hidden]` output. GDN decode runs ~60 launches per linear layer per sequence and streams the F32 state through the device four times per step because `recurrent_delta_step` is written as eleven separate elementwise/matmul ops, and `forward_batch` multiplies that by the number of sequences; the README's own conc=4 numbers (hybrid AWQ 1.5x vs dense AWQ 2.7x) are the signature of exactly that. The streamed-expert pool is the most mature piece: the byte-identity contract, coalesced parallel uncached reads and deferred reclamation are all real and the rejected alternatives were measured; what remains is a double copy on the miss path and a full BF16 dequantization per call on the F8-resident prefill path. The encoder is small and parity-verified, but it is single-sequence, uses O(n^2) F32 attention with a host-built n^2 mask, and bounds input only by `max_position_embeddings` (32768 for Qwen3-Embedding), which on a 24 GB machine is a multi-gigabyte transient allocation per request on a platform where allocation failure has been observed to become garbage rather than an error. The biggest single lever is kernel fusion of the two per-token loops: a fused, batched GDN recurrent step and a device-side grouped expert GEMV with on-device routing. Both are L-sized, both have the reference tests already in place to keep them honest, and both attack the only thing standing between these models and the bandwidth bound the dense paths already reach. The S-sized items below (one router readback, scalar affine weights, l2norm via the existing RMSNorm kernel, pre-cast LayerNorm, un-permute instead of per-expert index_add) are worth doing first because they are measurable in an afternoon and reduce the surface the kernels later replace.

findings.title: MoE decode routes through the CPU: two device syncs plus a per-expert launch loop per layer per step
findings.evidence: moe.rs:476-486 builds routing on device (`probs.arg_sort_last_dim(false)`, `narrow`, `gather`, `sum_keepdim`, `broadcast_div`), then dispatch_naive at :560-561 reads both back: `let top_idx_cpu: Vec<u32> = top_idx.flatten_all()?.to_vec1::<u32>()?; let top_vals_cpu: Vec<f32> = top_vals.flatten_all()?.to_vec1::<f32>()?;`. Each `to_vec1` on Metal is candle's `MetalStorage::to_cpu` (candle-core-0.11.0 src/metal_backend/mod.rs:2004-2020): allocate a blit buffer, encode a blit, `flush_and_wait_current()`. Then :576-589 loops `for (e, expert) in self.experts.resolve(&active)?` and per expert does `Tensor::from_vec(w.clone(), (n_tokens, 1), device)?.to_dtype(..)` (:580), `expert.forward(x_flat, ..)` (3 matmuls + silu + mul via MoeExpert::forward :121-133), `broadcast_mul`, and `a + weighted`. The module doc at :20-24 still describes a `scatter_add` dense gate that no longer exists.
findings.rationale: Per MoE layer per decode step this is 2 full pipeline drains + top_k x (8 launches + 1 host-to-device upload). OLMoE (16 MoE layers, top_k 8) pays 32 drains, ~1024 launches and 128 uploads per token; Qwen3-30B-A3B-class (48 layers) ~96 drains and ~3000 launches. OLMoE's active weights are ~2.6 GB (1.3B x BF16), i.e. ~17 ms at 150 GB/s, yet the README/ROADMAP report 8-10.6 tok/s (~100 ms): the gap is dispatch, not bandwidth. The GPU idles at every drain while the CPU re-encodes the next layer.
findings.proposal: Keep routing on the device for resident banks: (1) at load, stack each layer's expert projections into `[E, inter, hidden]` / `[E, hidden, inter]` tensors (GPT-OSS already ships stacked, see finding 5); (2) add a Metal 'grouped expert GEMV' kernel taking x `[m, hidden]`, the stacked weights, and a `[m, top_k]` U32 id buffer + `[m, top_k]` F32 weight buffer produced by the existing arg_sort/gather on device, computing gate/up for the selected experts in one launch, silu*up in a second, down + weighted accumulate in a third. Decode then has zero readbacks and ~4 launches per MoE layer. Keep `dispatch_naive`/`dispatch_sparse` as the CPU and fallback path and reuse `naive_and_sparse_dispatch_agree` as the contract test (extend it per finding 16). The streamed bank keeps the CPU path (it needs ids on the host to fetch) but can read `probs` once (finding 2).
findings.expected_benefit: Removes 2 syncs and ~70 launches per MoE layer per token. Rough bound from the code: OLMoE from ~100 ms/token toward the 17-25 ms bandwidth floor, i.e. 2-4x decode; on the 48-layer 30B-A3B class the same ratio. This is the 'custom fused MoE kernel' the README (line 499) already predicts as the next 2-3x for prefill; the decode win is the same kernel at m<=8.
findings.verify_how: On the M5: `OXYDLLM_PROFILE_DECODE=1` per-layer timing on OLMoE-1B-7B and Qwen3-30B-A3B before/after; count command-buffer commits per token (Metal System Trace) which should drop from ~2x layers to ~0; the deterministic coherence check and `naive_and_sparse_dispatch_agree` must stay green.

verdict.reason: Mechanism verified: moe.rs:560-561 does two `to_vec1` readbacks (candle metal_backend/mod.rs:2004-2019 `to_cpu` allocates a blit buffer and `flush_and_wait_current()` per call) and :576-589 runs per active expert `Tensor::from_vec(..).to_dtype(..)`, `expert.forward` (3 matmuls + act + mul, :121-133), `broadcast_mul`, add. Frequency (per MoE layer per step) is right and the ROADMAP perf backlog still lists 'decode path still naive dense-gate', so it is not rejected. But the scope is overstated: (a) the 'zero readbacks' win exists only for the Resident bank; the Streamed bank must have ids on the host for `fetch_many` (expert_stream.rs:249-262) and holds experts as separate per-expert `Arc<MoeExpert>` buffers (:281-293), so a stacked-weight grouped kernel cannot address them without argument-buffer indirection; (b) the '48-layer 30B-A3B class' streams on the 24 GB reference machine (BF16 60 GB; Qwen3.6-35B FP8 streams per CHANGELOG), so the 'same ratio' does not transfer; (c) a device-side id path bypasses `checked_expert_row` (CHANGELOG line 41: the detector for recycled-buffer garbage), so the kernel must clamp/validate ids; (d) one kernel per weight format (BF16 Standard, Fp8Resident, MXFP4 GptOss) makes L honest only for the first format. OLMoE (16 layers, 64 experts, top-8, README:569 13.6 tok/s) is the real target; 1.5-2.5x there is plausible, 2-4x is optimistic because attention, router and tiny-M GEMV efficiency remain.
verdict.corrected_benefit: Resident BF16 MoE (OLMoE class) decode 1.5-2.5x; no readback removal for streamed banks (they still get finding 2's single readback and the launch reduction only if a per-expert-buffer variant is written later).
verdict.corrected_proposal: Land findings 2 and 4 first (S). Then a grouped BF16 expert GEMV for the Resident Standard bank only: stack gate/up/down per layer at load, pass the device `[m, top_k]` U32 ids + F32 weights, validate ids in-kernel (clamp + flag) to keep the corruption detector, measure OLMoE with OXYDLLM_PROFILE_DECODE before touching MXFP4 or the streamed bank.

findings.title: Both dispatch paths read back two tensors and run five device ops only to produce data the CPU immediately consumes
findings.evidence: moe.rs:474-486: `let probs = softmax_last_dim(&logits_f32)?; let sorted_idx = probs.arg_sort_last_dim(false)?; let top_idx = sorted_idx.narrow(D::Minus1, 0, self.top_k)?.contiguous()?; let top_vals = probs.gather(&top_idx, D::Minus1)?; ... let denom = top_vals.sum_keepdim(D::Minus1)?; top_vals.broadcast_div(&denom)?`. Then dispatch_naive :560-561 and dispatch_sparse :614-615 each do two separate `to_vec1` readbacks (`top_idx` as u32, `top_vals` as f32). candle's `to_cpu` (metal_backend/mod.rs:2004-2020) commits and waits per call.
findings.rationale: At decode `probs` is `[n_tokens, E]` F32, i.e. 512 B per token at E=128: reading it back once and doing top-k + renormalisation on the CPU (a 128-element partial sort, ~100 ns) is cheaper than the five device launches (arg_sort is a full bitonic sort of the row) plus a second blit/commit/wait. The second wait is not free even with an empty queue: it allocates a staging buffer, encodes a blit and round-trips the command queue (~0.1-0.3 ms on Metal). On a 48-layer MoE that is ~5-15 ms per token of pure sync, plus 240 launches.
findings.proposal: In `forward`, when the bank's dispatch will run on the CPU anyway (both current paths), replace :476-486 by one `probs.to_vec1::<f32>()` (or `to_vec2`) and a CPU `top_k_rows(&probs, top_k, norm_topk) -> (Vec<u32>, Vec<f32>)`; pass the vectors to `dispatch_naive`/`dispatch_sparse` instead of tensors. Keep `checked_expert_row` semantics by checking the read-back probabilities are finite (the corruption detector then triggers on NaN/garbage floats instead of out-of-range indices). The prefill readback is `n_tokens x E x 4` bytes (0.5 MB at 1024 tokens x 128) and the CPU top-k ~0.1 ms, still far below one sync.
findings.expected_benefit: -1 pipeline drain and -5 launches per MoE layer per step on every MoE model (resident and streamed). Estimated 3-8% of decode time on 40-48-layer MoE models; subsumed by finding 1 for resident banks but remains the right shape for the streamed bank.
findings.verify_how: Count `to_cpu` blits per token with Metal System Trace (should halve), and compare `decode_ms` median over 5 runs on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-FP8 streamed and OLMoE resident. `corrupted_router_row_is_rejected` is replaced by an equivalent finite-check test.

verdict.reason: Verified moe.rs:474-486 (softmax, arg_sort_last_dim, narrow+contiguous, gather, sum_keepdim, broadcast_div: 5-6 launches) and the duplicated pair of readbacks at :560-561 and :614-615, each a candle `to_cpu` with its own blit + `flush_and_wait_current()` (metal_backend/mod.rs:2004-2019). Both dispatch paths consume the data on the CPU immediately, so one F32 `probs` readback plus a CPU top-k/renormalisation is strictly less device work. Benefit is real but at the low end: the second wait is on an empty queue (~0.1-0.2 ms), i.e. ~2-4% on 40-48-layer MoE and ~2% on OLMoE. Two determinism notes the proposal should state: CPU renormalisation sums top_k values in a fixed order that may differ in the last ULP from `sum_keepdim`, and exact probability ties may order differently than candle's arg_sort; both change bytes versus the previous build (acceptable per the CHANGELOG precedent for the F8 GEMV) but stay run-to-run deterministic. S effort is honest; `corrupted_router_row_is_rejected` becomes a finite/[0,1] range check on the read-back row.

findings.title: dispatch_sparse copies the entire output tensor once per active expert because candle's Metal index_add is out-of-place
findings.evidence: moe.rs:633-646: `let mut output = Tensor::zeros((n_tokens, hidden), ...)?; for (e, expert) in self.experts.resolve(&active)? { ... let x_subset = x_flat.index_select(&idx_t, 0)?; let expert_out = expert.forward(&x_subset, ..)?; let weighted = expert_out.broadcast_mul(&weights_t)?; output = output.index_add(&idx_t, &weighted, 0)?; }`. candle-core-0.11.0 src/metal_backend/mod.rs:1668-1678 `fn index_add(...) { let mut acc = self.device.zeros_impl(l.shape(), self.dtype())?; self.copy_strided_src(&mut acc, 0, l)?; ...` — a zero-fill, a full copy of `self`, then the `ia_*` kernel, per call.
findings.rationale: Per MoE layer per prefill chunk, the `[n_tokens, hidden]` BF16 output is zero-filled and copied once per active expert: with 128 experts, 1024 tokens and hidden 2048 that is 128 x (4 MB write + 4 MB read + 4 MB write) ~ 1.5 GB of memory traffic and 3 x 128 launches per layer, x 48 layers ~ 72 GB per 1024-token chunk, i.e. on the order of 0.4-0.5 s at 150 GB/s, comparable to the expert GEMM work itself (3.7 TFLOP at 4-8 TFLOPS ~ 0.5-1 s). This cost is invisible in the source because `index_add` looks like an in-place scatter.
findings.proposal: Replace the per-expert accumulate with an un-permute: compute each expert's `weighted` rows and collect them in routing order (`Tensor::cat` of the per-expert outputs, one write pass), build on the CPU the inverse permutation `inv[token*top_k + slot] -> row in cat order`, then `out = gathered.index_select(&inv_t, 0)?.reshape((n_tokens, top_k, hidden))?.sum(1)?`. That is one cat (E small copies totalling one pass), one gather and one reduction instead of E full copies, and it also makes the summation order deterministic per token. Alternatively a single `index_add` with concatenated ids (candle's `ia` kernel handles duplicate ids by looping per destination element) but the un-permute is cheaper and simpler to reason about.
findings.expected_benefit: Removes ~3E launches and ~E full passes over the output per MoE layer per prefill chunk; estimated 15-30% TTFT reduction on long prompts for 64-128-expert models (OLMoE TTFT 7.3 s on 256 words per the module doc is the baseline to beat). Zero effect on decode (n_tokens <= top_k path).
findings.verify_how: TTFT on a ~1.3k-token prompt for OLMoE and Qwen3-30B-A3B before/after; `naive_and_sparse_dispatch_agree` plus the new sparse-vs-per-token test (finding 16) must agree to 1e-5 on CPU; Metal: byte-identical greedy output on the deterministic coherence check (summation order changes, so compare logits tolerance, not bytes, on the first run).

verdict.reason: candle-core-0.11.0 metal_backend/mod.rs:1677-1678 confirmed: `index_add` does `zeros_impl(l.shape())` + `copy_strided_src(&mut acc, ..)` before the `ia_*` kernel, so moe.rs:645 `output = output.index_add(&idx_t, &weighted, 0)?` zero-fills and copies the whole `[n_tokens, hidden]` output once per active expert per prefill chunk. Correction to the arithmetic: OLMoE has 64 experts (README:569), not 128, so its figure halves; Qwen3-30B-A3B (128) and Qwen3.6-35B (256) are as stated, though for streamed banks the SSD re-read dominates TTFT so the relative gain is smaller there. The un-permute proposal is sound with candle's API: per-expert `weighted` rows -> `Tensor::cat` (one pass), host-built inverse permutation -> `index_select` (one pass), `reshape((n_tokens, top_k, hidden)).sum(1)` (one pass), and the per-token summation order becomes fixed (slot order), which is deterministic. Drop the alternative 'single index_add with duplicate ids': candle's Metal `ia` kernel loops over every id per destination element, so it would be O(n_tokens x n_tokens x top_k). S effort honest; verify with `naive_and_sparse_dispatch_agree` (moe.rs:853) at tolerance since the summation order changes.

findings.title: Per-expert host-to-device uploads of gate weights and token indices inside the hot dispatch loops
findings.evidence: moe.rs:579-580 (dispatch_naive): `let w_t = Tensor::from_vec(w.clone(), (n_tokens, 1), device)?.to_dtype(x_flat.dtype())?;` executed once per active expert; moe.rs:637-640 (dispatch_sparse): `let idx_t = Tensor::from_vec(token_idx.clone(), (n_selected,), device)?; let weights_t = Tensor::from_vec(per_expert_weights[e].clone(), (n_selected,), device)?.to_dtype(x_flat.dtype())?.reshape((n_selected, 1))?;` per active expert. On Metal `Tensor::from_vec` is `storage_from_cpu_storage` -> `new_buffer_with_data` (candle metal_backend/device.rs:253), a pool allocation under the device's buffer lock plus a memcpy, and `to_dtype` is a cast kernel.
findings.rationale: At decode with n_tokens == 1 the per-expert weight is a single scalar, yet it costs a device buffer allocation, a memcpy, a cast launch and a `broadcast_mul` launch per expert: top_k x layers = 384 allocations and 768 launches per token on a 48-layer model, all serialized on the engine thread. In prefill the two uploads per expert are 2E small allocations per layer.
findings.proposal: Decode: when `n_tokens == 1`, replace `w_t` + `broadcast_mul` by `expert_out.affine(w[0] as f64, 0.0)?` (one launch, no upload). When `1 < n_tokens <= top_k`, upload all active weights once as `[n_active, n_tokens]` (one `from_vec`, one cast) and `narrow(0, i, 1).t()` per expert. Prefill: upload `per_expert_tokens` and `per_expert_weights` concatenated once per layer (`[sum n_selected]` each, one cast) and `narrow` per expert by offset; with finding 3 the weights become a single `[n_tokens*top_k, 1]` multiply after the gather.
findings.expected_benefit: -1 allocation, -1 cast launch per active expert per layer at decode (~384 allocs + 384 launches per token on a 48-layer top-8 model, ~2-5 ms); -2E allocations per layer per prefill chunk. Small individually, but on the hottest loop of every MoE model.
findings.verify_how: `decode_ms` median over 5 runs on OLMoE and Qwen3-30B-A3B; the CPU tests in moe.rs cover both paths (naive path with n_tokens=2 and the single-expert test with n_tokens=8 go through the modified code).

verdict.reason: Code verified: moe.rs:579-580 `Tensor::from_vec(w.clone(), (n_tokens, 1), device)?.to_dtype(..)` per active expert in the decode path and :637-640 two uploads per expert in the sparse path; on Metal each `from_vec` is `new_buffer_with_data` (device.rs:253-267: a fresh MTLBuffer, buffers-map write lock, residency-set insert) plus a cast launch. But the per-token cost is small: 128 uploads on OLMoE (~1 ms of a ~75-100 ms token) and ~384 on a 48-layer streamed model (~1-2% of a ~250 ms token at 4 tok/s), inside the ~1% run-to-run band the CHANGELOG reports. The `affine(w as f64, 0.0)` replacement is only byte-identical if `w` is first rounded to the activation dtype on the CPU (`bf16(w)` as f64), because the current path multiplies by a BF16-cast weight; the finding does not say so. It is also naturally subsumed by finding 2, after which the per-expert weights already live on the CPU.
verdict.corrected_benefit: ~1% decode on MoE models; worth doing only as part of the finding-2 refactor, not on its own.
verdict.corrected_proposal: Inside the finding-2 CPU routing rewrite: at n_tokens == 1 use `expert_out.affine(f64::from(bf16::from_f32(w[0])), 0.0)`; for 1 < n_tokens <= top_k upload all active weights once as `[n_active, n_tokens]` and `narrow` per expert; in the sparse path upload the concatenated per-expert weights once and `narrow` by offset (and after finding 3, a single `[n_tokens*top_k, 1]` multiply after the gather).

findings.title: GPT-OSS resident load copies every expert out of the stacked tensors while the stacked device copies stay alive, doubling expert memory during load
findings.evidence: moe.rs:397-399: `let slice_expert = |t: &Tensor, e: usize| -> Result<Tensor> { t.narrow(0, e, 1)?.squeeze(0)?.contiguous() };` applied at :420-432 to `gu_blocks`, `gu_scales`, `gu_bias`, `dn_blocks`, `dn_scales`, `dn_bias` for every `e in 0..num_experts`. `gu_blocks` etc. come from `weights.get(..)` (:401-406) which hands out `&Tensor` into `ModelWeights`; `ModelWeights::load` (weights.rs:350-395) uploads every non-streamed tensor to the device in phase 2 (`.to_device(device)` at :395), and the loader keeps `weights` alive from loader.rs:1111 through the block loop and the final model construction (~:1441).
findings.rationale: `narrow(0,e,1).squeeze(0).contiguous()` on a device tensor is a device copy. For gpt-oss-20b the stacked expert tensors are ~10 GB (24 layers x ~425 MB of blocks+scales+bias) and live on the device for the whole load, so the per-expert copies push the load peak to roughly resident size + 10 GB (~23 GB on the 24 GB M5). The ROADMAP documents that allocation failure on Metal has produced silent corruption rather than an error, and the 2026-07-24 fix specifically keeps gpt-oss-20b resident, so the load-time peak matters even though steady state is fine.
findings.proposal: Short term (S): do not slice. Keep the six stacked tensors per layer and give `Mxfp4Linear` an expert offset: `mxfp4_matmul` already receives `blocks`/`scales` tensors, so passing `t.narrow(0, e, 1)?.squeeze(0)?` without `.contiguous()` works if the custom op honours `layout.start_offset()` (check `Mxfp4Matmul` in metal_ops.rs; if it does not, add the offset as a kernel argument). Alternatively add `ModelWeights::take(&mut self, name) -> Option<Tensor>` and have `load_gpt_oss` take `&mut ModelWeights` so the stacked tensors are dropped after slicing (peak becomes one layer's ~425 MB). Keeping the stacked layout is also what finding 1 needs.
findings.expected_benefit: Load-time device peak for resident gpt-oss-20b drops by ~10 GB; removes 6 x 32 device copies per layer at load (~1-2 s of load time). Eliminates a hidden path into the memory-exhaustion failure mode on the reference 24 GB machine.
findings.verify_how: On the M5 watch `memory_footprint`/Activity Monitor during `oxydllm run openai/gpt-oss-20b` (resident) before/after; the `gpt_oss_expert_matches_scalar_reference` test and the byte-identity streamed-vs-resident check cover correctness.

verdict.reason: `slice_expert` (moe.rs:397-399: `t.narrow(0, e, 1)?.squeeze(0)?.contiguous()`) does not copy. candle `Layout::narrow` only moves `start_offset` and keeps the strides (layout.rs:159-160), `Layout::is_contiguous` checks strides alone (layout.rs:112-114), and `Tensor::contiguous` returns `self.clone()` when the layout is contiguous (tensor.rs:2466-2468). So every per-expert `Mxfp4Linear` holds a view sharing the stacked tensor's storage: `Mxfp4Linear::new` checks only `elem_count` (mxfp4.rs:21-22), and `Mxfp4Matmul` binds `b_sl.1.start_offset()` / `s_sl.1.start_offset()` (metal_ops.rs:6826-6827), i.e. the custom op already honours the offset. There is no doubling of expert memory at load and no 6 x num_experts device copies per layer; keeping `weights` alive costs nothing extra because the views keep the same storage alive anyway. The 'short term: do not slice' proposal describes what the code already effectively does.

findings.title: F8-resident experts dequantize the whole projection to BF16 on every prefill call (m > 8)
findings.evidence: moe.rs:100-113: `fn linear(&self) -> Result<Linear> { let w = crate::common::metal_ops::f8_block_dequant_bf16(&self.bytes, &self.scales)?; Linear::new(w, None) }` and `fn forward(&self, x: &Tensor) -> Result<Tensor> { let m = x.dim(0)?; if (1..=8).contains(&m) && x.device().is_metal() && x.dtype() == DType::BF16 { return f8_gemv(x, &self.bytes, &self.scales); } self.linear()?.forward(x) }`. The dequantized `w` is a temporary dropped after one matmul; `dispatch_sparse` calls `expert.forward` once per active expert per layer per prefill chunk, and `Fp8Resident::forward` (:134-146) calls this three times (gate/up/down).
findings.rationale: For a streamed FP8 MoE (Qwen3.6-35B-A3B: 256 experts, 40 MoE layers) a 1024-token prefill chunk routes ~32 rows to each expert, so every expert takes the m > 8 branch: 3 dequant launches + 3 fresh BF16 allocations (2x the F8 bytes each) + 3 matmuls per expert, ~30k dequants and ~30k transient allocations per chunk, with memory traffic per projection of read F8 + write BF16 + read BF16 = 5x the F8 bytes. The decode path (m<=8) is already right; the prefill path undoes the point of caching in F8.
findings.proposal: Either (a) an F8 GEMM that dequantizes tile-staged inside the TensorOps path, as the README says the packed-quant GEMMs already do ('tile-staged dequantization, no dense-weight materialization'), reusing `maybe_mpp_quant_matmul`'s structure for the E4M3 + block-scale decode; or (b) cheaper interim: raise the native-GEMV ceiling to m <= 32 by chunking rows like `PackedQuantLinear::chunked_batch_gemv` (linear.rs:447-466, `gemv_max_m` 16/32), which already covers the per-expert row counts of typical prefill chunks on 128-256-expert models, so the dequant branch is only taken for very long chunks.
findings.expected_benefit: Streamed-FP8 prefill: per-expert bytes moved drop ~5x and ~90k launches per 1024-token chunk disappear; TTFT on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-FP8 should improve markedly (not measured in README; the 4.0 tok/s row is decode). Option (b) is an afternoon and captures most of it for 256-expert models.
findings.verify_how: TTFT on a ~1.3k-token prompt for Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-FP8 streamed before/after; `fp8_resident_expert_matches_standard` (Metal) extended with m=16 and m=32 rows must stay bit-exact for (b) or within tolerance for (a).

verdict.reason: Code accurate: moe.rs:100-113 `Fp8Cached::forward` takes the native F8 GEMV only for m in 1..=8 and otherwise calls `linear()`, which runs `f8_block_dequant_bf16` to a fresh BF16 temporary per call; `dispatch_sparse` calls `expert.forward` once per active expert per chunk, three projections each. But the finding overstates where it matters: `Fp8Cached` is built only by the streamed pool (expert_stream.rs:500-540, guarded by `self.device.is_metal()` and F8 dims), while resident FP8 is dequantized to BF16 at load (README 'FP8 on Apple Silicon doubles resident memory'). On the streamed 35B the cache (3.4 GB) is far below the ~60 GB of experts, so every prefill chunk re-reads each layer's experts from SSD at 3-5 GB/s; the dequant round trip (read F8 + write BF16 + read BF16, ~5x the F8 bytes at ~150 GB/s) is a few percent of the time already spent reading the same bytes from disk. Transient allocations are pool hits after the first expert (candle reuses same-size buffers). Option (b) moves ~8 MB per projection (4 x 8-row GEMVs each re-reading the weight) against ~10 MB for dequant+GEMM and adds launches, so it is not a clear win; only option (a) is a real improvement and only once measurement shows the dequant share.
verdict.corrected_benefit: A few percent of streamed-FP8 TTFT at most; nothing on decode or on resident models.
verdict.corrected_proposal: Add a tracing span around `Fp8Cached::linear()` in the sparse path and measure its share of a 1.3k-token streamed prefill on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-FP8; only if it exceeds ~10% build the tile-staged F8 GEMM (option a). Skip option (b).

findings.title: Streamed miss path copies every expert twice: a fresh zeroed Vec per pread, then a memcpy into a new Metal buffer
findings.evidence: expert_stream.rs:399-431 `read_one`: `let mut bytes = vec![0u8; len as usize]; self.files[meta.file as usize].read_exact_at(&mut bytes, offset)` — a new allocation per tensor per miss; then :445-447 `return Tensor::from_raw_buffer(&r.bytes, r.dtype, &r.dims, &self.device);` (Metal `new_buffer_with_data`, a second full copy), after which `RawRead` is dropped. The module doc at :7 claims reads go 'straight into a reusable scratch buffer', which the code does not do.
findings.rationale: On the streamed decode path misses dominate (Qwen3.6-35B-A3B at 4 tok/s holds ~7% of its experts in a 3.4 GB cache, so hundreds of MB are read per token). Each missed tensor costs: page-faulting a fresh calloc'd region as the kernel fills it (F_NOCACHE I/O lands in user pages), the pread itself, a memcpy into a Metal buffer, and an munmap. On unified memory the Metal buffer could be the pread destination, removing one copy and the fault/zero pass; a reused buffer removes the allocation churn too.
findings.proposal: Allocate (or reuse from a small per-thread pool) a shared-storage `MTLBuffer` of the tensor size, `pread` directly into its `contents()` pointer, and wrap it as the cache tensor. The codebase already owns Metal buffers outside candle for IQ weights (`GgufMatmul::Owned` + `mpp_owned_matmul`), and `Fp8Cached.bytes`/`Mxfp4Linear.blocks` are consumed only by this crate's custom ops, so an own-buffer tensor type (or `MetalStorage::new` via a thin wrapper) is the path. Keep the `Vec` path for CPU devices. Also fix the :7 doc either way.
findings.expected_benefit: Removes one full copy plus the page-fault/zero pass per missed tensor; per expert (~5-12 MB) roughly 0.5-1 ms of CPU work on a ~1.5-4 ms SSD read, i.e. 15-30% of per-miss cost when reads are not already parallel-saturating the SSD. Overall decode gain on streamed models bounded by the miss fraction; measure before committing.
findings.verify_how: Add tracing spans around `read_misses` and the build in `fetch_many`, run Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-FP8 at the pinned 3.4 GB cache and gpt-oss-20b at 4 GB, compare read-vs-build ms per token and the 3-run decode median; `streamed_expert_matches_direct_load` and `read_row_matches_narrow` keep byte identity.

verdict.reason: Verified and slightly stronger than stated. expert_stream.rs:420-423 allocates `vec![0u8; len]` per tensor per miss; :445-447 and :520-524 `Tensor::from_raw_buffer(.., &self.device)` resolve to candle `storage_from_slice` -> `new_buffer_builder().with_data()` -> `new_buffer_with_data` (device.rs:253-267, `newBufferWithBytes` = a second full memcpy plus residency-set insert). The doc at :7 ('reusable scratch buffer') is false. What the reviewer did not say: both `from_raw_buffer` calls are executed while holding `metal_alloc_lock()` (weights.rs:52-55, a global `Mutex<()>`), so the upload memcpy of every missed tensor is serialized across the rayon build threads of `fetch_many` (:271-281); the parallel build buys nothing for that step. Proposal constraints to add: the destination buffers must be fresh allocations (candle's pool `new_buffer` recycles free buffers without checking command completion, the hazard the graveyard exists for), and the tensor wrapper can be a thin custom op returning `MetalStorage::new(buf, dev, count, dtype)` exactly as the crate's ops do (metal_ops.rs RmsNormOp body). M effort and 'measure before committing' are honest.

findings.title: GDN decode step is eleven unfused ops per sequence per layer and streams the F32 state four times; no Metal kernel exists for it
findings.evidence: gdn.rs:240-258 `recurrent_delta_step`: `let q = (l2norm(q)? * (1.0 / (dk as f64).sqrt()))?; let k = l2norm(k)?; let g_exp = g.exp()?.unsqueeze(D::Minus1)?; let s = state.broadcast_mul(&g_exp)?; let kv_mem = k.matmul(&s)?; let delta = (v - kv_mem)?.broadcast_mul(&beta.unsqueeze(D::Minus1)?)?; let s = (s + k.transpose(D::Minus2, D::Minus1)?.matmul(&delta)?)?; let out = q.matmul(&s)?;` with `l2norm` (:114-117) itself `sqr`, `sum_keepdim`, `+eps`, `sqrt`, `broadcast_div`. Around it, `conv_forward` t==1 (:583-592) is `cat`, `broadcast_mul`, `sum_keepdim`, `narrow().contiguous()`, `silu`; `mix_segment` (:640-716) adds `to_dtype`, three `to_heads` reshapes/contiguous copies, two `expand_heads` copies and the final transpose/reshape copy. `rg -i 'delta|gdn|recurrent' src/common/metal_ops.rs` returns nothing: no fused kernel.
findings.rationale: Counting the decode path for one sequence: ~35 launches in `mix_segment` (20 in the recurrent step alone) plus ~16 in `project` and ~6 in `finish`, i.e. ~60 per linear layer, ~1400 per token on Qwen3.5-4B (24 linear layers). The state `[h, dk, dv]` F32 (2 MB per layer at 32x128x128) is materialized as a decayed copy, read by `k.matmul`, added into a third tensor and read again by `q.matmul`: ~18 MB of state traffic per layer, ~430 MB per token, ~14% of the AWQ 4B's 3.1 GB of weights. Qwen3.5-4B-AWQ decodes at 24.6 tok/s (README) against ~39-43 for the dense Qwen3-4B-AWQ in the maintainer's notes at a similar resident size: the ~35% gap is consistent with ~14 ms of launch overhead in a ~40 ms token.
findings.proposal: One Metal kernel `gdn_recurrent_step` with a threadgroup per (sequence, v-head): load q,k (dk) and v (dv), g, beta; l2-normalize q,k in threadgroup memory; for each dv column j compute kv_j = e^g * sum_i k_i S_ij, delta_j = (v_j - kv_j) * beta, then S_ij <- e^g S_ij + k_i delta_j and o_j = sum_i q_i S_ij in a single pass (S read once, written once, in place). Grid dimension over sequences so batched decode is one launch (see finding 9). A second small kernel (or the same one) for the causal conv window + SiLU. Keep the candle path as CPU reference; the fixture tests (`recurrent_step_matches_reference_and_chunked_prefill`, `full_layer_matches_reference_prefill_then_decode`) are the contract, run on Metal via a `fused_gdn_step_matches_candle` test like `fused_gated_norm_matches_fallback_on_metal`.
findings.expected_benefit: Per linear layer per token: ~60 -> ~25 launches and state traffic 18 MB -> 4 MB. On Qwen3.5-4B-AWQ an estimated +20-30% single-stream decode (toward the dense AWQ number), ~10% on the BF16 4B (bandwidth-bound), and most of the batched-decode gap in finding 9. Applies to every Qwen3.5/3.6 hybrid including the 35B-A3B MoE.
findings.verify_how: `OXYDLLM_PROFILE_DECODE=1` per-layer timings on Qwen3.5-4B-AWQ and BF16 before/after; Metal System Trace launch count per token; the 13-test Qwen3.5 battery (batched-vs-single byte identity will need the same kernel on both paths) and the gdn fixture tests at 1e-4.

verdict.reason: Verified gdn.rs:240-258 (recurrent step), :114-117 (l2norm = sqr, sum_keepdim, add, sqrt, broadcast_div), :583-592 (conv t==1: cat, broadcast_mul, sum_keepdim, narrow+contiguous, silu), :640-716 (to_dtype, three to_heads copies, two expand_heads copies, final transpose+reshape copy), :613-634 (`project`: 3-4 linears, to_h_t transposes/casts, sigmoid, softplus chain). `rg -i 'delta|gdn|recurrent'` over src/common/metal_ops.rs and src/common/kernels returns 0 hits: no fused kernel. The ~20 launches in the step and ~30-35 per mix_segment are the right order; state traffic at [32,128,128] F32 (2 MB decayed copy, read by k.matmul, outer-product add into a third tensor, read by q.matmul) is ~18 MB per layer as claimed. README:560 (Qwen3-4B-AWQ 38.5 tok/s) vs README:597 (Qwen3.5-4B-AWQ 24.6) confirms the gap the finding points at. Kernel design note: S (64 KB per head) exceeds Apple's 32 KB threadgroup memory, but it need not be staged: one thread per dv column reads its S column once and writes it once, with q/k/g/beta in threadgroup memory and simd reductions for the l2norms. Changes summation order versus candle's matmul (not byte-identical to the current build, but deterministic); the fixture tolerance 1e-4 at :890/:1179 is the contract. L is honest once the Metal test (like :1264) and both batched paths are included.

findings.title: forward_batch runs the recurrent step once per sequence, so GDN launch cost scales linearly with concurrency
findings.evidence: gdn.rs:768-792: `pub fn forward_batch(&self, x, token_counts, states: &mut [&mut Option<RecurrentState>]) { ... let (qkv, z, beta, g) = self.project(x)?; let mut cores = Vec::with_capacity(states.len()); let mut offset = 0usize; for (state, &t) in states.iter_mut().zip(token_counts) { let qkv_seg = qkv.narrow(1, offset, t)?.contiguous()?; let beta_seg = ...; let g_seg = ...; cores.push(self.mix_segment(&qkv_seg, &beta_seg, &g_seg, state)?); offset += t; } let core = Tensor::cat(&cores, 1)?; self.finish(&core, &z, x.dtype()) }`. block.rs:68-75 builds one `&mut Option<RecurrentState>` per segment from `s.cache.recurrent_mut()`. README line 594-598: Qwen3.5-4B-AWQ conc=4 aggregate 36.1 (1.5x) and BF16-INT4 30.3 (1.9x) versus dense Qwen3-4B-AWQ 17.6 -> 47.7 (2.7x) at line 608.
findings.rationale: Projections are batched once (good), but the ~35 per-sequence launches of `mix_segment` are repeated B times per linear layer: B=4 -> ~165 launches per layer, ~4000 per step across 24 layers (~40 ms of a ~110 ms step at the README's 9 tok/s per stream), B=8 -> ~7300. The per-head recurrence is embarrassingly parallel over sequences; `recurrent_delta_step` already works on any leading batch dim because every op is a batched matmul or broadcast over `[h, 1, dk] x [h, dk, dv]`.
findings.proposal: Partition segments into decode (t == 1, state present) and the rest. For the decode group: `Tensor::cat` the B states into `[B*h, dk, dv]` and the conv windows into `[B, k-1, c]`, run `conv_forward` and `recurrent_delta_step` once on the batched tensors, then `narrow` + `contiguous` per sequence to write states back. Cost is 2B small copies (2 MB each) instead of B x 35 launches. Prefill segments keep the per-segment chunked scan. Follow-up (bigger): hold all recurrent states in one slot-indexed pooled tensor in paged.rs so the cat/narrow disappear; with finding 8 the batched kernel consumes that layout directly.
