findings.title: Dense FP8 checkpoints are widened to BF16 at load on Metal, so the F8 ops here could halve their memory; the Metal cast op is otherwise unreachable in serving
findings.evidence: metal_ops.rs:6462-6468 `pub fn cast_f8e4m3_to_f32(t: &Tensor)` is called only from linear.rs:189 inside `Fp8Linear::forward`, which per call does `cast_f8e4m3_to_f32(&self.weight)` (F32, 4 B/elem), `apply_scale_inv` (another full pass), then `weight_f32.to_dtype(x.dtype())?.t()?` (linear.rs:228-229) before the matmul. But weights.rs:367-375 passes `preserve_fp8_weight && !device.is_metal()` to the loader, and weights.rs:144-153 casts every F8E4M3 tensor to F32 then to the runtime dtype on CPU when not preserved, so on Metal no `Fp8Linear` ever holds F8 bytes: the op and the kernel `cast_f8e4m3_f32` (metal:3912-3933) only run in linear.rs tests. Meanwhile `f8_block_dequant_bf16` (6708) and `f8_gemv` (6680) already implement exact block-scaled F8 serving for experts (moe.rs `Fp8Cached`).
findings.rationale: A dense FP8 checkpoint (Qwen3-8B-FP8 class; ROADMAP:255 mentions Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507-FP8 in the sweep) occupies 2 B/param resident on the 24 GB M5 although the file is 1 B/param and the engine already has a bit-exact F8 GEMV and a bit-exact device dequant. Keeping the per-forward F32 widening path alive for a device that never takes it is dead weight, and if it ever were taken it would be a 10 B/param-per-token disaster.
findings.proposal: Make `Fp8Cached` (or a new `AnyLinear::Fp8Resident { bytes, scales }`) the Metal representation for block-scaled F8 dense weights: loader keeps `preserve_fp8_weight` on Metal, `from_weight_with_scale_inv` builds the resident variant, forward uses `f8_gemv` for m <= DECODE_GEMV_MAX_M and `f8_block_dequant_bf16` + matmul (or the F8 mul_mm from finding 9) above. Then delete `CastF8E4M3ToF32` and its kernel, or keep `cast_f8e4m3_to_f32` only as the CPU/CUDA fallback it already is.
findings.expected_benefit: Resident memory for dense FP8 checkpoints halves (an 8B model goes from ~16 GB to ~8 GB of weights, which on the 24 GB M5 is the difference between fitting with KV room and not), with decode bytes per token halved on those models; removes ~60 lines of Rust + 22 lines of Metal that cannot run in production on the supported platform.
findings.verify_how: Load a block-scaled FP8 checkpoint before/after and compare `oxydllm estimate` / resident bytes; parity via the existing `fp8_resident_expert_matches_standard` pattern on a dense layer; decode tok/s should rise with the halved weight traffic once finding 5's geometry lands.

verdict.reason: Accurate: weights.rs:367-375 passes `preserve_fp8_weight && !device.is_metal()`, and 144-153 cast F8 -> F32 -> target dtype on CPU when not preserved; `AnyLinear::from_weight_with_scale_inv` (linear.rs:539-547) builds `Fp8Linear` only for an F8E4M3 tensor, so on Metal no `Fp8Linear` exists and `cast_f8e4m3_to_f32` (6462-6468, kernel metal:3912-3933) is reachable only from linear.rs tests; meanwhile `f8_gemv` (6680) and `f8_block_dequant_bf16` (6708) already replay the loader's cast chain bit-for-bit for experts. Dense FP8 checkpoints therefore sit at 2 B/param on the 24 GB M5, and the memory halving is real. The effort is understated: a resident-F8 `AnyLinear` variant needs loader changes (keep F8 + scale on Metal; `apply_weight_scale_inv` at weights.rs:246-290 currently folds at load), a prefill path (per-layer dequant+MPP GEMM or an F8 staged kernel), `estimate` accounting (loader.rs:930-933 doubles FP8 into BF16), and the F8 GEMV geometry of finding 5 so decode does not regress against candle's BF16 matvec (2x fewer bytes minus the ~1.2x QDET gap still nets a win, but it must be measured). That is a week of work with verification by execution on several checkpoints.
verdict.corrected_benefit: Resident weight memory halves for dense block-scaled FP8 checkpoints (an 8B model from ~16 GB to ~8 GB on the 24 GB M5), decode weight traffic halves once the F8 GEMV geometry is competitive; ~80 lines of Metal-only-in-tests code deleted.
verdict.corrected_proposal: As stated, but sequenced: land finding 5(b) and 12's F8 tests first, then the resident-F8 AnyLinear variant with the loader keeping `preserve_fp8_weight` on Metal, GEMV for m <= 8 and per-layer `f8_block_dequant_bf16` + MPP GEMM above; keep `cast_f8e4m3_to_f32` only if a CPU/CUDA caller remains.

findings.title: mxfp4_gemv_batch_bf16 recomputes exp2 per lane, loads block bytes one at a time, and indexes its accumulator by a runtime M
findings.evidence: metal_ops.rs:6822 `get_or_compile_quant_pipeline(device.device(), "mxfp4_gemv_batch_bf16")` with `m_batch` passed at runtime (6779-6783) and grid `n.div_ceil(8)` x 64 threads (6829-6840). quant_kernels.metal:3126 `const uint M = min(p.m_batch, (uint)GGUF_BATCH_MAX);`, :3138-3139 `float sumf[GGUF_N_DST][GGUF_BATCH_MAX]` then `for (uint m = 0; m < M; ++m) sumf[row][m] += acc;` (:3160) with runtime M; :3146-3153 `device const uint8_t *qs = blocks + base * 16 + 4 * il; const float scale = exp2((float)scales[base] - 127.0f); for (i < 4) { const uint8_t byte = qs[i]; ... }` — four 1-byte loads and one `exp2` per (row, block) in each of the 4 `il` lanes that share the block; :3154-3160 the x loads `y = x + m*K + ib*32 + y_off` do not depend on `row` but sit inside the `row` loop, so x is re-read 4x per block unless the compiler hoists it.
findings.rationale: This kernel moves ~1.2 GB of the ~3.5 GB per gpt-oss-20b token, so it is the single largest byte mover; the README's 14.3 tok/s versus a ~30 tok/s bandwidth bound says the sum of launch overhead (findings 2-3) and kernel efficiency is costing about half. A runtime-bounded loop over a register array is the classic trigger for thread-private-memory demotion on Apple GPUs, and `exp2` + 4 byte loads per 16-byte block per lane is avoidable work in the inner loop.
findings.proposal: Specialise M with `[[function_constant(0)]] uint M_CONST` (one pipeline per m in 1..=8, cached by name+constant), so `sumf` and the m-loop fully unroll; load the block bytes as one `uint` (`*(device const uint*)(blocks + base*16 + 4*il)`, 4-byte aligned by construction); compute the E8M0 scale as `as_type<float>((uint)scales[base] << 23)` with a zero guard for code 0 (exact for 1..=254, no transcendental); hoist the x loads out of the row loop into `float y[8]` per m.
findings.expected_benefit: If the kernel is currently ALU/issue-bound rather than bandwidth-bound (unknown without a trace), 1.2-1.5x on the expert GEMV, i.e. up to ~15-20% of gpt-oss decode; if it is already at bandwidth the change is neutral and costs nothing.
findings.verify_how: Add the MXFP4 GEMV at N=5760,K=2880 and N=2880,K=2880 to `quantized_matvec_bandwidth_probe` and print GB/s (bytes = N*K/2 + N*K/32); compare with candle Q4_0 matvec (same ~0.5 B/elem) as the floor; then Xcode GPU capture to read the occupancy and the 'thread memory' column for the kernel.

verdict.reason: Kernel verified at metal:3126-3161: `M = min(p.m_batch, 8)` runtime, `float sumf[4][8]` zeroed and accumulated under `for (m < M)` (3138-3139, 3155-3161), `exp2((float)scales[base] - 127.0f)` computed per (row, block) by each of the 4 `il` lanes that share the block (3146-3147), four single-byte `qs[i]` loads (3149-3153), and the `y = x + m*K + ib*32 + y_off` loads sit inside the `row` loop although they do not depend on `row` (3155-3157). The Rust side passes `m_batch` at runtime and compiles one pipeline (6779-6783, 6822), so M cannot unroll. First-principles: ~1.2 GB of expert weight per gpt-oss-20b token takes ~10 ms at bandwidth, while the per-lane instruction count here (byte loads, 8 dynamic `constant`-space LUT lookups, exp2, runtime-bounded loops) is within ~2x of that budget on the M5's ALUs, so issue-bound is plausible but unproven; the reviewer's 0.5 confidence is honest and the probe they name is the right test. Proposal is S and output-identical provided the E8M0 `as_type` path guards code 0 (would decode to 0.0 instead of 2^-127) and code 255 (becomes +inf instead of NaN) to stay bit-identical with `mxfp4::dequantize_mxfp4_f32`, the CPU reference the existing test uses. Add: replace the dynamic `constant float MXFP4_LUT16[16]` lookup with a register-only e2m1 decode, which is the likelier cost than exp2. Function-constant specialisation needs the pipeline cache key (1587) extended with the constant value.

subsystems.coverage_notes: Read lines 6387-7112 and 7796-8036 of metal_ops.rs in full; 7112-7796 skimmed by headings, with 7661-7722 (mxfp4 reference test) and the sink test's shape line read. Did not read the test bodies 7127-7660 (staged GEMM/crossover/bandwidth probes). Did not open NAN_INVESTIGATION, PERFORMANCE_INVESTIGATION_GGUF or LOAD_AND_HISTORY beyond a grep for FP8/MXFP4/sink numbers (none found). candle-metal-kernels 0.11 is not in the Linux cargo registry, so the claim that a blit encoder ends the live compute encoder rests on candle-core's allocate_zeros calling blit_command_encoder and on candle's single-live-encoder Commands design, not on reading that crate. Did not read mpp_gemm.metal or the MppOwnedMatvec/MppStagedMatmul bodies beyond their signatures, so the owned-weight finding covers pool reuse, not the Metal-4 residency question. Did not verify the MXFP4 nibble order against the GPT-OSS reference (README reports the model coherent end to end). No profiling was possible; all bandwidth/launch-cost magnitudes are argued from the code and the README's measured 14.3 tok/s.
missed: The sink-SDPA call site copies the entire K and V cache of every GPT-OSS layer on every decode step before the kernel reads it once more, and the op's contiguity rule is what forces it. `SdpaVectorSink::metal_fwd` bails unless q/k/v are contiguous (metal_ops.rs:7005-7007) and the kernel addresses heads as `k_base = k + kvh * kv_len * D` (quant_kernels.metal:3281-3282), so attention.rs:897-899 calls `k_seg.contiguous()` / `v_seg.contiguous()` unconditionally. But the cache hands back `contig_k.narrow(2, start, len)` of a `[1, n_kv, cap, D]` buffer (paged.rs:1254-1259, allocated at 1043-1045 with `cap = contig_buf_capacity(needed)` which is always larger than `needed`, 928-935), and `truncate_kv_window` narrows again along dim 2 (attention.rs:125, 128); with n_kv = 8 > 1 that view has stride[1] = cap*D != len*D and is not contiguous, so candle materialises both tensors: 2 x KVH x L x D x 2 B read plus written, i.e. ~32 MB read + 32 MB written per full-attention layer per token at L = 8k on gpt-oss-20b, two to three times the traffic of the kernel itself. The non-sink decode path already avoids exactly this with its `straight_in` check (attention.rs:869-882: `stride[3] == 1 && stride[2] == dims[3]`), and the FA op takes a `kv_head_stride` parameter derived by `kv_head_stride(layout)` (metal_ops.rs:1077, 1158-1192, 3564-3566). Fix (S, output-bitwise-identical): add `kv_head_stride: u32` to `SdpaSinkParams` and the Metal struct, replace the k/v contiguity bail with the straight-in condition, pass `k_l.stride()[1]`, and at the call site use `straight_in` as the SDPA branch does. Verify with `OXYDLLM_PROFILE_DECODE` or a Metal trace counting copy kernels per token on an 8k prompt, and A/B tok/s; this should be done before finding 4 so the kernel rewrite is measured on its own.

subsystems.assessment: The kernel layer is in two very different states. The parts that are live and recent are solid: the deterministic AWQ/GPTQ split-K epilogues are correct and bounds-safe, the TensorOps staged GEMMs (`gemm_staged`) double-buffer their dequant and handle the odd block sizes (Q3_K 110 B, Q6_K 210 B, Q8_0 34 B) with packed loads, the wide d=512 FlashAttention variant reads V in place with a proper n>=bc mask, and the IQ matvec keeps M compile-time with guarded unrolled loops, which is the right register discipline. The fragile part is what the task brief assumed was the bottleneck: the ten GGUF `gguf_*_gemv_bf16` / `_gemv_batch_bf16` / `_mul_mm_bf16` kernel families in quant_kernels.metal (about 2,400 lines, lines 686-3105) are not dispatched by any Rust code; GGUF K-quant decode at M<64 goes to candle's QMatMul with an F32 cast in and out per linear, so the measured ~50% bandwidth ceiling belongs to candle's f32 `mul_mv` plus cast overhead, not to the ports in this file, and the batched-decode weight-sharing the CHANGELOG credits for 1.5-1.7x concurrency scaling is no longer on the path. The biggest lever is therefore structural rather than micro-optimization: re-own the GGUF M=1..8 path on the `Owned`/`StagedWeight` route the IQ types already use (bf16 I/O, batch kernels), which the maintainer's own notes measured at +6% for the casts alone and which is the precondition for any further GEMV tuning. The second lever is cheap and certain: the deterministic AWQ/GPTQ GEMV still inherits the atomic kernels' F32 accumulator, so every packed-quant linear per token is a zero-fill dispatch, the GEMV, and a cast dispatch, where one dispatch writing bf16 would do. Beyond that, the recurring pattern across the live decode kernels (MXFP4, F8, sink SDPA, IQ matvec) is being load-instruction bound rather than weight-bandwidth bound: activations re-read per output row, byte-wise weight loads, runtime-bounded loops over register arrays, and one-simdgroup-per-head attention that cannot fill the GPU at long context. The prefill side is good where TensorOps is used and poor where it is not: the legacy flash_attn.metal path (which Gemma 2's softcap forces even on M5) does its softmax with one thread per row, and the packed-quant staged GEMM re-reads scales eight times per word with no double buffering. None of this is a correctness problem; the one numerical nit is fast-math `tanh` in the softcap kernels versus `precise::tanh` everywhere else.

findings.title: GGUF gemv/batch/mul_mm kernel suite (~2,400 lines) is dead code; live GGUF decode is candle's QMatMul
findings.evidence: quant_kernels.metal:686 `// GGUF GEMV kernels: bf16-aware ports of llama.cpp \`mul_vec_q_n_f32\` (MIT).`; :734 `kernel void gguf_q5_0_gemv_bf16(`, :1041 `#define GGUF_LEGACY_GEMV_BATCH(`, :1235 `kernel void gguf_q4k_gemv_bf16(`, :1333 `gguf_q4k_gemv_batch_bf16`, :2644 `kernel void gguf_q5_0_mul_mm_bf16(` ... :3058 `kernel void gguf_q3k_mul_mm_bf16(`. `grep -rn '"gguf_' src --include=*.rs` returns no hits and no format!-built names exist. linear.rs:263-265 `Small batches go to candle's \`QMatMul\` ... Large batches go to the staged TensorOps GEMM`; linear.rs:279-282 `enum GgufMatmul { Candle(QMatMul), Owned(StagedWeight) }`; metal_ops.rs:2979-2990 `matvec_kernel` returns Some only for Iq4Nl/Iq4Xs/Iq3S.
findings.rationale: Thirty kernels plus the `gguf_*_dequant_strip_into` helpers (lines 686-3105) are compiled into the quant library at first pipeline build in every process and nothing dispatches them; the in-file geometry comments (:1223 'Q4_K geometry: 1 simdgroup x N_DST=4 rows') and CHANGELOG :181/:254 describe them as the live fast path, and the parity tests CHANGELOG :108 mentions no longer reference them. Any tuning effort aimed at the 'GGUF GEMV bottleneck' lands on code that does not run.
findings.proposal: Decide explicitly: either delete lines 686-3105 plus `GgufParams`/`GgufBatchParams`/`GgufMatmulParams` (keep `GGUF_N_SIMDGROUP`/`GGUF_N_DST`/`GGUF_BATCH_MAX`, which `mxfp4_gemv_batch_bf16` uses), or re-wire them per kernels-2. In both cases add a unit test that extracts every `kernel void <name>` from the `include_str!` Metal sources and asserts the name appears in some Rust string literal, so dead kernels fail CI.
findings.expected_benefit: Roughly 40% less quant-library source to compile at startup; removes a misleading surface for future work. No runtime perf change by itself.
findings.verify_how: Run the grep above on M5; delete the range and confirm `cargo test` plus a GGUF decode smoke run are unaffected; time the first `get_or_compile_quant_pipeline` before/after.

verdict.reason: Accurate on the core fact: `grep -rn '"gguf_' src --include=*.rs` returns nothing, no format!-built names exist, and every GGUF decode with m < min_m goes to candle (linear.rs:339-351 `x.to_dtype(DType::F32)` ... `candle_core::Module::forward(inner, &x_2d)`), while `matvec_kernel()` (metal_ops.rs:2979-2990) only names the three `mpp_mv_iq*` kernels in the MPP library. So the 30 `gguf_*_gemv/_gemv_batch/_mul_mm_bf16` kernels at quant_kernels.metal:734-3101 are compiled and never dispatched. The retirement is undocumented: the history is squashed at 42943bf (2026-08-26) which already uses QMatMul, no CHANGELOG entry mentions dropping the path, and alpha.13 (CHANGELOG:108) still lists parity tests for these kernels. Two corrections to the proposal: (1) `GgufBatchParams` and `GgufMatmulParams` plus `GGUF_MM_BM/BN/TG` are LIVE, used by `mxfp4_gemv_batch_bf16` (:3119 `constant GgufBatchParams &p`) and `mxfp4_mul_mm_bf16` (:3202 `constant GgufMatmulParams &p`, :3206/:3213-3219 `GGUF_MM_BN/BM`), so deleting them breaks gpt-oss; only `GgufParams` (:695) and the typedefs/helpers in 686-3101 are dead. (2) The CI name-check must also parse macro instantiations (`AWQ_DET_KERNEL(w4a16_gemv_bf16, ...)` at :3712ff, `GGUF_LEGACY_GEMV_BATCH(...)`, `MPP_MATVEC_KERNEL(...)`), since those kernels are `kernel void NAME(`. Severity is maintainability-medium, not high: Metal compiles the source once per process and macOS caches the binary by source hash, so the ~61% of file (not 40%) that is dead costs nothing per token; the real cost is the misleading surface and the undocumented reversal of a measured +6% path. Keep the 'decide explicitly' framing, because kernels-2 depends on the decision.
verdict.corrected_benefit: Removes ~2,400 dead lines and the misleading comments/CHANGELOG lineage; no runtime change. The CI check prevents the next silent retirement.
verdict.corrected_proposal: Either delete quant_kernels.metal:686-3101 except `GGUF_N_SIMDWIDTH/N_DST/N_SIMDGROUP/BATCH_MAX`, `GgufBatchParams`, `GgufMatmulParams`, `GGUF_MM_BM/BN/TG` (all used by the live mxfp4 kernels), or re-wire per kernels-2; add a test that extracts kernel names from both `kernel void <name>` and `<MACRO>_KERNEL(<name>,` lines of all four include_str! sources and asserts each appears in a Rust string literal; add one CHANGELOG line stating why the GGUF fast path was retired.

findings.title: GGUF K-quant decode pays F32 cast-in/cast-out per linear and runs candle's f32 mul_mv; bf16 ports exist but are unused
findings.evidence: linear.rs:347-351 `x_f32_owned = x.to_dtype(DType::F32)?; ... candle_core::Module::forward(inner, &x_2d)`, :375 `out.to_dtype(self.out_dtype)`; the staged GEMM takes only m >= MPP_GEMM_MIN_M=64 (metal_ops.rs:2546, :3085-3088). findings.rationale: Per decode token on a 36-layer model: ~253 linears x (cast kernel over [1,K] + candle `kernel_mul_mv_q*_f32` + cast kernel over [1,N]) = ~500 extra dispatches plus an F32 activation copy, on the dominant GGUF workload (Q4_K_M). The dead ports were measured at +6% (25.64 -> 27.18 tok/s on Q5_0 4B) precisely because they remove these casts, and owning the kernel is the precondition for any geometry/vectorization tuning toward the 76% Ollama reaches.
findings.proposal: Route K-quant/legacy/Q8_0 weights through the `Owned(StagedWeight)` path the IQ types use: add `WeightKind::Q4K/Q5K/Q6K/Q2K/Q3K/Q8_0/Q4_0/...` arms to `matvec_kernel()` pointing at `gguf_*_gemv_bf16` (M=1) and `gguf_*_gemv_batch_bf16` (M=2..8) with the per-type threadgroup geometry the comments document (Q4_K 1 simdgroup x 4 rows at :1223; Q5_K 2x2; Q6_K 2x1; Q2_K 2x4; Q3_K 2x2; legacy/Q8_0 2x4), reinstating the parity tests. Keep the staged TensorOps GEMM for M >= 64; M in 9..63 can use `gguf_*_mul_mm_bf16` or candle.
findings.expected_benefit: +3-6% decode on Q4_K_M/Q5_K/Q6_K/Q8_0 models from the casts alone (previously measured), removal of the F32 activation copy, and an owned kernel to tune further.
findings.verify_how: Qwen3-4B-Q4_K_M steady-state tok/s before/after; temp-0 output comparison against the candle path (the haiku bit-identity check the notes used); dispatch count per token in a Metal System Trace.

verdict.reason: Verified: linear.rs:339-351 casts x to F32 and runs candle's `QMatMul`, and `finish()` (:366-376) casts the F32 result back to `out_dtype`, for every GGUF linear with m below `min_m()` (metal_ops.rs:3083-3091: 64 for Q4_0/1, Q5_0/1, Q4K; 128 for Q8_0/Q2K/Q3K/Q5K/Q6K) — so all decode and small-batch GGUF traffic pays 2 cast dispatches plus an F32 activation copy per linear. candle 0.11's Metal `fwd` (quantized/metal.rs:372-375) sends m==1 to `fwd_mv` (the f32 `kernel_mul_mv_*`), so the per-token mechanism is as claimed. The maintainer's own note (PERFORMANCE_INVESTIGATION_GGUF.md 'Decomposizione del guadagno (+6%)': 'Costo dei 2 cast bf16↔f32 della candle path: ~1-2 ms/token = 3-6%', and later 'Q5_K/Q6_K +6-11% sul baseline candle') measured exactly this on candle 0.10; the mul_mv kernels did not change in 0.11, so it should reproduce. Implementability: `StagedWeight` already retains candle's own buffer (2eed4aa 'reading the weight in the buffer candle keeps it in rather than copying it'), which removes the 2x-memory objection that the May version hit; the bf16 kernels take `GgufParams{in,out}` and the geometry is documented in-file (:1223 'Q4_K geometry: 1 simdgroup x N_DST=4 rows'). Two caveats that do not change the verdict: the gguf kernels sit in the quant library (`get_or_compile_quant_pipeline`) while `MppOwnedMatvec` uses the MPP library, so a new op or a move of the kernels is needed; and for M in 9..63 keep candle's `call_quantized_matmul_mm_t` (ggml's simdgroup-matrix GEMM) rather than the 16x16 scalar `gguf_*_mul_mm_bf16` tiles, which are the kernels alpha.12.1 found 3.7x too expensive at small M. The retirement reason is undocumented, so this is measure-first per the ROADMAP; confidence ~0.65 rather than 0.75.

findings.title: Concurrent GGUF decode (M=2..8) likely lost the shared-weight batch kernels and may have regressed to per-row weight streaming
findings.evidence: The batch kernels share one weight read across M rows: :1333 `gguf_q4k_gemv_batch_bf16` with the m loop inside the block loop `for (uint m = 0; m < M; ++m)` (:1392), likewise :1041-1095 (legacy macro), :1161, :1561, :1757, :1935, :2177. None is dispatched (see kernels-1); linear.rs:320-358 sends every m < 64 to candle's QMatMul. CHANGELOG :165 'aggregate throughput on Qwen3-4B-Q4_K_M goes from 14.9 to 52.1 tok/s at concurrency 2' and :181 (M>=2 previously '3.7x more expensive than two serial ones') are attributed to these kernels.
findings.rationale: candle's quantized Metal matmul dispatches its `kernel_mul_mv_*` with one threadgroup column per activation row, so the weight is streamed once per batched row; aggregate decode throughput at concurrency 2-8 would then be close to flat instead of the 1.46x/1.62x/1.69x the CHANGELOG records. I could not execute anything, so this is a hypothesis grounded in the dispatch code; the fix is the same re-wire as kernels-2.
findings.proposal: Measure first. If confirmed, the fix is kernels-2's re-wire of `gguf_*_gemv_batch_bf16` for M=2..8 (and the chunked dispatch above 8 the packed-quant path already has, linear.rs:447-469).
findings.expected_benefit: Restores 1.5-1.7x aggregate throughput scaling at concurrency 2-8 on GGUF checkpoints if the regression is real.
findings.verify_how: On M5 run Qwen3-4B-Q4_K_M with 1, 2, 4 and 8 concurrent clients (scripts/stress_baseline.py) and compare aggregate tok/s to the CHANGELOG :165 numbers (14.9 -> 52.1 at c=2).

verdict.reason: The stated mechanism is wrong: candle 0.11 does NOT run `kernel_mul_mv_*` once per activation row for M>=2. `QMatMul`'s Metal `fwd` (candle-core-0.11.0/src/quantized/metal.rs:372-375) takes the mv path only when `src_shape.dim(D::Minus2) == 1`; otherwise it calls `call_quantized_matmul_mm_t` (:414), ggml's tiled `kernel_mul_mm` which dequantizes a weight tile into threadgroup memory once and multiplies it against all M rows with simdgroup matrices. So weight bytes are not re-streamed per row and aggregate throughput should not be flat. What remains is a weaker, different question: ggml's mul_mm at M=2..8 pads to 64-row tiles and llama.cpp itself keeps mul_mv below `ne11_mm_min`, so candle's path may be slower than the retired `gguf_*_gemv_batch_bf16` (which processed M rows against one weight read in registers, :1392-1400) — but that is a tile-overhead effect of unknown size, not a 'per-row streaming' regression, and the CHANGELOG:165 numbers (14.9 -> 52.1 tok/s at c=2) were measured against the project's own 16x16 scalar mul_mm, not against ggml's. Keep only the measurement; the fix, if any, is kernels-2.
verdict.corrected_benefit: Unknown until measured; candle's mul_mm already shares the weight read across M rows, so any gap at c=2..8 is tile overhead, likely well under the 1.5x the finding implies.
verdict.corrected_proposal: Run scripts/stress_baseline.py on Qwen3-4B-Q4_K_M at c=1/2/4/8 and compare to CHANGELOG:165/:181; only if aggregate scaling is clearly below 1.4x at c=2 fold the `gguf_*_gemv_batch_bf16` re-wire into kernels-2.

findings.title: Deterministic AWQ/GPTQ GEMV still uses an F32 accumulator: zero-fill + GEMV + cast = three dispatches per linear per token
findings.evidence: :3355 `device float*         out,` (also :3427, :3511, :3577; wrappers :3650-3708 `device float* out [[buffer(4)]]`); every output is written exactly once: :3415 `out[j * PACK_FACTOR + pack_position<BITS>(k)] = sum;`, :3563 `out[o] = sum;`. Host metal_ops.rs:2078-2086 `let out = Tensor::zeros((m, out_features), DType::F32, x.device())?; out.inplace_op1(&W4A16Matmul {..})?; out.to_dtype(x.dtype())`; doc :1697-1699 'Written as an InplaceOp1 on the F32 accumulator because the op needs four input tensors and CustomOp3 tops out at three'. The zero-fill was a requirement of the retired atomic kernels only (:51 '`out` must be host-zeroed (atomic_fetch_add accumulates)').
findings.rationale: Per packed-quant linear per decode token: a fill kernel, the GEMV, a cast kernel, plus an F32 write and read of [m,N]. On Qwen3-4B (36 layers x 7 linears) that is ~500 extra dispatches per token; the same cast mechanism was measured at 1-2 ms/token (3-6%) on the GGUF path, and at 35.5 tok/s (28 ms/token) this is the same order as the 3.7% the det epilogue cost (CHANGELOG :96). The four-input limitation is already solved in the same file: `MppOwnedMatvec` is a CustomOp1 on `x` that captures the weight and allocates its own BF16 output (metal_ops.rs:3240-3242).
findings.proposal: Template the det impls on the output type (`device T* out`, `out[..] = T(sum)`; batch variants likewise) and instantiate `_bf16`/`_f16` outputs; convert `W4A16Matmul`/`GptqMatmul` to `CustomOp1` on `x` capturing qweight/qzeros/scales, allocating the output in x's dtype with `device.new_buffer` (no `zeros()`, no `to_dtype`). Keep the bench-only atomic variants on the F32 accumulator.
findings.expected_benefit: Two fewer dispatches per packed-quant linear (~500/token on a 36-layer model) and no F32 round trip; ~3-6% decode throughput on AWQ/GPTQ/compressed-tensors checkpoints.
findings.verify_how: tok/s on Qwen3-4B-AWQ and Qwen3-1.7B-GPTQ-Int8 before/after; Metal System Trace dispatch count per token; the 48-run bitwise determinism test must still pass (in-kernel bf16 rounding equals the cast).

verdict.reason: Verified end to end. Host: metal_ops.rs:2078-2086 `Tensor::zeros((m, out_features), DType::F32)` -> `out.inplace_op1(&W4A16Matmul{..})` -> `out.to_dtype(x.dtype())`, and `gptq_matmul` at :2510 does the same; the doc at :1697-1699 gives the CustomOp3 three-input limit as the reason. Kernels: every deterministic path writes each output exactly once — `awq_gemv_det_impl` :3415 `out[j * PACK_FACTOR + pack_position<BITS>(k)] = sum;`, batch :3484, `gptq_gemv_det_impl` :3563 `out[o] = sum;`, gptq batch :3644 — so the zero-fill is a leftover of the atomic variants (:51 '`out` must be host-zeroed (atomic_fetch_add accumulates)'). Candle's `zeros_impl` (metal_backend/mod.rs:2081-2087 `.with_zeros(size)`) is extra work per call either way, and the cast is a compute dispatch, so each packed-quant linear per token carries two avoidable commands plus an F32 [m,N] write/read; on a 36-layer model that is ~500 commands/token. The precedent is in the same file: `f8_gemv_bf16` already writes `out[o] = bfloat(sum)` (:3821) into a buffer allocated with `device.new_buffer(n_out, DType::BF16, ..)` (:6630), and `MppOwnedMatvec` is a CustomOp1 on `x` capturing the weight (:3240-3242). The det impls are already templated on `T`, so `device T* out` + `T(sum)` is a mechanical change; in-kernel `bfloat(sum)` is RNE like candle's cast, so the 48-run determinism test and byte-identity should hold. Expected 3-6% is the right order (the same two-cast mechanism measured 1-2 ms/token on GGUF); severity 'high' is at the boundary but defensible on AWQ, the model class where the det epilogue already cost 3.7% (CHANGELOG:96).

findings.title: AWQ det M=1 kernel: 4-byte loads per thread, under-filled grid on narrow outputs, 4-way bank conflicts in the epilogue
findings.evidence: :3393 `uint ww = qweight[i * p.packed_out + j];` :3394 `float xv = float(x[i]);` (one 4-byte weight and one 2-byte activation load per k per thread); TG (TGW=32, S=32)=1024 threads via :3712 `AWQ_DET_KERNEL(w4a16_gemv_bf16, bfloat, 4, 32u, 32u)`, grid = packed_out/32 threadgroups with classes at packed_out < 512 / < 1024 (metal_ops.rs:1807-1815). Epilogue :3404 `partials[(ks * TGW + tid.x) * HALF + h] = ...` and :3413 `sum += partials[(s * TGW + tid.x) * HALF + ...]` put adjacent lanes HALF=4 words apart. The retired atomic geometry used TARGET_THREADS=32768 (metal_ops.rs:2302) and measured 36.8 vs det 35.5 tok/s (CHANGELOG :96).
findings.rationale: For Qwen3-4B down_proj (in=9728, out=2560): packed_out=320 -> 10 threadgroups for a 12.4 MB weight, i.e. one 1024-thread TG per core on a 10-core M5, each thread walking 304 k-rows with scalar 4-byte loads; q/k/v/o are similar. That is latency-bound memory-level parallelism, consistent with AWQ sitting at ~59% of bandwidth where the perf notes had the W4A16 atomic kernel at 71%. The strided partials layout adds 4-way TG-memory bank conflicts on both the store and the S-deep reduction, twice per output.
findings.proposal: (1) Each thread handles a `uint2`/`uint4` of consecutive packed words (16/32 output columns, acc[16]/acc[32]), keeping the simdgroup on 256/512 contiguous bytes with 2-4x fewer load instructions. (2) For the narrow class (packed_out < 512) use TGW=8..16 with S=64 so down_proj gets 20-40 threadgroups instead of 10. (3) Store partials SoA, `partials[(h * S + ks) * TGW + tid.x]`, which is conflict-free; keep the fixed reduction order so determinism is preserved. The GPTQ det loop (:3539-3546) has the same scalar-load structure and the `scale_v` multiply inside the per-element FMA could be hoisted per group.
findings.expected_benefit: 5-15% AWQ decode (59% -> ~70% of bandwidth, where the atomic kernel already stood); smaller gain for GPTQ.
findings.verify_how: `quant_gemv_bench` per shape (gate_up 2560x19456 and down_proj 9728x2560 at m=1) before/after; `xcrun metal` register report; tok/s on Qwen3-4B-AWQ; determinism test.

verdict.reason: Code facts check out: :3393 `qweight[i * p.packed_out + j]` is one 4-byte word per lane per k, `float xv = float(x[i])` a uniform 2-byte load; class 0 (packed_out < 512, metal_ops.rs:1807-1815) maps to `AWQ_DET_KERNEL(w4a16_gemv_bf16, bfloat, 4, 32u, 32u)` (:3712) = 1024-thread TGs, so Qwen3-4B down_proj (packed_out=320) gets 10 TGs; the partials layout `(ks * TGW + tid.x) * HALF + h` (:3404/:3413) puts adjacent lanes 4 words apart, a 4-way bank conflict on both the store and the S-deep reads. But two things shrink the benefit: (a) across a simdgroup the word loads ARE coalesced (32 adjacent words = 128 contiguous bytes per i), so the per-lane 'scalar' load is not the uncoalesced pattern the rationale implies; wider per-lane loads only raise bytes in flight. (b) The atomic kernel with TARGET_THREADS=32768 geometry (:2302) — the reviewer's own 'where the atomic kernel already stood' reference — measured only 3.7% faster end to end (36.8 vs 35.5, CHANGELOG:96), and the ROADMAP's own backlog entry puts the det-geometry gap at ~1.2x on the q_proj class at the micro-bench; a 5-15% end-to-end claim is therefore optimistic, 2-5% is the honest band. Also `quant_gemv_bench` named in verify_how no longer exists in the tree (no reference in src or Cargo), so the paired harness must be recreated. Not rejected by the ROADMAP; it is explicitly in the performance backlog.
verdict.corrected_benefit: 2-5% AWQ decode end to end (the atomic geometry ceiling was +3.7%); larger only if wider loads lift the kernel above where the atomic variant stood.
verdict.corrected_proposal: Do the two zero-risk parts first: SoA partials `partials[(h * S + ks) * TGW + tid.x]` (conflict-free, same reduction order) and `uint2` weight loads per lane (two consecutive words, acc[16]); re-measure the narrow class with TGW=16,S=64 before touching GPTQ. Recreate a paired det/atomic micro-bench (the one CHANGELOG:96 describes) since it is gone.

findings.title: IQ matvec (`matvec_owned`) uses one output row per simdgroup, so activations are re-read 4x the weight bytes per row
findings.evidence: :897 `const uint row = tg * MV_ROWS + sg;` (one row per simdgroup, 4 per TG); :911-922 per 32-weight span: `dequant32(wrow + s / SPB, (s % SPB) * 32u, w, 1u, 32u);` then `device const bfloat4* xa = (device const bfloat4*)(a + s * 32u);` with eight `float4(xr[i])` loads; dispatch metal_ops.rs:3254-3265 `width: n.div_ceil(MPP_MATVEC_ROWS)`, TG `32 * MPP_MATVEC_ROWS`; only Iq4Nl/Iq4Xs/Iq3S use it (metal_ops.rs:2979-2990).
findings.rationale: At IQ4 each row streams K/2 bytes of weight but 2K bytes of activation through L1: per span 16 weight bytes in 4 packed loads versus 64 activation bytes in 8 loads, so the kernel is load-instruction bound rather than weight-bandwidth bound. ggml's `mul_vec_q_n` amortizes x over N_DST=4 rows per simdgroup for this reason (the dead port at :1245-1252 does too). unsloth UD-Q4_K_XL files keep most FFN weight in IQ4_XS, so this is their decode GEMV.
findings.proposal: Template `matvec_owned<Block, M, R>` with R=2..4 rows per simdgroup: load the span's `float4`s once, apply to R row pointers (`acc[M][R]`), TG of 4 simdgroups covers 8-16 rows; keep M compile-time with guards. For R=4 decode 16-weight half-spans to bound `w[]` registers.
findings.expected_benefit: 1.3-1.8x on the IQ matvec at M=1; 10-25% decode on IQ4_XS-dominant models.
findings.verify_how: Decode tok/s on a UD-Q4_K_XL Qwen3 model before/after; the CPU-decoder parity tests for IQ kernels cover correctness.

verdict.reason: Verified: mpp_gemm.metal:897 `const uint row = tg * MV_ROWS + sg;` gives one output row per simdgroup; per 32-weight span :912 `dequant32(..)` (IQ4_XS: 17 bytes of weight) against :913-921 eight `float4(xr[i])` loads = 64 bytes of activation per row, so activation traffic through L1 is ~4x the weight bytes and the loop is load-instruction bound; dispatch metal_ops.rs:3254-3265 confirms 4 rows per TG. Only the three IQ kinds use it (:2979-2990), i.e. the unsloth UD-Q4_K_M/XL files that keep most FFN weight in IQ4_XS (CHANGELOG:7). The maintainer's own commit fd8097d reports this kernel at 'three quarters or more of candle's Q4_K rate', and candle's Q4_K is itself ~50% of bandwidth per the performance notes, so the kernel sits near 35-40% of bandwidth: there is headroom for the 1.3-1.8x claimed. Amortizing x over R rows per simdgroup is exactly ggml's N_DST design (also visible in the dead port at :1245-1252); the register budget caveat (w[32] per row, so half-spans at R=4) is correct. The CPU-decoder parity tests cover correctness. Effort S is plausible (template parameter + dispatch width + the existing `MPP_MATVEC_KERNEL` macro).

findings.title: `sdpa_vector_sink_bf16`: runtime-indexed 128-float accumulator and one simdgroup per head cannot fill the GPU at long context
findings.evidence: :3286 `float acc[SDPA_SINK_MAX_D];` indexed by runtime `D = p.head_dim` loops (:3287-3289, :3296-3298, :3302-3304 `acc[d] = acc[d] * corr + w * (float)vj[d];`); :3291 `for (uint j = tiisg; j < p.kv_len; j += 32)` walks the entire KV length with one simdgroup; dispatch metal_ops.rs:7066-7077 `width: h` threadgroups of `width: 32` threads; final :3320-3325 D sequential `simd_sum`s.
findings.rationale: A thread array indexed with a runtime bound normally lands in private (stack) memory, adding ~2D private loads/stores per KV position on top of the bf16 V loads; and 64 heads x 32 lanes = 2048 threads total regardless of kv_len, so at gpt-oss context lengths each lane serially processes kv_len/32 positions with a dependent exp/rescale chain. CHANGELOG :174 measured +17% at short context; attention's share grows linearly with context.
findings.proposal: (1) Template on D (64 for gpt-oss, 128) with `#pragma clang loop unroll(full)` loops so `acc` stays in registers (the `matvec_owned` pattern at mpp_gemm.metal:905-908). (2) Split KV across G simdgroups per head (TG = 32*G, each with its own m/l/acc over positions j = sg mod G), combine the G partials through threadgroup memory before folding the sink; pick G from kv_len (1 below 512, up to 8 above 4k).
findings.expected_benefit: 1.5-3x on this kernel at kv_len >= 2k on gpt-oss decode; negligible below 256 tokens.
findings.verify_how: gpt-oss-20b decode tok/s at 256 vs 8k context before/after; the existing scalar-reference parity test extended with kv_len unaligned to G*32.

verdict.reason: Verified: :3286 `float acc[SDPA_SINK_MAX_D];` (MAX_D=128, :3249) indexed only by runtime `D = p.head_dim` loops (:3287-3289, :3296-3298, :3302-3304), no bound the compiler can prove, so the array is dynamically indexed; :3291 `for (uint j = tiisg; j < p.kv_len; j += 32)` makes one simdgroup walk the whole KV length; dispatch :7066-7077 is `width: h` TGs of 32 threads, called once per sequence segment (attention.rs:899). On gpt-oss-20b that is 64 simdgroups (2048 threads) per layer per token regardless of context, and each lane also reads its own full K row and V row serially (`kj[d]`, `vj[d]`), so lanes of a simdgroup touch 32 different rows per load instruction. At 8k context each lane does 256 dependent exp/rescale steps over D=64 with scalar loads; the kernel cannot approach bandwidth. Templating on D (the `matvec_owned` pattern at mpp_gemm.metal:905-908) and splitting KV over G simdgroups with a threadgroup combine is the standard two-pass sdpa_vector design; the sink fold at :3313-3318 moves after the combine. Benefit ~0 at short context (CHANGELOG:174's +17% was measured there) and grows with context; medium severity is right because gpt-oss sliding-window layers cap half the layers at 128 keys.

findings.title: `mxfp4_gemv_batch_bf16` reloads activations per output row, loads weights byte-wise and computes exp2 per (row, block) per lane
findings.evidence: :3146 `const float scale = exp2((float)scales[base] - 127.0f);` per (row, block), recomputed by each of the 4 lanes (il) that share a block; :3147-3152 four 1-byte loads `qs[i]`; :3154-3161 `for (uint m ...) { ... for (uint j = 0; j < 8; ++j) acc += (float)y[j] * w[j]; }` nested inside `for (uint row = 0; row < GGUF_N_DST; ++row)` (:3141), so the same 8 activations are reloaded for each of the 4 rows.
findings.rationale: Per 8-weight quarter block per lane at M=1: 4 weight-byte loads + 1 scale load + 1 exp2 + 32 activation loads (4 rows x 8), i.e. ~1 activation load per half byte of weight; the kernel is load-instruction bound. E8M0 -> float is an exact bit placement (`as_type<float>(s << 23)` for 1 <= s <= 254) and needs no transcendental. This is the resident-expert decode GEMV for gpt-oss.
findings.proposal: Hoist the activation loads out of the row loop: load `y[0..8]` per m once per block as two `bfloat4` (8 floats x M registers; for M in 5..8 do two passes of 4 rows); load the 4 weight bytes as one `packed_uchar4`; replace exp2 with the bit shift (guarding s==0 and s==255). Keep the dequant-once-per-row register design.
findings.expected_benefit: ~3x fewer load instructions per block at M=1; 1.3-1.8x on the expert GEMV, translating to a decode gain proportional to the expert-FFN share on gpt-oss-20b.
findings.verify_how: MXFP4 parity tests (CHANGELOG :198) and gpt-oss-20b decode tok/s with experts resident.

verdict.reason: Verified: :3146 `const float scale = exp2((float)scales[base] - 127.0f);` is computed per (row, block) by each of the 4 lanes sharing a block; :3147-3152 four `qs[i]` byte loads; the activation loads `y[j]` (:3155-3159) sit inside `for (uint row ...)` (:3142) so the same 8 activations are reloaded for every one of the 4 rows (32 activation loads per 16 weight bytes at M=1). This is the resident gpt-oss expert decode GEMV (`Mxfp4Matmul` -> 'mxfp4_gemv_batch_bf16', metal_ops.rs:6820). E8M0->float as `as_type<float>(uint(s) << 23)` is exact for 1..254 and arguably more correct than fast-math `exp2`, which may be off by an ulp for integer inputs; parity tests exist (CHANGELOG:198). One addition the proposal should include: `sumf[GGUF_N_DST][GGUF_BATCH_MAX]` is looped with runtime `M = min(p.m_batch, 8)` (:3127, :3154, :3168) — the same pattern as kernels-10 — so while hoisting loads, make the m-loop `unroll(full)` over GGUF_BATCH_MAX with a guard. gpt-oss-20b resident decode (12.3 tok/s, CHANGELOG:14) is ~25% of bandwidth for ~2 GB of active MXFP4 bytes, so the expert GEMV has real headroom; medium severity with upside.

findings.title: `f8_gemv_bf16`: branchy per-byte E4M3 decode with a redundant bf16 round, 1-byte row-per-thread loads
findings.evidence: :3769-3783 `f8_weight_value`: exponent branches + `ldexp`, then :3782 `return float(bfloat(float(bfloat(val)) * sc));`; :3804 `device const uchar* wrow = w + ulong(o) * p.in_features;` and :3808 `acc += float(x[i]) * f8_weight_value(wrow[i], sc);` (thread per output row o = tgid.x*32+tid.x, scalar 1-byte and 2-byte loads, lanes of one simdgroup `in_features` bytes apart); batch :3851-3853 `for (uint r = 0; r < p.m; ++r) acc[r] += float(x[ulong(r) * p.in_features + i]) * wv;` with runtime-bounded r over `acc[8]`.
findings.rationale: Every E4M3 value is exactly representable in bf16 (3 mantissa bits, exponent in range), so the inner `bfloat(val)` round is a no-op and the whole decode is a pure function of one byte, i.e. a 256-entry table. The per-element cost is ~10 ALU + 2 scalar loads for one byte of weight. CHANGELOG :67 shows +12% from this kernel on streamed decode, where SSD reads dominate; with a warm expert cache or resident FP8 this kernel is the per-token cost.
findings.proposal: `constant float F8_LUT[256]` holding the bf16-exact values (NaN at 0x7F/0xFF); `packed_uchar4` weight loads along i and `bfloat4` activation loads (4 elements per step, sequential accumulation so the summation order and the `float(bfloat(v * sc))` rounding stay bit-identical); compile-time M with guards for the batch variant.
findings.expected_benefit: 2-4x on the kernel itself; system-level gain only when experts hit the cache (resident FP8 models, high hit-rate streaming).
findings.verify_how: The 48-run determinism and parity tests (CHANGELOG :77) must pass bitwise; Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-FP8 decode with a pinned warm cache before/after.

verdict.reason: Verified: `f8_weight_value` :3769-3783 is three branches plus `ldexp`, then `float(bfloat(float(bfloat(val)) * sc))`; every E4M3 value (3 mantissa bits, exponents 2^-9..2^8 including subnormals) is exactly representable in bf16, so the inner round is a no-op and the decode is a pure function of the byte — a 256-entry `constant float` LUT with `float(bfloat(LUT[v] * sc))` keeps the output bit-identical. :3804-3808 reads `wrow[i]` one byte at a time with lanes `in_features` bytes apart (row-per-lane), and the batch variant's `for (uint r = 0; r < p.m; ++r)` over `acc[8]` (:3851-3853, :3858) has NO provable upper bound (no `min`), so `acc` is dynamically indexed and lives in scratch — the surest spill case in the file. Scope is narrower than a reader might assume: dense FP8 checkpoints are dequantized to BF16 at load (CHANGELOG:101 item 2), so these kernels serve only `MoeExpert::Fp8Resident` (streamed Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-FP8), where SSD misses dominate unless the cache is warm; the reviewer states this. Severity medium, effort S, bitwise tests exist (:5672 `f8_gemv_parity_and_determinism`).

findings.title: Batch det kernels loop over register accumulators with a runtime bound (`m_rows`/`p.m`), risking private-memory spills
findings.evidence: :3439-3444 `float acc[AWQ_BATCH_MAX][PACK_FACTOR]; for (uint m = 0; m < m_rows; ++m) { for (uint k ...) acc[m][k] = 0.0f; }` with `m_rows = min(p.m, AWQ_BATCH_MAX)` (:3431) and the same runtime loops at :3465-3474 and :3482-3496; gptq batch :3593-3596; f8 batch :3851. Contrast mpp_gemm.metal:905-908 `#pragma clang loop unroll(full) for (uint r = 0; r < M; ++r) { if (r < m) {` with compile-time M.
findings.rationale: A loop with a runtime trip count cannot be fully unrolled, so `acc[m][k]` is dynamically indexed; the Metal compiler then typically places the 64-float array in private memory and each FMA becomes load/FMA/store. This path serves concurrency 2-8 on every packed-quant checkpoint (CHANGELOG :115/:131) and the FP8 batch GEMV.
findings.proposal: Loop `for m in 0..AWQ_BATCH_MAX` with `#pragma clang loop unroll(full)` and a uniform `if (m < m_rows)` guard, or instantiate M as a template parameter per batch class (2, 4, 8) as `MPP_MATVEC_KERNEL` does.
findings.expected_benefit: If the spill is present, 1.3-2x on the batch GEMV at m=4-8 (aggregate concurrent throughput on AWQ/GPTQ); none otherwise.
findings.verify_how: Compile with `xcrun -sdk macosx metal -c` and check the shader profiler's spill/private-memory counters, or microbench m=1 vs m=4 vs m=8 with `quant_gemv_bench` and look for a super-linear per-row cost.

verdict.reason: Code matches: :3431 `m_rows = min(p.m, AWQ_BATCH_MAX)`, :3439-3444/:3469-3474/:3482-3496 runtime-bounded loops over `acc[8][PACK_FACTOR]`, gptq :3593-3596, f8 :3851, versus the compile-time `M` + `unroll(full)` pattern at mpp_gemm.metal:905-908. The effect is real on this toolchain — the maintainer's commit fd8097d says specialising the IQ matvec on the row count 'so its accumulators stay in registers' took it from half to three quarters of candle's rate — but it is not certain for the AWQ/GPTQ batch loops: `min(p.m, 8u)` hands LLVM a provable max trip count of 8, which is exactly its default upper-bound full-unroll threshold, so those loops may already be unrolled and `acc` promoted. The cases without any bound are the ones that certainly spill: `f8_gemv_batch_bf16` (`r < p.m`, :3851/:3858) and the sink kernel's `D` loops (kernels-7); `mxfp4_gemv_batch_bf16` (:3154) is in the maybe class. The proposal is cheap and safe (same summation order), so do it everywhere, but the 1.3-2x upside applies to the unbounded loops first.
verdict.corrected_benefit: Certain gain only where the bound is unprovable (f8 batch, sdpa sink); AWQ/GPTQ/MXFP4 batch kernels may already be unrolled by LLVM's upper-bound unroller — verify before expecting a change.
verdict.corrected_proposal: Apply `#pragma clang loop unroll(full)` over the compile-time maximum with a uniform `if (m < m_rows)` guard (or a template M per batch class) to awq/gptq batch, f8 batch, mxfp4 batch and the sink kernel; confirm with `xcrun -sdk macosx metal -c quant_kernels.metal -Rpass-missed=loop-unroll` and the Xcode shader profiler's spill counter which kernels actually changed, then micro-bench only those.

findings.title: `mpp_fa_impl` stages V through threadgroup memory per KV block although the wide variant shows it can be read in place
findings.evidence: :1229-1232 `for (uint i = lane; i < uint(FA_BC * D); i += 32u) { uint row = i / uint(D); tg_v[i] = (int(row) < bc) ? vb[size_t(kv0) * D + i] : bfloat(0.0f); }` executed per KV block by one simdgroup (D iterations per lane), plus `threadgroup bfloat tg_v[FA_BC * D]` (:1526); the wide kernel instead masks :1400 `if (n >= bc || kv_pos > q_pos ...)` and reads V in place (:1466-1470; comment :1468 'staging it would copy the whole head's V through threadgroup memory once per query block'). Scores use `exp()` after a per-element `* p.scale` (:1240-1241, :1210).
findings.rationale: At D=128 each 32-key block costs 128 scalar bf16 loads+stores per lane (plus the P zero-fill at :1215) before P.V can run, comparable to the matmul2d work of a 32x32x128 tile; `tg_v` also doubles the threadgroup footprint (8 KB at D=128, 16 KB at D=256) while each TG is a single simdgroup (dispatch width 32, metal_ops.rs:3708-3712), limiting resident simdgroups per core.
findings.proposal: Mirror the wide kernel: mask `n >= bc` to -inf in the score pass, read V via `tensor(vb + kv0*D, dextents{D, bc}, {1, D})`, delete `tg_v`. Optionally fold `scale * log2e` into one multiply and use `exp2` for both the rescale and P.
findings.expected_benefit: 10-20% on prefill attention at D=128/256 (V copy and its barrier phase removed, higher occupancy); TTFT gain grows with prompt length.
findings.verify_how: MPP FA parity tests; TTFT on a 4k-token prompt for Qwen3-4B (d=128) and Qwen3.5 (d=256).

verdict.reason: Verified: `mpp_fa_impl` stages V per KV block through `tg_v` — :1229-1232 `for (uint i = lane; i < uint(FA_BC * D); i += 32u) { ... tg_v[i] = (int(row) < bc) ? vb[size_t(kv0) * D + i] : bfloat(0.0f); }` — D loads + D stores per lane per 32-key block, plus the `tg_p` zero fill (:1226-1228), all inside a single-simdgroup TG (dispatch width 32, metal_ops.rs:3698-3703) with `threadgroup bfloat tg_v[FA_BC * D]` (:1529) = 8 KB at D=128 / 16 KB at D=256, which bounds resident TGs per core. The wide D=512 variant proves the alternative compiles and passes parity: it masks `n >= bc` to -inf in the score pass (:1400) and reads V in place with `tensor(vb + kv0*D, dextents{DC, bc}, {1, D})` (:1469-1470), with the comment at :1466-1468 stating why. `mpp_fa_bf16_d64/d128/d256` (:1534-1536, selected at :3657-3660) all use the staging version, so every non-512 head width on M5 is affected. Benefit 10-20% on the attention kernel is plausible (the copy phase and its barrier are serialized against the two tensor-op matmuls, and occupancy rises); TTFT impact scales with attention's share, i.e. with prompt length. Effort S is honest since the wide kernel is the template; the exp2/log2e fold is a free extra.

findings.title: flash_attn.metal softmax/rescale runs one thread per query row (8-32 of 128 threads active) and the softcap gate forces Gemma 2 onto it even on M5
findings.evidence: :418 `for (uint i = tid; i < br_act; i += tg_size)` — one thread per row does the max, both exp passes over `p.bc` columns and :456-458 `for (uint dd = 0; dd < p.d; dd++) { o_acc[i * p.d + dd] *= exp_factor; }` serially (scalar kernel :184-232 identical); 128 threads per TG (metal_ops.rs:1200) with tiles from `fa_tile_sizes` (metal_ops.rs:993-995: d64->(32,32), d128->(16,32), d256->(8,16)); six `threadgroup_barrier`s per KV block (:365, :392, :415, :463, :472, :503). The TensorOps path requires `softcap.unwrap_or(0.0) == 0.0` (metal_ops.rs:1486-1491), so Gemma 2 (attn softcap 50) prefill lands here.
findings.rationale: At d=256 the per-row rescale is 256 serial multiplies by 8 threads while 120 idle, repeated per 16-key block, and the MMA phase has only 2 S-tiles for 4 simdgroups; the FA4 conditional-rescale skip only helps when `shift < 8`. This is also the only path on M1-M4 and on macOS < 26.
findings.proposal: (1) Softmax by simdgroup-per-row: lanes across columns with `simd_max`/`simd_sum`, exp2 vectorized; (2) distribute the O rescale over all threads (`for kk = tid; kk < br_act*d; kk += tg_size`); (3) merge the mask pass (:394-414) into the S-store loop to drop one barrier; (4) add `precise::tanh` softcap to `mpp_fa_impl`'s score pass (next to mpp_gemm.metal:1240 `float val = sT[i] * p.scale;`) and relax the gate so Gemma 2 uses the TensorOps kernel.
findings.expected_benefit: 2-4x on the softmax phase, 20-40% on this kernel at d=256 or small br; Gemma 2 prefill moves to the kernel measured 1.96-3.6x faster than the candle-class path.
findings.verify_how: FA parity tests (the d256 GQA+prefix case, CHANGELOG :138); TTFT on Gemma-2-9B on M5, and on an M2/pre-macOS-26 machine for the non-MPP path.

verdict.reason: Facts verified: flash_attn.metal:418 `for (uint i = tid; i < br_act; i += tg_size)` does max, both exp passes and the :456-458 `o_acc *= exp_factor` rescale with one thread per row (same in the scalar kernel :184-232); 128 threads per TG (metal_ops.rs:1198) and `fa_tile_sizes` d256 -> (8,16) (:992-996) so 8 of 128 threads are active in softmax and the MMA phase has 2 S-tiles for 4 simdgroups; six barriers per KV block (:365, :392, :415, :463, :472, :503); the TensorOps gate (:1486-1491) requires `softcap.unwrap_or(0.0) == 0.0`, so Gemma 2 (supported, README:96; attn softcap, head_dim 256) prefill runs this kernel even on M5 although `mpp_fa_bf16_d256` exists. But the four sub-proposals have very different value. (4) is small and squarely on the verified platform: add a `softcap` field to `MppFaParams`, apply `val = p.softcap * precise::tanh(val / p.softcap)` right after `float val = sT[i] * p.scale;` at mpp_gemm.metal:1198 (and :1394 in the wide variant), relax the gate — Gemma 2 then gets the kernel measured 1.96-3.6x faster. (1)-(3) rework a kernel that on the maintainer's M5 is only reached with softcap or `OXYDLLM_DISABLE_MPP`; it matters for M1-M4 and macOS < 26 (supported but unverified by execution), so it is a secondary-platform M-effort item, not a medium-severity M5 item.
verdict.corrected_benefit: Gemma 2 prefill on M5 moves from the one-thread-per-row kernel to the TensorOps kernel (the measured 1.96-3.6x class); the legacy-kernel softmax rework is deferred to when a pre-M5 machine can measure it.
verdict.corrected_proposal: Ship only the softcap in `mpp_fa_impl`/`mpp_fa_wide_impl` and relax the `softcap == 0.0` gate at metal_ops.rs:1487 (extend the FA parity test with softcap=50 at d=256). File the simdgroup-per-row softmax, distributed O rescale and barrier merge for flash_attn.metal as a backlog item for the non-MPP platforms.

findings.title: Staged packed-quant GEMM (`mpp_gemm_quant_impl`) re-reads scales 8x per word per k and single-buffers the tile
findings.evidence: :116-146 `awq_stage_tile`: per packed word `for (uint s = 0; s < PF; ++s) { ... float scale = float(scales[g * uint(p.n) + uint(col0) + o]); ... sB[kk * uint(TN) + o] = bfloat(v); }` (:137-144) with `g` constant across a 64-k tile at group_size >= 64, `qzeros` per word (:135); :1081 `threadgroup bfloat sB[QBK * TN];` single buffer; :1049-1060 stage -> barrier -> `op.run` -> barrier with no overlap, whereas `gemm_staged` (:765-828) double-buffers `sB0/sB1` (:794-806).
findings.rationale: Per 64x64 tile step: 512 weight-word loads versus 4096 scattered 2-byte scale loads and 512 zero loads, so dequant is ~10x the instruction count of reading the tile, and the tensor units idle during it. This is the prefill GEMM for AWQ/GPTQ/compressed-tensors at M >= 64, i.e. TTFT; the measured 1.96x over candle at M=64 (header comment :6-7) leaves staging as the limiter.
findings.proposal: Stage `scale[TN]`/`zero[TN]` once per group into threadgroup memory (two slices indexed by `kk >> group_shift` when a tile straddles a group at group_size 32/64), unpack a word to 8 values and store contiguous columns (apply `AWQ_PACK_ORDER` at index time), and adopt the two-slot double buffer from `gemm_staged`.
findings.expected_benefit: 1.3-2x on the staged packed-quant GEMM; TTFT on AWQ/GPTQ prompts >= 64 tokens.
findings.verify_how: `mpp_gemm_perf_probe` on 2560x9728 at M=64/256/1024 for w4/gptq4 before/after; staged packed-quant parity tests on partial tiles and group sizes 32/64 (CHANGELOG :138).

verdict.reason: Verified: `awq_stage_tile` (mpp_gemm.metal:116-146) loads one `qweight` word and one `qzeros` word per (k, word) and then, per word, 8 `scales[g * n + col0 + o]` 2-byte loads (:140) with the pack-order permuted index, writing `sB[kk * TN + o]` — at group_size 128 and QBK=64 every k row of the tile re-reads the same 8 zeros and 64 scales, so a 64x64 tile costs 512 weight loads against 512 zero loads and 4096 scale loads (L1 hits, but 10x the instruction count). `mpp_gemm_quant_impl` (:1042-1056) single-buffers `sB` with stage -> barrier -> `op.run` -> barrier, while the GGUF `gemm_staged` (:794-806) already double-buffers `sB0/sB1`, so the pattern is in the same file; `threadgroup bfloat sB[QBK * TN]` at :1081 confirms the single slot. This is the AWQ/GPTQ/compressed-tensors prefill GEMM for m >= 64 (linear.rs:484-493 via `maybe_mpp_quant_matmul`), i.e. TTFT on real prompts. The group-straddle note for group_size 32/64 is correct (QBK=64 never straddles a 128 group). 1.3-2x on the staged GEMM is plausible given the GGUF stager's measured 5553-5925 GFLOPS (commit 2eed4aa) vs this path's 1.96x-over-candle; `mpp_quant_staged_perf_probe` (metal_ops.rs:6248) exists to measure it. Effort M honest.

findings.title: Retired `*_atomic` kernels (~600 lines) duplicate the det main loops and ship in the production library for a benchmark only
findings.evidence: :52 `inline void awq_gemv_atomic_impl(`, :118 batch, :371 `gptq_gemv_atomic_impl`, :433 batch, with 16 `kernel void *_atomic` wrappers at :217-333 and :547-641; metal_ops.rs:1563-1569 `/// Selects the retired atomic split-K epilogue ... Production never sets this` `pub static QUANT_GEMV_ATOMIC`. The det impls repeat the main loop verbatim (:3387-3396 vs :85-104).
findings.rationale: Four copies of the AWQ main loop and four of the GPTQ loop (atomic, det, batch-atomic, batch-det) must be edited together for kernels-4/5/10, and the whole source is compiled at first pipeline build in every process.
findings.proposal: Factor the per-thread accumulation into `awq_accumulate<T,BITS,M>(..., thread float (&acc)[M][PF])` / `gptq_accumulate<...>` shared by both epilogues; guard the atomic epilogue and wrappers with `#ifdef OXYDLLM_BENCH_ATOMIC` that only `quant_gemv_bench` defines (pass a preprocessor define to the compile), or delete them once kernels-4/5 are measured det-only.
findings.expected_benefit: ~600 fewer production lines, one main loop to tune; no runtime change.
findings.verify_how: `quant_gemv_bench` builds with the define; unit tests and the determinism test pass.

findings.title: Softcap kernels use fast-math `tanh` while GeLU and both attention paths use `precise::tanh`
findings.evidence: :215 `out[gid] = cap * tanh(x[gid] / cap);` (:227, :239 likewise); same file :16 `return 0.5f * x * (1.0f + precise::tanh(inner));`; flash_attn.metal:166 and :401 `val = p.softcap * precise::tanh(val / p.softcap);`; comment :204 'Used by Gemma2 attention scores (cap=50) and Gemma2/Gemma4 logits (cap=30)'.
findings.rationale: Metal's default `tanh` under fast-math carries a few-ulp error; on final logits at cap 30 that can reorder near-tied top tokens between the fused kernel, the CPU reference `(x/cap).tanh()*cap`, and the FA-scored attention path, making temp-0 cross-path parity fragile. The elementwise kernels are memory-bound, so precision is free here. The same kernels also do a per-element integer `gid / half_n` (:31 etc.) and scalar bf16 loads.
findings.proposal: Use `precise::tanh` in the three softcap kernels; optionally vectorize the gated/mul kernels to 4 elements per thread (`bfloat4`) and dispatch a 2-D grid so the row/col split needs no division.
findings.expected_benefit: Bit-consistent softcap across paths; negligible perf change (vectorization is a minor instruction-count win on a memory-bound op).
findings.verify_how: Compare `softcap_bf16` against `(x/cap).tanh()*cap` bitwise on random logits before/after; existing gated_silu parity tests for the vectorized variants.

findings.title: Q4_K/Q6_K `stage_tile` lane mapping writes the staged tile with ~4-way threadgroup bank conflicts
findings.evidence: :682-684 `uint col = t / subs; uint sub = t % subs;` (subs = 2 at BK=64), so adjacent lanes are (col, sub=0) and (col, sub=1); :706-709 `out[0] = ...; out[tn_stride] = ...` at `sB + kk*64 + col` with kk differing by 32 between the pair, i.e. 32*64 bfloat = 4096 bytes apart (same bank), and 16 columns of 2-byte values share 8 bank words; same mapping in the generic stager :649 and Q6_K :727. Comment :194-197: the staging cost 'decides how much the dequantisation costs per multiply'.
findings.rationale: Each 32-lane threadgroup store touches ~8 distinct banks, so the 32 stores per lane per tile serialize ~4x; the dequant stage is the non-tensor-unit part of the GGUF prefill GEMM and is overlapped only by the double buffer.
findings.proposal: Map `col = t % tn, sub = t / tn` so consecutive lanes write consecutive columns (adjacent 2-byte slots), in all three stagers.
findings.expected_benefit: A few percent on the staged GGUF GEMM at M >= 64 (prefill TTFT); uncertain without a profiler.
findings.verify_how: `mpp_gemm_perf_probe` Q4_K/Q6_K variants before/after; Q4_K mul_mm parity tests.

subsystems.coverage_notes: All four in-scope Metal files were read in full. Callers were checked only as far as needed to establish liveness and dispatch geometry: metal_ops.rs (FA tile sizes and router 991-1060/1150-1260/1480-1590, AWQ/GPTQ dispatch 1690-1860/2064-2100/2240-2330, MPP constants 2540-2560/2975-3010, IQ matvec and MPP FA dispatch 3225-3290/3640-3720, sink SDPA 7040-7095), linear.rs (255-380, 447-560), attention.rs (800-860). Not done: I did not read candle 0.11's quantized.metal / quantized metal.rs, so kernels-3 (per-row weight streaming for M=2..8 on the candle path) is a hypothesis to measure, not a verified fact; I could not compile or run any Metal code, so register-spill claims (kernels-7, kernels-10) and bank-conflict claims (kernels-5, kernels-16) are reasoned from the source, not profiled; I did not audit the Rust FA threadgroup-bytes bounds, the RoPE/norm kernels (out of scope), iq_quant.rs, or the GGUF loader's Owned/StagedWeight construction; git history is shallow (51 commits, squashed import at 42943bf), so I could not find when or why the GGUF fast-path dispatch was removed, only that it was already gone at import. The ROADMAP's rejected list and constant audit were read; none of the findings re-propose a rejected item.
missed: The gpt-oss expert PREFILL GEMM `mxfp4_mul_mm_bf16` (quant_kernels.metal:3197-3240) is a 16x16-thread scalar tile: `GGUF_MM_BM = 16; GGUF_MM_BN = 16; GGUF_MM_TG = 256` (:2287-2289), and per 32-element k block it stages `w_tile[16][32]` through threadgroup memory (:3223 `mxfp4_dequant_strip_into`, which also calls `exp2` per element at :3192), hits `threadgroup_barrier` twice (:3224, :3233), and each thread computes one output with a scalar loop `for (uint j = 0; j < MXFP4_BLOCK; ++j) partial += (float)x_chunk[j] * (float)w_tile[n_off][j];` (:3229-3231), re-reading its own 32 activations per block. For gpt-oss-20b's expert shapes (K=2880 -> 90 barrier pairs per output tile; routed-token M in the hundreds at prefill) this is every active expert's up/gate/down GEMM on the path that decides TTFT, running on scalar FMAs with no simdgroup matrices and no TensorOps, while the same file family already has a staged TensorOps GEMM pattern (`gemm_staged`, mpp_gemm.metal:765-828, with a `stage_tile` per block type and double buffering) that measured 1.96x-3.6x over candle's GEMM. The ROADMAP lists 'MXFP4 prefill' under the TensorOps roadmap, so it is known but not rejected or shipped; an MXFP4 `stage_tile` (16 bytes + one E8M0 byte per 32 columns, decoded with the existing `MXFP4_LUT16`) into `gemm_staged` is a day or two of work with the existing MXFP4 parity tests (CHANGELOG:198) as the oracle, and should be worth several-x on gpt-oss prefill. None of the 13 findings touches it.

subsystems.assessment: The tokenizer wrapper and chat-template layer are compact (1.1k + 0.5k lines), well-commented, and the GGUF builder is the strongest part: it owns the pipeline table instead of trusting candle, has a regression matrix for the prefix-space repair, and an exact-ids test against a reference tokenizer.json for Gemma 4. Per-token cost in this scope is essentially nil (decode is a hash lookup plus a small decoder chain, and the streaming logic lives upstream in engine_loop), and per-request cost is dominated by things that are trivially cacheable (a fresh minijinja Environment and a full template compile on every request). What is fragile is fidelity, not speed: the GGUF path marks every non-NORMAL token type (2..=5) as a skip-on-decode special token, which strips USER_DEFINED tokens such as Qwen's <tool_call> from streamed content and so diverges from both llama.cpp and the sibling tokenizer.json path; the `llama` SentencePiece kind added on 2026-09-04 never prepends the dummy `▁` (add_space_prefix) and builds a Unigram model from what are BPE-by-score vocabularies, with only a trim-tolerant round-trip test guarding it; the Jinja environment differs from transformers/minja in three independent, mechanical ways (no trim_blocks/lstrip_blocks, alphabetised map keys and compact separators in tojson, no loop_controls feature); and the server injects a tool-calling system instruction even when the template renders tools natively, so tool-heavy prompts carry every schema twice with contradictory output-format instructions. Stop-sequence derivation also over-registers: foreign chat markers that the vocabulary does not know are BPE-fragmented and installed as multi-token stop sequences, so a model that spells another family's marker in plain text is cut off. The biggest lever is a parity harness rather than any single fix: for each local checkpoint, compare (a) rendered prompt bytes against transformers.apply_chat_template and (b) prompt ids against tokenizer.json / llama-tokenize over a few thousand words; nearly every finding here is S-effort once such a harness makes the divergence visible, and the maintainer's own stated standard ("a tokenizer that is nearly right is worse than one that refuses") is currently met only for the Gemma 4 and byte-level BPE GGUF paths.

findings.title: GGUF builder marks USER_DEFINED tokens as skip-on-decode specials, stripping <tool_call>/<think> text from generated content
findings.evidence: src/tokenizer.rs:860-866: `// Aligns with llama_token_type: non-normal/non-byte = special.\n if matches!(value_to_u32(v)?, 2..=5) && let Some(tok) = tokens.get(idx) { specials.push(AddedToken::from(tok.clone(), true)); }` followed by `tokenizer.add_special_tokens(specials)`. src/tokenizer.rs:335-338: `pub fn decode(&self, ids) { self.inner.decode(ids, true) }`; tokenizers-0.23.1 tokenizer/mod.rs:901-912 filters `!skip_special_tokens || !self.added_vocabulary.is_special_token(token)`. Consumers: src/server/routes/engine_loop.rs:487 `tokenizer.decode(window_ids)` (streamed content) and :834 `tokenizer.decode(&tracker.output_ids)` (final content); src/server/routes/chat.rs:727-730 `parse_tool_call_tag_blocks` requires the literal `<tool_call>`/`</tool_call>` in that text. llama_token_type: 1 NORMAL, 2 UNKNOWN, 3 CONTROL, 4 USER_DEFINED, 5 UNUSED, 6 BYTE; convert_hf_to_gguf types added tokens with special=false that do not look like `<|…|>` (Qwen's `<tool_call>`, `</tool_call>`, `<think>`, `</think>`) as USER_DEFINED, and llama.cpp's token_to_piece always emits USER_DEFINED text (it drops only CONTROL when special=false). The tokenizer.json path keeps them too (special=false in added_tokens), so the same Qwen3 model behaves differently as GGUF vs safetensors.
findings.rationale: Every decode of generated text on the GGUF path runs with skip_special_tokens=true, so any token the builder flagged special disappears from the stream and from the final content. Type 4 is exactly the class of tokens a model is supposed to emit as text (tool-call and thinking markers), so on Qwen2.5/Qwen3/Qwen3.5 GGUFs the tag parser never sees `<tool_call>`; only the bare-JSON fallback in try_parse_tool_calls (chat.rs:816) can rescue a lone call with no surrounding text, and parallel calls or calls after reasoning text are returned as plain content. Thinking detection survives because engine_loop resolves `<think>` by id, which hides the problem from the think path.
findings.proposal: In build_tokenizer, map token types individually: 2 (UNKNOWN) and 3 (CONTROL) -> `AddedToken::from(tok, true)`; 4 (USER_DEFINED) -> `AddedToken::from(tok, false)` added via `add_tokens` (still an added token, so it matches atomically in input text and keeps its id, but survives decode); 5 (UNUSED) may stay special. Keep from_gguf_content's own `special_token_ids` map including type 4 so `special_token_id("<think>")` and the constrained-decoding exclusion (constrain.rs:712) keep working. Add a unit test next to run_gguf_pre_tokenizer_case: a type-4 token must round-trip through `decode()` unchanged while a type-3 token is stripped.
findings.expected_benefit: Tool calls on Qwen-family GGUF checkpoints parse the same way as on the safetensors variant (streamed content shows the tags, parallel calls and reasoning-then-call work); behaviour matches llama.cpp. No performance change.
findings.verify_how: On the M5: `Tokenizer::from_gguf_file(qwen3.gguf).decode(&[id])` for id = token_to_id("<tool_call>") returns "" today and must return "<tool_call>"; confirm the type with gguf-py (`reader.fields['tokenizer.ggml.token_type'].parts` at that id == 4). Then send the same tools request to the GGUF and safetensors variants of Qwen3-4B and compare `tool_calls` (count, streamed content).

verdict.reason: Accurate. src/tokenizer.rs:858-870 pushes `AddedToken::from(tok.clone(), true)` for every token whose tokenizer.ggml.token_type is 2..=5 and calls `tokenizer.add_special_tokens(specials)`; `decode()` at src/tokenizer.rs:335-338 is `self.inner.decode(ids, true)`; tokenizers-0.23.1 tokenizer/mod.rs:901-911 filters `!skip_special_tokens || !self.added_vocabulary.is_special_token(token)` and added_vocabulary.rs:258-260 answers from `special_tokens_set`, which `add_special_tokens` populates. Generated content is decoded with that function (engine_loop.rs:487 streamed window, :834 final content, :873 reasoning), there is no id-based `<tool_call>` handling anywhere in engine_loop.rs (grep empty), and chat.rs:727-730 only finds calls by the literal `<tool_call>`/`</tool_call>` text, so on a GGUF every type-4 token vanishes before the parser sees it. On the tokenizer.json path the special flag comes from the file (Qwen's `<tool_call>`/`<think>` are special=false), so the same model diverges between formats. Mitigation the reviewer already credits: the JSON fallback at chat.rs:816-826 rescues a lone call whose stripped content is exactly one JSON object; parallel blocks and reasoning-then-call fall through to plain content. The think path survives because `special_token_id` (tokenizer.rs:359-364) also falls back to `token_to_id`, so ids resolve either way. Proposal is implementable as stated: `add_tokens` with special=false keeps the existing id and atomic matching; to mirror the HF file exactly use `AddedToken::from(tok, false).normalized(false)`. `from_gguf_content` (tokenizer.rs:271-282) keeps its own type-2..=5 map, so `special_token_id_values()` for constrain.rs:712 is unchanged. The converter type assignment (USER_DEFINED for added tokens that are special=false and not `<|...|>`-shaped) cannot be checked on this machine; confidence 0.65 is honest, but it is consistent with llama-server emitting `<think>` as text on Qwen3 GGUFs. Severity high is justified: silent, format-dependent loss of tool-call parsing on a supported path, S effort, no perf cost.

findings.title: SentencePiece `llama` kind never prepends the dummy prefix and ignores tokenizer.ggml.add_space_prefix
findings.evidence: src/tokenizer.rs:587-612 sentencepiece_pipeline: normalizer `Replace::new(" ", "\u{2581}")`, pre-tokenizer `Split(" ", MergedWithPrevious)`, decoder `[Replace("\u{2581}"," "), ByteFallback, Fuse]` — no `Prepend("\u{2581}")` and no trailing `Strip`. src/tokenizer.rs:726: `let sentencepiece = model_kind == "gemma4" || model_kind == "llama";` so both kinds share this pipeline; `rg add_space_prefix src` finds no reader of the key. src/tokenizer.rs:17-27: from_dir tries `from_gguf_file` before the sibling tokenizer.json fallback, so since 131b905 (2026-09-04, "accept the SentencePiece vocabulary every Llama 1 and 2 era converter writes") a TinyLlama/Llama-2/Phi-3 GGUF uses this pipeline instead of the HF tokenizer it used before. The only test, tokenizer.rs:918-940, asserts `back.trim() == text.trim()`, which a missing dummy prefix cannot fail. Reference behaviour: llama.cpp SPM vocab defaults add_space_prefix=true (the converter writes false only for Gemma) and prepends ' ' to the first raw-text fragment and to each fragment after a control token; the HF legacy Llama-2 export has normalizer `Sequence[Prepend("▁"), Replace(" ","▁")]` and decoder ending in `Strip(" ", start=1)`.
findings.rationale: For every chat turn of a Llama-2-family GGUF the first token after each special token differs from what the model was trained on (`▁[INST]` vs `[INST]`; `▁`+`<0x0A>`+`Hi` vs `<0x0A>`+`Hi`). The model still answers (which is why the round-trip test and a quick smoke run look fine), but the prompt ids are not the reference ids, which the maintainer's own GGUF test doc treats as a bug class. Gemma 4 is unaffected because its file sets add_space_prefix=false, so the exact-ids test does not cover this.
findings.proposal: Read `tokenizer.ggml.add_space_prefix` (default true for `llama`, false for `gemma4`) in build_tokenizer and pass it to sentencepiece_pipeline; when true, use normalizer `Sequence[Prepend("\u{2581}"), Replace(" ", "\u{2581}")]` and append `Strip(" ", 1, 0)` to the decoder chain, mirroring the HF legacy Llama export (the per-segment Prepend reproduces llama.cpp's after-each-special-token space). Keep from_dir preferring tokenizer.json when present.
findings.expected_benefit: Prompt ids identical to llama-tokenize and the HF tokenizer for Llama-2, TinyLlama, Mistral-7B v0.1/v0.2, Vicuna and similar GGUFs; removes a per-turn distribution shift at zero runtime cost.
findings.verify_how: On the M5: `llama-tokenize -m tinyllama-1.1b-chat-v1.0.Q4_0.gguf -p $'<|user|>\nHi</s>'` vs `Tokenizer::from_gguf_file(..).encode(..)`; today the GGUF path lacks id 29871 (`▁`) before each `<0x0A>`. Extend the ignored TinyLlama test to compare ids with the TinyLlama tokenizer.json (available on HF) instead of a trimmed round trip.

verdict.reason: Accurate. `sentencepiece_pipeline` (src/tokenizer.rs:587-612) has normalizer `Replace(" ", "\u{2581}")`, pre-tokenizer `Split(" ", MergedWithPrevious)` and decoder `[Replace, ByteFallback, Fuse]`; grep for `add_space_prefix|Prepend|Strip::` in src/tokenizer.rs returns nothing, and line 726 `let sentencepiece = model_kind == "gemma4" || model_kind == "llama";` routes both kinds through it. The doc comment at 583-586 says the pipeline was copied from the checkpoints that use it, i.e. Gemma's tokenizer.json, which is the one SentencePiece family that sets add_dummy_prefix=false; the Llama-2 legacy export (Prepend normalizer + trailing Strip) differs exactly as claimed. `from_dir` (tokenizer.rs:16-19) does prefer a sibling tokenizer.json, so only GGUF-only folders are affected, and the only `llama`-kind test (918-940) compares `back.trim() == text.trim()`, which cannot see a missing leading `\u{2581}`. The maintainer's own contract in the Gemma test doc (942-950: 'a tokenizer that is nearly right is worse than one that refuses') makes exact ids the standard. ROADMAP line 110 rates legacy SPM GGUFs 'only if these legacy models matter', but the path shipped (131b905), so medium is right. Proposal is sound: tokenizers' normalizer runs per segment between added tokens, so a `Prepend` reproduces llama.cpp's space-after-each-control-token behaviour; default true for `llama`, false for `gemma4`, override from `tokenizer.ggml.add_space_prefix`. S effort, zero runtime cost.

findings.title: Unigram-from-scores is not the SentencePiece-BPE segmentation llama.cpp and HF use; only an 11-string exact-ids test guards it
findings.evidence: src/tokenizer.rs:772-800: `// No merge list: a SentencePiece file states the scores instead, and the pieces are picked to maximise their sum rather than merged pairwise.` … `let unigram = Unigram::from(vocab, unk_id, byte_fallback)`. llama.cpp's SPM tokenizer (llm_tokenizer_spm_session) is a priority-queue pairwise merge ordered by piece score, and transformers' LlamaConverter.extract_merges turns the same scores into rank-ordered BPE merges; Llama/Gemma .model files are BPE-type SPM with score = -rank, not Unigram models. The exact-ids test (tokenizer.rs:966-997) covers Gemma 4 on 11 short strings; the `llama` kind has only the trim-tolerant round trip (918-940).
findings.rationale: Viterbi max-sum over -rank scores and greedy rank-ordered merging agree on most words but not all: with pieces ab:-1, bc:-2 and single chars at about -29000, BPE yields [ab, c] (sum -29101) while Viterbi yields [a, bc] (sum -29002). Each disagreement is a different id sequence than the model was trained on, invisible to a round-trip test and unlikely to surface in 11 strings. Since this is the only tokenizer a GGUF-only Llama-2/TinyLlama user gets, the gap matters more than its rarity suggests.
findings.proposal: Add an ignored exact-ids test for a `llama`-kind GGUF against its HF tokenizer.json (TinyLlama ships one) over a few thousand words of mixed text (README prose, code, non-Latin, digits), and widen the Gemma 4 corpus the same way. If mismatches appear, replace the Unigram branch with a BPE built from score-ordered merges the way HF's converter does (for each piece, every (left,right) split present in the vocab, ordered by the piece's score); the BPE construction path at 755-776 already exists.
findings.expected_benefit: Either proof that the Unigram approximation is exact on real vocabularies, or a fix that makes `llama`-kind GGUF ids identical to llama.cpp/HF. Test only: no runtime cost.
findings.verify_how: Run the new test on the M5 with TinyLlama and Gemma 4 checkpoints present; count mismatching strings. Cross-check a mismatch with `llama-tokenize` to see which side llama.cpp agrees with.

verdict.reason: Accurate. src/tokenizer.rs:772-800 builds `Unigram::from(vocab_with_scores, unk_id, byte_fallback)` whenever a SentencePiece GGUF has no merge list, and the comment at 772-774 states the approximation knowingly ('picked to maximise their sum rather than merged pairwise'). Llama/Gemma `.model` files are BPE-type SentencePiece whose scores are merge ranks, and both llama.cpp (score-ordered pairwise merge) and the HF converter (score-ordered merges into a BPE model) merge greedily; Viterbi max-sum over the same scores agrees on most but not all inputs, and the reviewer's counterexample is valid. Coverage is as described: the exact-ids test (966-997) is 11 Gemma 4 strings; the `llama` kind has only the trim-tolerant round trip. Test-gap at medium and S effort are right; the proposed fix path (derive merges by enumerating each piece's split points, ordered by piece score) is implementable on the existing BPE builder at 755-776, with the caveat not to copy HF's O(V^2) pairwise scan at load (enumerate splits per piece instead, O(V*len)). The ignored-test pattern with `checkpoint assente, salto` already exists, so the test fits the house style.

findings.title: Hardcoded foreign chat markers are BPE-fragmented into multi-token stop sequences on every model
