findings.evidence: src/tokenizer.rs:421-430 unconditional marker list (`<|eot_id|>`, `<|eom_id|>`, `<|end_of_text|>`, `<|im_end|>`, `<|im_start|>`, `<|endoftext|>`, `<turn|>`, `<end_of_turn>`); src/tokenizer.rs:439-466 `fn push_sequence(..) { let Ok(ids) = tok.encode(content) …; if let Ok(roundtrip) = tok.decode_with_special(&ids) && roundtrip != content { return; } if !out.contains(&ids) { out.push(ids); } }` with no length restriction, plus `let with_newline = format!("{}\n", content); push_sequence(..)`. Wired for every served model at src/models/manager.rs:1205 and matched as a suffix of generated ids at src/engine.rs:392-396 `|| has_matching_stop_sequence(all_tokens, self.sequences)` / :172-176.
findings.rationale: On a vocabulary that lacks a marker, `encode` splits it into ordinary byte-level pieces (`<|`, `eot`, `_id`, `|>` on Qwen; `<`, `end`, `_of`, `_turn`, `>` on Llama 3) and the byte-level decoder reproduces the text exactly, so the round-trip check passes and the fragments become a stop sequence. Any answer that spells another family's marker in plain text — a developer asking for a Llama 3 or Gemma chat template, a llama.cpp config, fine-tuning data — ends with finish_reason=stop mid-answer. That is the audience of a local inference server. Per-step cost of the extra ~14 sequences is negligible; the issue is correctness.
findings.proposal: In push_sequence accept only sequences whose marker is atomic in this vocabulary: `ids.len() == 1 || self.special_token_ids.contains_key(content)` (then the `\n` variant is a legitimate two-token sequence); drop markers the vocab does not know. Single-id markers are already covered by stop_token_ids, so this reduces stop_token_sequences to the `marker\n` forms of real special tokens.
findings.expected_benefit: No spurious truncation when a model quotes another family's chat markup; identical behaviour for genuine stop tokens.
findings.verify_how: Prompt Qwen3 with "Print the Llama 3 chat template verbatim, including the <|eot_id|> markers" and inspect finish_reason/length before and after. Unit test with the WordLevel fixture in tokenizer.rs tests: markers absent from the vocab must not appear in `stop_token_sequences()`.

verdict.reason: Mechanism verified: src/tokenizer.rs:421-430 appends eight foreign markers unconditionally; `push_sequence` (439-455) only rejects a marker whose round trip through `decode_with_special` differs, which a byte-level BPE never fails, and has no length guard; `manager.rs:1205` wires the result for every model and engine.rs:172-176/392-396 match it as a suffix of the generated ids. So a Qwen answer that spells `<|eot_id|>` in its canonical fragmentation does stop early. Two corrections to the proposal. (a) `special_token_id` (tokenizer.rs:359-364) falls back to `inner.token_to_id`, so `stop_token_ids` (377-408) already covers every atomic marker whether or not it is flagged special; after the reviewer's change `stop_token_sequences` would hold only `[id]` entries (redundant) and `[id, \n]` entries (unreachable, the single id stops first), i.e. the function becomes a no-op in practice. (b) That also removes the one legitimate use of multi-token sequences: a model whose own template marker is not atomic in its vocab (ChatML-as-prose fine-tunes on a Llama-2 vocabulary), which is presumably why the list exists. The cheaper and safer change is to gate on the model's own template rather than on atomicity.
verdict.corrected_benefit: No spurious finish_reason=stop when a model quotes another family's chat markup; models whose own marker is fragmented in their vocabulary keep their stop sequence; redundant single-id and unreachable `marker\n` entries disappear from the per-step suffix scan.
verdict.corrected_proposal: In `stop_token_sequences` push a sequence only when the marker (before the `\n` suffix) is one of `self.special_tokens` values or appears literally in `self.chat_template` (`template.contains(marker)`); skip markers that encode to a single id (already in `stop_token_ids` via the token_to_id fallback). Add a unit test on the WordLevel fixture (tokenizer.rs:1003-1030) with a template that names `<|im_end|>`: foreign markers absent from the template must not appear, the template's own marker must.

findings.title: Jinja environment lacks trim_blocks/lstrip_blocks that transformers and minja enable, changing whitespace of non-dash-stripped templates
findings.rationale: With trim_blocks the newline after each `%}` is removed; here it is kept, so such templates render three or four extra newlines per turn relative to the reference prompt the model was trained on. Templates that dash-strip everywhere (Qwen3, Llama 3.x, gpt-oss) are unaffected, which is why the harmony test passes, but the engine claims template compatibility with HF checkpoints in general and currently diverges from both references on this class.
findings.proposal: Add `env.set_trim_blocks(true); env.set_lstrip_blocks(true);` (leave keep_trailing_newline false, matching Jinja2). If the environment is cached per model (finding 8), set it there.
findings.expected_benefit: Byte-identical prompts to transformers for templates that use plain `{% %}` tags; no change for dash-stripped templates.
findings.verify_how: Render the TinyLlama template for [system,user] with and without the flags and diff against `tokenizer.apply_chat_template(msgs, tokenize=False)`; assert Qwen3/Llama-3.1/gpt-oss renders are unchanged. Add the zephyr template as a unit test with the reference string.

verdict.reason: Accurate. src/chat_template.rs:28-35 builds `Environment::new()`, registers the callback, filter and functions and adds the template; nothing calls `set_trim_blocks`/`set_lstrip_blocks`. minijinja-2.19.0 environment.rs:263-269 documents trim_blocks 'Defaults to `false`' and :280 provides `set_lstrip_blocks`. transformers' `_compile_jinja_template` passes `trim_blocks=True, lstrip_blocks=True` and minja's chat_template uses the same options, so any multi-line template written with plain `{% %}` tags (zephyr/TinyLlama, StableLM-era templates) renders extra newlines here relative to the training prompt; dash-stripped templates (Qwen3, Llama 3.x, gpt-oss) are unaffected, as are one-line templates (Llama-2, Mistral v0.1). The existing tests (chat_template.rs:357-375 single-line template; 447 gpt-oss real template) will not change. Two-line change, S effort, moves every affected template toward the reference with no risk to the verified ones; medium severity is right since it is a rarely-taken path today.

findings.title: tojson renders alphabetised keys, compact separators and null optional fields, so tool schemas differ from the reference rendering
findings.evidence: src/chat_template.rs:296 `let json_string = serde_json::to_string(&value)` on a minijinja Value; :60 `tools: opts.tools` (serde_json::Value) enters the context through serde. minijinja-2.19.0 value/mod.rs:244 `#[cfg(not(feature = "preserve_order"))] pub(crate) type ValueMap = std::collections::BTreeMap<Value, Value>;` and value/serialize.rs:430-433 `SerializeStruct::end … fields.sort_unstable_by(|(a,_),(b,_)| a.cmp(b))`; Cargo.toml:30 enables only `features = ["builtins"]` (no preserve_order) and Cargo.lock's serde_json 1.0.149 has no indexmap dependency. transformers' tojson is `json.dumps(x, ensure_ascii=False, indent=None, separators=None)`, i.e. insertion order with `", "` and `": "`. src/server/routes/types.rs:32-40 `FunctionDefinition { description: Option<String>, parameters: Option<Value>, strict: Option<bool> }` has no skip_serializing_if, so absent fields serialise as null.
findings.rationale: Qwen3's `{{- tool | tojson }}` (and Llama 3.x / Mistral equivalents) therefore emits `{"function":{"description":…,"name":…,"parameters":{"properties":…,"required":…,"type":"object"},"strict":null},"type":"function"}` where the model was trained on `{"type": "function", "function": {"name": …, "description": …, "parameters": {"type": "object", "properties": …, "required": …}}}`. Key order, spacing and spurious `"strict": null` all move the prompt away from the distribution the tool-calling fine-tune saw; past `tool_call.function.arguments | tojson` is reordered the same way. Each is small, but together they are the single largest byte-level difference between oxydllm's tool prompts and the reference.
findings.proposal: Enable `preserve_order` on minijinja (adds indexmap) and on serde_json; add `#[serde(skip_serializing_if = "Option::is_none")]` to the optional FunctionDefinition fields; and implement a Python-style compact `serde_json::ser::Formatter` (begin_object_key writes ", " after the first key, begin_object_value writes ": ", begin_array_value writes ", ") used by tojson_filter when `indent` is None.
findings.expected_benefit: Tool definitions and historical tool calls render byte-identical to transformers; should measurably improve tool-call format adherence on Qwen/Llama native templates (magnitude unmeasured). Also removes the double serialise/parse for the indent path.
findings.verify_how: Render the Qwen3 template with one tool via apply_chat_template and diff against `tokenizer.apply_chat_template(msgs, tools=[tool], tokenize=False)`; run a small tool-calling set (e.g. 50 BFCL-style prompts) before/after and compare parse success.

verdict.reason: All three sub-claims verified. Ordering: Cargo.toml:26/30 enable only `builtins` on minijinja and no feature on serde_json; Cargo.lock 2789-2795 lists serde_json's dependencies as itoa/memchr/serde/serde_core/zmij with no indexmap, so `serde_json::Value` maps are BTreeMaps and `tools_value = serde_json::to_value(&tool_config.tools)` (chat.rs:1641-1643) is already alphabetised before it reaches the template; minijinja value/mod.rs:244 `ValueMap = BTreeMap` and value/serialize.rs:438 `fields.sort_unstable_by(..)` sort struct fields too. Separators: `tojson_filter` (chat_template.rs:296) uses `serde_json::to_string` (no spaces) while transformers' tojson is `json.dumps(..., separators=None)` (`, ` and `: `). Nulls: `FunctionDefinition` (types.rs:33-40) has `#[serde(default)]` but no `skip_serializing_if`, so `strict: null` and `description: null` are rendered. Qwen3's `{{- tool | tojson }}` therefore emits a byte-different schema from the reference. Proposal is implementable: `preserve_order` on both crates plus a ~30-line `serde_json::ser::Formatter` for the no-indent path. One caveat to budget for: `preserve_order` on serde_json is crate-wide, so check constrain.rs schema iteration and any test that compares serialised strings; still S.

findings.title: Tools are injected twice for native-tool templates: in the system message and through the template's `tools` variable
findings.evidence: src/chat_template.rs:60 `tools: opts.tools` goes into the Jinja context (Qwen3, Llama 3.1+, Mistral v3, gpt-oss templates render their own tools block from it). The caller src/server/routes/chat.rs:1647 `let needs_tool_instr = has_tools;` … :1653 `extra_parts.push(tools_system_instruction(&tool_config.tools, &tool_config));` prepends/merges a system message, and :1690-1696 passes `tools_value` to apply_chat_template in the same request. chat.rs:646-681 tools_system_instruction uses `serde_json::to_string_pretty(tools)` and instructs "respond ONLY with a valid JSON object … {\"tool_calls\": [..]}", which contradicts the native template's `<tool_call>` instruction; CHANGELOG line 97 records models echoing that injected shape inside the tags.
findings.rationale: Every tool-bearing request on a native-tool model prefills each schema twice (pretty-printed JSON tokenises roughly 1.5-2x the compact form), occupies the extra KV blocks for the whole request, and gives the model two conflicting output formats. For 5-10 tools that is on the order of 1-3k extra prompt tokens per turn, repeated on every turn of an agent loop (the prefix cache only saves the unchanged prefix, not the per-turn re-render of a changed system message).
findings.proposal: Gate the injection on the template: pass `tools` to the template and skip tools_system_instruction when the template references tools (e.g. `template.contains("tools")`), and inject the instruction only for templates without native tool support or for the no-template fallbacks. Optionally expose a per-request/per-model override.
findings.expected_benefit: 1-3k fewer prompt tokens per tool-heavy request on Qwen/Llama/Mistral/gpt-oss (lower TTFT and KV use), and a single, consistent tool-call format instruction.
findings.verify_how: Log `prompt_tokens` (chat.rs:1718 debug line) for a 5-tool request on Qwen3-4B before/after; confirm tool_calls still parse via the tag parser and that the gpt-oss harmony path is unchanged.

verdict.reason: The double injection is real: chat.rs:1647 `let needs_tool_instr = has_tools;` (has_tools = `!tool_config.tools.is_empty()`, :1574) unconditionally prepends/merges `tools_system_instruction` (:1653, pretty-printed schemas plus the `{"tool_calls": [...]}`-only instruction at :646-680) and the same request passes `tools_value` to `apply_chat_template` (:1690-1696), which Qwen3/Llama 3.1/Mistral/gpt-oss templates render again; no `supports_tools`-style gate exists (grep empty), and CHANGELOG:97 documents models echoing the injected shape inside the tags. Two corrections. (a) Frequency: the injected system message sits at the start of the prompt and is byte-identical across turns while tools and tool_choice are unchanged, so with the prefix cache the extra 1-3k tokens are prefilled once per conversation, not on every turn; what persists is the KV occupancy and the conflicting instruction. (b) Dropping `tools_system_instruction` entirely for native templates removes the only prompt-side carrier of `tool_choice=required`/forced and `parallel_tool_calls=false` (chat.rs:648-664); post-hoc enforcement at :807/:830-845 only filters and truncates, so the model would not be told. Gate the schema dump, keep the one-line policy.
verdict.corrected_benefit: 1-3k fewer prompt tokens and KV blocks per tool-bearing request on native-tool templates (once per conversation with the prefix cache warm, every request when it is not), and one consistent output-format instruction instead of two that contradict each other; tool_choice and parallel policy still reach the model.
verdict.corrected_proposal: When `tokenizer.chat_template()` contains `tools`, skip the `<tools>` schema block and the 'respond ONLY with a valid JSON object' sentence and inject only `choice_instruction`/`parallel_instruction` (and only when choice_mode != Auto or parallel_tool_calls is false); otherwise keep today's full instruction. Verify with the `prompt_tokens` debug line (chat.rs:1718) on a 5-tool Qwen3-4B request and confirm `<tool_call>` parsing and the gpt-oss harmony path are unchanged.

findings.title: A fresh minijinja Environment and a full template compile on every request (and twice on the system-retry)
findings.evidence: src/chat_template.rs:26 `let template = preprocess_template(template);` (copies the whole template and runs `.replace("[::-1]", "|reverse")`), :28-38 `let mut env = Environment::new(); … env.add_template("chat", &template).context(..)?; let tmpl = env.get_template("chat").unwrap();` per call. Callers: src/server/routes/chat.rs:1690 per request, again at :1307 on the system-message retry; src/main.rs:1271/1281 per CLI turn. minijinja 2.19 parses slice steps natively (compiler/parser.rs:458-469 `step = Some(..)`, value/ops.rs:133 `pub fn slice(value, start, stop, step)`), so the `[::-1]` rewrite is vestigial.
findings.rationale: Environment::new builds the builtin filter/test/function tables and add_template lexes, parses and compiles the template (gpt-oss harmony is ~17 KB, Llama 3.x ~8 KB, Qwen3 ~5 KB) for every request, on the tokio worker thread, even though the template is fixed per model. Rough bound: a few hundred microseconds to ~1 ms per request, i.e. ~1-3% of TTFT for short prompts on small models, and compile errors surface at first request instead of at load.
findings.proposal: Compile once per model at load: build an `Environment<'static>` with `add_template_owned("chat", template)`, the trim settings and filters, store it as `Arc<Environment<'static>>` in Tokenizer (or a ChatTemplate struct), and per request do `env.get_template("chat")?.render(&ctx)`. Drop preprocess_template. Optionally run render+encode under spawn_blocking for long prompts.
findings.expected_benefit: Removes O(template size) parse/compile work per request (the existing `template_ms` debug field will show it); template syntax errors are reported at model load.
findings.verify_how: Compare the `template_ms` value in the "prompt preparation timings" debug log for gpt-oss-20b and Qwen3 before/after; the retry path should show the same drop.

findings.title: minijinja `loop_controls` feature is not enabled, so templates using {% break %}/{% continue %} fail to compile with a 500
findings.evidence: Cargo.toml:30 `minijinja = { version = "2.19.0", features = ["builtins"] }`; minijinja-2.19.0 Cargo.toml `default = [builtins, debug, deserialization, macros, multi_template, adjacent_loop_items, std_collections, serde]` (no loop_controls) and `loop_controls = []`; compiler/parser.rs:855/862 gate `break`/`continue` behind `#[cfg(feature = "loop_controls")]`. src/chat_template.rs:35-36 `env.add_template("chat", &template).context("Failed to compile chat template")?` turns that into chat.rs:1696-1702 `template_render_failed` for every request; the system-message retry cannot help.
findings.rationale: transformers compiles templates with `jinja2.ext.loopcontrols`, so template authors may use `{%- break %}`; any such checkpoint is unusable for chat here although the fix is a Cargo feature flag with no runtime cost.
findings.proposal: Add `"loop_controls"` to the minijinja feature list in Cargo.toml; add a unit test rendering `{% for m in messages %}{% if loop.index0 > 0 %}{% break %}{% endif %}{{ m.role }}{% endfor %}`.
findings.expected_benefit: Templates with loop controls render instead of failing; zero cost otherwise.
findings.verify_how: The proposed unit test fails today with a syntax error from add_template and passes with the feature enabled.

findings.title: strftime_now panics the handler task on an invalid strftime directive instead of returning a template error
findings.evidence: src/chat_template.rs:349 `Ok(chrono::Local::now().format(&fmt).to_string())` after only length (334-342) and newline (343-348) checks. chrono's `DelayedFormat` Display returns `Err(fmt::Error)` when the format contains `Item::Error` (unknown or truncated `%` directive), and std's blanket `ToString::to_string` panics on a Display error ("a Display implementation returned an error unexpectedly").
findings.rationale: The format string comes from the model's chat template; a template with `strftime_now("%")` or `%Q` panics the axum task on every request (connection dropped, no structured error), while the existing guards show the function was meant to fail safely on bad input.
findings.proposal: Validate first with `chrono::format::StrftimeItems::new(&fmt).parse()` and map the error, or format via `std::fmt::Write` into a String (`write!(out, "{}", now.format(&fmt)).map_err(|_| minijinja::Error::new(InvalidOperation, "invalid strftime format"))`).
findings.expected_benefit: Bad templates yield a 500 with a message instead of a panic; no runtime cost.
findings.verify_how: Unit test `strftime_now("%".to_string())` panics today under `cargo test`; after the fix it returns Err.

findings.title: encode builds a full Encoding (per-token Strings, offsets, masks) only to copy out the ids; encode_fast avoids it
findings.evidence: src/tokenizer.rs:300-306 `let encoding = self.inner.encode(text, false)…; Ok(encoding.get_ids().to_vec())` (same at 326-331). tokenizers-0.23.1 tokenizer/mod.rs:837-850 `encode` -> `encode_single_sequence(.., OffsetType::Byte)` -> pre_tokenizer.rs:225-235 materialises `(token.id, token.value, offsets, word, type_id)` per token; `encode_fast` (mod.rs:795-806) uses `OffsetType::None` -> pre_tokenizer.rs:212-220 `(token.id, String::with_capacity(0), (0, 0), None, 0)` with no per-token allocation. Called per request at src/server/routes/chat.rs:1707 on the async worker, plus for stop strings (:1730-1736) and at load for stop sequences.
findings.rationale: Per request the current path performs N String allocations and N offset pairs for an N-token prompt that are immediately dropped; for a 32k-token prompt that is on the order of a few milliseconds of allocator traffic on a tokio worker, for no information used.
findings.proposal: Use `self.inner.encode_fast(text, false)` / `encode_fast(text, true)` in `encode` and `encode_with_special_tokens`.
findings.expected_benefit: Removes O(N) allocations per encode; small (sub-percent of prefill) but free, and reduces worker-thread stall on long prompts.
findings.verify_how: Compare the `encode_ms` value in the "prompt preparation timings" debug log on a 20-30k-token prompt before/after; existing round-trip tests cover correctness.

findings.title: GGUF header (tokens, merges, scores) is parsed twice per load and the token array is cloned three times
findings.evidence: src/tokenizer.rs:225-229 `pub fn from_gguf_file(..) { let header = GgufHeader::read(gguf_path)…; Self::from_gguf_content(&header.content) }` and src/common/gguf_weights.rs:130 `let header = GgufHeader::parse(&mmap[..])` for the same file, whose `metadata: header.content.metadata` is retained (:155); src/models/manager.rs:1044-1050 loads the tokenizer first, then the model, sequentially. Inside the tokenizer: src/tokenizer.rs:243-250 `let tokens_arr: Vec<String> = … .filter_map(|v| v.to_string().ok().cloned()).collect()` (clone 1), gguf::build_tokenizer:733 `value_to_string_array(.."tokenizer.ggml.tokens")` (clone 2), :757-760 `let vocab: Vocab = tokens.iter().enumerate().map(|(i,t)| (t.clone(), i as u32)).collect()` (clone 3).
findings.rationale: For Qwen3 (151,936 tokens + 151,387 merges + token_type) the metadata is several MB of small strings; parsing it twice and cloning the token list three times is a few hundred thousand avoidable allocations on the load critical path, roughly tens of milliseconds per load. Small against a multi-second load but pure waste.
findings.proposal: Make `from_gguf_content` pub(crate) and have the GGUF load path hand the already parsed `Content` (or `GgufWeights.metadata`) to the tokenizer instead of re-reading the file; inside, let build_tokenizer return its `tokens` Vec alongside the tokenizer so from_gguf_content reuses it, and pass `vocab` by moving the strings (collect `(String, u32)` from `tokens.into_iter()` after the last use).
findings.expected_benefit: Roughly 20-60 ms less GGUF load time (estimate; ~0.5% of a 10 s load) and ~450k fewer allocations.
findings.verify_how: Time the load span (`load_completed_ms` debug line) for a Qwen3 GGUF before/after, or instrument from_gguf_file with an Instant.

findings.title: Named chat templates (tool_use/rag) are ignored in both tokenizer_config.json array form and GGUF metadata
findings.evidence: src/tokenizer.rs:134-145 `parse_chat_template`: `serde_json::Value::Array(arr) => arr.iter().find(|v| v.get("name")… == Some("default")).or_else(|| arr.first())…` always picks the default; src/tokenizer.rs:234-238 reads only `content.metadata.get("tokenizer.chat_template")`, while llama.cpp also writes `tokenizer.chat_template.<name>` entries listed in `tokenizer.chat_templates`. transformers selects the `tool_use` template when tools are passed and that name exists.
findings.rationale: Checkpoints that ship named templates (Command-R family and some Mistral exports) get their default template for tool requests, so native tool rendering is lost and only the injected system instruction remains; a rarely taken path, but silent.
findings.proposal: Keep all named templates in Tokenizer (`HashMap<String, String>` plus default) from both sources, and in chat.rs apply_chat_template select `tool_use` when `tools.is_some()` and present, else default.
findings.expected_benefit: Native tool prompts for named-template models; matches transformers' selection rule.
findings.verify_how: Unit test with a tokenizer_config.json whose chat_template is `[{name: default, template: A}, {name: tool_use, template: B}]`: a tools request must render B.

findings.title: CLI `run` silently falls back to the plain "User:/Assistant:" format when the chat template fails
findings.evidence: src/chat_template.rs:90-126 `format_plain_chat` emits `System: … User: … Assistant: `; src/main.rs:1271-1272 `let mut prompt = server::apply_chat_template(&tokenizer, &messages, thinking, None, None).unwrap_or_else(|_| crate::chat_template::format_plain_chat(&messages));` and again at 1281-1282, with no log of the error. The server path deliberately surfaces the same failure (CHANGELOG: "a failed apply_chat_template no longer falls back to a plain-text render with a 200 OK; the error now propagates as a structured 500").
findings.rationale: A template error in the CLI (missing loop_controls, a raise_exception, a syntax error) turns into a prompt format the model was never trained on, producing incoherent or non-stopping replies with no diagnostic, which is the exact class of silent downgrade the server path was fixed to avoid.
findings.proposal: Propagate the error in `run` (exit with the template error), or at minimum print the error once before falling back, mirroring the server behaviour.
findings.expected_benefit: Template problems are visible in the CLI instead of masquerading as model quality issues.
findings.verify_how: Run `oxydllm run` on a model whose template contains `{% break %}` (or an intentional syntax error) and observe that today the session proceeds with a `User:`/`Assistant:` prompt without any message.

missed:
`reasoning_content` never reaches the template. `ChatMessage` carries it (src/server/routes/types.rs:71 `pub reasoning_content: Option<String>`) and the server emits it in responses (chat.rs:1447 `data.reasoning_content.push_str(&text)`), but `TemplateMessage` (src/chat_template.rs:278-287, built at :46-56) has only role/content/tool_calls/tool_call_id/name, so the field is dropped on the way into the Jinja context. The Qwen3 and Qwen3.5 templates test `message.reasoning_content is string` and, for assistant turns after the last user query (i.e. inside a tool-call loop), re-render `<think>
{reasoning}
</think>

` before the content; transformers and vLLM pass the field through, so the model sees the reasoning it produced before calling the tool. oxydllm always takes the empty branch, so in every agentic loop on Qwen3-family models the assistant's own prior reasoning is silently removed from its history, a per-turn distribution shift on a supported, frequently used path. Fix is S: add `#[serde(skip_serializing_if = "Option::is_none")] reasoning_content: Option<&'a str>` to `TemplateMessage` and map `m.reasoning_content.as_deref()`, with a unit test rendering the Qwen3 template for [user, assistant(tool_call, reasoning), tool] and asserting the `<think>` block appears.

subsystems.assessment: The build/CI surface is unusually thorough for a one-maintainer project: pinned toolchain, MSRV floor on an arm64 runner, a weekly toolchain sweep, cargo audit, per-arch CUDA compile checks, reusable build workflow, multi-arch Docker manifests, and a release gate that refuses to publish without a green CI run on the tagged SHA. The release profile is sane (opt-level 3, thin LTO, codegen-units 1, unwind kept, which the EngineSlotGuard self-heal silently depends on). What is fragile is that the only CI leg for the only verified platform cannot prove it exercised anything: 77 Metal tests skip silently when Device::new_metal(0) fails and nothing asserts a device, so the macos-26 job is green whether or not the VM has a GPU, and the 6.3k lines of MSL that are include_str!'d and compiled at runtime are never compiled in CI at all. The second fragility is drift between the documented contributor contract and the executed one: CONTRIBUTING demands clippy --all-targets, hooks and CI run plain clippy, and a CPU-only --all-targets run fails today on one let-else in test code (a direct consequence of the uninhabited-enum trick used to keep the CPU build honest). Docker images are built without build.rs because .dockerignore and both Dockerfiles omit it, so the per-arch CUDA images lose exactly the compiled-cap warning that was written for them, and the ci.yml path filter omits build.rs and the Dockerfiles, which can also strand a release behind the 20-minute verify-ci poll. The dependency graph carries avoidable compile weight (aws-lc-sys as TLS provider, OTEL metrics/logs signals that are never built, tokenizers compiled twice because candle-core 0.11 pins 0.22 non-optionally) and the CI/Docker recipes install OpenSSL packages that no crate links. Structurally, metal_ops.rs at 8k lines (54 percent tests) and 101 cfg(feature = "metal") sites following one copy-pasted pattern are the biggest maintainability levers; a CPU stub module with the same signatures would delete most of the cfgs at zero runtime cost. The biggest single lever is making the macOS job fail loudly when no Metal device is present and adding an MSL compile test, because today the kernel suite could regress on main with CI fully green.

findings.title: CPU-only clippy --all-targets fails on an irrefutable let-else in gguf_weights tests; hooks and CI never lint test targets
findings.evidence: clippy_cpu.log: 'error: irrefutable `let...else` pattern --> src/common/gguf_weights.rs:757:9 ... `-D irrefutable-let-patterns` implied by `-D warnings`' then 'could not compile `oxydllm` (bin "oxydllm" test)'. Source 757-761: `let LinearWeight::Candle { tensor: restored, .. } = depermute_qk_rows(...).unwrap() else { panic!(...) };`. src/common/linear.rs:18-20: `#[cfg(not(feature = "metal"))] pub enum StagedWeight {}` and gguf_weights.rs:45 `Owned(StagedWeight)`, so off Metal the Owned variant is uninhabited and the pattern is irrefutable. Grep for `let LinearWeight::` and `matches!(.., LinearWeight::Owned` found only this site plus line 894 which is already under `#[cfg(feature = "metal")]`. CONTRIBUTING.md:56 'Run `cargo clippy --all-targets`' and :71 'No clippy warnings on `--all-targets`'; .githooks/pre-commit:8 `cargo clippy -- -D warnings`; ci.yml:104,129,158,249 all run `cargo clippy ... -- -D warnings` without --all-targets.
findings.rationale: Test modules (396 #[test] fns, 46 #[tokio::test]) are never linted anywhere, so the documented rule is unenforced and the first person who follows CONTRIBUTING literally on a Linux box hits a hard error. Only one site exists today, so the fix is trivial; the rule should then be enforced so it stays at zero.
findings.proposal: Replace the let-else at gguf_weights.rs:757 with a match that names the other arm (which already compiles clean in non-test code at :416/:438/:459): `let restored = match depermute_qk_rows(&interleaved, n_heads, head_dim, &dev).unwrap() { LinearWeight::Candle { tensor, .. } => tensor, LinearWeight::Owned(_) => panic!("a candle weight comes back as one") };`. Then add `--all-targets` to .githooks/pre-commit:8 and to the four clippy steps in ci.yml (104, 129, 158, 249) so test code is linted under -D warnings on both feature sets.
findings.expected_benefit: CONTRIBUTING, hooks and CI agree; test code gets the same lint bar as library code; no more latent --all-targets breakage.
findings.verify_how: On the M5: `cargo clippy --no-default-features --all-targets -- -D warnings` fails before the patch at gguf_weights.rs:757 and passes after; `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings` (Metal) should also pass; then watch the updated CI jobs.

verdict.reason: Accurate. gguf_weights.rs:757-761 is a by-value `let LinearWeight::Candle{..} = depermute_qk_rows(..).unwrap() else { panic!() }` inside the un-gated `#[cfg(test)] mod tests` (line 721-722); linear.rs:18-20 makes `StagedWeight` an uninhabited enum off Metal and gguf_weights.rs:45 `Owned(StagedWeight)`, so by-value the Owned arm is empty and the let-else is irrefutable. The scratchpad clippy_cpu.log confirms it is the only error: line 509 'error: irrefutable let...else pattern', 519 '-D irrefutable-let-patterns implied by -D warnings', 522 'could not compile oxydllm (bin "oxydllm" test)'. Enforcement gap is real: .githooks/pre-commit:8 `cargo clippy -- -D warnings`; ci.yml:104,129,158,249 all without --all-targets; CONTRIBUTING.md:56/71 demand --all-targets. My grep agrees only :757 and :894 (the latter under cfg metal) touch the pattern. One amendment to the proposal: write the replacement as a match on a reference (as the non-test sites at :416/:438/:459 do, `LinearWeight::Owned(w) => ...` on `&LinearWeight`, which the CPU clippy log proves lint-clean) rather than a by-value `Owned(_) => panic!` arm, since a by-value wildcard over an empty payload is exactly what min_exhaustive_patterns treats as redundant and could trade the irrefutable error for an unreachable_patterns warning on the CPU build. Severity medium and effort S are fair; the enforcement half (--all-targets in hook and four CI steps) is what keeps it at zero.

findings.title: Contributor workflow documents a test target, a feature and a download step that do not exist, and the pre-commit hook only builds on macOS
findings.evidence: CONTRIBUTING.md:46-49: 'Architecture regression tests download small model checkpoints on first run and are gated behind the `arch_regression` feature: cargo test --test arch_regression'. Cargo.toml [features] has only default/cuda/metal (lines 7-10); there is no tests/ directory (`ls tests` -> No such file); src/models/arch_regression.rs:1-18 is `#[cfg(test)] mod tests` building synthetic hidden=32 models with `rand_t`, no download code (grep for download/hub/HF_ found nothing). .githooks/pre-commit:8 runs `cargo clippy -- -D warnings` on the default feature set, which is `default = ["metal"]` (Cargo.toml:8) pulling candle-metal-kernels/objc2-metal; every Linux CI job (ci.yml:104,158,249) has to pass --no-default-features for the same reason. pre-commit:11 also runs `cargo audit`, which fetches the advisory DB over the network on every commit. .githooks/pre-push:5 runs `cargo test --release -- arch_ edge_`, again default (Metal) features.
findings.rationale: CONTRIBUTING explicitly supports Linux/CUDA and CPU contributors, but the hooks it tells them to install cannot run there, and the documented test command fails with 'no test target named arch_regression'. Stale docs cost every new contributor one round-trip and erode trust in the rest of the document.
findings.proposal: CONTRIBUTING: replace lines 46-49 with `cargo test arch_ edge_` and drop the download/feature sentence. Hooks: detect platform (`case "$(uname -s)" in Darwin) F="";; *) F="--no-default-features";; esac`) and pass `$F --all-targets` to clippy and `$F` to the pre-push test; move `cargo audit` out of pre-commit into pre-push (or keep it in CI only, where it already runs) so an offline commit is not blocked.
findings.expected_benefit: Hooks work on all three documented platforms; documented commands match the tree; commits are not blocked by network access.
findings.verify_how: On a Linux box with hooks enabled, `git commit` of a trivial change currently fails in clippy (metal feature); after the patch it passes. `cargo test --test arch_regression` fails today; `cargo test arch_ edge_` passes (18 tests).

findings.title: macOS CI cannot tell whether a single Metal test ran: 77 tests skip silently when no device exists and the MSL sources are never compiled in CI
findings.evidence: metal_ops.rs:3720-3722: `fn metal_device_or_skip() -> Option<Device> { Device::new_metal(0).ok() }` used 58 times in the 74-test module; 19 further sites use `let Ok(dev) = Device::new_metal(0) else { return; }` (13 metal_ops, 2 linear, 1 each gdn/gguf_weights/moe/sampling, e.g. gguf_weights.rs:815-817). The only non-skip use is paged.rs:2377 `Device::new_metal(0).unwrap_or(Device::Cpu)`, which also degrades silently. ci.yml:112 `runs-on: macos-26`, :129 `cargo clippy --release -- -D warnings`, then 'Unit tests (Metal — CPU-only tests, no GPU needed)': `cargo test --release -- --test-threads=4`. Kernel sources are include_str!'d and compiled only at runtime: metal_ops.rs:521 FFN_METAL_SOURCE, :912 FA_METAL_SOURCE, :1561 QUANT_METAL_SOURCE, :2541 MPP_GEMM_SOURCE (6316 lines of .metal under src/common). No CI step invokes the Metal compiler.
findings.rationale: Every kernel-parity, AWQ/GPTQ GEMV, FlashAttention, GGUF dequant and MPP test is written to pass by returning early. If the macos-26 VM exposes no Metal device the job is a CPU re-run of the Linux job; if it does, nobody knows which tests actually executed. A syntax error in quant_kernels.metal would only surface on the maintainer's machine at runtime. For a Metal-first engine this is the largest hole in the safety net.
findings.proposal: (1) Add `OXYDLLM_REQUIRE_METAL=1` to the check-macos job env and make the skip helpers honour it: `fn metal_device_or_skip() -> Option<Device> { match Device::new_metal(0) { Ok(d) => Some(d), Err(e) => { if std::env::var_os("OXYDLLM_REQUIRE_METAL").is_some() { panic!("Metal device required: {e}") } None } } }` and route the 19 let-else sites through a shared `crate::common::test_support::metal_device_or_skip()`. (2) Add one `#[cfg(feature = "metal")]` test that calls `newLibraryWithSource_options_error` on each of the four sources with the language version each needs (MPP needs Version4_0, the others the baseline), so MSL compile errors fail CI. (3) If the hosted runner turns out to have no Metal device, the loud failure is the signal to move this job to a self-hosted M-series runner or mark it as compile-only honestly.
findings.expected_benefit: CI either proves the Metal suite ran (74+ tests, four kernel libraries compiled) or fails visibly; silent zero-coverage becomes impossible.
findings.verify_how: Push a branch with a deliberate typo in src/common/ffn_kernels.metal: today check-macos stays green; after the change it must fail. Also run `OXYDLLM_REQUIRE_METAL=1 cargo test --release metal_` locally on the M5 and confirm the test count matches the number of tests in fused_kernel_parity_tests.

verdict.reason: The facts hold: metal_ops.rs:3720-3722 `fn metal_device_or_skip() -> Option<Device> { Device::new_metal(0).ok() }` used 58 times, 74 #[test] fns from line 3713 to EOF, 17 more `let Ok(dev) = Device::new_metal(0) else { return }` sites across src/, paged.rs:2377 `unwrap_or(Device::Cpu)`; the four kernel sources are include_str! at :521/:912/:1561/:2541 and compiled only via new_library_with_source at :549/:941/:1612 and newLibraryWithSource_options_error at :2592; ci.yml:112 macos-26, :132 `cargo test --release -- --test-threads=4`, and the step is literally named 'CPU-only tests, no GPU needed'. So CI genuinely cannot say whether a Metal test ran. But 'high' overstates it on this project's own terms: the ROADMAP's verification-by-execution rule means the M5 suite is the real gate (CHANGELOG 'Unreleased: 351 unit tests green', ROADMAP:71 full suite executed on every toolchain 1.94.1-1.97.1), so this is a CI-visibility gap, not a correctness risk on a supported path. The proposal is also riskier than stated: GitHub's arm64 macOS VMs expose an Apple paravirtual Metal device whose feature set is not the M5's (no Metal 4 TensorOps, possibly different bf16/simdgroup behaviour), so OXYDLLM_REQUIRE_METAL=1 in the hosted job turns 77 skips into either a permanent red or flaky kernel-parity failures on a GPU nobody ships on; part (2) does not avoid the device question either, since newLibraryWithSource is a device method, and `xcrun metal` on Xcode 26 runners needs the separately downloaded Metal Toolchain component. Cheaper and safer: first make the skip visible, not fatal.
verdict.corrected_proposal: Step 1 (report mode): route all 75 skip sites through one `crate::common::test_support::metal_device_or_skip()` that prints a fixed marker (`eprintln!("SKIP no-metal-device: {name}")`) and, in the check-macos job, run `cargo test --release -- --nocapture 2>&1 | tee test.log` followed by a step that counts the marker and the executed metal_ops tests and writes both to the job summary (`$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY`). Also run the existing diagnostic `the_tensor_ops_library_compiles_here` (metal_ops.rs:7591-7612) and the three sibling library compiles as `cargo test --release -- --ignored metal_library` so a compile verdict appears in the log. Step 2: after a few runs you know what macos-26 actually exposes; only then add a `require-metal` job input that fails on a nonzero skip count, or honestly rename the step to compile-only and keep the M5 as the kernel gate. Keep the skip-counting helper off the shipped binary (it is #[cfg(test)]), so it does not add to the four undocumented env switches the ROADMAP flag audit already objects to.
verdict.corrected_benefit: CI states, per run, how many Metal tests executed and whether the four MSL libraries compiled on that runner, without betting the job's colour on an unknown paravirtual GPU; the loud-failure switch is added only once the answer is known.

findings.title: Docker images are compiled without build.rs, so the CUDA images lose the compute-cap validation and the runtime cap-mismatch warning written for them
findings.evidence: Dockerfile:39 `COPY rust-toolchain.toml ./`, :46 `COPY Cargo.toml Cargo.lock ./`, :55 `COPY src ./src`; Dockerfile.cpu:26/32/37 identical; neither copies build.rs. .dockerignore starts with `**` and whitelists only Cargo.toml, Cargo.lock, src/, .cargo/, rust-toolchain.toml, Dockerfile, Dockerfile.cpu (no `!build.rs`). Cargo auto-detects build.rs only when present, so the image builds with no build script. build.rs:18-33 validates CUDA_COMPUTE_CAP (`cargo::error=... not a supported compute capability`) and emits `cargo:rustc-env=OXYDLLM_COMPILED_CAP={cap}`; src/models/loader.rs:703-714 reads `option_env!("OXYDLLM_COMPILED_CAP")` to warn 'Binary compiled for sm_{compiled_cap} but hardware is sm_{cap}'; main.rs:537 and :1563 read `option_env!("OXYDLLM_BUILD_TS")` so `--version` prints no build date. main.rs:534-536 comment blames 'the Docker dummy-build layer doesn't always reapply the build-script env', which misdiagnoses it.
findings.rationale: The per-arch images (:cuda-ada, :cuda-hopper, ...) are exactly where a user is most likely to run the wrong arch, and the warning that exists for that case can never fire in them. The build-time validation that rejects unsupported caps is also skipped, so a bad `--build-arg CUDA_ARCH` only fails deep inside cudarc/candle-kernels.
findings.proposal: Add `!build.rs` to .dockerignore and `COPY build.rs ./` immediately after the Cargo manifest COPY in both Dockerfiles (before the stub build so the dependency layer is cached with the script). Fix the comment at main.rs:534-536 to say the env is absent only when build.rs is not in the build context. Optionally pass `--build-arg OXYDLLM_BUILD_TS_OVERRIDE=$(git log -1 --format=%ct)` from build.yml for reproducible timestamps.
findings.expected_benefit: Docker binaries carry the compiled cap and build date; invalid CUDA_ARCH fails at cargo build with the curated message; `oxydllm --version` inside a container matches the tarball.
findings.verify_how: `docker build -f Dockerfile.cpu -t t .` then `docker run --rm t --version`: today prints `oxydllm 0.0.0-alpha.15` with no `+YYYYMMDD` suffix; after the change it prints the date. For CUDA: `docker build --build-arg CUDA_ARCH=75 .` should fail in build.rs with the supported-caps list.

verdict.reason: Fully verified. Cargo.toml:1-5 and :12-14 declare no `build = ` key, so Cargo auto-detects build.rs only if present. .dockerignore starts with `**` and whitelists only Cargo.toml, Cargo.lock, src/, .cargo/, rust-toolchain.toml, Dockerfile, Dockerfile.cpu (no `!build.rs`); Dockerfile:39/46/55 and Dockerfile.cpu:26/32/37 copy only rust-toolchain.toml, the manifests and src. build.rs:12-17 emits OXYDLLM_BUILD_TS, :19-33 validates CUDA_COMPUTE_CAP via `cargo::error=` and emits OXYDLLM_COMPILED_CAP; Dockerfile:25-28 sets `CUDA_COMPUTE_CAP=${CUDA_ARCH}` so the validation would run if the script existed. loader.rs:703-714 reads `option_env!("OXYDLLM_COMPILED_CAP")` for the sm mismatch warning; main.rs:537 and :1563 read OXYDLLM_BUILD_TS, and the comment at main.rs:534-536 ('the Docker dummy-build layer doesn't always reapply the build-script env') misdiagnoses it: build.rs emits only rerun-if-env-changed, so a present script's env is reapplied; it is simply absent from the context. Beyond --version, main.rs:528-540 compares a release's published_at against build_ts, so a container with build_ts=0 feeds that comparison a zero, which is a supported-path (CPU image) UX defect, not only a CUDA one. Proposal (`!build.rs` plus `COPY build.rs ./` before the stub build in both Dockerfiles, fix the comment) is correct and S.

findings.title: ci.yml path filter omits build.rs, Dockerfiles, .dockerignore, .githooks and build.yml; release verify-ci then aborts for tags on such commits
findings.evidence: ci.yml:13-19 and :22-28 `paths: [src/**, Cargo.toml, Cargo.lock, rust-toolchain.toml, install.sh, .github/workflows/ci.yml]`. build.rs, Dockerfile, Dockerfile.cpu, .dockerignore, .githooks/*, .github/workflows/build.yml are not listed, yet build.rs is compiled into every binary and build.yml is what release.yml and nightly.yml call. release.yml verify-ci polls `gh run list --commit $SHA --workflow ci.yml` 20 times with `sleep 30` and ends with 'CI did not complete within 20 minutes ... Either CI was never triggered ... exit 1'.
findings.rationale: A change to build.rs (the compute-cap table is edited whenever a new sm_ is added) or to build.yml ships to main with no compile check, and if a release tag lands on a commit whose only changes are filtered paths (CHANGELOG + Dockerfile tweak), the release job waits 20 minutes and then fails with a misleading message. The `ci-ok` required check also never reports on such PRs.
findings.proposal: Add `build.rs`, `Dockerfile`, `Dockerfile.cpu`, `.dockerignore`, `.githooks/**`, `.github/workflows/build.yml` to both paths lists (or drop the filter and rely on Swatinem caching; the fmt/audit jobs are seconds). In release.yml, treat 'no CI run found for this SHA' as an immediate error rather than a 20-minute poll by checking `gh run list` once for an empty payload before entering the loop.
findings.expected_benefit: No untested build-script or workflow changes on main; release failures surface in seconds with an accurate cause.
findings.verify_how: Open a PR that only edits build.rs: today no CI workflow runs (Checks tab shows nothing for ci.yml); after the change the full matrix runs.

verdict.reason: The filter is as cited: ci.yml:13-19 and :22-28 list only src/**, Cargo.toml, Cargo.lock, rust-toolchain.toml, install.sh, .github/workflows/ci.yml; build.rs is absent although every binary compiles it. release.yml:40-69 polls `gh run list --commit $SHA --workflow ci.yml` and exits 1 after the loop. Three corrections shrink it. (1) The loop is `seq 1 20` with `sleep 30` (release.yml:40,64): 10 minutes, not 20; the message at :67 is itself wrong. (2) A release tag normally sits on the version-bump commit, which touches Cargo.toml and Cargo.lock and therefore does trigger CI; the abort needs a tag on a CHANGELOG/Dockerfile-only commit, which is rare. (3) Adding Dockerfile, Dockerfile.cpu, .dockerignore, .githooks/** and build.yml to ci.yml's paths is wasted compute: ci.yml's own header (:4-5) says it does not build Docker images, and it never calls build.yml (only nightly.yml:71 and release.yml:74 do), so a Dockerfile edit would run the full eight-job Rust matrix and still test nothing about the Dockerfile. Only build.rs belongs in the list; a broken build.rs today surfaces at the next nightly (nightly.yml via build.yml) rather than never. The ci-ok 'required check' claim is unverifiable from the repo (branch protection is not in it), though ci.yml:298-318 does gate correctly on needs.*.result.
verdict.corrected_proposal: Add only `build.rs` to both `paths:` lists in ci.yml:13-19 and :22-28. In release.yml verify-ci, run `gh run list ... --json databaseId` once before the loop and fail immediately with 'no CI run exists for $SHA (CI is path-filtered; push a commit that touches src/ or Cargo.toml, or dispatch ci.yml manually)' when the payload is `[]`; fix the ':67' message to say 10 minutes or change `seq 1 40`.
verdict.corrected_benefit: build.rs changes get the compile check on the PR instead of at the next nightly; a tag on a filtered commit fails in seconds with the real cause instead of 10 minutes later with a misleading one. No extra CI runs for Docker/hook edits that ci.yml cannot test.

findings.title: Release Metal binaries are built on macos-14 while CI validates on macos-26
findings.evidence: build.yml:37 `runs-on: macos-14` for 'Build · macOS arm64 (Metal)' with `cargo build --release` at :49; ci.yml:112 `runs-on: macos-26` for check-macos. The Metal 4 path is selected at runtime (metal_ops.rs:2588 `opts.setLanguageVersion(MTLLanguageVersion::Version4_0)` via newLibraryWithSource), so the shipped binary's behaviour is host-dependent, but the toolchain/SDK that produced it is two major OS versions behind the one that was tested.
findings.rationale: The artifact users install is not the artifact CI tested; any objc2-metal or candle-metal-kernels change that starts depending on a newer SDK symbol will pass CI and fail in the release build, and GitHub retires older macOS images on a rolling basis (macos-13 already gone), which would break the release pipeline without a code change.
findings.proposal: Set build.yml:37 to `macos-26` (or define `MACOS_RUNNER: macos-26` once in both workflows), so release and CI use the same image; if an older deployment target is wanted for compatibility, set `MACOSX_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET` explicitly instead of relying on the runner age.
findings.expected_benefit: One tested toolchain per release; no surprise when GitHub drops macos-14.
findings.verify_how: Trigger nightly.yml via workflow_dispatch after the change and confirm the macOS artifact builds and `oxydllm --version` reports as before; compare `otool -l target/release/oxydllm | grep -A3 LC_BUILD_VERSION` between the two runner images.

findings.title: Release profile: thin LTO never A/B'd against fat, and the unwind dependency of the engine self-heal is undocumented
findings.evidence: Cargo.toml:55-58 `[profile.release] opt-level = 3 / lto = "thin" / codegen-units = 1`; no `panic` key. grep over CHANGELOG and all five design notes for lto/codegen-units/panic=abort returned nothing, so the choice was not measured. src/models/manager.rs:966-973: `impl Drop for EngineSlotGuard { fn drop(&mut self) { let panicked = std::thread::panicking(); ...` and the test at manager.rs:1599-1603 asserts `t.join().is_err()`; CHANGELOG alpha.15 line 42 describes this as the engine-loop self-heal. With codegen-units = 1 the only LTO effect left is cross-crate (oxydllm <-> candle-core/tokenizers/axum), which is what fat vs thin decides.
findings.rationale: Decode is GPU-bound so the CPU-side per-token path (sampling.rs, scheduler, tokenizer decode, Metal command encoding in metal_ops) is where cross-crate inlining matters; fat LTO is a one-line, zero-risk experiment that nobody has run. Separately, `panic = "abort"` is the standard size/speed knob people reach for, and here it would silently disable the self-heal because `thread::panicking()` never runs; nothing in Cargo.toml says so.
findings.proposal: Add a comment above [profile.release]: `# panic must stay unwind: EngineSlotGuard (models/manager.rs) relies on thread::panicking() to self-heal a panicked engine loop.` Then run one A/B of `lto = "fat"` with scripts/stress_baseline.py --quick (decode_tps, ttft_ms, cold_load_ms) and binary size; keep fat only if decode_tps or ttft improves beyond run-to-run noise.
findings.expected_benefit: Documented invariant; possibly a few percent on CPU-bound phases (sampling, tokenizer, scheduling) at no runtime risk; if no gain, the measurement closes the question.
findings.verify_how: `cargo build --release` with each setting, `./scripts/stress_baseline.py --quick --models <one small GGUF, one AWQ>` three times each, diff the CSVs; compare `ls -l target/release/oxydllm`.

findings.title: OpenSSL dev/runtime packages are installed in 14 places but no crate links OpenSSL; the actual TLS cost is the aws-lc-sys C build
findings.evidence: Cargo.toml:19 `reqwest = { version = "0.13.3", features = ["blocking", "json"] }` (default features on). Registry reqwest-0.13.3/Cargo.toml: `default = ["default-tls", "charset", "http2", "system-proxy"]`, `default-tls = ["rustls"]`, `rustls = ["__rustls-aws-lc-rs", "dep:rustls-platform-verifier", "__rustls"]`. Cargo.lock contains no openssl, openssl-sys or native-tls package (grep), only openssl-probe; clippy_cpu.log shows `Compiling aws-lc-sys v0.45.0`, `Compiling aws-lc-rs v1.18.1`, `Compiling rustls v0.23.45`, `Checking rustls-platform-verifier`, no openssl. Yet `apt-get install ... pkg-config libssl-dev` appears in ci.yml (msrv, rust-latest, check-linux-cpu, check-linux-cuda x5 matrix, check-linux-arm64-cpu, check-linux-arm64-cuda x4), build.yml (all Linux jobs), Dockerfile:30 and Dockerfile.cpu:17, and the runtime stages install `libssl3` (Dockerfile:62, Dockerfile.cpu:44). toolchains.yml also installs libssl-dev.
findings.rationale: Every Linux job pays an apt-get update + install for a library that is never linked, and the runtime images carry libssl3 for nothing. The real native cost is aws-lc-sys (a large C/C++ crypto library compiled with cc on every clean build, including inside each of the 10 CUDA matrix jobs and both Docker builders) for a client that only talks to huggingface.co and api.github.com.
findings.proposal: Delete `pkg-config libssl-dev` from the apt lines in ci.yml, build.yml, toolchains.yml and both Dockerfile builders, and `libssl3` from both runtime stages (keep ca-certificates: rustls-platform-verifier reads the system store). Optionally swap the provider: `reqwest = { version = "0.13.3", default-features = false, features = ["rustls-no-provider", "charset", "http2", "system-proxy", "blocking", "json"] }` plus `rustls = { version = "0.23", default-features = false, features = ["ring", "std", "tls12", "logging"] }` and one line in main(): `rustls::crypto::ring::default_provider().install_default().ok();` — ring builds in a fraction of aws-lc-sys's time.
findings.expected_benefit: Removes ~15-30 s of apt from each Linux job and ~5 MB from each runtime image with zero behaviour change; the ring swap removes the slowest C build from every clean CI/Docker build (typically tens of seconds to over a minute on the 2-core runners).
findings.verify_how: `cargo tree -i openssl-sys` prints 'nothing to print' (no dependency). Remove the apt lines on a branch and watch all Linux jobs pass; `ldd target/release/oxydllm | grep ssl` on a Linux build is empty. For the ring swap, time `cargo build --release --no-default-features` from a clean target before/after and run `oxydllm pull <small model>` to confirm TLS still works.

findings.title: OpenTelemetry stack compiles metrics and logs signals that are never used and is not feature-gated
findings.evidence: Cargo.toml:42-46 `opentelemetry = "0.32.0"`, `opentelemetry_sdk = "0.32.1"`, `opentelemetry-otlp = "0.32.0"`, `tracing-opentelemetry`, `opentelemetry-http` all non-optional with defaults. Registry opentelemetry-otlp-0.32.0: `default = ["http-proto", "reqwest-blocking-client", "trace", "metrics", "logs", "internal-logs"]`; opentelemetry_sdk-0.32.1: `default = ["trace", "metrics", "logs", "internal-logs"]`. The only consumer is src/telemetry.rs (160 lines): :96-104 builds exactly one `opentelemetry_otlp::SpanExporter::builder().with_http()...` and :16-25 a `TraceContextPropagator`; grep for opentelemetry outside telemetry.rs hits only chat.rs (header extraction). No metrics or logs exporter exists; Prometheus (src/server/routes/metrics.rs) carries metrics. clippy_cpu.log: `Checking opentelemetry-proto v0.32.0`, `Checking prost v0.14.4`, `Compiling prost-derive`.
findings.rationale: opentelemetry-proto's generated prost code for metrics and logs is compiled into every build (CPU CI, CUDA matrix, Docker) for signals the binary cannot emit. Trimming is a manifest-only change; gating the whole stack behind a cargo feature would additionally let the CPU/CI builds skip prost entirely.
findings.proposal: `opentelemetry-otlp = { version = "0.32.0", default-features = false, features = ["http-proto", "reqwest-blocking-client", "trace"] }` and `opentelemetry_sdk = { version = "0.32.1", default-features = false, features = ["trace"] }` (internal-logs optional). Second step: an `otel` cargo feature (in `default`) wrapping the five crates and `telemetry::init`'s OTLP branch, so `--no-default-features` builds drop the stack.
findings.expected_benefit: Fewer generated-proto modules compiled in every build; with the feature, CPU/CI builds shed opentelemetry-proto, prost and friends entirely. No runtime change for the default build.
findings.verify_how: `cargo tree -e features -p opentelemetry-proto | grep -E 'metrics|logs'` shows the features gone; `cargo build --release` still succeeds and `--otel-endpoint http://localhost:4318` still exports spans (telemetry::tests::base_endpoint_gets_traces_signal_path stays green).

findings.title: tokenizers is compiled twice: candle-core 0.11 pins 0.22 non-optionally while oxydllm asks for 0.23
findings.evidence: Cargo.toml:29 `tokenizers = { version = "0.23.1", default-features = false, features = ["onig"] }`. Cargo.lock reverse lookup: `tokenizers 0.22.2` is depended on by `candle-core 0.11.0`; registry candle-core-0.11.0/Cargo.toml:273-276 `[target.'cfg(not(target_arch = "wasm32"))'.dependencies.tokenizers] version = "0.22.0" features = ["onig"] default-features = false` with no optional flag and no feature gating it. clippy_cpu.log: `Checking tokenizers v0.22.2` and `Checking tokenizers v0.23.1` (onig_sys is shared, only the Rust crate is duplicated). Cargo.lock also shows two gemm stacks (0.18 via ug, 0.19 via candle) and two cudarc (0.17 via ug-cuda, 0.19 via candle) that are candle's problem, not ours.
findings.rationale: tokenizers is one of the heavier pure-Rust crates in the graph; compiling it twice in every CI job and Docker build is pure waste. CHANGELOG alpha.13 line 101 says the bump to 0.23.1 came with the candle bump, not because of a needed 0.23 API.
findings.proposal: Set `tokenizers = { version = "0.22", ... }` so both resolve to 0.22.2 (if the 0.23 API is actually needed, note which call and keep it; otherwise revisit when candle-core 0.12 bumps its pin). Alternatively ask upstream to make candle-core's tokenizers dependency optional, since candle-core itself only uses it for examples/utilities.
findings.expected_benefit: One tokenizers build instead of two in every clean build (tens of seconds on the 2-core runners, more inside the 10-job CUDA matrix).
findings.verify_how: After the edit `cargo tree -d | grep tokenizers` prints nothing; `cargo test --release --no-default-features tokenizer::` stays green (6 tests + 2 ignored).

findings.title: Debug environment variables: the ROADMAP decision is still open and the names have drifted (OXYD_ prefix, undocumented OXYD_PROFILE_EVERY, stale CHANGELOG names)
findings.evidence: Reads (all verified): profile.rs:32 `OXYDLLM_PROFILE` via OnceLock; profile.rs:23 `std::env::var("OXYD_PROFILE_EVERY")` (different prefix, read on every report_every() call, not cached); sampling.rs:587 second independent OnceLock on `OXYDLLM_PROFILE` gating `eprintln!` at :599 (CONTRIBUTING:74 'No println! in library code; use tracing'); gdn.rs:42 `OXYDLLM_GDN_DEBUG` OnceLock, 11 call sites; metal_ops.rs:2584 `OXYDLLM_DISABLE_MPP` inside the per-device `or_insert_with` (read once per device); gguf_header.rs:574 `OXYDLLM_GGUF` only in an `#[ignore]` probe. README.md:420-422 documents OXYDLLM_PROFILE, OXYDLLM_GDN_DEBUG, OXYDLLM_DISABLE_MPP but not OXYD_PROFILE_EVERY. CHANGELOG:125 and :170/178 still name `OXYDLLM_GDN_CHUNK` and `OXYDLLM_PROFILE_DECODE`, neither of which exists in src/ (grep). ROADMAP 'Flags and environment variables': 'Either document them as such or gate them behind a feature; leaving them undocumented and always-on is the worst of the three.' Per-token cost is nil: every hot-path read is OnceLock'd and the probes early-return.
findings.rationale: Not a performance problem (verified) but a surface-area one: three naming conventions, two separate caches of the same variable, one undocumented knob, and release notes that point at variables that no longer exist. The ROADMAP asked for a decision two months ago; the cheapest decision is to make the list the code.
findings.proposal: Create `src/env.rs` with `pub const PROFILE: &str = "OXYDLLM_PROFILE"; pub const PROFILE_EVERY: &str = "OXYDLLM_PROFILE_EVERY"; pub const GDN_DEBUG...; pub const DISABLE_MPP...;` plus one `pub fn profile_enabled() -> bool` OnceLock used by both profile.rs and sampling.rs; rename OXYD_PROFILE_EVERY to OXYDLLM_PROFILE_EVERY and add it to README:420; switch sampling.rs:599 to `tracing::info!`; add a `## Renamed` line to CHANGELOG Unreleased for GDN_CHUNK/PROFILE_DECODE. Optionally gate the module behind a `debug-env` cargo feature that is on by default so release builds can opt out.
findings.expected_benefit: One registry to grep, README and code agree, no duplicate OnceLocks, CONTRIBUTING rule honoured.
findings.verify_how: `grep -rn 'env::var("OXYD' src/` lists only src/env.rs after the change; `OXYDLLM_PROFILE=1 oxydllm run <model>` still prints the phase table and the top_p probe lines now arrive via tracing.

findings.title: 101 cfg(feature = "metal") sites follow one copy-pasted pattern that a CPU stub module would delete
findings.evidence: mod.rs:72-73 `#[cfg(feature = "metal")] pub mod metal_ops;`. Count per file: linear.rs 27, gguf_weights.rs 17, attention.rs 16, rope.rs 6, moe.rs 5, loader.rs 4, gdn/ffn/awq 3 each, total 101 (cuda: 2). The pattern, e.g. linear.rs:327-336: `GgufMatmul::Owned(w) => { #[cfg(feature = "metal")] { ... super::metal_ops::mpp_owned_matmul(&x_2d, w)? ... } #[cfg(not(feature = "metal"))] match *w {} }`; linear.rs:120-126 `#[cfg(feature = "metal")] let mm = |x2| match super::metal_ops::maybe_mpp_matmul(x2, weight_t)? {..}; #[cfg(not(feature = "metal"))] let mm = |x2| x2.matmul(weight_t);`; attention.rs:809-850 three pairs of `#[cfg(feature = "metal")] let use_X = ...; #[cfg(not(feature = "metal"))] let use_X = false;` and :853/:868/:896/:917 cfg'd blocks calling metal_ops. The uninhabited `StagedWeight` (linear.rs:18-20) exists only to make `match *w {}` typecheck, and is what made finding 1 trip.
findings.rationale: Each new kernel adds two cfg blocks per call site; the CPU build is correct only because every author remembered the `match *w {}` dance. A CPU `metal_ops` module exposing the same signatures (`maybe_mpp_matmul -> Ok(None)`, `flash_attention_metal_available -> false`, `mpp_owned_matmul -> bail!`) collapses call sites to plain code with no cfg, is optimised out entirely (constant false / None), and keeps the single cfg at the module boundary. A full backend trait is heavier than needed because there is only one accelerated backend; the stub gives the same decoupling at zero dispatch cost.
findings.proposal: Split `metal_ops.rs` into `metal_ops/mod.rs` with `#[cfg(feature = "metal")] mod imp; #[cfg(not(feature = "metal"))] mod stub; pub use ...;` where stub.rs defines every pub fn with the same signature returning `Ok(None)`, `false`, or `candle_core::bail!("Metal only")`, and `StagedWeight` becomes a real (empty-payload) struct in both builds. Then delete the `#[cfg(not(feature = "metal"))]` arms in linear.rs, gguf_weights.rs, attention.rs, rope.rs, moe.rs, ffn.rs, gdn.rs, awq.rs. Do it file by file; the CPU CI job is the regression test.
findings.expected_benefit: Roughly 80 of 101 cfg sites removed; new kernels touch one stub line instead of N call sites; CPU and Metal builds share one control flow, so test-only breakage like finding 1 cannot recur.
findings.verify_how: `grep -rc 'feature = "metal"' src/ | awk -F: '{s+=$2} END{print s}'` drops from 101 to the stub boundary count; `cargo clippy --no-default-features --all-targets -- -D warnings` and the Metal build both pass; stress_baseline.py shows unchanged decode_tps (the stub is never compiled on Metal).

verdict.reason: Counts and pattern verified exactly: `grep -rc 'feature = "metal"' src/` totals 101 (linear.rs 27, gguf_weights.rs 17, attention.rs 16, rope.rs 6, moe.rs 5, loader.rs 4, gdn/ffn/awq 3 each; cuda total 2). linear.rs:327-336 is the `#[cfg(feature = "metal")] { ... mpp_owned_matmul ... } #[cfg(not(feature = "metal"))] match *w {}` shape; linear.rs:128-130 the paired `let mm` closures; attention.rs:809-850 three `let use_X = ...` / `let use_X = false` pairs. The stub-module idea is sound and the 'about 80 of 101' estimate matches the per-file sum (linear 27 + gguf_weights 17 + attention 16 + rope 6 + moe 5 + gdn/ffn/awq 9 = 80); on Metal nothing changes, so no perf or numerics risk. One part of the proposal costs something real: making `StagedWeight` an inhabited empty struct on CPU discards the type-level proof that the CPU build cannot reach an Owned weight (`match *w {}` is a compile-time guarantee; `bail!` is a runtime one) and forces stubs for owned_dims/owned_rows/owned_from_rows (gguf_weights.rs:416/438/459) as well. The cheaper variant keeps the proof.
verdict.corrected_proposal: Create `metal_ops/{mod.rs, imp.rs, stub.rs}` as proposed, but keep `StagedWeight` uninhabited off Metal (move linear.rs:18-20 into stub.rs) and stub only the gate and fusion entry points that call sites test or call unconditionally: `maybe_mpp_matmul`/`maybe_mpp_quant_matmul -> Ok(None)`, `flash_attention_uses_hardware_path`/sdpa gates `-> false`, the eight `*_fused` ops returning the candle fallback the call sites already use, and `mpp_owned_matmul(&Tensor, &StagedWeight) -> Result<Tensor>` whose body is `match *w {}`. That deletes the `let use_X = false` pairs, the `let mm` closure pairs and the cfg'd fused-op calls (attention.rs, rope.rs, ffn.rs, gdn.rs, moe.rs, most of linear.rs) while the handful of `GgufMatmul::Owned`/`LinearWeight::Owned` matches keep their one-line `match *w {}` arm. Do it file by file with the CPU job as the regression test, after finding 1 lands.
verdict.corrected_benefit: Roughly 65-70 of the 101 cfg sites disappear and new fusions touch one stub line; the CPU build keeps its compile-time proof that no Owned weight exists, so the class of error in finding 1 stays a compile error rather than becoming a runtime bail.

findings.title: metal_ops.rs is 8036 lines, 54 percent of it a single test module; split by the seven op families its own header lists
findings.evidence: wc -l: 8036 lines (next largest file is chat.rs at 2970). metal_ops.rs:3713-3714 `#[cfg(test)] mod fused_kernel_parity_tests {` runs to EOF: 4323 lines holding 74 #[test] fns; 43 pub fns and 246 fns total. The module doc (:11-31) already partitions the content: attention (sdpa, flash_attention_metal_prefill, sdpa_vector_sink), elementwise fusions (8 fns), packed-int quant (w4a16/w8a16/gptq + 3 dequantizers), FP8 (3), MXFP4, TensorOps GEMM (mpp_* + gates), plus four include_str! kernel sources at :521, :912, :1561, :2541. 551 unwrap/expect calls live in this file (most in tests).
findings.rationale: Every kernel change recompiles and re-lints an 8k-line unit, test filtering by family needs name conventions, and reviewers cannot see which family a diff touches. The split is mechanical because the doc comment already names the seams and the helpers (`metal_device_or_skip`, `build_awq_triplet`) are shared only by tests.
findings.proposal: `src/common/metal_ops/{mod.rs, attention.rs, fused.rs, packed_quant.rs, fp8.rs, mxfp4.rs, mpp.rs, library.rs (compile/cache + MPP_RUNTIME_BROKEN)}` with `mod.rs` re-exporting the current pub API unchanged, and the test module split alongside (`attention_tests.rs`, ...) sharing one `test_support.rs` holding `metal_device_or_skip` and the AWQ fixture builders (which also lets finding 3's OXYDLLM_REQUIRE_METAL hook live in one place). Pair with finding 12 so the stub module is written against the new layout.
findings.expected_benefit: Smaller review surface per kernel family, faster incremental `cargo check`/`cargo test` on kernel work (only the touched submodule re-parses), and a natural home for the per-family parity tests.
findings.verify_how: `cargo test --release metal_ops::attention` runs only that family; public call sites in linear.rs/attention.rs compile with no path changes; `wc -l src/common/metal_ops/*.rs` shows no file above ~1500 lines.

verdict.reason: Numbers are right: metal_ops.rs is 8036 lines (chat.rs 2970 next), `#[cfg(test)] mod fused_kernel_parity_tests` starts at :3713 and holds all 74 tests to EOF (4323 lines, 54 percent), 45 pub fns, 248 fns, and the module doc at :11-31 does name the seven families. The claimed compile-time benefit is illusory, though: rustc's unit is the crate, incremental compilation is already query/function-granular, and parsing 8k lines is milliseconds, so splitting into submodules does not make `cargo check`/`cargo test` on kernel work measurably faster. What remains is review ergonomics and test filtering, plus git-blame churn on the single most-edited file in a Metal-first engine, which argues for the smallest cut. The cheap 54 percent win is moving the test module out as-is.
verdict.corrected_proposal: Replace lines 3713-8036 with `#[cfg(test)] mod fused_kernel_parity_tests;` and move the body verbatim to `src/common/metal_ops/fused_kernel_parity_tests.rs` (or convert metal_ops.rs to metal_ops/mod.rs with that one submodule), hoisting `metal_device_or_skip` and the AWQ fixture builders into `src/common/test_support.rs` so the 17 other-file `let Ok(dev) = Device::new_metal(0) else` sites can share it (this is the piece finding 3 also needs). Leave the 3.7k non-test lines in one file; split by family only if a second accelerated backend ever appears.
verdict.corrected_benefit: metal_ops.rs drops to about 3700 lines with zero API churn and a one-line diff at the seam; one skip helper for all 75 Metal-gated tests; blame history on the kernel code is preserved.

findings.title: Duplicated helpers: byte-identical clamp_to_char_boundary, two fmt_size with different output, two GGUF header readers that already disagree on v1 files, and a CLI re-implementation of the server's streaming decode
findings.evidence: main.rs:1107-1113 and src/server/routes/engine_loop.rs:383-389 are the same `fn clamp_to_char_boundary(s: &str, idx: usize) -> usize` body. main.rs `fn fmt_size(bytes: usize)` prints `"{:.2} GB"` while src/models/hub.rs `fn fmt_size(bytes: u64)` prints `"{:.2}GB"` (no space), so the same size renders two ways in `list` vs `pull`. src/common/gguf_header.rs:98-170 `struct Cursor` with `fn len()` that reads u32 for `VersionedMagic::GgufV1` and u64 otherwise, MAX_DEPTH 64, MAX_DIMS 4; src/models/gguf_probe.rs:128-172 a second `struct Cursor` whose `string()` always reads `self.u64()` for the length and whose `skip_value` has no depth bound, so the probe mis-parses GGUF v1 headers that GgufHeader::parse handles; the `#[ignore]` test gguf_header.rs probes::the_two_readers_agree_on_every_local_file exists because they can drift. main.rs:1225-1400 (the `run` REPL) re-implements incremental decode: `tokenizer.decode(&output_ids)` then `clamp_to_char_boundary`, `trim_end_matches('\u{FFFD}')`, `hold_back_bytes` from `stop_text_markers()`, `find_first_stop_marker`, thinking split; engine_loop.rs:392-400 `emit_suffix` does the same U+FFFD hold-back for the server.
findings.rationale: Each pair is a place where a fix lands once and the other copy stays wrong: the GGUF v1 divergence is already real (rarely hit, but the probe silently returns Unknown or a wrong verdict for v1 files), and the CLI streaming path will miss any fix to stop-marker or UTF-8 handling made in the server path.
findings.proposal: Move `clamp_to_char_boundary`, `emit_suffix`, `find_first_stop_marker` and the hold-back logic into `src/common/text_stream.rs` (an `IncrementalDecoder { ids, decoded_len }` with `push(token) -> Option<String>`) used by both engine_loop.rs and main.rs; one `fmt_size(u64)` in `src/common/mod.rs`; implement `gguf_probe::inspect_header` on top of `GgufHeader::parse(&bytes)` mapping `Err` to `HeaderVerdict::Unknown` and iterating `header.tensors` for the SUPPORTED_TYPES check, then delete the second Cursor and un-ignore the agreement test as a fixture-based unit test.
findings.expected_benefit: One implementation each for UTF-8 safe streaming, size formatting and GGUF header parsing; the v1 divergence disappears; the CLI inherits every server-side streaming fix.
findings.verify_how: After the refactor `grep -rn 'fn clamp_to_char_boundary\|fn fmt_size\|struct Cursor' src/` shows one hit each; http_compat_tests streaming tests stay green; `oxydllm run <model>` output for a prompt ending mid-multibyte-character matches `/v1/chat/completions` stream output byte for byte; run the un-ignored two-readers test over ~/.oxydllm/models.

verdict.reason: Each duplicate exists: `clamp_to_char_boundary` is byte-identical at main.rs:1107-1113 and engine_loop.rs:382-388; main.rs:1027-1034 `fmt_size(usize)` prints `"{:.2} GB"` while hub.rs:859-868 `fmt_size(u64)` prints `"{:.2}GB"` and hub.rs:874-882 adds a third `fmt_size_f` with `"{:.2} GB"` (so three formatters, not two); gguf_probe.rs:147-150 `fn string(&mut self) { let n = self.u64()? ... }` and :183 `(c.u32(), c.u64(), c.u64())` read v2+ widths unconditionally while gguf_header.rs:134-136 switches on `VersionedMagic::GgufV1 => u64::from(self.u32()?)`; the agreement test is `#[ignore]` at gguf_header.rs:486-488. But the consequences are smaller than claimed. The v1 divergence is harmless by design: gguf_probe.rs:15 documents that the probe fails open ('Unknown so a download proceeds'), a v1 header's u32 counts read as u64 are garbage that the bounds checks turn into `HeaderVerdict::Unknown` (:181-217), and GGUF v1 files are practically extinct; `skip_value` needs no depth bound because every nesting level consumes at least 12 bytes of a range-bounded buffer. The CLI/server streaming paths are also not the same algorithm: engine_loop.rs:394-402 `emit_suffix` only holds back U+FFFD, the server's stop handling is the separate stable-prefix machinery at :426-449, while main.rs:1226 derives `hold_back_bytes` from `stop_text_markers()` and :1357-1380 does marker search and flush itself; a shared `IncrementalDecoder` can therefore carry only the char-boundary and U+FFFD hold-back (about 15 lines), so 'the CLI inherits every server-side streaming fix' overstates it.
verdict.corrected_proposal: Move `clamp_to_char_boundary` and `emit_suffix` (the U+FFFD hold-back) into `src/common/text_stream.rs` and call them from main.rs:1330/1345-1347/1358/1377/1399 and engine_loop.rs:395/836; keep one `fmt_size(u64)` in src/common (pick the spaced form, update the hub.rs:1110-1115 test) and delete main.rs:1027 and hub.rs:874. Leave the two GGUF readers as they are: the probe is a deliberately lenient pre-download sniff that must never block, the header reader is the strict loader; at most add a one-line comment at gguf_probe.rs:147 saying v1 lengths are not handled and fall through to Unknown. Do not promise a shared stop-marker path until the two policies are deliberately unified.
verdict.corrected_benefit: One UTF-8 streaming helper and one size formatter, consistent `list`/`pull`/`estimate` output; no behaviour change on either streaming path and no risk to the fail-open download gate.

findings.title: All 396 tests live in one bin-crate test binary: no lib target, no tests/ directory, integration suites rebuilt with every unit test
findings.evidence: Cargo.toml:12-14 declares only `[[bin]] name = "oxydllm" path = "src/main.rs"`; no `[lib]`. test_cpu.log:231 `Running unittests src/main.rs (target/debug/deps/oxydllm-f658793048806418)` is the only test binary; `ls tests` -> no such directory. routes/mod.rs:5-6 `#[cfg(test)] mod http_compat_tests;` (1672 lines, 46 #[tokio::test] HTTP-level tests through tower::oneshot) and src/models/arch_regression.rs (798 lines, `#[cfg(test)] mod tests`) are integration-style suites compiled into the unit test binary; 66 `#[cfg(test)]` modules in 55 files; the hook (pre-push:5) and CI (ci.yml CUDA job) select suites by name prefix (`arch_ edge_`).
findings.rationale: With a single bin target every test run links the full 50k-line crate plus every test module, `cargo test --lib` / `--test <name>` partitioning is impossible, doc-tests cannot run, benches cannot link the crate, and suite selection depends on naming discipline (`arch_`, `edge_`, `metal_`). A `src/lib.rs` that `pub mod`s the existing modules with a 30-line `main.rs` calling `oxydllm::cli::main()` unlocks `tests/http_compat.rs`, `tests/arch_regression.rs`, `benches/`, and `cargo doc`.
findings.proposal: Add `src/lib.rs` re-exporting the current module tree (`pub mod common; pub mod models; pub mod server; ...`), shrink main.rs to argument parsing + `oxydllm::run(args)`, move http_compat_tests.rs to `tests/http_compat.rs` and arch_regression.rs to `tests/arch_regression.rs` (they already use only pub paths or can via `pub(crate)` -> `pub` on a handful of items), and change pre-push/CI to `cargo test --test arch_regression`. CONTRIBUTING's existing `cargo test --test arch_regression` line then becomes true.
findings.expected_benefit: Selective test runs (`cargo test --lib` for the 3.9 s unit set, `--test http_compat` for the HTTP suite), parallel test binaries, criterion benches for the sampling/scheduler hot paths, and rustdoc for the crate.
findings.verify_how: `cargo test --test arch_regression` lists 18 tests; `cargo test --lib` finishes faster than the current single-binary run; `cargo doc --no-deps` succeeds.

findings.title: No automated dependency updates; cargo audit failing CI is the first and only signal for advisories
findings.evidence: .github/ contains ISSUE_TEMPLATE, PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md, res/, workflows/ and nothing else (no dependabot.yml or renovate.json). pre-commit:11 `cargo audit` and ci.yml audit job `run: cargo audit` are the only dependency checks. CHANGELOG alpha.13 line 102: 'Security and unsoundness bumps: crossbeam-epoch 0.9.20 (RUSTSEC-2026-0204, also failing CI's cargo audit), quinn-proto (RUSTSEC-2026-0185), and anyhow/memmap2/rand advisories' — i.e. the advisory broke every PR's CI until a manual bump landed. Cargo.lock holds 410 packages with 4 windows-sys, 3 hashbrown, 3 getrandom, 2 thiserror, 2 base64 (0.13.1 from 2021) versions.
findings.rationale: A published advisory currently turns every open PR red (audit is in ci-ok's needs) until the maintainer hand-bumps; a scheduled lockfile PR converts that into a reviewable diff that usually lands before the advisory, and keeps the duplicate-version count from growing.
findings.proposal: Add `.github/dependabot.yml` with `package-ecosystem: cargo`, weekly schedule, `groups: { minor-and-patch: { update-types: [minor, patch] } }`, plus `package-ecosystem: github-actions` for the pinned `@v6/@v7/@v8` actions; keep cargo audit as the gate. Optionally make the audit job `continue-on-error` with a separate scheduled audit that opens an issue, so an upstream advisory does not block unrelated PRs for hours.
