findings.expected_benefit: Advisories arrive as PRs instead of CI outages; actions and lockfile drift are reviewed in small weekly diffs.
findings.verify_how: After adding the file, the Dependabot tab shows cargo and github-actions jobs; the first grouped PR should bump the oldest transitive crates (base64 0.13 via spm_precompiled is upstream-pinned and will be skipped, which is fine).

subsystems.coverage_notes: Read in full: Cargo.toml, build.rs, all five workflows, both git hooks, CONTRIBUTING.md, Dockerfile, Dockerfile.cpu, .dockerignore, docker-compose.yml, rust-toolchain.toml, the CPU clippy and test logs, the ROADMAP sections the task named plus Exit-from-alpha, Performance backlog, Parked and Known suspicions. Skimmed only: install.sh (header, service/build greps), scripts/stress_baseline.py (docstring and argparse), src/models/arch_regression.rs (header and test list), CHANGELOG.md (headings and build/CI-related lines of the top sections). Source files were opened at the specific ranges quoted in the findings (gguf_weights.rs 700-900, linear.rs 1-140 and 320-345, attention.rs cfg sites, metal_ops.rs header/2560-2610/3713-3722, profile.rs, gdn.rs 30-60, sampling.rs 575-600, telemetry.rs 1-120, main.rs 425-460/530-548/1107-1130/1215-1240/1322-1350/1555-1575, loader.rs 695-715, encoder.rs 520-555, manager.rs 955-1050, gguf_probe.rs 1-30/95-230, gguf_header.rs 1-25/95-200, hub.rs/estimate.rs/chat.rs/engine_loop.rs via grep only). Not done: no cargo invocations (per instructions), so the Metal-feature `clippy --all-targets` result and the fat-LTO A/B are unmeasured; did not fetch GitHub Actions logs to check whether the macos-26 runner actually exposes a Metal device (finding 3 is written to hold either way); did not read objc2-metal's target gating to prove the Metal default cannot build on Linux (inferred from CI always passing --no-default-features on Linux); did not read the four non-ROADMAP design notes beyond a grep for lto/codegen/panic; did not audit every unwrap/expect in chat.rs handlers beyond the serde_json::to_string and handle-take sites listed (all invariant-protected); did not inspect install.sh's download/verification logic or the full release-body templates for correctness.
missed: The CI matrix compiles every test binary with the shipped binary's profile. Cargo.toml:55-58 sets `[profile.release] opt-level = 3, lto = \"thin\", codegen-units = 1`, and every job runs `cargo test --release` (ci.yml:106, :132, :161, :223) with no `CARGO_PROFILE_*` or `RUSTFLAGS` override anywhere in .github/workflows (grep is empty). Since Cargo 1.57 `cargo test --release` uses the release profile for the test executable, so each of the eight jobs codegens the 56k-line crate twice (bin plus test harness) through a single codegen unit followed by a thin-LTO step that has one unit to work on, i.e. serial LLVM on the hottest part of the build while Swatinem's cache covers only dependencies. codegen-units = 1 is the right choice for the distributed binary (build.yml) but buys nothing for a test run, and Rust's float codegen is IEEE-strict regardless of LTO or unit count, so the kernel-parity tolerances are unaffected. Add `[profile.ci] inherits = \"release\" codegen-units = 16 lto = false` (or export `CARGO_PROFILE_RELEASE_CODEGEN_UNITS=16 CARGO_PROFILE_RELEASE_LTO=off` in ci.yml's env) and use `--profile ci` in the four test steps; keep build.yml untouched. I could not measure the saving from this machine (no cargo runs allowed), so verify by comparing the 'Unit tests' step wall time in the Actions tab before and after; the expectation from the profile shape is minutes per job on the macOS and arm64 runners, which are the slowest and most quota-limited.

subsystems.assessment: The single-model request/decode path is clean from a locking standpoint: one OS thread per model owns the Engine, the scheduler, the KV caches and the trackers, so there is no Arc<Mutex> clone, no cross-thread Tensor drop and no tokio mutex on the per-token path; the only lock on the hot path is the per-device gpu_lock around engine.step() plus roughly 300 uncontended std::Mutex acquisitions per step from the OnceLock pipeline caches (about 8-10 per layer), which is well under 0.1 percent of a step and not a lever. The request channel is bounded with 429 on overflow, the response channel is unbounded but guarded by is_closed() disconnect detection, and the candle 0.11 Metal mitigations are still necessary: candle-core 0.11.0's device.rs inserts into the residency set under two different RwLocks (private_buffers in new_buffer, buffers in allocate_buffer/new_buffer_with_data) and synchronize() is wait_until_completed() on a shared Arc<Commands>, so the hazards the CHANGELOG describes are real on this exact version. What is fragile is everything that touches the device from a thread other than the engine thread, which is exactly the multi-model story the server advertises (on-demand loads, keep-alive and LRU eviction): metal_alloc_lock only serializes the loader's own rayon workers, while phase-2 uploads, loader drains, GGUF parallel uploads and the final Engine drop all run outside gpu_lock and can overlap another model's decode. The Unreleased drop guard (EngineSlotGuard) holds a Sender clone for the life of the loop, so an idle engine blocked in blocking_recv never sees the shutdown flag: keep-alive and LRU eviction now leak the model and a later request double-loads it, and even for a busy engine the eviction is fire-and-forget (budget released and slot removed before anything is dropped, with Metal buffers reclaimed only at some later sync by whichever thread happens to synchronize). The biggest lever is therefore not throughput but correctness and memory on that path: fix the guard, make eviction acknowledged, and put the device-touching half of a load and the Engine drop under gpu_lock. Secondary headroom is at load time, where the FP8 scale fold runs single-threaded after the parallel phase and same-dtype tensors are copied twice. Finally, the gpu_lock.rs header's claim that scheduling and sampling happen outside the lock is false today; with two models on one device the whole step, including CPU sampling, KV-quant packing and streamed-expert SSD reads, is serialized.

findings.title: EngineSlotGuard keeps a request Sender alive, so an idle engine never exits on eviction (model leaks, later request double-loads)
findings.evidence: manager.rs:1184 `let engine_tx = request_tx.clone();` ... :1257-1261 `let _slot_guard = EngineSlotGuard { manager: manager_thread, model_id: model_id_thread.clone(), request_tx: engine_tx, }; engine_loop(engine, tokenizer, request_rx, shutdown, model_id_thread);` — the guard (and its Sender) lives on the engine thread for the whole loop. engine_loop.rs:640 `if shutdown.load(Ordering::Acquire) { break; }` is only reached at the top of an iteration; when idle the loop sits in :656 `match request_rx.blocking_recv() { Some(req) => ..., None => break }`. Eviction (manager.rs:570-573 and :702-705) only does `self.slots.remove(&id); ... s.store(true, Ordering::Release);` — it drops the slot's Sender but the guard's clone keeps the channel open, so blocking_recv never returns None and the flag is never read.
findings.rationale: An evicted model is by definition idle (keep-alive expiry) or at least usually idle (LRU), i.e. blocked in blocking_recv with no remaining sender other than the guard's. Nothing ever sends on that channel again (the slot is gone, so get_or_load spawns a fresh load with a new channel). The engine thread, its weights and its KV pool therefore stay resident forever while kv_budget has already been released and a second copy may be loading. On a 24 GB M5 this defeats the Unreleased 'loading a model that does not fit now evicts idle ones' feature and can double-commit unified memory, the silent-corruption class the ROADMAP calls D1. The only test (engine_panic_removes_stale_slot) exercises the panic path, not shutdown.
findings.proposal: Do not store a strong Sender in the guard. Either (a) store `request_tx.downgrade()` (tokio WeakSender) and in Drop do `self.weak.upgrade().is_some_and(|s| slot_tx.same_channel(&s))`, or (b) store the `Arc<AtomicBool>` shutdown and compare `Arc::ptr_eq(&slot.shutdown, &self.shutdown)`. Additionally make eviction wake the loop explicitly: replace the AtomicBool with a `tokio::sync::Notify`/`watch` or simply have the loop use `request_rx.blocking_recv()` only while `!shutdown`, with eviction also dropping every Sender (which (a)/(b) achieves).
findings.expected_benefit: Restores keep-alive and LRU eviction: evicted models actually free their weights and KV pool; no double residency after eviction + reload. Memory effect equals the full size of every evicted model (GBs).
findings.verify_how: Load a model, let keep-alive expire (or trigger LRU by loading a second model), then check `ps`/Activity Monitor RSS and `GET /v1/models/running`; today RSS does not drop and a thread dump shows the engine thread parked in blocking_recv. After the fix RSS drops and the thread exits; add the test from finding 9.

verdict.reason: Verified in code. manager.rs:1184 `let engine_tx = request_tx.clone();` and :1256-1261 build `EngineSlotGuard { request_tx: engine_tx, .. }` on the engine thread, and the guard outlives `engine_loop` (it is declared before the call and dropped after it returns). The only consumer of `shutdown` is engine_loop.rs:640-642 at the top of an iteration; when the engine has no pending work the loop parks in :656 `request_rx.blocking_recv()`, which returns `None` only when every `Sender` is gone. All three eviction paths (manager.rs:570-573 LRU, :702-705 keep-alive, :1342-1346 post-load over-budget) do exactly `kv_budget.release`, `slots.remove`, `store(true)`: the slot's Sender is dropped but the guard's clone keeps the channel open, nothing ever sends on it again (a reload creates a new channel at :1183), so an idle evicted engine never wakes, never reads the flag, and its weights, KV pool and the whole per-model MetalDevice stay resident. The guard shipped in alpha.15 (CHANGELOG 'A panicking engine loop no longer leaves a model permanently unusable') and the Unreleased 'loading a model that does not fit now evicts idle ones' feature depends on the broken path, so this is a real high-severity leak on the headline feature. The proposal is sound and S: storing `Arc<AtomicBool>` and comparing `Arc::ptr_eq(&slot.shutdown, &self.shutdown)` is the smallest fix (no channel involvement); `tokio::sync::mpsc::WeakSender` + `same_channel` also works. No `Notify` is needed: once the guard holds no Sender, dropping the slot's Sender makes `blocking_recv` return `None` for an idle loop, and a busy loop already sees the flag at :640. Note `evict_expired_removes_idle_slot` (:1681) cannot catch this because it never runs a loop (see finding 9).

findings.title: Eviction is fire-and-forget: KV budget released and slot removed before the engine drops anything, and freed Metal buffers are only reclaimed at the next sync by whichever thread syncs
findings.evidence: manager.rs:570-573 `self.kv_budget.release(kv_bytes); self.slots.remove(&id); if let Some(s) = shutdown { s.store(true, Ordering::Release); }` then get_or_load immediately continues (:598-620) to `spawn_load(...)`. The engine only notices at engine_loop.rs:640 after finishing its current step, then drops `engine` at the end of `engine_loop` (:992-1003) with no drain and no lock. candle-core 0.11.0 metal_backend/device.rs:130-150 `drop_unused_buffers` runs only from `wait_until_completed`/`flush_and_wait_current`, so a dropped Tensor's MTLBuffer is kept in the pool (strong_count 1) until some thread synchronizes the device.
findings.rationale: The new load's phase 1 (rayon, host RAM) and phase 2 (device uploads) start while the old model is still fully resident; the KV budget is handed to the new model before the old pool is gone. On unified memory this is a transient over-commit of up to one full model, exactly the regime in which the maintainer measured silent weight corruption (loader.rs:858-921 fingerprint retry exists because of it). Even after the drop, the buffers are only returned when another thread syncs; if no model remains loaded, nothing syncs and the memory stays allocated.
findings.proposal: Make eviction acknowledged: give each slot a `std::sync::mpsc::Receiver<()>`/`oneshot` (or keep the thread's JoinHandle) that the engine thread signals after `drop(engine)`; in get_or_load/evict_lru_for_bytes wait for that signal (tokio spawn_blocking join with a bounded timeout) before releasing kv_budget and spawning the load. On the engine thread, end `engine_loop` with `{ let _g = gpu_lock.acquire(); drop(engine); let _ = device.synchronize(); }` so buffers are reclaimed immediately and under the device lock (see finding 3).
findings.expected_benefit: Removes the double-residency window during evict+load (up to one model size of unified memory), makes 'evict to make room' actually make room before the room is used, and prevents the fingerprint-retry path from firing spuriously because of a not-yet-dropped predecessor.
findings.verify_how: With two models whose sum exceeds the budget, request B while A is resident; log timestamps of 'evicting LRU model', the old engine's drop, and the new load's first device upload; today the upload precedes the drop. Watch peak memory with `vm_stat`/`footprint` on the M5.

verdict.reason: The ordering claim is accurate (manager.rs:570-573 releases kv_budget and removes the slot before anything is dropped; the Engine is dropped only when `engine_loop` returns at engine_loop.rs:1003 with no drain), but two parts are wrong and the severity collapses once finding 1 is fixed. (1) Today the 'window' is unbounded only because of finding 1 (the idle engine never exits); that is finding 1, not a second defect. After the guard fix an idle loop exits as soon as the slot's Sender drops (the `blocking_recv` returns `None`), and a busy loop exits at the end of its current step (tens of ms for decode, up to ~1 s for a 4096-token prefill chunk), while the new load's device uploads start only after its tokenizer load and the whole CPU phase 1 (weights.rs:365-388, seconds). The uploads practically never precede the drop; what overlaps is phase 1's anonymous host memory with A's last step. (2) 'Buffers are only reclaimed when another thread syncs; if no model remains loaded nothing syncs' is false here: every load calls `loader::select_device_at` (manager.rs:1053) which does `Device::new_metal(0)` (loader.rs:745), and candle 0.11 `MetalDevice::new` (metal_backend/mod.rs:2026-2053) creates a fresh command queue, `buffers`/`private_buffers` maps and `ResidencySet` per call. The Engine holds the last clones of that device, so dropping it drops the `Arc<RwLock<BufferMap>>` and releases every MTLBuffer with no synchronize at all; no other thread can sync that device. So the proposed `{ gpu_lock; drop(engine); device.synchronize() }` tail is unnecessary.
verdict.corrected_benefit: Bounds the evict-then-load overlap to zero instead of one engine step; mainly makes the sequence observable and testable (log/ack), not a memory win of 'one model size'.
verdict.corrected_proposal: Keep the engine thread's `JoinHandle` (or a `std::sync::mpsc::SyncSender<()>` signalled right after `engine_loop` returns) in `SlotState::Ready`; on eviction hand the handle(s) to the spawned load thread (never block the manager under its tokio Mutex) and have that thread join them with a bounded timeout before phase 1 begins. Do not add gpu_lock or a synchronize around the drop: the model owns its MetalDevice. Fix finding 1 first; this is a follow-up.

findings.title: Model-load device work (phase-2 uploads, GGUF parallel uploads, loader drains) and the Engine drop run outside gpu_lock, racing another model's decode on the same device
findings.evidence: weights.rs:392-403 phase 2: `let dev_t = cpu_t.to_device(device)...; if i % 16 == 15 { drain_metal(device, name)?; } } drain_metal(device, "post-load")?;` — no gpu_lock anywhere in `ModelWeights::load`; gpu_lock is acquired only in warm_up_model (manager.rs:847-848), engine_loop.rs:686 and embeddings.rs:59. gguf_weights.rs:655-660 and :700-701 create device tensors from rayon workers under `metal_alloc_lock` only. loader.rs:858 `drain_metal(device, "model load")` and :921 fingerprint drain also run unlocked. candle-core 0.11.0 device.rs: `new_buffer` (op outputs) inserts into `residency_set` under `private_buffers.write()` (:205-229) while `new_buffer_with_data` (to_device) inserts under `buffers.write()` (:251-266) — two different locks, so a loader upload and a decoding engine's output allocation insert concurrently; `synchronize()` (mod.rs:2368) is `wait_until_completed()` on the shared `Arc<Commands>` (device.rs:41), i.e. a cross-thread drain while the engine thread encodes.
findings.rationale: The CHANGELOG alpha.13 entry documents exactly these two candle 0.11 hazards (unsynchronized MTLResidencySet mutation -> GPU reads zeros; synchronizing from one thread while another encodes -> corrupted state) and fixes them for the loader's own rayon threads via metal_alloc_lock. metal_alloc_lock is not taken by the engine's forward (it cannot be: every op allocates), so the protection does not extend to 'model B loads while model A decodes', which is the normal on-demand multi-model flow. The comment at engine_loop.rs:17-20 claims the gpu lock serializes 'the forward pass against concurrent model loads' — it does not, because the loader never takes it.
findings.proposal: Acquire `gpu_lock_for(device)` around every device-touching section of a load: in `ModelWeights::load` wrap phase 2 (optionally per 16-tensor chunk so a concurrent engine gets a step between chunks), wrap `parallelise_tensor_load` for GGUF, wrap the loader's KV-pool allocation + drain + fingerprint check (loader.rs:840-925) and the draft load, and take the lock around `drop(engine)` at the end of engine_loop (finding 2). Keep metal_alloc_lock for intra-load rayon serialization. Document the invariant once in gpu_lock.rs: 'any thread that creates, drops or synchronizes Metal resources on a device holds its GpuLock'.
findings.expected_benefit: Closes the only remaining path on which the documented candle 0.11 corruption can occur in production (multi-model). Cost: a concurrently served model pauses for the device phase of a load (seconds), which is the correct trade versus silent zeros in weights.
findings.verify_how: On the M5: serve model A under a continuous decode loop, trigger a load of model B (BF16 safetensors and a GGUF), compare A's outputs to a single-model reference and run B's weight fingerprint check; repeat 20x. With the locks the run is byte-stable; without, the CHANGELOG's own symptom (zeroed buffers / NaN) is expected intermittently.

verdict.reason: The lock-absence is accurate (grep: `gpu_lock` is acquired only at engine_loop.rs:686, embeddings.rs:59 and manager.rs:847-848; weights.rs:390-403, gguf_weights.rs:560-567/655-660/700-701 and loader.rs:858-925 never take it), but the claimed mechanism does not exist because models do not share a candle device. Each load thread calls `loader::select_device_at` (manager.rs:1053), which calls `Device::new_metal(0)` (loader.rs:745); candle 0.11 `MetalDevice::new` (metal_backend/mod.rs:2026-2053) builds a new `command_queue`, a new `Commands`, new `buffers`/`private_buffers` RwLocks and a new `ResidencySet::new(&device)` on every call. So model B's `new_buffer_with_data` inserts into B's residency set under B's lock (device.rs:253-266), B's `drain_metal` -> `synchronize()` -> `wait_until_completed()` (mod.rs:2368, device.rs:170-176) waits on B's own queue, and A's engine encodes into A's `Commands`; the 'shared Arc<Commands>' and 'two different locks on one residency set' hazards are intra-device, exactly what `metal_alloc_lock` already covers for a load's own rayon workers. The only state shared across devices in this subsystem is oxydllm's pipeline caches, keyed by `registry_id` under a Mutex (metal_ops.rs:524-561, :916, :1587), which is thread-safe. Taking gpu_lock around phase 2 would pause a served model for the seconds of another model's uploads to defend against a hazard with no mechanism and no repro, contrary to the maintainer's measure-first rule. What is true is that the comment at engine_loop.rs:17-20 and :582-585 overstates the lock as serializing 'the forward pass against concurrent model loads'; gpu_lock.rs:5-7 gives its real purpose (GPU contention between engine loops). That is a one-line doc fix, not a correctness finding.

findings.title: gpu_lock covers the entire engine.step() including CPU sampling, KV-quant packing and streamed-expert SSD reads; gpu_lock.rs documents the opposite
findings.evidence: engine_loop.rs:685-688 `let step_result = { let _gpu = gpu_lock.acquire(); engine.step() };`. engine.rs:996-1115 `step()` does `scheduler.schedule(...)`, `plan_prefill_inputs`, `run_forward_pass` (which calls into MoE layers that invoke `StreamedExperts::fetch_many` -> expert_stream.rs:254-310 pread + rayon build + graveyard drain), then `sample_prefill_outputs` / `sample_decode_outputs` (CPU), then `run_speculative_decode`, all before returning. gpu_lock.rs:16-17 says `Scheduling and sampling happen **outside** the lock, so the only serialised portion is the actual GPU compute.`
findings.rationale: With one model per device this is harmless. With two models on one device (the multi-model feature) model B's step waits for A's CPU-only tail: top-k/top-p sampling over vocab-size logits per sequence, grammar masks, KV packing on the CPU, and on streamed MoE models the SSD miss fetch (hundreds of ms per batch of misses). The GPU is idle during all of that, so aggregate throughput of two co-resident models is bounded by the sum of their CPU tails instead of overlapping them. The header comment is stale and misleads anyone reasoning about lock scope.
findings.proposal: Short term (S): fix the gpu_lock.rs header to state the actual contract. Medium term (M): split `Engine::step` into `forward(&mut self) -> Logits` (GPU + readback, under the lock) and `finish(&mut self, logits)` (sampling, retire, prefix-cache bookkeeping, outside the lock), and in engine_loop hold `_gpu` only across `forward`. Expert fetches remain under the lock because they create device buffers (finding 3), but their read-side (pread into host memory) could be hoisted before taking the lock once the router decision is known.
findings.expected_benefit: Only for multiple models on one device: overlap of model A's sampling/KV-pack CPU time with model B's GPU time; the gain equals the CPU tail fraction of a step (several percent for high-concurrency sampling, far more on streamed MoE where SSD misses dominate).
findings.verify_how: Serve two small models on the M5 with concurrent clients; measure aggregate tok/s before/after. Use OXYDLLM_PROFILE=1 (profile.rs) to size the sampling tail vs forward.

verdict.reason: Mechanism verified: engine_loop.rs:685-688 holds `_gpu` across `engine.step()`, and engine.rs:996-1115 runs `scheduler.schedule` (:1012), `plan_prefill_inputs`/`build_batch_input` (:1038-1039), `run_forward_pass` (:1056), CPU `sample_prefill_outputs`/`sample_decode_outputs` (:1070-1085), `run_speculative_decode` (:1091-1099) and `retire_finished` (:1102) inside it; gpu_lock.rs:16-17 states the opposite. Worth is small: it only matters when two models are both actively decoding on the same M5 at once, which the Unreleased LRU eviction makes rare (a second model that does not fit evicts the first), and since every model owns its own MetalDevice/command queue (manager.rs:1053 -> loader.rs:745) the lock is purely a contention policy that gpu_lock.rs:5-7 asserts without a measurement in the ROADMAP. The split-step refactor (M) is therefore premature; the cheapest experiment is to measure two small co-served models with the lock scope unchanged vs removed before designing a split.
verdict.corrected_benefit: Accurate lock documentation now; a multi-model overlap win (sampling tail, roughly 5-20% of a decode step at 8 sequences) only if co-serving on one device becomes a measured use case.
verdict.corrected_proposal: Rewrite gpu_lock.rs:16-17 and engine_loop.rs:17-20/:582-585 to say the lock covers the whole `Engine::step` (scheduling, forward, CPU sampling, speculative decode) and exists for submission contention between engine loops on one physical GPU, not for candle-state safety across models. Defer the forward/finish split until an A/B of two co-served models with and without the lock shows the lock itself is the bottleneck.

findings.title: Decode-path expert streaming shares the global rayon pool with model loads, so a concurrent load stalls streamed decode
findings.evidence: expert_stream.rs:384-388 `let reads: Vec<(usize, RawRead)> = flat.par_iter().map(|(slot, name, row)| Ok((*slot, self.read_one(name, *row)?))).collect()` and :272-282 `misses.par_iter().zip(reads.into_par_iter()).map(|(&e, tensors)| ... build_standard / build_gpt_oss ...)` run on the default global pool from the engine thread, inside `fetch_many` (:254 holds `self.state` for the whole call). weights.rs:365-380 `names.par_iter().map(|name| load_tensor_with_dtype(...))` and gguf_weights.rs:560-567 `infos.par_iter().map(|entry| build_tensor(...))` use the same global pool for thousands of CPU-heavy tasks.
findings.rationale: Rayon workers prefer their local deques and steal from peers before draining the global injector, so a par_iter injected from the engine thread while a load's thousands of tasks are in flight waits until those are nearly done. For a streamed MoE model (gpt-oss-20b, Qwen3.6-35B-FP8) a per-step miss batch that normally takes tens of ms can be delayed by the whole phase-1 of another model's load (seconds), and the engine thread is blocked inside `par_iter().collect()` for that time while holding gpu_lock. `fetch_many` also holds the LRU `state` mutex across the blocking IO and the rayon join, which is harmless today (single caller) but is a latent serialization point if a prefetcher ever appears.
findings.proposal: Give `StreamedExperts` its own `rayon::ThreadPool` (e.g. `ThreadPoolBuilder::new().num_threads(available_parallelism/2).thread_name(..).build()`) stored in the struct and run `read_misses`/build via `self.pool.install(|| ...)`. Optionally move the loaders to a separate low-priority pool as well. Release `state` before the reads and re-acquire for insertion (misses are computed under the lock, inserted after).
findings.expected_benefit: Streamed decode latency becomes independent of concurrent loads; removes multi-second stalls while another model loads. No single-model effect.
findings.verify_how: Serve gpt-oss-20b streamed, run a decode client, trigger a load of a 4B BF16 model; plot per-token latency around the load. Expect a multi-second gap today, none with a dedicated pool.

verdict.reason: Mechanism verified: there is no `ThreadPoolBuilder` or `.install(` anywhere in src (grep), so `read_misses` (expert_stream.rs:384-387 `flat.par_iter()`) and the build (:272-282 `misses.par_iter().zip(reads.into_par_iter())`) run on the global pool from the engine thread while `fetch_many` holds `self.state` (:254) and the caller holds gpu_lock; loader phase 1 (weights.rs:365-383) and GGUF (gguf_weights.rs:560-567) flood the same pool, and rayon services injected jobs only after local and stolen work, so the miss batch waits. The scenario is narrower than claimed: a streamed MoE model is by definition one that does not fit resident, and its reported footprint is resident bytes plus the cache budget sized to what remains (CHANGELOG alpha.14), so a concurrent second-model load on the same 24 GB box triggers `evict_lru_for_bytes` (manager.rs:538-573) against the streamed model (it has the oldest `last_used`, see 'missed') rather than co-existing with it. The stall only appears when two models genuinely fit together, which on the M5 means a small dense model loading beside a streamed MoE with a tiny cache. Holding `state` across the IO is harmless today (single caller) and releasing it, as proposed, would open a duplicate-fetch race if a second caller ever appeared; leave it.
verdict.corrected_benefit: Streamed miss latency independent of concurrent CPU-heavy loads in the rare co-resident case; no single-model effect.
verdict.corrected_proposal: Give `StreamedExperts` its own `rayon::ThreadPool` (built once in `new`, sized to available_parallelism) and wrap `read_misses` and the build in `self.pool.install(..)`; keep `state` held as today. Do this after finding 1 and after eviction becomes in-flight-aware, which are the fixes that actually decide what happens when a second model is requested.

findings.title: apply_weight_scale_inv is a single-threaded F32 pass over every scaled weight, run after the parallel phase
findings.evidence: weights.rs:246-293 `fn apply_weight_scale_inv(tensors: &mut FxHashMap<String, Tensor>)` ... `for weight_name in weight_names { ... let weight_f32 = weight.to_dtype(DType::F32)...; let scaled_f32 = apply_scale_inv(&weight_f32, &scale_inv_f32)...; let scaled = scaled_f32.to_dtype(weight_dtype)...; tensors.insert(weight_name, scaled); }` — a plain sequential loop called at :386 after the `par_iter` phase (:365) and before phase 2. On Metal, phase 1 passes `preserve_fp8_weight && !device.is_metal()` = false (:374), so FP8 weights are already BF16 here and each one is promoted to F32, multiplied by the tiled scale grid (`broadcast_as(...).contiguous()` materializes a full F32 scale tensor per weight) and cast back, on one core.
findings.rationale: For an FP8 checkpoint (Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507-FP8, Qwen3.6-35B-FP8 non-expert weights) every projection does three full-size passes (BF16->F32, F32 mul with a materialized F32 scale, F32->BF16) of host memory traffic on a single thread: roughly 16 bytes read+written per parameter, i.e. tens of GB of traffic for a 4B model at single-core bandwidth, several seconds of pure serial time inside a load that is otherwise parallel. The per-tensor rayon closure already has the mmap and the name of the scale companion.
findings.proposal: Fold the scale inside the phase-1 closure: when `scale_inv_names.contains(&format!("{name}_scale_inv"))`, load the scale from the mmap in the same task, do the F32 multiply there (keeping the F32 promote-and-cast chain bit-for-bit identical so the byte-identity contract with expert_stream.rs holds), and skip the post-pass. Keep `apply_weight_scale_inv` only for the CPU/CUDA `preserve_fp8_weight` case or delete it.
findings.expected_benefit: FP8 safetensors load time drops by the whole serial fold (parallel speedup ~ number of performance cores for that phase, several seconds on a 4B model, proportionally more on larger checkpoints).
findings.verify_how: Time `ModelWeights::load` (log at the 'model loaded' line) for Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507-FP8 before/after; confirm byte identity of the first-forward fingerprint (loader.rs weight_fingerprint) and of the streamed-vs-resident expert test.

verdict.reason: Verified. weights.rs:246-293 is a plain `for weight_name in weight_names` loop called at :388 after the parallel phase 1 and before phase 2; per weight it does `to_dtype(F32)` (:267), `apply_scale_inv` (:280), which for block-wise grids materializes a full-size F32 scale tensor via `broadcast_as(..).contiguous()` (:230-233), and `to_dtype(weight_dtype)` (:284); candle's CPU unary/binary ops are single-threaded, so this is one core moving roughly 28 bytes per parameter (2r+4w promote, 4w tile, 8r+4w mul, 4r+2w cast). On Metal phase 1 passes `preserve_fp8_weight && !device.is_metal()` = false (:374), so FP8 weights have already been dequantized to BF16 in parallel and are promoted a second time here. The scale tensor is loaded in the same `par_iter` with `force_f32` (:369), and `scale_inv_names` is already computed (:334-338), so folding inside the closure is straightforward: load the companion scale from the mmap in the same task and run the identical BF16 -> F32 -> `apply_scale_inv` -> BF16 chain, which keeps the bytes identical to today's output and to the contract documented at expert_stream.rs:13-20. Keep `apply_weight_scale_inv` for the CPU/CUDA `preserve_fp8_weight` path and its tests (:600-720). Effort S, benefit a few seconds of serial time per FP8 load on a 4B model (tens of GB of single-core traffic), more for larger non-expert sets. Not in the ROADMAP's rejected or audit lists.

findings.title: Dead Metal mitigation code in load_tensor_with_dtype: it is only ever called with Device::Cpu, so its metal_alloc_lock guards, drains and the FP8-on-Metal branch are unreachable
findings.evidence: The only call site is weights.rs:370-379 `let t = load_tensor_with_dtype(&mmap, name, &Device::Cpu, dtype, preserve_fp8_weight && !device.is_metal(), force_f32, f8_names.contains(name))?;`. Inside, :94 `if file_is_f8 && device.is_metal() && !keeps_file_dtype(name) { ... metal_alloc_lock().lock() ... drain_metal(device, name)?; return Ok(t_dev); }`, :119-125 `let _guard = device.is_metal().then(|| metal_alloc_lock().lock().unwrap()); let t = mmap.load(name, device)...; drain_metal(device, name)?;`, :160-167 and :190-199 likewise, plus :288 `drain_metal(scaled.device(), &weight_name)?;` in apply_weight_scale_inv on CPU tensors — all conditioned on a device that is always CPU. The doc comment at :72-79 still describes device-side casts and a 'failed device-side cast retries via CPU' fallback (:170-200) that can never run.
findings.rationale: A reader (or the ROADMAP item 'if fixed upstream we delete metal_alloc_lock') sees the lock being taken around every tensor load and concludes the load path is protected per-tensor; the actual protection is the sequential phase 2, and the real users of metal_alloc_lock are expert_stream.rs and gguf_weights.rs. The dead CPU-fallback path also doubles the function's size and keeps three error-message variants alive that cannot be produced. This is the kind of structure that makes finding 3 easy to miss.
findings.proposal: Rename to `load_tensor_cpu(mmap, name, dtype, preserve_fp8, force_f32, file_is_f8)`, drop the device parameter, the three guard/drain blocks and the device-cast fallback; remove the drain in apply_weight_scale_inv; move the 'why metal_alloc_lock exists' comment next to its remaining users. Keep `metal_alloc_lock` and `drain_metal` as the shared helpers they are.
findings.expected_benefit: Roughly 80 lines removed, the lock's real scope becomes visible, and the two-phase invariant ('phase 1 never touches the device') is enforced by the type signature instead of by a call-site argument.
findings.verify_how: cargo build with the device parameter removed compiles only if no other caller exists (grep confirms none); existing weights.rs unit tests and the FP8 load fingerprint check cover behaviour.

verdict.reason: Verified by grep: the only call site is weights.rs:370-379 and it passes `&Device::Cpu`. Hence :94 `if file_is_f8 && device.is_metal() ..` (with its `metal_alloc_lock` at :107 and `drain_metal` at :114), the guard at :119-123, the cast guard at :160-167 and the CPU-fallback branch at :183-203 (including its `metal_alloc_lock` at :190-193) are unreachable, and the doc comment at :76 'A failed device-side cast retries via CPU' describes a path that cannot run (F8 is handled explicitly at :148-160 before the fallback, and CPU float casts do not fail). `drain_metal` at :288 in `apply_weight_scale_inv` is a no-op on CPU tensors because `drain_metal` gates on `device.is_metal()` (:60). The live users of `metal_alloc_lock` are expert_stream.rs:446/:473/:520 and gguf_weights.rs:657/:700; the ROADMAP backlog item 'If fixed upstream we delete metal_alloc_lock and the loader drains' is exactly the audit that these dead guards would mislead. Proposal (drop the device parameter, delete the three guard/drain blocks and the fallback, move the lock rationale next to its real users) is S and behaviour-preserving; the phase-1 'never touches the device' invariant then lives in the signature.

findings.title: Same-dtype tensors are copied twice during load (mmap -> host Vec in phase 1, host Vec -> MTLBuffer in phase 2) and the whole model is resident in anonymous host memory between the phases
findings.evidence: weights.rs:365-383 phase 1 collects `Vec<(String, Tensor)>` of CPU tensors for every name (`mmap.load(name, &Device::Cpu)` at :121 copies the mmap slice into a fresh Vec even when `t.dtype() == target_dtype`, returned unchanged at :138-140). Phase 2 :392-398 `let cpu_t = tensors.remove(name)...; let dev_t = cpu_t.to_device(device)...; drop(cpu_t);` — candle's `storage_from_cpu_storage` (metal_backend/mod.rs:2179) copies again via `new_buffer_with_data`. Nothing is uploaded until every tensor has been materialized on the host.
findings.rationale: For the common BF16-file -> BF16-runtime case the host copy carries no information: the bytes in the mmap are already in the runtime layout. The load therefore does two full memcpys of the model (the second single-threaded in phase 2) and holds one full model of non-reclaimable anonymous memory at the phase boundary, on top of the file-backed page cache. On a 24 GB M5 loading a 13 GB checkpoint this is the difference between fitting and swapping, and it is a few seconds of memcpy on every cold and warm load.
findings.proposal: In phase 1 return an enum per name: `Materialized(Tensor)` for tensors that needed a cast/scale fold, `Direct` for same-dtype tensors. In phase 2 upload `Direct` entries straight from the mmap slice (`mmap.get(name)?.data()` -> `Tensor::from_raw_buffer(bytes, dtype, dims, device)` under the same sequential/drained regime), so they are copied once and never occupy anonymous host memory. Optionally stream phase 1 in chunks of N names so `Materialized` tensors are uploaded and dropped before the next chunk is decoded, bounding host residency to a chunk.
findings.expected_benefit: One fewer full-model memcpy on every load (seconds for 10+ GB models) and a host-memory peak reduced from ~1x model to ~chunk size; lets larger checkpoints load on 24 GB without paging.
findings.verify_how: Measure wall time of `ModelWeights::load` and peak RSS (`/usr/bin/time -l`) for a BF16 safetensors model (e.g. Qwen3-4B) before/after; confirm the post-load fingerprint and a greedy-decode transcript are unchanged.

verdict.reason: The double copy is real: phase 1 `mmap.load(name, &Device::Cpu)` (weights.rs:121) goes through candle safetensors.rs:115-123 `convert_slice` -> `Tensor::from_slice`, which copies the mmap bytes into a CPU Vec even when `t.dtype() == target_dtype` (returned unchanged at :138-140); phase 2 `to_device` (:393-395) copies again via `storage_from_cpu_storage` -> `new_buffer_with_data` (candle mod.rs:2179, device.rs:253-266). But the memory claim is overstated: phase 2 removes and drops each host tensor right after its upload (:392-397), so anonymous host memory shrinks as device residency grows and the peak is about 1x the model either way (the mmap pages are reclaimable page cache); the proposal does not change that peak and cannot be 'the difference between fitting and swapping'. The time saved is only the phase-1 copy, which is parallel across rayon workers: roughly one model's worth of multi-core memcpy plus Vec page faults, i.e. well under a second per 10 GB on an M5, not 'seconds'. The proposal is also heavier than needed: `mmap.load(name, device)` is already the single-copy path (safetensors.rs:123 `Tensor::from_slice` -> mod.rs:2096 `storage_from_slice` -> `new_buffer_with_data`), so no new enum or `from_raw_buffer` plumbing is required.
verdict.corrected_benefit: One fewer parallel memcpy and one fewer allocation per same-dtype tensor on every safetensors load (sub-second per 10 GB on an M5), and less allocator churn; no change to peak residency.
verdict.corrected_proposal: In phase 1 skip names whose file dtype (available from `mmap.tensors()` as at :343-348) equals the runtime dtype and that are neither `keeps_file_dtype` nor scale-fold targets; in phase 2 call `mmap.load(name, device)` for those names inside the same sequential loop with the same every-16 `drain_metal`. Verify with the load-time log and the `weight_fingerprint` consistency check at loader.rs:917.

findings.title: No test proves that eviction terminates the engine thread and frees the model; the existing tests only check slot removal
findings.evidence: manager.rs:1681-1695 `fn evict_expired_removes_idle_slot()` asserts only `mgr.list_running().len() == 0` after `evict_expired()`; :1583-1608 `engine_panic_removes_stale_slot` covers the panic path; engine_loop.rs tests (:1139-1160 `drive_one_request`) drop the sender so the loop exits via `None`, never via the shutdown flag while idle. Nothing spawns a real `engine_loop` with an `EngineSlotGuard`, sets `shutdown`, and joins the thread.
findings.rationale: Finding 1 is a regression introduced by a drop guard whose purpose was correctness; a thread-join-with-timeout test would have caught it immediately and will guard the acknowledged-eviction change in finding 2. The StubModel in engine_loop.rs already makes such a test cheap on CPU.
findings.proposal: Add a test that builds an Engine over StubModel, runs `engine_loop` on a spawned thread with an `EngineSlotGuard` wired to a real `SharedModelManager` slot, lets it go idle (no requests), then performs `evict_expired()` through the manager and asserts the thread's JoinHandle completes within e.g. 2 s and that the slot is gone and kv_budget restored. Mirror it for `evict_lru_for_bytes` and for a loop that is mid-step when shutdown is set.
findings.expected_benefit: Pins the eviction lifecycle (the headline Unreleased feature) and prevents the leak class from recurring.
findings.verify_how: Write the test before fixing finding 1: it must fail (join times out) on 9e77e56 and pass after the guard change.

verdict.reason: Verified. manager.rs:1681-1695 `evict_expired_removes_idle_slot` inserts an aged dummy slot and asserts only `list_running().len() == 0`; :1583-1608 `engine_panic_removes_stale_slot` and :1610-1633 `engine_guard_leaves_replaced_slot_alone` only exercise the guard's Drop; engine_loop.rs:1151-1158 drops `req_tx` before calling `engine_loop` so the loop exits through `blocking_recv() == None`, never through `shutdown` while idle. No test runs a real `engine_loop` with an `EngineSlotGuard` holding a Sender, sets `shutdown`, and joins the thread, which is precisely why finding 1 shipped. The proposed test is cheap with `StubModel`; note the Engine holds a non-Send `Box<dyn BatchModel>` (engine_loop.rs:1153-1155), so the test must construct the Engine inside the spawned thread, as production does at manager.rs:1248-1261. Write it first: it must hang/time out on 9e77e56 and pass after the guard change; add the mid-step variant (shutdown set while `has_pending_work`) and one for `evict_lru_for_bytes`.

findings.title: Every custom Metal kernel dispatch takes a global Mutex and hashes a string key to fetch its pipeline (~300 acquisitions per decode step)
findings.evidence: metal_ops.rs:524-525 `static FFN_PIPELINES: OnceLock<Mutex<HashMap<(u64, &'static str), ComputePipeline>>>`, :537-547 `let cache = FFN_PIPELINES.get_or_init(...); let key = (device.registry_id(), kernel_name); let mut guard = cache.lock()...; if let Some(p) = guard.get(&key) { return Ok(p.clone()); }`; identical pattern for FA_PIPELINES (:916-945), QUANT_PIPELINES (:1587-1612), MPP_PIPELINES (:2553, :2655-2666), plus `metal_supports_mma` (:1021-1030) locked on every FA call (:1165). 28 call sites across 26 `metal_fwd` impls; a decode step on a quantized model issues on the order of 8-10 of these per layer (q/k/v/o GEMV, gate/up/down, fused activation, decode SDPA).
findings.rationale: Per acquisition: an uncontended std::Mutex lock/unlock, SipHash of the kernel-name bytes, HashMap probe, and an objc retain + release for the `ComputePipeline` clone/drop. At ~100-150 ns each and ~300-400 per step on a 36-layer model this is ~30-60 us per step, under 0.1 percent of a 30-70 ms step. It is not a throughput lever today; it is listed because the brief asked for the count, and because the global Mutex becomes a contention point if the step is ever split across threads or models stop serializing on gpu_lock.
findings.proposal: Resolve the pipeline once per op instance: give each custom-op struct an `OnceLock<ComputePipeline>` (or a small per-model `PipelineSet` built at load) so the hot path does a single atomic load and no hashing. Alternatively keep the global cache but key on a `u16` kernel id instead of `&str` and switch to `RwLock`.
findings.expected_benefit: Tens of microseconds per step; measurable only on very small models (Qwen3-0.6B class at 100+ tok/s) and only as a fraction of a percent.
findings.verify_how: Count acquisitions by temporarily incrementing an AtomicU64 in each getter and printing it per step; measure tok/s on Qwen3-0.6B-Q4_K before/after.

findings.title: GpuLock is an unfair std Mutex re-acquired within microseconds; with two models on one device the other engine can be starved despite yield_now
findings.evidence: gpu_lock.rs:25-33 `pub struct GpuLock { inner: Arc<Mutex<()>> } ... pub fn acquire(&self) -> MutexGuard<'_, ()> { self.inner.lock().unwrap_or_else(|e| e.into_inner()) }`. engine_loop.rs:685-688 releases the guard right after `engine.step()`, then does CPU post-processing (:689-984) and :985 `std::thread::yield_now();` before looping back to :686. std's Mutex on macOS has no FIFO fairness.
findings.rationale: A busy engine releases and re-acquires the lock after at most a few hundred microseconds of tracker work; a second engine waiting in `lock()` wins only if the scheduler happens to run it in that window, and `yield_now()` is a hint, not a handoff. Under two concurrently busy models one can see a large share imbalance, which users of the multi-model feature will perceive as one model being 'slow' rather than both being half-speed.
findings.proposal: Replace the Mutex with a fair primitive: `parking_lot::FairMutex` or a ticket lock (AtomicU64 next/serving + Condvar) inside GpuLock, keeping the API; drop `yield_now()` once fairness is enforced.
findings.expected_benefit: Predictable per-model share under multi-model load; no single-model effect.
findings.verify_how: Serve two models on the M5 with one saturating client each; compare per-model tok/s. Expect near-equal shares with a fair lock, skewed shares today.

findings.title: expert_stream.rs claims reads go into a reusable scratch buffer, but read_one allocates a fresh zeroed Vec per tensor per miss; the LRU state Mutex is held across the SSD reads
findings.evidence: expert_stream.rs:6-7 doc: `fetches misses with positioned uncached reads (pread + F_NOCACHE) straight into a reusable scratch buffer` and :11 `upload from the scratch buffer to the device in a single copy`. Code :420-423 `let mut bytes = vec![0u8; len as usize]; self.files[meta.file as usize].read_exact_at(&mut bytes, offset)` per tensor, with the Vec dropped after `build_*` (:272-282). :254 `let mut state = self.state.lock().unwrap();` is taken before `read_misses` (:271) and held through the rayon build, the LRU insertion and the graveyard drain (:310). :264 `else if !misses.contains(&e)` is an O(n^2) dedup on a Vec.
findings.rationale: Each miss batch pays mmap/munmap and page-fault cost for tens to hundreds of MB of fresh anonymous memory (a 64 MB vec!-zeroed buffer is ~4000 16 KB page faults on Apple Silicon, roughly a millisecond, per tensor, per miss), then a second copy into the MTLBuffer. The doc describes the better design (a scratch arena reused across batches) that was never implemented, so a future reader will assume the cost is already gone. Holding `state` across blocking IO is fine with one caller but turns any future prefetcher or stats poller into a stall.
findings.proposal: Keep a per-pool `Mutex<Vec<Vec<u8>>>` scratch arena sized to the largest expert; in `read_one` take a buffer (`Vec::with_capacity` + `set_len` after `read_exact_at`, or reuse), return it to the arena after the device copy. Compute misses under `state`, release the lock for `read_misses`/build, re-acquire for insertion/eviction. Replace `misses.contains` with a sort+dedup after the loop.
findings.expected_benefit: A few percent of per-miss cost on streamed decode (page faults and zeroing) and a doc that matches the code; the lock change is latent-only.
findings.verify_how: OXYDLLM_PROFILE=1 on streamed gpt-oss-20b: compare the MoE phase ms/token with and without the arena at a pinned cache size; or instrument `read_misses` with Instant around the par_iter.

subsystems.coverage_notes: Read in full: src/gpu_lock.rs, src/common/weights.rs, src/models/manager.rs, src/server/routes/engine_loop.rs, src/common/expert_stream.rs, src/common/profile.rs. metal_ops.rs was read only at the statics/pipeline-cache sections (lines ~515-560, 910-960, 1010-1040, 1330-1370, 1560-1625, 2545-2690) plus a grep of all OnceLock/Mutex/static/atomic sites; the kernels and op bodies were not reviewed, and the per-layer dispatch count in finding 10 is an estimate from call sites rather than a trace. To confirm callers I read engine.rs step() (996-1140), embeddings.rs (35-110), chat.rs (1780-1845), loader.rs (835-930), server/routes/mod.rs (225-275) and grep context in gguf_weights.rs; scheduler, paged.rs (KV-quant packing), awq.rs and the rest of engine.rs were not read. candle-core 0.11.0 metal_backend/device.rs and mod.rs were inspected for lock structure and synchronize(), but candle-metal-kernels (ResidencySet and Commands internals) is not vendored on this Linux box, so the residency-set thread-unsafety and cross-thread synchronize corruption are taken from the maintainer's CHANGELOG/ROADMAP statements plus the two-lock structure visible in device.rs; finding 3's confidence reflects that. tokio 1.52.2 bounded.rs was checked for WeakSender/same_channel. Of the design notes I read the ROADMAP's 'Constant and flag audit' and 'Rejected / do-not-do' sections and grepped it for overlap; the other four notes were not read. No runtime measurement was possible (no Metal, no cargo); all quantitative estimates are argued from the code.
missed: Eviction never checks for in-flight work, so it can kill running generations. `evict_lru_for_bytes` (manager.rs:538-546) picks the Ready slot with the smallest `last_used`, and `evict_expired` (manager.rs:680-688) compares `last_used` against the keep-alive (default 900 s, main.rs:700); but `last_used` is written only at request admission in `get_or_load` (manager.rs:620) and at slot install (:1314), never while sequences are being generated. The engine loop tests `shutdown` at the top of every iteration even when `engine.has_pending_work()` (engine_loop.rs:640-642), then drains every tracker with `EngineEvent::Error("Model unloaded")` (engine_loop.rs:989-1003). So a request for model B that does not fit evicts an actively decoding model A (the CHANGELOG Unreleased entry says it 'evicts idle ones', but idleness is not a criterion), and a single generation longer than keep-alive (realistic for a streamed MoE at 2-4 tok/s producing a long answer, or a long batch admitted at once) is aborted mid-stream by `evict_expired`. Today this is partly masked by finding 1 only for idle engines; for busy ones the kill is live. Fix (S): publish per-slot in-flight state (e.g. an `Arc<AtomicUsize>` incremented in `enqueue_request` and decremented on StreamEnd/abort, or bump `last_used` from the loop while trackers are non-empty), make both evictors skip busy slots and report 'insufficient memory, model X busy' to the new load's waiters, and have the loop honour `shutdown` only when idle or after finishing its running batch. Add a test with a long-running StubModel request plus `evict_lru_for_bytes`, asserting the request completes rather than erroring.

reconcile.assessment: The five documents split cleanly by age. The ROADMAP (Jul-Aug 2026) is accurate on what it records as fixed but its "Now / Near-term / Constant audit" lists are about two months stale: since then the code shipped the own GGUF header reader with IQ4_XS/IQ4_NL/IQ3_S decode, the pull-time header precheck, estimate composition, the D1 verification loop (fingerprint read-back plus halving retry in loader.rs), the device-reported memory ceiling (recommendedMaxWorkingSetSize) that retired KV_POOL_FRACTION/KV_TOTAL_FRACTION to non-Metal fallbacks, the growth half of "Version B" (BlockAllocator::growing with segmented pools), a measured PrefillPacer replacing PREFILL_CHUNK_THRESHOLD, and README documentation of the three surviving debug env vars. The two May documents (PLAN_COMPARISON, PERFORMANCE_INVESTIGATION_GGUF) are largely historical and in one respect actively misleading: the ten-type bf16 GGUF GEMV/mul_mm suite they describe at length is no longer on any dispatch path (QLinear routes decode to candle's QMatMul with an F32 activation cast and prefill to the TensorOps staged GEMM; no "gguf_q*" kernel name is referenced from metal_ops.rs), which leaves roughly 2,300 lines of dead Metal still compiled into QUANT_METAL_SOURCE and a stale README claim about batched GGUF decode kernels. The NaN document's Phase-3 warmup workaround is still in place after the candle 0.11 bump, and the LOAD document's parallel safetensors materialization was deliberately reverted to a sequential, drained device phase as a candle 0.11 workaround, so model load for high-tensor-count checkpoints is now bounded by that serialization rather than by the per-tensor MTLBuffer cost the doc measured. The PLAN_COMPARISON "MXFP4 removed" and "MoE not started" rows are simply stale (both shipped). What remains open and is worth doing, roughly by value: (1) the GCD mask cache, since JsonConstraint::allowed walks the whole vocabulary through a cloned automaton on the CPU for every token of every constrained sequence with no memoization; (2) streaming tool-call deltas (chat.rs still buffers the whole completion when tools are present); (3) deleting the dead GGUF kernels and fixing README:608; (4) the loader's device phase (sequential to_device + drain every 16 tensors, serialized under metal_alloc_lock) and the upstream reports that would let it go; (5) an MPP staged GEMM for MXFP4 prefill (gpt-oss M>8 still uses the naive-tiled own mul_mm); (6) MoE decode, which does two device-to-host readbacks per MoE layer per token plus one accumulate chain per active expert; (7) splicing token ids across turns in run_interactive so the prefix cache no longer depends on tokenizer round-trip; (8) the shrink half of the lazy KV pool and a live GlobalKvBudget. Files read (by sed/grep in this session): the five docs, CHANGELOG.md (1-110), Cargo.toml, README.md (selected lines), src/common/{paged.rs, weights.rs, metal_ops.rs (selected ranges), attention.rs, linear.rs, moe.rs, prefix_cache.rs, mask.rs, mxfp4.rs, gguf_weights.rs, gguf_header.rs (grep), iq_quant.rs (grep), expert_stream.rs (grep), quant_kernels.metal and mpp_gemm.metal (kernel inventories)}, src/{constrain.rs, sampling.rs, engine.rs, tokenizer.rs, gpu_lock.rs, telemetry.rs, main.rs (grep)}, src/models/{loader.rs, manager.rs, hub.rs, gguf_probe.rs, estimate.rs, arch_defaults.rs, parsers/hf_parser.rs (grep)}, src/scheduler/{mod.rs, sequence.rs}, src/server/routes/{chat.rs, engine_loop.rs, mod.rs, http_compat_tests.rs (grep)}, .github/workflows (grep), scripts/. Not covered: kv_quant.rs, gdn.rs, encoder.rs and the embeddings route, OTEL, arch_regression.rs internals, flash_attn.metal and awq.rs bodies, the soak harness (not in the repo), category-B hardware constants, and whether any candle upstream issues were actually filed (no links in the repo; no network check performed).

items.evidence: Abort path: src/scheduler/mod.rs:372-388 `abort_sequence` -> `seq.clear_caches()` -> src/common/paged.rs:1392-1410 `clear()` frees each block with `alloc.free(bid)` (refcounted) and retires the contig buffer; registration into the prefix cache happens only after a completed prefill, src/engine.rs:668-679 `prefix.register(&seq.all_tokens, info.num_cached_blocks, &new_block_ids)`. No test aborts a sequence mid-prefill and then reuses its prefix.
items.note: The code reads safe on inspection (shared blocks are refcounted, aborted-before-register sequences are never cached), but the anomaly was reproduced only under an aborted-request sequence and no test pins it; a CPU test that aborts during a chunked prefill and re-issues the prompt is cheap.
